https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.text: Scottish Crime copy Composite: Guardian Design/Getty/Strathclyde Police View image in fullscreen Scottish Crime copy Composite: Guardian Design/Getty/Strathclyde Police The Saturday read Organised crime The final hit: Is Glasgow’s 25-year gruesome gangland feud finally over? The double assassination of two Scots in the Costa del Sol may have ended the war between the Lyons and the Daniels – but the crimes haven’t gone away Robyn Vinter Sat 1 Aug 2026 01.00 EDT Share It was a warm evening in Fuengirola on the Costa del Sol last year when two Scottish men met a violent end. The punters of Monaghans seafront bar had barely finished watching the Nations League final on 8 June when a car pulled up outside. A masked gunman emerged and headed to the table of 46-year-old Eddie Lyons Jr, shooting him at point-blank range. The assassin turned the gun on Lyons’ friend, the bar’s owner Ross Monaghan, 43, but it jammed. Grainy CCTV captured Monaghan racing inside the bar, pursued by the gunman, and falling to the ground, where he was shot three times while crawling on his hands and knees. The shooter fled the scene and, allegedly, the country too. View image in fullscreen The Irish pub in the coastal city of Fuengirola in the Costa del Sol where two Scottish men were shot dead. Photograph: Jorge Zapata/EPA This double murder in a public place was the apex of 25 bloody years of feuding between two Glasgow families and their allies in organised crime: the most untouchable gang in Scotland , the Lyons, and their bitter rivals, the Daniels. Earlier this month, police said they had noticed a lull in violence coming out of the criminal underworld. Could Scotland’s most deadly criminal war be over? After a particularly unpleasant six-month spell of attacks and firebombings across “the length and breadth” of Scotland, there had been “a clear and obvious downturn of activity”, Police Scotland said. “The cause of that downturn was without question multi-factorial, including the resolution of differences within the serious and organised crime community,” the force wrote in an update to the Scottish Police Authority. View image in fullscreen ‘Torchings’ at the Cut Steakhouse in Bothwell in Lanarkshire could be linked to organised crime. Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian Police Scotland will not comment on whether they intervened to mediate, though this is a known police tactic in other forces. Karyn McCluskey, the pioneer behind Scotland’s Violence Reduction Unit, said in this case it was more probable that the gangs had changed their approach in response to heat from the police. “If you’re a good organised crime group, you don’t commit violence, because that’s just what brings the police down on you,” she said. A total of 64 people were arrested in less than a year, the Police Scotland report said, after 84 incidents of violence. Search and arrest warrants recovered seven firearms and “assorted weapons” and more than 90 safeguarding plans were put in place to protect vulnerable members of the public caught up in the feud. Police were also given a boost when – between March and June 2020 – officers in 13 European countries infiltrated an encrypted communications service called EncroChat used by crime bosses and their subordinates all over the world. The breach allowed police to investigate figures at the very top of the underworld, watching them ordering drugs, weapons or assassinations in real time. As of 2023, the hack was responsible for 6,558 arrests worldwide, including more than 3,000 in the UK. Defendants are still appearing in front of judges month after month based on evidence gathered from EncroChat. Origins of the feud The beginning of this very specific feud can be traced back 25 years and has been compared to the plot of a gangster movie, somewhere between The Godfather and Guy Ritchie’s Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels. In 2001, a £20,000 stash of drugs belonging to the Daniel clan was stolen by associates of the Lyons family, and, it is suspected, the teenage Monaghan and Eddie Lyons Jr. View image in fullscreen Ross Monaghan and Eddie Lyons Jr were murdered in a double assassination in Spain. Photograph: Iain McLellan/Spindrift Photo Agency/Mike Gibbons This did not go down well with the Daniels’ patriarch, Jamie Daniel, a highly territorial scrap-metal dealer who turned a hand to dealing heroin, eventually building a criminal empire. He was a man people knew not to cross. He was linked to beatings and a sniper murder of a rival drug dealer, a crime that is still technically unsolved. “He had the reputation of being one or two steps ahead of the police and pretty much untouchable,” said a former detective inspector, David Moran, in a 2018 documentary. View image in fullscreen Kevin ‘Gerbil’ Carroll was shot in an Asda car park in Robroyston. Photograph: Strathclyde police It was Kevin “Gerbil” Carroll who did a lot of the dirty work and his increasing hubris began to pour jet fuel on an already roaring fire. Around 2005, amid a spate of gangland killings, Glasgow was labelled the murder capital of the UK. Police were handing out dozens of threat-to-life warnings, known as Osman warnings, to gang members and their families every year. Gerbil, Jamie Daniel’s son-in-law and chief enforcer, was volatile and notorious for his “alien abduction” kidnap and torture routine, where his victims were often found at night injured and in their underwear claiming to have no memory of what happened to them. In 2006, in revenge for being shot, he desecrated the grave of the eight-year-old son of Eddie Lyons Sr, which appeared to cross a line. Michael Lyons was killed in a daylight ambush, which the judge described as a ‘cold-blooded, premeditated execution’. Only weeks later, two Daniel hitmen wearing “old man” rubber masks carried out a daylight ambush at a garage, killing an innocent member of the Lyons family, 21-year-old Michael Lyons. A judge described the attack as a “cold-blooded, premeditated execution”, before handing out the longest jail terms in Scottish legal history to the men responsible – 32 and 35 years in prison. Fearing for his life, Eddie Lyons Sr’s son Steven Lyons fled abroad, conducting business from Spain and slowly taking over the job of running the business from his father. Next came a murder so audacious it would cause reverberations across the Scottish criminal underworld that are still felt to this day. In January 2010, the Daniels’ enforcer Gerbil was shot dead by two masked men in a busy Asda car park in Robroyston. He was in the back of a three-door Audi, and his associates in the front seats ran, leaving him a sitting duck, to be shot 13 times in the head and chest. View image in fullscreen Steven Lyons and William Paterson at the high court in Glasgow in February 2008. Photograph: Iain McLellan/Spindrift Photo Agency William “Buff” Paterson became the key suspect and during the trial his defence read out a list of 99 people who had reasons to want Gerbil dead. Despite this, he was convicted of the murder. View image in fullscreen Steven ‘Bonzo’ Daniel, who was targeted for assassination by the Lyons family, was ambushed on the M8 motorway at Port Dundas after a car chase and left for dead. Photograph: Spindrift Photo Agency An uneasy successor When the patriarch Jamie Daniel died of cancer in 2016 without leaving an obvious successor, the role of mob boss fell – somewhat uneasily, some people say – on the shoulders of Jamie’s nephew, Steven “Bonzo” Daniel, who became a primary target for the Lyons family. Bonzo is known for distinctive scarring across his face, caused by a 2017 machete and meat cleaver attack so severe his jaw detached, his nose was nearly severed and his tongue shredded. It is said that he survived only because the attack happened close to a hospital. He was taking over at a time of great change in organised crime. Gangs began to enter uncharted territory, moving operations on to the dark web and finding new partnerships overseas.Unlike previous generations who lived relatively modestly and conducted their business semi-privately, these TikTok-friendly gangsters were living outwardly glamorous lifestyles in exotic locations, photographed with Botox, filler and Turkey dental work. Steven Lyons was expanding the family’s business from Spain and later Dubai, forging links with Ireland’s largest gang, the Kinahans, through his associate, Ross “Miami” McGill. McGill was formerly the head of the Rangers’ “Union Bears” ultra fans and now leads a young Scottish enforcer gang called Tamo Junto (Portuguese slang meaning “we are together”). He is currently on the run. View image in fullscreen Ross McGill was the former head of Rangers football club’s ultra fan group, the Union Bears. Photograph: Mark Runnacles/Getty Members of Tamo Junto and a Daniels-aligned group calling themselves the A-Team have posted anonymous TikTok videos each ridiculing the deaths of gangland figures such as Gerbil, Monaghan and Eddie Jr. They have taunted one another with threats in the style of memes as they meted out violence on the ground, filming attacks and firebombings and posting them online. Steven Lyons’s links to the Kinahan cartel would be his undoing. Detectives working on information gathered during the EncroChat breach targeted the Kinahans’ money manager, Johnny Morrissey, and as a result gathered enough evidence on Steven Lyons to arrest him, his wife and more than a dozen other key figures earlier this year. View image in fullscreen Steven Lyons is escorted by police officers at the Bali police headquarters in Denpasar, Indonesia, on 31 March. Photograph: Sonny Tumbelaka/AFP/Getty Steven Lyons’s arrest and the assassination in Spain of his brother and Monaghan was a “decapitation” of the powerful Lyons gang, the former Police Scotland superintendent Martin Gallagher said. The downturn in violence observed by police represents a shift in thinking among those who are left. “Things are just falling into place with what the new normal will be,” Gallagher said. “Although that doesn’t look like crime occurring to the general public – so nobody’s house is being set on fire, no lorry is being driven through somebody’s front door, as has occurred – that means they’re focusing on what they want to do to make money – which is import drugs.” He added: “There’s still crime happening, it’s just not as obvious and they’re not trying to bump each other off.” Last week, police found a cocaine stash worth £1.7m in Moodiesburn, a village on the outskirts of Glasgow. A 34-year-old man has been charged. Graeme Pearson, a former police officer and Labour MSP, said: “The business is too lucrative to suddenly die overnight. It’s like running a seam of gold. If you know the gold’s there, you’ll keep going back to it.” Explore more on these topics Organised crime The Saturday read Scotland Spain Drugs Europe Crime Glasgow Share Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/j.text: Nirmal Purja had been leading an expedition on Broad Peak along with climbers from Nepal, Pakistan, Oman, China and the US. Photograph: Nirmal Purja/PA View image in fullscreen Nirmal Purja had been leading an expedition on Broad Peak along with climbers from Nepal, Pakistan, Oman, China and the US. Photograph: Nirmal Purja/PA Mountaineering World-renowned climber Nirmal Purja among 11 struck by avalanche on Pakistan mountain Rescuers say four bodies found in search for team caught in Broad Peak avalanche, after trackers showed rapid descent Peter Beaumont and Shah Meer Baloch in Islamabad Fri 31 Jul 2026 11.35 EDT First published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 22.54 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The world-renowned Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja – a former British special forces member – is among 11 climbers caught in a deadly avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak. The Alpine Club of Pakistan said “seven climbers have been spotted via aerial drone footage” adding that “their identities and condition cannot yet be verified”. Rescuers had said earlier on Friday that four bodies had been found and efforts were under way to retrieve them despite the harsh weather. Three of the dead have been identified: Pur Bahadur Gurung, a Nepali citizen, Nadhira Alharthy, who was the first Omani to climb Everest, and US climber Mallory Geis. Their bodies have been transported to a hospital. Purja, also known as Nims Dai, made history in 2019 after climbing all of the world’s 14 peaks over 8,000 metres in just over six months, cutting years off the previous record. He later led the first team to summit K2, the world’s second-highest mountain in winter, a highly coveted achievement. View image in fullscreen Nirmal ‘Nims’ Purja and his Project Possible team are congratulated after successfully scaling all 14 mountains above 8,000 metres in just over six months. Photograph: Skanda Gautam/Zuma Wire/Rex/Shutterstock Purja has also attracted controversy, however, including a high-profile claim, which he denied , of sexually inappropriate behaviour. Also among those missing are the US climber Mallory Geis, a Chinese national, Wang Zhong, and Pakistani and Nepali high-altitude workers. As night fell on the mountain on Friday, visual searches for any survivors, including with the use of drones, were halted. Search efforts have been hampered by the weather and the fact that unlike in Nepal, where there is a well-established network of private helicopter search and rescue operations, helicopters are less available in Pakistan and run by the military. Map showing location of Broad Peak Trackers carried by the climbers showed a rapid loss of altitude, suggesting the team had been caught in an avalanche. Purja’s tracker, however, shifted location after the initial rapid descent. The GPS data suggested the avalanche occurred close to 9am local time at 6,579 metres (21,585ft), between camp two and camp three on the mountain’s west ridge, the most popular ascent route. According to Climbing magazine , Geis’s tracker showed a sudden descent of 543 metres, while Alharthy’s tracker showed a much-larger descent of 1,651 metres. View image in fullscreen Broad Peak, on the border of Pakistan and China, is the 12th highest mountain in the world at 8,047 metres. Photograph: Naveed Hussain/Alamy Commenting on the rescue efforts, a spokesperson for police in the mountainous Gilgit-Baltistan region said “preliminary reports indicate that four bodies have so far been recovered”, adding that the condition of the remaining climbers was still being verified. A statement by the Alpine Club of Pakistan (ACP) suggested an avalanche had struck a group of climbers around midday on Thursday. “The entire team has been out of communication since the avalanche,” the statement said, as teams with helicopters and drones were sent to help with rescue efforts. The statement added: “Every possible effort is being made to ensure that helicopter support and all available rescue resources are mobilised at the earliest opportunity, subject to weather and operational conditions.” Irfan Arshad Khan, the ACP’s president, said: “We can confirm the death of three climbers, as we received two dead bodies and a body part of another climber.” Purja’s business partner, Mingma Gyabu Sherpa, who is also a member of the Nepali house of representatives, said data appeared to show continuing movement from Purja’s tracking device after the initial incident. “Initially, it appeared that he had been swept downhill by the avalanche,” he told the Nepali news site Kantipur. “But after the point where the tracking had stopped, the location appears to have shifted again.” Mingma added that one Pakistani and one Nepali climber had set out overland towards the suspected avalanche site to check reports that one climber’s location appeared to be near the base of the mountain. “We have received information that one person’s location appears to be near the foot of the mountain. A search team has gone there to verify it,” he said. Mingma cautioned that they did not have any indication of Purja’s condition, simply that the location of the tracker had shifted. In person, Purja was striking for his confidence and self-belief . His rapid chain of ascents of the world’s tallest mountains demonstrated strength and a talent for logistical organisation, using the exploit to showcase what he felt were the overlooked abilities of Nepali climbers. His profile was boosted after he starred in a 2021 Netflix documentary on the feat. The previous record for climbing all 14 was seven years; his record was surpassed in 2023. View image in fullscreen Purja, after being part of the all-Nepali mountaineering team that became the first to scale K2 in winter, arrives at Tribhuwan international airport in Kathmandu in January 2021. Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/AP Purja was leading an expedition for his company, Elite Exped, on Broad Peak, the world’s 12th-highest mountain at 8,047 metres, when the avalanche occurred. The ACP received “deeply concerning” reports on Thursday that an avalanche had struck the team. ‘It’s not about ego’, says speed climber who tamed world’s 14 highest peaks Read more The expedition includes five Nepali climbers, as well as US, Pakistani, Omani and Chinese nationals. Another foreign climber was also part of the group, said the ACP’s vice-president, Karrar Haidri. “The club prays for the safety and successful rescue of all the climbers and stands in solidarity with their families and the international mountaineering community during this difficult time,” the ACP said in a statement. View image in fullscreen Nims Purja on Manaslu, the world’s eighth-highest mountain, in Nepal Photograph: Supplied Purja, who is also a British citizen after joining the British army in 2003, opted to use supplementary oxygen for his ascents, justifying his choice by the huge size of the challenge he had set himself. Purja had written on X this week that he was close to becoming the first person to climb all 14 mountains over 8,000 metres twice without oxygen. “Broad Peak, I ask for nothing but safe passage up and back down,” he wrote. “I take zero mountains for granted. Not one. The moment my foot leaves basecamp, it’s 100%. Always has been. Always will be. “My purpose has never been about me. It’s about what I represent. It’s about showing YOU that your own mountains – whatever they are – are climbable.” Explore more on these topics Mountaineering Pakistan Nepal Oman China South and central Asia Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Donald Trump en route to Camp David where he and his cabinet are meeting to discuss the war and its fallout. Photograph: Manuel Balce Ceneta/AP View image in fullscreen Donald Trump en route to Camp David where he and his cabinet are meeting to discuss the war and its fallout. Photograph: Manuel Balce Ceneta/AP US-Israel war on Iran Iran strikes tankers under US escort in Hormuz strait as Trump gathers cabinet to discuss war Energy prices have soared again since fighting between US and Iran resumed two weeks ago as conflict spreads across Middle East William Christou in Beirut Fri 31 Jul 2026 10.48 EDT First published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 10.11 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Iran has said it struck two tankers trying to pass through the strait of Hormuz under the escort of the US military as Donald Trump gathered his cabinet to discuss the stalling war and rising prices as midterm elections in the US loom. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Friday that the “non-compliant oil tankers … were struck and brought to a halt, while four other oil tankers quickly changed course and returned to their previous positions”. The military body said the ships had tried to pass through the strait via an “undeclared route” and under US aerial escort. Iran and the US have said ships should pass through the strait via two competing routes, with Iran bombing ships that take the southern route, close to the coast of Oman, and the US bombing ships that violate its blockade of Iranian ships and ports. View image in fullscreen Vessels in the strait of Hormuz near Oman. The strait has been almost completely closed to traffic for the last two weeks. Photograph: Reuters The strait has been almost completely closed to traffic since Iran and the US returned to fighting two weeks ago, sending energy prices soaring. On Thursday, the price of crude oil pushed past $90 a barrel when the US struck Iran in retaliation for its targeting of US bases in Jordan. Fighting continued on Friday, with the Kuwaiti defence ministry reporting that it had shot down Iranian drones targeting “vital and military facilities” without any casualties. In Lebanon, the Israeli military carried out a huge detonation overnight near the ancient Beaufort Castle. It said it was targeting Hezbollah tunnels and infrastructure. The explosion was heard across south Lebanon and covered nearby towns in ash, while photos showed the affected area levelled by the force of the blast. Lebanese officials accused Israel of violating the ceasefire by carrying out the detonation. The Israeli military said it was ensuring the security of its northern residents. View image in fullscreen Smoke rises behind Beaufort Castle in Lebanon after an Israeli military strike in June. The area was hit by Israel again on Friiday in a massive explosion that covered towns in ash. Photograph: Léo Corrêa/AP Trump has tried to open the strait of Hormuz by force, but increasingly intense US strikes on Iran have yielded few results . The price of gas and groceries remain high in the US as a result of the energy disruption, complicating Republicans’ chances at the ballot box in November’s midterm elections. On Friday, Trump brought his cabinet together at the Camp David retreat in Maryland to try to chart a path forward for the war. The White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, said at a briefing last week that the cabinet meeting would be “a lot of fun and something different for the cabinet to experience together”. Top of the agenda will be the Iran war, which Trump promised would last a few weeks but has now dragged on for five months. A Reuters-Ipsos poll this week found that one in three Americans support the war, the lowest polling since the war began. View image in fullscreen A gas station in Miami. Energy companies have posted record profits as a result of the war in Iran. Photograph: Marta Lavandier/AP Support in Congress is also waning, with the US Senate narrowly rejecting a symbolic vote to express disapproval of the war. The war powers resolution asking the president to stop the war failed in a 49-50 vote. Inflation caused by the war is a boon for Democrats, who are hoping to wrest control of the house from the Republicans. Energy companies have posted record profits as a result of the conflict, with ExxonMobil’s profits doubling and Chevron reporting more than five times its profits in the same time period last year. Pakistani security personnel stand guard on Monday outside a polling station during the first phase of general elections in Mirpur. Photograph: Amiruddin Mughal/EPA View image in fullscreen Pakistani security personnel stand guard on Monday outside a polling station during the first phase of general elections in Mirpur. Photograph: Amiruddin Mughal/EPA Kashmir Pakistan accused of fatally shooting 30 unarmed protesters in Kashmir Local civil rights group alleges authorities removed evidence of killings amid communications blackout Shah Meer Baloch in Islamabad Tue 28 Jul 2026 12.41 EDT Last modified on Wed 29 Jul 2026 00.11 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google At least 30 people are alleged to have been killed in Pakistan-administered Kashmir in the past two days as part of what has been claimed is a brutal state crackdown that has engulfed the disputed region for weeks. According to a local civil society group, Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), the Pakistani security services fired on tens of thousands of peaceful protesters, killing 25 people on Monday and five more on Tuesday. A wave of protests and violence in Pakistani Kashmir started in June. The state has imposed a severe communication shutdown in response, including an internet blackout that cut the region off from the rest of Pakistan, and began carrying out mass arrests. Amnesty International on Tuesday called for Pakistani authorities to lift the communications blackout. JAAC and their supporters had taken to the streets to call for electoral reform in the heavily militarised region. Monday marked the first phase of an election disputed by local groups who say a system of reserved seats for refugees from Indian-administered Kashmir now living across Pakistan gives outsiders too much control over the region. SA Khan, a spokesperson for JAAC, accused Pakistan’s security agencies of firing on unarmed protesters in Mirpur on Tuesday and then removing the evidence. “Security forces have taken away the dead bodies and locked away the hospital in Mirpur,” he said. “We have the photos and video evidence of dead bodies lying on streets in a pool of blood. The security forces abducted the dead bodies to erase the evidence.” A local resident in Mirpur, requesting anonymity for fear of retribution by the authorities, said the violence had erupted early on Tuesday afternoon when people gathered to protest against killings the previous day. “The bodies were shifted to hospital and then they went missing. Now, all shops nearby have been closed after the violence,” they said. The Guardian could not independently verify the death toll as media were prevented from accessing the area and the internet blackout remained in place, making it hard to reach local communities. Pakistani media have largely ignored the protests and alleged killings. Pakistani authorities have rejected the accusation of state involvement in the killing of civilian protesters. In a press conference over the weekend, the information minister, Atta Tarar, alleged that the protests in Pakistani-administered Kashmir were receiving “funds and instructions” from India. JAAC spokesperson Khan rejected the accusations that the unrest was sponsored by India. “It is nothing new: people asking for political or economic rights are termed India-sponsored or anti-state in Pakistan, same goes in India,” he said. The protests, led by JAAC, have been ongoing for a year, demanding political and economic rights for local people, as well as electoral reforms. Pakistan-administered Kashmir has been rocked by bouts of deadly violence in recent years. The protests that began in June, calling for the abolition of 12 reserved seats for refugees from Indian-administered Kashmir, have prompted the deadliest crackdown in years. Locals say the reserved seats are used by the central government to retain control over the region and destabilise regional politics. About 40 people were alleged to have been killed when violence erupted in June and the government accused protesters of killing police. The local government responded by proscribing JAAC as a terrorist organisation, arresting and detaining its political workers en masse and responding to protests with force. It prompted the UN rights chief, Volker Türk, to call for an investigation into the deadly violence. Isabelle Lassée, Amnesty International’s action regional director for south Asia, said: “The disturbing reports emerging from Rawalakot are consistent with the Pakistani authorities’ long history of unlawful violence against protesters in Jammu and Kashmir. A prompt, independent, and transparent investigation must be ordered into the security forces’ use of force against protesters. “So long as an internet and mobile services blackout remains in place, it will severely impede the independent verification of the full extent of the situation on the ground. We urge the Pakistani authorities to restore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area.” Explore more on these topics Kashmir Pakistan Amnesty International South and central Asia Protest Human rights news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Indranil Aditya/NurPhoto/Shutterstock India India’s Cockroach movement threatens to restart protests after mass student arrests Cockroach Janta party says government has broken promise, with detentions in Delhi, Assam, West Bengal and Bihar Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi Tue 28 Jul 2026 03.23 EDT First published on Mon 27 Jul 2026 20.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google India’s youth-led “Cockroach” movement, whose nationwide protests forced the resignation of the education minister , has accused the government of backtracking on its promise not to act against student protesters and has threatened to restart demonstrations. The Cockroach Janta party (CJP), which organised mass protests over exam paper leaks and other irregularities, said it had received reports of hundreds of students being detained or “harassed” by police. Police cases were filed against students in Delhi, Assam, West Bengal and Bihar, all states ruled by Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). The CJP had agreed to call off the demonstrations on Saturday after the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, resigned and senior BJP ministers assured the group no punitive action would be taken against protesters. But on Monday, the CJP accused the Modi government of reneging on the agreement. “If the government does not honour the agreement and release everyone detained or arrested, we will be compelled to resume the protest,” a CJP spokesperson, Ashutosh Ranka, told reporters. At least 100 people have been arrested, many on stringent, non-bailable charges, according to the CJP. ‘I will die for this cause’: how India’s cockroach meme became the biggest challenge to Modi’s grip on power Read more On Monday, Neha Bora, the head of the All India Students Association, who became an important figurehead of the CJP movement, travelled to Bihar to put pressure on the authorities to withdraw cases against all protesters in the state. A police officer was suspended in Bihar for using an assault rifle to disperse student protesters on Saturday. In West Bengal, where the BJP recently took power, the hardline chief minister, Suvendu Adhikari, inferred that all the protesters last week were Muslims. Cases have been filed against many participants under a draconian new state law. The CJP has set up a legal fund to help cover the expenses of protesters implicated in criminal cases by the police, said Saurav Das, another spokesperson for the group. The youth-led movement has won millions of followers on social media since it was launched in May by a 30-year-old public relations graduate, Abhijeet Dipke. Hundreds of thousands of protesters, mainly students, rallied last week in New Delhi and other cities, demanding Pradhan’s resignation and broader reforms of the examination system. View image in fullscreen Saurav Das, a spokesperson for the Cockroach movement, addresses a press conference in New Delhi on Monday as his co-spokesperson, Ashutosh Ranka, and Kapil Sibal, an Indian lawmaker, look on. Photograph: Priyanshu Singh/Reuters Demonstrations in the Indian capital turned violent on 20 July when huge crowds attempted to march to parliament from the Jantar Mantar protest site. Police fired teargas and used batons to disperse them, causing clashes and a wave of detentions. The protests were an unprecedented show of dissent against the Modi government, which has cracked down on critics and opposition over its 12 years in power. Pradhan’s resignation was the first time a senior minister in the Modi government had been forced out by public pressure. The chief justice of India called for an independent investigation after a petition was filed in the supreme court alleging police brutality at the Delhi protest, stating that the “right to peaceful, lawful protest is absolutely guaranteed” under the Indian constitution. The issue also reverberated in parliament on Monday, as opposition lawmakers demanded a response from the government over last week’s police crackdown. The government has promised to act on the issues that sparked the protests, and announced a panel to oversee an overhaul of India’s examination system. On Monday, it introduced a measure in parliament seeking tougher penalties for exam paper leaks. Narendra Modi has never been challenged so publicly and so widely. Photograph: Altaf Hussain/Reuters View image in fullscreen Narendra Modi has never been challenged so publicly and so widely. Photograph: Altaf Hussain/Reuters First Edition newsletter India Monday briefing: ​How the Cockroach ​protests ​have expose​d the ​cracks in ​India’s government In today’s newsletter: Across ​the country, a ​younger generation is turning private disillusionment into public defiance​ against a government that once felt untouchable Hettie O'Brien Mon 27 Jul 2026 01.47 EDT Last modified on Mon 27 Jul 2026 01.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. As flames engulfed parts of France and Spain this weekend, in India, the prime minister, Narendra Modi, was trying to put out a very different kind of fire. Thousands of people arrived in Delhi on Saturday to demand the resignation of his education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan. When he stepped down in the early afternoon, the protests turned into a triumphant block party. But the Cockroach protests that have swept through India this summer are about much more than a single minister. They have humiliated Modi and undermined the indomitable power of his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) that has ruled India for the past 12 years. They’re also a lesson in using humour to political advantage. Modi likes to present himself as an infallible messiah , but young people have mocked the prime minister online and in the streets, calling him a “56-inch monkey” (a reference to Modi boasting about his ample 56-inch chest), and parodied his social media addresses. “Hating Modi is cool on the internet now, after years of criminalising dissent,” one told a reporter. Now the protesters have secured a victory, will their calls for revolution continue? For this morning’s newsletter, I spoke to our south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen , who has been reporting on the “Cockroaches” in Delhi , about what their anger stems from and what it means for the BJP. That’s after a roundup of the biggest stories of the weekend. Weekend roundup Wild fires | Authorities in France battled to contain a huge wildfire near Bordeaux in the south-west as Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, warned Spain and the Iberian peninsula were suffering the effects of the climate emergency. Germany | A man suspected of driving a van into a crowd near Berlin’s Pride festival then going on a knife rampage in an Islamist terror attack has been shot dead by police , German officials have said. Iran | The US has paused strikes on Iran for a second night as top military officials advised Donald Trump to halt his bombing campaign, and diplomatic negotiations have continued to avoid a return to all-out war. UK politics | Britain’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is to indicate he will put the climate crisis and overseas development at the heart of UK international relations by taking up the country’s seat on the board at the World Bank. UK news | Five Palestine Action activists face being sentenced as terrorists for breaking windows and throwing red paint at a branch of Barclays Bank in Lancashire. In depth: ‘What if all cockroaches come together?’ View image in fullscreen The Cockroach Janta party has tasted victory and might widen the scope of the changes they seek. Photograph: Indranil Aditya/Reuters It started as a sardonic joke . On 16 May, Abhijeet Dipke, an Indian student at Boston University, posted on X: “What if all cockroaches come together?” It was a tongue-in-cheek response to India’s chief justice, who had called unemployed young Indians “cockroaches”. Online, thousands of people responded to Dipke’s message. Realising he had tapped into something big, Dipke flew to Delhi on 6 June and went to Jantar Mantar, its famous protest ground. The protests drew young people from across the country, and the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) – a play on the BJP’s name – created a website listing their demands, including reform of India’s education system. India has a young population who are better educated than ever before, but it has proven a weak point for the BJP, with the country’s universities crumbling and its economy failing to provide jobs for many graduates. Millions of young people spend years prepping for gruelling public exams in the hope of securing a decent job, and their parents go into debt or sell their land to fund these studies. To make matters worse, these exam papers are routinely leaked and sold to the highest bidder. “Anyone rich enough can buy the answers,” Hannah tells me. This is devastating for millions of young people, forcing them to retake tests for which they’ve already studied. After a medical entrance exam was leaked in May, at least 12 students took their own lives; some left notes behind saying they could not bear the thought of resitting the test. The leaks are a potent symbol of institutional corruption, inflaming the anger that young people feel towards a political system that is failing them. Thief, thief Sonam Wangchuk, an engineer and education reformer from Ladakh, joined the protest on 28 June and declared he would go on indefinite hunger strike until the education minister resigned. “The idea of a hunger strike has a particularly powerful resonance in India,” says Hannah. “Gandhi put his life on the line several times with his hunger strikes for independence.” Delhi police forcibly removed Wangchuk from Jantar Mantar on 18 July and took him to hospital, supposedly for the sake of his health. Footage of his hospital stay went viral, and the Cockroach party called for a march on parliament. On Monday, tens of thousands of people started to fill Delhi’s streets. “In my whole time covering India, I’ve never seen so many people turning out,” Hannah says. The mood was jubilant, but by the afternoon, things had turned violent as the police began firing teargas and using batons on the protesters. Despite that, many of the protesters stayed put, and Hannah went back to Jantar Mantar in the following days. “It was the place to be in India,” she says. “There were people camping out, delivery guys bringing pizza and biryani, people cooking food. It had become about more than just the education minister resigning. More, even than education.” The protesters’ very public displays of contempt – graffiti of Modi’s name under the image of a urinating dog; people stamping on a poster of his face and chanting “thief, thief” – would have seemed unimaginable just two weeks ago. “People were just revelling in the opportunity to speak their mind,” Rahul Bhatia, a writer and author of The New India, who attended the protests on Saturday, tells me. “It was delightful. It made people think: things are possible.” Modi lost control of the narrative Pradhan’s resignation is a major victory for the Cockroach protesters. He is a Modi loyalist and former organiser for the RSS, the Hindu supremacist group closely affiliated with the BJP (for more on its sinister ideology, it’s worth reading this fascinating 2020 piece by Samanth Subramanian). “It creates a crack in the BJP’s armour,” Hannah says. Modi has projected an image of total authority, but this is one of the first instances where he has bent to popular will. He demands unflinching loyalty from his ministers. They may now be questioning whether their positions are quite as secure as they thought. India has taken a sharp turn towards autocracy under the BJP. Its main media channels are controlled by (or intensely favourable to) the government, and most of them gave minimal coverage to the protests, so young people resorted to sharing information and anti-government memes on social media. The party is no stranger to social media (its “troll army” is adept at smearing digital opponents, and the government tried to shut down the Cockroach party’s X account in early July), but it has lost control of the narrative. Modi’s last-ditch attempt to engage protesters with two reels he posted to his then 101 million Instagram followers on Thursday night (after which he gained over 1 million more, an impressive number, though still fewer than Beyoncé’s 299 million) seemed contrived and stilted. “He has been crucified online for those videos,” Hannah says. Is this the start of something bigger? It’s tempting to compare the Cockroach protests to other youth uprisings that have led to regime change in south Asia. But “a quick look at the outcome of people’s movements in India is not encouraging,” the novelist Arundhati Roy wrote in a recent piece for Equator magazine. “Revenge is surely being planned and will be visited on those [the government] sees as the main instigators.” After people took to the streets in 2019 to protest against the BJP’s controversial new citizenship act, the government swiftly outlawed gatherings in several places and detained protesters. The real test of the BJP’s power will come at election time. It is one of the world’s richest and most formidable parties, and has attempted to capture India’s electoral machinery, pushing for reforms to its voting map that would tilt power further in Modi’s favour. In West Bengal, a state the BJP had never won before, it “revised” the electoral roll and excluded more than 9.1 million voters from the register, securing a decisive victory earlier this year. “It seems like the BJP has much less support than people actually think,” Bhatia says. But after these protests, Modi will be doing all that he can to maintain his party’s grip on power. https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text: In 2024, M&S reported a third of underwear sales were made by people under 30. Photograph: Yui Mok/PA View image in fullscreen In 2024, M&S reported a third of underwear sales were made by people under 30. Photograph: Yui Mok/PA Marks & Spencer Knickers in a twist: why M&S selling crotchless panties isn’t as outrageous as it seems Some have called it ‘S&M’, but partnership with Ann Summers is less a scandal than another step in a century of evolving underwear trends, experts say Lauren Cochrane Sat 1 Aug 2026 04.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T he news that Marks & Spencer is selling Ann Summers crotchless knickers on their website has been greeted – as might be expected – with outrage online, being described as everything from “tawdry” to “S & M” . But it could be this is just the latest evolution in what the UK’s biggest underwear retailer has available for the smalls drawer. In recent years, the store has sold vastly different options through its own products, ranging from full-brief knickers to thongs, period knickers and those that can be used by women who wear stomas . The introduction of other brands in clothing came five years ago, with underwear included. Ann Summers – which is selling bras and chemises as well as knickers on the M&S website – lines up alongside lingerie brands including Pour Moi and Calvin Klein. Catherine Shuttleworth, the chief executive of retail consultancy Savvy, sees it as part of wider strategy. “They’ve started introducing brands to bring them into sectors that probably isn’t their core,” she says. “And this is another one. It’s just a little bit more eye-catching.” View image in fullscreen The offending crotchless thong being sold by M&S, which has been called ‘tawdry’ Photograph: M&S Shuttleworth describes M&S underwear as a “national obsession” and there’s little doubt the store remains a must-visit for anyone restocking their underwear drawer. If its long-term popularity might have meant it was perceived as a bit mumsy for younger people, that has changed recently. In 2024, the store reported that people under 30 made up a third of underwear sales – double that of 2023. View image in fullscreen The Ann Summers knickers are sold on M&S’s website alongside other retailers including Pour Moi and Calvin Klein. Photograph: M&S Shuttleworth says the introduction of Ann Summers could be about continuing to engage this demographic. “They are always innovating for every stage of your life,” she says. “And I think this is a gap in their category. Ann Summers is a byword for sex, isn’t it?” This echoes the message coming from the retailer itself. In a statement, an M&S spokesperson said: “Our ‘brands at M&S’ strategy is all about giving customers greater choice through carefully selected third-party brands that complement our existing M&S offer. Ann Summers is one of the latest brands to join [M&S online], helping broaden our underwear and nightwear offer.” There is also, of course, the publicity factor. “It doesn’t really matter whether they sell any crotchless pants or not, we’re all going to be talking about it,” says Shuttleworth. “You might also go online to look. You might not buy those, but you’ll think: ‘I could do with replacing my pants.’” M&S has sold underwear since the 1920s and fitted bras since 1947 . It was the first retailer to sell pre-shrunk cotton underwear in 1965, and by 1976 knickers were the biggest export – nearly 4m pairs were sold internationally every year. Fashion dictated different styles – from the “hip-hugger” styles in the 60s to thongs, which reached the apex of popularity in the mid- 00s. In 2016, the store sold 60m pairs of knickers a year, with Brazilian knickers replacing the thong. The style, which reveals some of the wearer’s bum, made up 10% of those sales. By 2021, thongs were back , thanks to the popularity of low rise jeans. According to the retailer’s website, the No 1 bestseller now is a five-pack of white full briefs. View image in fullscreen Experts have said that M&S have always followed trends, including lace designs a world away from basics. Photograph: PR Image Lorraine Topper, a researcher at The Underpinnings Museum , argues the reaction around the crotchless knickers is disproportionate – because the store does stock sexier styles along with basics. “M&S have always followed fashion with regard to their lingerie designs,” she says. “For some reason, it’s the multipack of full briefs that sticks in people’s heads when you talk about their underwear, rather than, for example, the beautiful lace designs from the Rosie Exclusively range.” She describes the outrage as “a fuss over nothing … Open-crotch underwear for women was the norm before the 1920s so this type of garment isn’t quite as scandalous as we might first think.” Explore more on these topics Marks & Spencer Retail industry Underwear news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Business Economics Diversity & equality in business Small business Retail

Politicians have described how alcohol is readily available throughout the day, including at daytime lobbying events. Photograph: Mark Kerrison/In Pictures/Getty View image in fullscreen MPs socialise on the terrace outside the House of Commons. Politicians have described how alcohol is readily available throughout the day, including at daytime lobbying events. Photograph: Mark Kerrison/In Pictures/Getty Politics ‘MPs have had their stomachs pumped’: concerns over ‘alcohol-soaked’ culture in Westminster Alcohol is embedded in profession where long hours, loneliness and lobbying are the norm, report finds Denis Campbell Sat 1 Aug 2026 03.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 04.40 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Parliament is “Britain’s last alcohol-soaked workplace” where MPs are offered free drinks as early as midday despite alcohol-related scandals, a report has reveal ed. Drinking is commonplace and some MPs have had their stomachs pumped after consuming so much alcohol that they ended up in hospital, one disclosed. Alcohol is “embedded” in how Westminster works, driven by loneliness among MPs, socialising in order to meet ministers, and drinks being served at daytime and evening events. View image in fullscreen The Churchill Room bar on the terrace of the House of Commons. Photograph: Lisa Ryder/Alamy Those are the findings of a survey of 190 MPs and their staff which shows that Westminster’s drinking culture endures, despite rising concern and a string of incidents, including an MP’s researcher allegedly having had her drink spiked in Strangers’ bar in parliament and the revelation that the Labour MP Neil Coyle was at one time drinking up to 200 units of alcohol a week – the equivalent of 10 pints a night. The spiking led to a police investigation and the temporary closure of Strangers’ bar. The report, by the Institute of Alcohol Studies (IAS) thinktank, said: “The findings suggest that Westminster remains a highly unusual workplace where alcohol is embedded in professional life, networking, lobbying and socialising in ways that would be exceptional in most other UK workplaces. View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey, visit a pub during a trip to Essex. The report found alcohol was embedded in networking, lobbying and socialising for those working in Westminster. Photograph: Richard Pohle/Pool Times Media Ltd/AP “Participants described alcohol as being available throughout the working day, frequently provided for free, and often intertwined with career advancement.” Twenty-four MPs, 58 Westminster staff and 108 constituency office personnel shared their experiences and views. One MP, describing how readily available alcohol was at Westminster, said: “Going to a meeting at noon and alcohol’s available. Of course, I’m not used to that in my old job.” The free alcohol at events on the parliamentary estate, which organisations arrange to help them lobby MPs, emerged as a particular issue. Another MP said: “Where else in a work environment would you go, unless it was the works Christmas do, and there was free alcohol there for you? It just wouldn’t happen in real life.” A third said: “You can start drinking here from 12 o’clock onwards and go around and consume large amounts of alcohol, and it’s relatively freely available.” A fourth described events as a “legitimised opportunity to drink alcohol”, while a fifth said this routine provision of alcohol helps to create a “casual attitude to drinking”. Hannah Spencer, the Green party MP elected at the Gorton and Denton byelection in February, received a mixed reaction from MPs when in April she labelled Westminster’s drinking culture “unprofessional and worrying” and said it led to cases of “questionable and dangerous behaviour”. She remarked that “you can smell the alcohol when people are in between votes”. View image in fullscreen Hannah Spencer said she found Westminster’s drinking culture ‘unprofessional and worrying’ after being elected as an MP this year. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian The IAS report also found that: 42% of the MPs interviewed had been offered an alcoholic drink at a work meeting or event on a weekly basis during the previous six months; 13% said that occurred daily. 22% had concerns about a colleague’s drinking. Parliament’s long and unusual working hours, the loneliness many MPs experience being away from home, the pressures of the job and socialising in order to advance their careers can all act as catalysts for drinking. The report added: “The availability of alcohol was seen to encourage unhealthy behaviour in general, from affecting colleagues’ sleep and stress levels to potentially normalising high-risk drinking, with one MP referring to colleagues having had their stomachs pumped in hospital and going back into Westminster the following day.” Some MPs said the findings should prompt Westminster to rethink its attitude to alcohol. The Labour MP Cat Smith said: “We wouldn’t accept a surgeon operating after a drink or a driver getting behind the wheel – so why should we accept legislators voting on the laws of the land after one? “If we’re serious about being a professional workplace, we have to ask hard questions about practices like late night votes that sit alongside on-tap bars.” Beccy Cooper, who was a public health consultant before entering parliament as a Labour MP in 2024, said the report was a wake-up call. In a foreword to the report, she suggested that parliament should draw up its first formal workplace policy on alcohol. She added: “Two findings stood out to me. Almost one in 10 respondents reported a negative experience because of someone else’s drinking at work and 70% either didn’t know, or weren’t sure, how to raise a concern about a colleague’s drinking. “That combination – real, measurable harm and no clear route to address it – is exactly the kind of gap we need to address.” View image in fullscreen Some MPs said Westminster should rethink its attitude to alcohol and parts of the job such as late night votes that sit alongside bars on-site. Photograph: House of Commons/PA Katherine Severi, the IAS’s chief executive, said Westminster should limit the provision of free alcohol to evening events as part of a renewed drive to make it a more modern workplace, which many MPs and staff support. “Very few professions these days would allow free alcohol from midday, or regularly host outside organisations sponsoring events where drinking is the norm during working hours,” she added. The report also said that the commercialisation of parliament as an events venue contributed to MPs’ drinking. In 2023, parliament’s independent complaints and grievance scheme said alcohol was a “frequent factor” in its investigations into alleged misconduct at Westminster. In its findings of 30 investigations it undertook between 2021 and 2022, it added that drinking in parliament’s array of bars was “leading to intimidating behaviour like shouting and swearing”. In July 2023, Daniel Greenberg, the parliamentary standards commissioner, said alcohol had led to “behaviour problems” at Westminster and suggested the sale of alcohol on the state be kept under review. A parliament spokesperson said everyone working there had been reminded to use alcohol responsibly, but hinted that immediate changes were unlikely. “Any changes to parliament’s provision of alcohol would ultimately be a matter for members to decide on. The estate is a unique working environment that includes public access and events,” they said. “Parliament’s behaviour code makes clear that everyone should be treated with respect at all times, and those who choose to drink alcohol on the estate must do so responsibly.” Westminster’s efforts to promote more responsible drinking include greater provision of no- and low-alcohol products and venue staff’s right to refuse to serve anyone who is, or looks likely to become, intoxicated. If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it ( iOS / Android ) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’. SecureDrop If you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via our SecureDrop platform. Our guide at theguardian.com/tips lists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each. Photograph: San Francisco department of animal care and control San Francisco San Francisco pitbull rescued after two days trapped in railway tunnel Pup named Roo, who ran away from home, was found curled up next to rail track – and was ‘thrilled’ to be rescued Uwa Ede-Osifo Fri 31 Jul 2026 19.07 EDT Last modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 19.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A two-year-old pitbull who ran away from home braved two days in a dim San Francisco railway tunnel before being rescued. Caltrain operators spotted the pup named Roo on his first day in the tunnel. Looking at the dog’s unmoving body, they had assumed he had been fatally struck by a train, according to a recent social media post from the San Francisco animal care and control shelter. On the second day, after Roo was seen moving, police officers set out on foot in the tunnel with a flashlight. View image in fullscreen Caltrain operators helping the pup named Roo. Photograph: San Francisco Department of Animal Care & Control They found Roo, lying curled next to a rail track, and led the dog out of the dark into the light of day. “He was terrified at first, then was thrilled to be rescued,” the animal shelter wrote in the post. The pup is a recent adoptee, who ran away after being “spooked”. Fortunately, Roo was microchipped. He has since been reunited with his owner. The San Francisco area has rallied around other dogs in distress as of late. Menlo Park firefighters rescued a missing dog that was found swimming in the San Francisco Bay, as seagulls followed in pursuit. Photograph: AP Sonya Massey Illinois officer who killed Sonya Massey denied medical release from prison Sean Grayson, diagnosed with colon cancer, was sentenced to 20 years for killing Massey in Springfield in 2024 Associated Press Fri 31 Jul 2026 17.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A former Illinois sheriff’s deputy won’t get an early medical release from his two-decade prison sentence for killing Sonya Massey inside her home after the Black woman called 911 about a possible prowler, state officials decided on Friday. Sean Grayson had been diagnosed with colon cancer prior to the 2024 shooting, and his attorney noted in January that the cancer had advanced to his liver and lungs. The three-member Illinois prisoner review board voted unanimously on Friday to deny Grayson’s application for early medical release, panel spokesperson Liz Mitchell said in an email. Grayson, who is white, was convicted in October of second-degree murder for Massey’s killing, a case that sparked protests over systemic racism and a US justice department review. View image in fullscreen Bodycam footage shows Sonya Massey and Sean Grayson outside her home in Springfield. Photograph: Illinois state police/AP Body-camera footage showed Grayson and another deputy enter Massey’s home in Springfield, Illinois. Minutes later, Grayson shot the 36-year-old single mother in the face as she moved a pot of hot water from the stove and told him: “I rebuke you in the name of Jesus.” Grayson was given 20 years, the maximum possible sentence, in January. He filed for early release from prison in May, six months into his sentence, according to a copy of his application published by Capitol News Illinois. Grayson apologized for Massey’s death at his January sentencing but in the release application wrote she had “attacked me with a pot of boiling water”. Attorney Daniel Fultz, who has represented Grayson, declined to comment. In a letter to the board opposing Grayson’s release, Sangamon county state’s attorney John Milhiser said the former deputy’s medical condition was already considered at sentencing. “To release Grayson under these circumstances would be a miscarriage of justice,” he wrote, “and an insult to Sonya Massey’s memory and family.” Representing Massey’s family, attorneys Ben Crump and Antonio Romanucci said on Friday that the board “made the right decision”. “The board recognized what this family has said from the start,” they said in a statement. “No one is above accountability, and a badge does not provide an early way out.” Democratic governor JB Pritzker said in a statement that Illinois law requires the prisoner review board to consider medical release requests. He called Massey’s killing “a profound loss”. “Sonya was innocent, unarmed, and calling law enforcement for help,” he said. “It was a painful reminder that too many innocent Black Americans have faced this kind of violence – and they deserve justice.” Explore more on these topics Sonya Massey US crime US policing Illinois news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Photograph: Rodrique Ngowi/AP Massachusetts Jurors in Lindsay Clancy murder trial visit home where children were killed Defense lawyers say Clancy was ill with postpartum psychosis when she killed three children in January 2023 Associated Press Fri 31 Jul 2026 15.50 EDT Last modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 18.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Jurors walked through the Massachusetts home where Lindsay Clancy strangled her three children, a rare visit on Friday that let them see first-hand the place where an outwardly ordinary family life unraveled into tragedy . After being driven past two businesses relevant to the narrative of the January 2023 killings, jurors were escorted in groups of six to view the inside of the house, including the basement where the children died. During the roughly 40-minute visit, the jury also saw the yard where Clancy was found after jumping from a second-story window. Journalists were kept away by a police barricade, but court officers could be seen through the trees escorting jurors to and from the bus along the site of the Clancy family’s former driveway. The home now has a new owner. Lindsay Clancy’s husband told police children were dead, court hears Read more Clancy herself did not attend the visit to the home, which she has not seen since the day of the killings. Her lawyers say Clancy was in the grip of postpartum psychosis , a rare mental illness linked to the stress, sleep deprivation and hormonal changes that follow childbirth. Jurors in US criminal cases often are expressly told not to visit the scene of the events in question. There are a number of rationales for not doing so – among other things, the site may have changed in the interim between an alleged crime and a trial. But courts sometimes allow juries to make a supervised excursion as a group, for reasons that can include assessing distances or features not thought to come across fully in photos. Such excursions have happened in a number of high-profile cases, including the 2023 murder trial of the South Carolina attorney Alex Murdaugh ; the 2022 sentencing trial of Parkland, Florida, school shooter Nikolas Cruz ; the 2015 Massachusetts murder trial of former New England Patriots player Aaron Hernandez ; and the 1995 murder trial of OJ Simpson . Jurors in Clancy’s trial retraced the route her ex-husband, Patrick Clancy, took when she asked him to pick up takeout food and medicine for Cora, their five-year-old, on the night of the killings. He returned to find the children dead and Clancy badly injured and bleeding in the yard. The panel was driven past the restaurant – about 5.5 miles from the family’s former home in Duxbury, a suburb south of Boston – and the pharmacy, about a mile from the house. Lindsay Clancy’s ex-husband testifies about day she killed their three children Read more Prosecutors say the errands were a ruse to get her husband out of the house. They say Lindsay Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, acted intentionally and is criminally responsible for the deaths of children Cora, five; Dawson, three; and Callan, eight months. Her lawyers do not dispute that Clancy killed the children, but they say she had bipolar disorder and her condition worsened when she took antidepressants prescribed after the birth of her third child. Clancy believed a voice was telling her to “kill the children so you can kill yourself”, according to her lawyers. Lindsay Clancy is paralyzed from the waist down after trying to kill herself that night. Clancy faces life in prison without parole if convicted of murder. If found not guilty due to a lack of criminal responsibility, she would be committed to a state mental health facility. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org . In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. On May 5, the minority government led by Liberal leader Ilie Bolojan was dismissed following a no-confidence vote in Parliament initiated by the former ruling partner PSD, and populist, ultranationalist AUR party (in opposition). The rift between the Liberals and USR, on the one hand, and the Social Democrats, on the other, has deepened and leaves no room for even a tentative rapprochement. More importantly, the conflict between the right-of-centre and left wing blocs threatens to jeopardise the reforms provided for in the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNNR) and, implicitly, the funding that the European Commission gives Bucharest in exchange. PSD says it considers itself an opposition party, and warns that it will not vote under pressure for any law stipulated in the PNRR. The Liberals criticise this position, which they see as a form of blackmail. President Nicuşor Dan is in turn criticised over his passive approach of the crisis and his leniency towards the Social Democrats, widely regarded as the initiators of the crisis. A growing number of political actors mention snap elections as a possibility. Waiting for the sovereign rating Amid persistent political uncertainty, the financial rating agency Fitch will release on the last day of the month its decision on Romania’s sovereign credit rating and the country’s outlook, the finance ministry announced. Ministry officials had technical discussions on Tuesday with Fitch Ratings officers. Bucharest promised that sustained efforts are carried on to complete the reforms and investments undertaken in the PNRR, as well as to step up fund absorption under the 2021-2027 Multiannual Financial Framework and the SAFE program. Similar talks were also held with Moody’s. Currently, all three major rating agencies (S&P, Moody’s and Fitch) have a ‘negative’ outlook linked with Romania’s sovereign rating, which places the country at the bottom of the investment-grade scale. From Paris to Kyiv Romania is an active and reliable partner in the efforts to strengthen European security, president Nicuşor Dan said in Paris, after talks within the “Coalition of the Willing” in support of Ukraine. Together with other European leaders, president Dan also attended the parade organised on the National Day of France. It was a good opportunity to reaffirm the strong ties between Romania and France, united by a strategic partnership and a friendship built over time, the Romanian leader emphasised after the French holiday. The 37 countries in the Coalition of the Willing for Ukraine renewed their commitment to continue military support and to have solid security guarantees in place once the conflict ends. Investing in the defence and security of Ukraine is an investment in our own security, and Ukraine must be able to negotiate peace from a position of strength, president Nicuşor Dan believes. On Wednesday, the president took part in the Ukraine-Southeast Europe Summit in Kyiv. The leaders attending the summit signed a joint declaration reaffirming their support for the independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine, as well as for its European Union and NATO accession. According to Nicuşor Dan, the talks also focused on regional connectivity. On the sidelines of the meeting, Nicuşor Dan had a meeting with president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to discuss coordination on prevention and early warning mechanisms in case of drone incidents. Supreme Court ruling collides with European law The Court of Justice of the European Union ruled on Thursday that the decision of Romania’s High Court of Cassation and Justice to extend the enforcement of the statute of limitations in criminal cases for the period 2014-2018 is not in line with EU law. The European court also ruled that the Supreme Court’s decision on the statute of limitations does not apply to pending cases. “The Court explains that, in view of the importance of the principle of res judicata in EU law, that law does not require that decisions having the authority of res judicata which have found, applying the decision of the HCCJ of 2022, that criminal liability for instances of serious fraud affecting the financial interests of the Union is time-barred be called into question.” In May 2022, the Constitutional Court issued a ruling regulating the suspension of the limitation period in criminal matters in force in 2018 – 2022. Subsequently, the Supreme Court held that the Constitutional Court ruling applies retroactively to 2014. The High Court of Cassation and Justice claims that it has applied European law ‘always in good faith’, and its approach to the limitation of criminal liability was not a choice between EU law and the European Convention on Human Rights. The High Court of Cassation and Justice stands not with a particular case law solution or to a specific outcome of a case, but with the fundamental values ​​of the rule of law, the Court emphasised. European football competitions begin Romanian football champion Universitatea Craiova qualified for the Champions League second qualifier round, after a double win against ML Vitebsk (Belarus). Craiova has a spectacular period, as this week they also added the Super Cup to their trophy list, after outplaying the runner-up Universitatea Cluj last season, both in the championship and the Cup final. The latter left the Europa League and will play in the Conference League alongside fellow Romanians CFR Cluj and FCSB. Newsflash Newsroom , 18.07.2026, 14:00 DEFENSE – Romania signed the final two contracts on Friday for the procurement of helicopters and radar systems under the European SAFE Programme, which is designed to strengthen the defence industry and military capabilities of EU member states. The two contracts are worth more than €1 billion. Combined with the other individual agreements signed by the end of May, the total value of Romania’s SAFE-related contracts now stands at €7.5 billion. Romanian Defence Minister Radu Miruță said that, by 2030, two further agreements remain to be concluded: a contract with Norway covering an air defence system, and a €200 million joint project with Ukraine for the production of drones. The Romanian Ministry of Defence’s total investment under the SAFE Programme amounts to €8.33 billion, with the largest share allocated to the German defence company Rheinmetall, with which seven contracts have been signed. MIGRANTS – Romania’s General Prosecutor’s Office questioned AUR MP Dan Tanasă on Friday over Facebook posts in which he urged Romanians to boycott immigrant workers. Judicial sources said the investigation concerns allegations of incitement to violence, hatred or discrimination against certain groups of people. Following the hearing, George Simion, leader of the Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR), responded online, accusing the authorities of launching politically motivated attacks against his party, which is in opposition in the Romanian Parliament. The case stems from a Facebook post in which Dan Tanasă called on Romanians to refuse deliveries made by foreign workers. Last year, several violent and xenophobic incidents targeted foreign delivery couriers, with some being physically assaulted or robbed while carrying out deliveries. MAGISTRATES – Romania’s Superior Council of Magistracy (CSM) has rejected the criticism contained in the European Commission’s Rule of Law Report, arguing that the document does not point to any systemic deterioration of the Romanian justice system. The CSM also maintains that the report contains factual inaccuracies, including the claim that the Council’s disciplinary decisions are communicated with undue delay, thereby affecting magistrates’ right to appeal. The Ministry of Justice welcomed the report’s overall conclusions, stating that the country’s recent judicial reforms have helped safeguard the independence of the judiciary. In its report, published on Friday, the European Commission warned that Romania has made little progress in strengthening safeguards for the independence of senior prosecutors and in investigating corruption within the judicial system. The Commission also noted that the broader assessment of the justice system had been suspended following a ruling by Romania’s High Court of Cassation and Justice, and recommended that the country improve both the efficiency and governance of its judicial system. CYBER ATTACK – Romania’s relevant authorities are investigating the cyberattack that recently targeted the National Agency for Cadastre and Land Registration. As a result of the attack, all of the agency’s IT systems are currently offline, including its email services and the electronic cadastre and land registry application. However, the data managed through these systems remain secure and have not been compromised. Romania’s National Cyber Security Directorate (DNSC) said that its immediate priority is to restore the functionality of public services, the agency’s applications and its IT infrastructure. The DNSC identified the group behind the attack as “ByteToBreach”, describing it as a financially motivated threat actor that has been active since 1 June 2025 and is suspected to be of Algerian origin. UNIONS – Trade unions in Romania’s healthcare sector have announced that more than 400 medical facilities across the country will take part in a two-hour warning strike on Monday, in protest against the government’s economic and social policies. During the strike, only emergency services will be fully maintained, while routine medical activity will be reduced to one third of its normal capacity. Representatives of the Sanitas Federation have warned that a nationwide general strike could follow from 28 July if their demands remain unmet. Meanwhile, trade union federations representing the education sector have also criticised the government’s approach to education in its public sector pay legislation. They have called on Parliament to amend what they describe as “a serious injustice”. The unions argue that the proposed legislation deepens pay disparities, further undermines the attractiveness of the teaching profession, and risks accelerating the decline of Romania’s education system. PAY LAW- The draft of Romania’s new unified public sector pay law, which overhauls the way salaries for state employees are calculated, has been published and is set to enter parliamentary debate in Bucharest. The legislation, which is due to come into force on 1 December 2026, stipulates, among other provisions, that no public sector employee will see their pay reduced as a result of the reform. Under the proposed system, salaries that currently exceed the new pay scale will be frozen. Where the new grading system would otherwise result in a lower salary, the difference compared with the employee’s November 2026 pay will be maintained temporarily and gradually phased out as future salary increases take effect. The legislation, which is a milestone under Romania’s National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP), was discussed on Friday by representatives of the Presidential Administration and the parties that made up the former governing coalition: the Social Democratic Party (PSD), the National Liberal Party (PNL), the Save Romania Union (USR) and the Democratic Union of Ethnic Hungarians in Romania (UDMR). The Social Democrats said they would not support the bill if its implementation resulted in lower incomes for public sector employees, while the Liberals and the USR expressed satisfaction with the draft legislation. Trade unions, however, have firmly rejected the proposed law, arguing that it deepens inequalities across the public sector and risks becoming little more than a symbolic exercise aimed at fulfilling a milestone under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan. IRAN – Iran launched fresh attacks on Saturday morning targeting US facilities hosted by Arab states in the region. The drone and missile strikes came after the United States carried out attacks against Iranian targets for the seventh consecutive night, hitting radar installations, military infrastructure, underground weapons storage sites and naval equipment. The main objective of the US air campaign is to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which has been blocked by Iran, with Tehran claiming the right to control maritime traffic through the strategic waterway. The latest escalation in violence followed Iran’s attack on a commercial vessel off the coast of Oman, despite having signed an interim agreement extending the ceasefire and guaranteeing freedom of navigation through the strait. Several US officials told Reuters that a second American objective was to prepare the ground for potential further operations. Newsflash Newsroom , 18.07.2026, 20:00 EBOLA – The number of confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo has surpassed 2,180, according to the latest official figures. Authorities in Kinshasa say that 864 of those infected have died. There is no specific treatment for this strain of the virus, which has a fatality rate of between 25% and 50%. Other strains of Ebola can have mortality rates as high as 90%. The ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has prompted the United States to impose travel restrictions on its citizens in the country. Under the measures, Americans are not permitted to return home on commercial flights unless, after leaving the DRC, they spend three weeks in a third country. In June, Romania’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs raised its travel advisory for the Democratic Republic of Congo to Level 8 on a nine-point scale and advised Romanian nationals to avoid all travel to the country. MOLDOVA – Moldova’s Prime Minister-designate, Vasile Tofan, is due to seek a vote of confidence from Parliament on Tuesday for his proposed cabinet and governing programme. Tofan has made only four changes to the ministerial line-up, retaining most of the team assembled by his predecessor, Alexandru Munteanu. On Friday, he said the government’s programme was in its final stages of preparation and would focus on restoring public trust in government, reviving the economy, and securing the signing of Moldova’s European Union accession treaty by the end of 2028. Like his predecessor, Tofan is not a member of the ruling Party of Action and Solidarity (PAS), which holds a commanding majority in Parliament, but comes instead from Moldova’s business community. WILDFIRE – More than 17,000 vegetation fires were recorded in Romania last year, with the number of such incidents having risen in recent years, the General Inspectorate for Emergency Situations has warned. Firefighters say vegetation fires can spread rapidly, particularly during periods of extreme heat, posing a serious threat to people and wildlife, as well as homes, farmland and forests. The authorities have reiterated that burning vegetation is strictly prohibited under Romanian law. Those found responsible face substantial fines ranging from 7,500 to 15,000 lei (€1,400–€2,900) for individuals and from 50,000 to 100,000 lei (€9,500–€19,000) for companies and other legal entities.
