Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Tom Armstrong, who lives in the area, said it was good that rightwing politicians were drawing attention to small boat crossings. Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/The Guardian Immigration and asylum On the ground in the English seaside town rightwing influencers say is being ‘invaded’ Some in Dover say their town is being exploited by content creators and politicians, but others claim there is a genuine problem Kevin Rawlinson Sat 1 Aug 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 07.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google I f you believe rightwing influencers and politicians, Dover and the wider Kent coast has been the site of an “invasion” for years now. And, for an online audience of millions, they and their camera crews have been the vanguard in the nation’s defence. Indeed, if you believe all you see on the algorithms of amateur Channel watchers, the shadow home secretary, Chris Philp , braved a hail of French gunfire as he took to the water in a fishing boat this week; an attempt by the French authorities, he suggested, to deter him in his mission of highlighting the small boats crisis. The inconvenient truth behind Philp’s attempt to self-police our borders is that nothing of the sort happened. The French government said he simply passed by a routine training exercise that involved firing live rounds. With its sloping pebble beach and sunbathers and dog-walkers enjoying the summer sunshine by its marina this week, Dover does not look much like the frontline of a war zone. Are the rightwing figures who regularly visit the town to create social media content exploiting it for their own careers, or are they seeking solutions to a genuine problem? “They’re using Dover a bit,” said one resident, Alison Drake. “People making all these videos and that is not really doing much, is it?” View image in fullscreen The frontline of a war zone? The Dover seafront, where rightwing influencers and politicians flock to make content for social media about an ‘invasion’. Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/The Guardian Some said that creating tension where there was none before was all part of the plan. “What they’re trying to do is play on fear with all of these stunts,” said Razia Shariff, who runs the Kent Refugee Action Network (Kran), a charity that provides education for refugee and asylum-seeking young people. Whether or not the selfie stick-toting influencers who descend on the south coast need to capture the supposed “invasion” is, for some, a moot point. Some of those living in the area insisted the relentless focus on the issue – and on the region – was at least keeping the problem in the public eye. “They’re letting the people know that the French are not doing anything,” Tom Armstrong said. Armstrong is avowedly anti-immigration and said the “country is being devalued” by it. He said rightwing politicians were helping that cause. “You’ve got to draw attention,” he said. Later, he added: “We’ve got to know the truth.” Philp claimed to have been exposing the small boats crisis during his jaunt across the Channel. While Drake agreed that rightwing figures highlighting the issue might prompt action, she added: “Everyone knows about it, it’s about time they did something about it. They don’t do anything. So, it’s all very well everyone keep going on about it, but no one does anything. They know it’s happening.” View image in fullscreen Alison Drake said despite the attention on Dover, no one was doing anything about the small boat crossings. Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/The Guardian Few people have had more opportunity to solve the small boats crisis than Philp who, as immigration minister in the early 2020s, oversaw a sharp increase in crossings. In contrast, organisations such as Kran are working to alleviate some of the challenges caused by the way migration has been handled by successive governments. The young people Kran helps are taking part in a summer scheme at an academy in Kent this week. Shariff spoke glowingly of some of their predecessors’ achievements. One, she said, had arrived in the UK as a child refugee and now worked as a nurse in local hospitals. “Others have set up their own businesses against all the odds. They get on with their lives and they try.” Carol, who lives in Dover and did not want to give her surname, suggested the focus should be more on the work of organisations such as Kran than on politicians such as Philp and Nigel Farage . The Reform leader has repeatedly referred to small boat crossings as an “invasion”. Standing on the Dover seafront in 2024, he described the site as the “frontline of the great national debate on immigration”. Carol did not recognise the picture the Reform leader painted of the town, as she stood on almost the same spot he had occupied two years ago. “I mean, look, it’s pleasant enough,” she said, nodding towards the beach. View image in fullscreen Carol worries that Dover being used as the backdrop for content about small boat crossings could deter tourists from visiting. Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/The Guardian People there were sunbathing in the warm weather, while children played in the water and others took an opportunity to go out in the sea in small vessels. “I think it is unfair that Dover is headlined in that way. Because you can sit on the beach, enjoy the area.” Carol said it was frustrating that Dover and other nearby towns were so often used as the backdrop for social media content focusing on the small boats crisis and feared it could deter people from visiting an area that needs a lift. “It’s a bit rundown, like many towns. It’s a bit sad. So it’s not a great place to shop, by all means, but the seafront’s lovely. And the surrounding countryside is lovely. I’m sure it isn’t helping. Dover has got that image.” Explore more on these topics Immigration and asylum Kent Chris Philp Nigel Farage news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story French riot police used teargas on people trying to board small boat, charity claims ICE-linked security firm reports UK revenue slump after asylum contract ends Home Office used ‘AI hallucinated’ information to refuse asylum claim, judge suggests Tory MP accuses French navy of firing ‘warning’ shots near him in Channel Home Office blocking evacuation of dozens of women and children from Gaza UK to continue sending potential trafficking victims to France despite court ruling Immigration bill amendment will allow removal of Rochdale gang leader Mahmood’s cutting of protections for UK-France ‘one in, one out’ asylum deal ruled unlawful Jamaican man who has lived in UK for 26 years facing deportation No 10 shares ‘public’s shock’ at reports of convicted people smuggler living in UK Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

Photograph: Mael Dubiez/SDIS33/EPA View image in fullscreen A firefighter works to contain a wildfire near Saumos, in the Gironde department of France, on Wednesday. Photograph: Mael Dubiez/SDIS33/EPA France Analysis Will brutal wildfires force French leaders to take climate crisis seriously? Angelique Chrisafis Campaigners worry politicians will have moved on by time of elections in which Marine Le Pen is expected to challenge Fri 31 Jul 2026 00.00 EDT Share As dozens of forest wildfires burned across France this week amid the summer’s fourth brutal heatwave and increasing air pollution, some wondered whether voters’ first-hand experience of the climate emergency would change the political debate ahead of next year’s presidential election. The Green leader, Marine Tondelier , who cut short a tour of France on medical advice that at seven months pregnant she should avoid breathing smoke-filled air in the south-west near a huge wildfire in Gironde, said the political class still had its head in the sand. She said the government had ignored her plea for cross-party crisis talks to declare a national state of emergency on the climate this summer. She called for a new “climate welfare state” in France to help those whose lives were being affected as about 260,000 people were evacuated because of wildfires across the country. But French politicians focused instead this week on arguments over budgets, crisis planning and criticisms over the levels of state funding for emergency services and equipment to fight fires, including water-bombing planes. The more complex longer-term issues of cutting emissions and structural societal changes to address climate heating were largely left aside. View image in fullscreen Emmanuel Macron meets forest police and firefighters in Noisy-sur-Ecole, near Fontainebleau. Photograph: Mohammed Badra/Pool EPA/AP The president, Emmanuel Macron , said it was not the time to analyse lessons to be learned while France was still in “full battle” against fires. Macron, whose decade as president comes to an end next spring, returned to his war vocabulary of the 2020 Covid pandemic. As the Gironde wildfire burned an area four times the size of Paris, Macron flew to the crisis operations centre in Bordeaux, saying France was facing its “hardest situation since the second world war”. He also said the situation was “totally atypical”, suggesting the wildfire was out of the ordinary. Climate experts said growing numbers of forest fires had been predictable amid rising temperatures. Most political parties will not clarify their full election manifestos – and positions on the climate crisis – until this winter, and some climate campaigners worry that by then the fires and heatwaves may be less present in the media and people’s minds. Marine Le Pen, who leads the far-right anti-immigration National Rally (RN), is seen as having a good chance of reaching the final round vote in the presidential race. During the second round of the last contest, in 2022, Le Pen said: “I have never been a climate sceptic”. But the following year she said the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change was “alarmist”, and some RN politicians have in the past questioned the role of human activity in climate heating. View image in fullscreen Marine Le Pen said in 2022 she had ‘never been a climate sceptic’. Photograph: Philippe Magoni/Reuters The RN has also opposed the workings of the EU’s green deal, which is designed to make the EU carbon neutral by 2050. But since the heatwaves of the start of the summer, key figures in Le Pen’s party have sought to stress that the RN is not a climate crisis denier. This week, the RN focused more on the heroism of firefighters and alleged underfunding of fire services by the state than on long-term environmental action. The radical left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon earlier in July proposed reorganising French regions into “eco-regions” to ensure water supply and deal with the climate crisis. Rémi Lefebvre, a professor of political science at the University of Lille, said of the current wildfires’ impact on the presidential campaign: “Ecology will probably be talked about more during the election campaign, but I’m not convinced that it will reconfigure French political life.” He said serious wildfires in previous years had not forced a change of direction and French politics had shown itself to be “too short-termist” to dig deep into changing models of society. Lefebvre said Le Pen did not take a stance of denying climate change “because that is no longer possible … we’ve passed that point”. But he said the broader issue was political inaction on climate challenges. He said a lot of French people felt those in charge were powerless to react. Photograph: Image courtesy of Stephanie Postle Krupa/the Krupa family View image in fullscreen Maria and Czeslaw Krupa with two family members outside the Tauron Arena in Kraków. Photograph: Image courtesy of Stephanie Postle Krupa/the Krupa family Brexit ‘It was a big shock’: new border rules left couple stuck in Kraków after living in UK for 80 years Maria and Czeslaw Krupa, who arrived as children of displaced Polish veterans, told they have no post-Brexit rights to return home to Bury Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent Thu 30 Jul 2026 12.59 EDT First published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 09.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T wo Polish citizens who have lived in the UK for nearly 80 years after their parents fled the second world war have spoken of their terrifying experience after being told they did not have post-Brexit rights to return to the UK. In May, while visiting Poland, they learned that although they had been welcomed as refugees after the war, they now needed special post-Brexit paperwork to return to their home in Bury, Greater Manchester . Maria Krupa, 85, and her husband, Czeslaw, 92, who met in the UK and went on to marry and settle in Bury, were issued with “ aliens’ registration cards ” and have travelled extensively as adults without anyone asking them for their immigration status. View image in fullscreen Maria and Czeslaw Krupa in Kraków airport. Photograph: Image courtesy of Stephanie Postle Krupa/the Krupa family Czeslaw, who came from Lviv which was then part of Poland , and Maria, who left her home town in what is now Belarus as an infant, had travelled to Poland in May to meet surviving family members. But Ryanair refused to allow them to board the flight for their return journey on the grounds that they had neither proof of the right to live in the UK nor the new electronic travel authorisation (ETA) now required for foreign tourists entering the UK. “It was a big shock,” said Maria. “We were very, very disappointed and a bit upset because my husband takes a lot of medicine because of a stroke to his spinal cord.” They had arrived in Southampton in 1947 and 1948 as the young dependants of displaced Polish service members who had been evacuated from their homes in 1940 and later became part of Gen Władysław Anders’s Polish army that served in Persia, India, the Middle East and Africa. Anders’s army played a key role in the defeat of the Third Reich and had integrated into the British military command structure after friction with the Soviets in 1942. “We tried to explain to Ryanair that our fathers fought for Poland and England in the war, but they refused to let us on the plane because they said they would have to pay a big fine,” said Maria. “My husband was really upset,” she said, explaining that Czeslaw used a mobility scooter and was on a lot of medication after the stroke. He has difficulty getting in and out of cars and “just wanted to get home”, she said. View image in fullscreen Czeslaw Krupa, left, with his brother and cousin in Africa in 1944. Photograph: Image courtesy of Stephanie Postle Krupa/the Krupa family They are speaking out to help others who might be in the same position. “It was a big, big shock because we never heard of this and we never thought for one minute that after nearly 80 years someone would tell us we couldn’t go home,” said Maria. Kate Smart, the chief executive of Settled, who helped the Krupas, said the charity was seeing “thousands of cases” like the Krupas’. “It is a really common occurrence, almost on a daily basis,” she said. The EU settlement scheme was launched in 2019 to give EU citizens living in the UK the documentary evidence needed to travel as they had done under the pre-Brexit, free-movement rules. Many of the people seen by Settled are elderly people who have British children and grandchildren. “They have nobody in their family circle who thinks like immigrants so they don’t talk about things like ‘settled status’,” said Smart. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Preview latest after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Maria Krupa as a child in Karachi, then part of India, where her father was stationed in 1943. Displaced Polish people were housed in refugee camps. Photograph: Image courtesy of Stephanie Postle Krupa/the Krupa family Maria said she had never thought to get a British passport as she had never needed it in the previous 80 years and it had never crossed her mind. “It was really important. I didn’t think of it as sort of weakening my identity. I love England. I mean, I always say, I’m very grateful to England, you know, to have taken so many people, you know thousands after the war. But I just thought it was important that we stay Polish,” she said. After being forced to leave the airport late on a Sunday night in May, they returned the next day with an ETA but the couple had to pose as tourists, claiming they lived in Poland as the online form would not accept their British address. View image in fullscreen Maria and Czeslaw Krupa celebrate Czeslaw’s 90th birthday in Bury. Photograph: Image courtesy of the Krupa family Maria said: “When we arrived in England we were terrified. We had to be careful about what we said. We were terrified because they started asking questions and we thought we are not going to lie again and have to tell the truth.” After going to Citizens Advice in Bury, they were connected with Settled. Smart commended the Home Office resolution centre for its swift action. The charity withdrew the initial no-time-limit application the Home Office advised the family to make and instead successfully applied for EU settled status. She appealed to the government to take note of the issues with the EU settlement scheme, arguing “a process should have kicked in at the airport” when an issue such as this one arose. A spokesperson said the Home Office would encourage people to check their immigration status before they travel, but anyone in a similar situation to the Krupas should make a no-time-limit application to get the paperwork they needed to travel in and out of the country. “Anyone settled in the UK without up-to-date evidence of their status is encouraged to make a no-time-limit application. This will give them access to an eVisa and facilitate seamless future travel,” they said. Photograph: Halyna Kavun/Alamy View image in fullscreen A young woman looking at the Bundestag building in Berlin. Talks about the youth mobility agreement have been deadlocked. Photograph: Halyna Kavun/Alamy Brexit Analysis What the EU wants from Andy Burnham Jennifer Rankin in Brussels and Lisa O’Carroll in London European leaders have made positive noises about the new UK PM, but he is likely to face the same restrictions as Starmer Tue 21 Jul 2026 07.31 EDT Last modified on Wed 22 Jul 2026 13.30 EDT Share Andy Burnham is unknown in Brussels, but that will soon change. In his schedule for the autumn is an EU-UK summit that may underscore the same dilemmas that have confronted previous British prime ministers in the relationship with Europe. EU leaders were quick to offer congratulations to Britain’s prime minister, the seventh since the 2016 Brexit referendum. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said she looked forward to strengthening the EU-UK partnership “for the security of our shared continent” and “the prosperity of people on both sides of the Channel”. The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, invited Burnham to visit Berlin “very soon”, noting that the UK and Germany’s “deep connection is particularly evident in these times”. Georg Riekeles, a former adviser on the commission’s Brexit taskforce, told the Guardian: “People don’t know what to expect. But he also starts with a blank sheet of paper … and that can be an advantage.” The main concern, said Riekeles, who is now an associate director at the European Policy Centre, was whether Burnham would be “on the same trajectory” in terms of defence and security cooperation, energy and the “very positive agenda” on economic issues. One EU diplomat observed: “For a British prime minister it is not necessarily a bad thing to be little known. If you are well known it is probably because you were prominent on one side or the other of the Brexit debate.” Burnham’s most notable statement on the EU was his wish to see Britain rejoin in his lifetime , while speaking to the Guardian at the Labour party conference in September 2025. But during campaigning in the leave-voting constituency of Makerfield, he made it clear reversing Brexit was not a priority , because “Britain would be stuck in a permanent rut if we are just constantly arguing”. Michael Jacobs, who advised the former prime minister Gordon Brown, said Burnham’s statement on rejoining “felt like it was from the heart” but was also politically astute. “It tells pro-Europeans that he is one of them. But it tells leave voters that it’s not his political priority for now, and he is not going to relitigate the Brexit arguments.” Among the first calls Burnham had after entering No 10 were with von der Leyen, Merz and the French leader, Emmanuel Macron. He has appointed Hamish Falconer as the Europe minister, replacing Nick Thomas-Symonds. The latter’s departure is a blow to the UK-EU reset talks started by Starmer, but some claimed they had lost momentum and Falconer would bring fresh energy. One of his first calls after being appointed was to the European trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič. Elected as an MP in 2024, Falconer brings a wealth of international experience, with a decade spent in the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, a stint in the National Crime Agency, and a career dealing with international terrorism, hostage recovery and countering human trafficking. He served as Middle East minister under Starmer. The return of Johnny Reynolds, as business secretary, will help in talks aimed at protecting European trade from China, and tricky negotiations to scrap an upcoming 10% tariff on exports of British cars to the EU and vice versa . Under Starmer, the UK and EU signed a security and defence pact and cooperated closely on Ukraine. Despite failing to agree British participation in a €150bn EU defence loans scheme, the two sides moved on. In Starmer’s final week in office the UK signed an agreement to participate in the EU’s €90bn (£77bn) loan for Ukraine, meaning British companies can provide more weapons funded through the scheme. Now Burnham inherits the reset agenda launched by Starmer. The two sides are due to sign a trio of agreements at the summit: a deal to reduce paperwork and certification for fresh food in an effort to ease trade barriers for British exporters; linking emissions trading systems; and a youth exchange scheme enabling 18- to 30-year-olds to work, study, travel and volunteer in the EU and UK. Ireland’s Europe minister, Thomas Byrne, told reporters this month that he expected “positive continuity, at the very least”. Ireland, which holds the EU Council’s rotating presidency until the end of the year, will be involved in the diplomatic preparations for the summit, the date of which is yet to be decided. “There are tricky issues there, and I think we can get them over the line,” Byrne said. Talks have been deadlocked over the youth mobility agreement . EU member states think the UK’s proposed cap of 50,000 youth visas is too low and they oppose their nationals paying the NHS surcharge and higher rate of tuition fees for foreign students. But Some diplomats see a middle ground whereby EU students get a discount on foreign fees but pay above the domestic rate. Jacobs suggested Burnham may raise the cap on numbers. “The idea that leave voters regard such a scheme as a form of immigration was always slightly absurd, and I think Burnham will see that as a relatively easy win to offer pro-Europeans.” But when it comes to the UK-EU economic relationship, Burnham will face the same constraints as Starmer. Earlier this year the EU rejected an attempt by Starmer to negotiate a single market for goods , minus the free movement of people. EU member states suggested the UK could join the European Economic Area, but that would require accepting the free movement of people and making payments to the EU budget with no voting rights in shaping new EU rules. Jacobs said: “Given Burnham’s sensitivity to the immigration concerns of his own Makerfield voters, and of many others, the idea that he would seek to re-enter the single market by allowing free movement and making a massive financial payment to the EU budget (which is what the EU would demand) seems implausible. “On the substantive issues, I think he will do pretty much what Starmer has been trying to do with the so-called ‘reset’, and he will come up against the same barriers in Brussels.” Explore more on these topics Brexit Andy Burnham Labour Foreign policy European Union Europe news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story ‘It was a big shock’: new border rules left couple stuck in Kraków after living in UK for 80 years The EU that the UK left no longer exists Brexit rule change means British teens in EU face soaring student fees for UK degrees EU urged to exempt UK from car rules that could be worst Brexit impact yet EU halves duty-free steel quota but UK and other partners given better rate Europe’s media look on in bemusement at post-Brexit ‘revolving door’ of UK prime ministers Two-thirds of EU citizens back UK rejoining bloc, survey finds Revealed: Brexit voting areas have seen faster growth in foreign workers since EU referendum UK could keep special pre-Brexit terms if it rejoined EU, Michel Barnier says Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Paul Quayle/Alamy View image in fullscreen MPs have warned of ‘utter chaos and miles of tailbacks’ unless EU’s entry-exit system is updated. Photograph: Paul Quayle/Alamy UK news France and UK to increase staffing at border controls in effort to avert travel chaos Disruption at Channel crossings expected to rise amid new fingerprint and facial recognition checks Matthew Weaver Sun 12 Jul 2026 09.33 EDT First published on Sun 12 Jul 2026 08.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google France and the UK have agreed to increase staffing at border controls in response to warnings of travel chaos caused by new fingerprinting and facial recognition checks. Disruption at Channel crossings is expected to rise sharply next weekend at the start of the summer holiday season, with MPs saying there would be “utter chaos and miles of tailbacks” unless the EU’s entry-exit system (EES) is fixed or checks are suspended. The EU has rejected calls to suspend the system, but French officials have reportedly assured the UK transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, that more staff will be deployed to ease queues. On Sunday, Alexander announced £20m of UK government funding to help reduce delays. The Department for Transport said the money would increase capacity for processing vehicles, reduce wait times and ease congestion. Alexander said her French counterpart, Philippe Tabarot, had agreed that high levels of resourcing at border points were essential to enable smoother journeys for passengers over the summer period. French border police have offered to put more of its officers on UK soil to ensure passport booths are better staffed at Dover, Folkestone and London St Pancras station, from where the Eurostar departs, according to the Sunday Times . The exact level of any staffing commitment from France is unclear. A spokesperson for the DfT said: “Heidi Alexander and her French counterpart agreed that high levels of resourcing at border points are essential to enable smoother journeys for passengers over the summer period.” Alexander told Tabarot that biometric kiosks used to take fingerprints and facial scans were not working. The DfT pointed out that checks could be carried out on coach passengers and lorries, by French border police on UK soil. But instead they are having to manually register car passengers without biometrics while the French authorities wait for new kiosks and tablets to be ready. Two-thirds of EU citizens back UK rejoining bloc, survey finds Read more Alexander said: “As well as the over £20m we have given to increase booths for passport checks and minimise disruption, I have raised holidaymakers’ concerns directly with the EU commissioner for transport to make sure they are playing their part to reduce delays during the busiest travel period of the year. “I will do everything in my power to help holidaymakers on their way.” The port of Dover said EES checks at the start of the May half-term holiday led to four-and-a-half hours of delays. It expects almost 50% more vehicles to travel through Dover this summer. About 12,000 cars a day are expected at Dover next weekend – more than three times as many than usual. After a visit to the port by home affairs select committee MPs, Karen Bradley, the committee chair, said last week: “We saw for ourselves that there is going to be utter chaos next week unless the French authorities step up.” On Tuesday, the EU said there were 20 “difficult spots” , which are thought to include Dover, caused by the new checks. But it dismissed a request by airports and airlines to suspend the EES. The new system is designed to address the weakness in border controls exposed by the terrorist attacks in Brussels and Paris in 2015 and 2016. It was delayed several times before it finally began being introduced in phases last October. Since April, UK passengers entering and exiting Schengen countries, have to register at the border by scanning their passport, plus having their photo and fingerprints taken. https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text: View image in fullscreen Kyiv, Ukraine People hold flares during a memorial event at Independence Square in Kyiv, marking the fourth anniversary of the Olenivka prison attack . On 29 July 2022, dozens of Ukrainian soldiers died in the bombardment of the Russian-controlled jail of Olenivka in the eastern Donetsk region. Photograph: Genya Savilov/AFP/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Lviv, Ukraine A woman is in tears upon seeing an apartment building hit by a Russian missile strike in Lviv. Donald ⁠Trump cast doubt this week on allowing Ukraine to build Patriot missiles , saying in an interview he was ‘not sure’ about the move. The US president told the Financial Times: ‘It’s a ​very extraordinary weapon, and we have to be ⁠a little bit careful ​of who ​we licence ​to.’ Photograph: Roman Baluk/Reuters Share View image in fullscreen Odesa, Ukraine Residents and visitors relax on a beach on the outskirts of Odesa as smoke from a fire rises in the background following a Russian missile strike. Russia has been accused of violating Polish airspace after a missile exploded in a field in the east of the country, triggering Nato air defences, in the midst of a massive air raid that killed 13 people in neighbouring Ukraine . Photograph: Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Ares, France Firefighting vehicles line up along a road to suppress a wildfire near Ares. Global heating made hot, dry and windy weather at least 20 times more likely in Spain and twice as likely in France, experts from the World Weather Attribution (WWA) consortium have calculated . The finding is the latest to pin the blame for the continent’s sweltering and deadly summer firmly on the heating caused by the burning of oil, gas and coal. Photograph: Baz Ratner/AFP/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Saumos, France Firefighters and civilian volunteers refill a water tanker during night-time wildfire suppression operations in Gironde. Severe wildfires have burned across Spain and France since early July, killing people, destroying thousands of homes and forcing more than 300,000 people to flee . Photograph: Fabrice Sapte /ABACA/Shutterstock Share View image in fullscreen Ceuta, Spain Migrants try to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. At least 57 people died trying to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after as many as 50,000 migrants entered the tiny territory from Morocco in a matter of hours, triggering a political crisis for the Madrid government and unleashing a barrage of criticism from other EU countries. Photograph: Antonio Sempere/AP Share View image in fullscreen Fnideq, Morocco A member of the security forces stands guard as people attempt to cross from the northern Moroccan town of Fnideq to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez , who arrived in Ceuta on Friday, described the influx of as many as 50,000 migrants as ‘a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity’ and said he would use all the state resources at his disposal to guarantee the safety of the people of Ceuta. Photograph: AP Share View image in fullscreen Gaza Palestinians take cover following an Israeli airstrike in Gaza. Donald Trump has declared a breakthrough in negotiations over the disarmament of Hamas and the withdrawal of Israeli forces but Israel has yet to respond officially to the plan and government officials have voiced scepticism over the deal. Photograph: Mohammed Saber/EPA Share View image in fullscreen Deir al-Balah, Gaza Adults and children survey the wreckage of homes destroyed in an Israeli military attack in Deir al-Balah. Israel has pointed to Hamas’s failure to disarm as justification for its continued strikes and refusal to allow any reconstruction in Gaza, and for Israeli forces’ steady edging forward from the demarcation line agreed in October. Photograph: Ali Jadallah/Anadolu/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Qusra, West Bank Children stand outside a mosque that was burned during an attack by Israeli settlers in the West Bank village of Qusra. On its wall, Hebrew graffiti reads ‘Revenge Benayahu’, referring to an Israeli settler killed during clashes with Palestinians in the village of Tell. Photograph: Léo Corrêa/AP Share View image in fullscreen Anzah, West Bank Palestinians gather in front of a building containing shops and flats that were demolished by Israeli forces, citing the lack of a building permit, in Anzah. Israel said it was preparing a major military operation in the West Bank after four Palestinians and two Israelis were killed during a confrontation that began after armed settlers entered a Palestinian village with support from the Israeli military. Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Yatsushiro, Japan A man walks past collapsed houses in Yatsushiro following the 28 July earthquake. The death toll from the powerful quake has risen to 30 , as the search continues for survivors trapped in a badly damaged shopping centre, a paper mill and collapsed homes across the south-west of the country. Photograph: Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Menasha, Wisconsin, US Residents survey damage after a tornado ripped through the town of Menasha. A rare and powerful tornado developed over north-east Wisconsin on Monday, lasting 26 minutes and carving a 12-mile path of destruction in western parts of Appleton and Menasha before dissipating over Lake Winnebago. Photograph: Scott Olson/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Central Valley of California, US Aurora and her six-year-old daughter, who were detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and sent to a family detention centre in Texas, pose for a portrait with Aurora’s ankle monitor in the Central Valley of California. The Trump administration arrested a record number of immigrants last month , according to newly released government data that reveals how US immigration agents are quietly but steadily ramping up operations across the country. Photograph: Carlos Barría/Reuters Share View image in fullscreen Pyongyang, North Korea Youths and students dance at the plaza of the Arch of Triumph to mark the 73rd anniversary of the end of the Korean War in Pyongyang. Russia and North Korea are close to completing a bridge that will form the first road link ever built between the countries, amid concerns the two increasingly close allies are creating infrastructure to boost military cooperation in the Ukraine war. Photograph: Kim Won Jin/AFP/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Nairobi, Kenya Revellers in cowboy attire dance to country music during International Cowboy Day celebrations at Ngong racecourse. Observed annually on the fourth Saturday of July, International Cowboy Day celebrates the history, culture and enduring legacy of cowboys and cowgirls around the world. Photograph: Luis Tato/AFP/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Spain US photographer Spencer Tunick gives instructions to the participants of his new performance. Entitled Gran Spectrum, it’s a tribute to the gay community, with participants painted in the colours of the rainbow flag. Photograph: Angel Medina G/EPA Share View image in fullscreen Paris, France The peloton cycles up Rue Lepic on the ascent of the Butte de Montmartre during the 21st stage of the 113th edition of the Tour de France . Tadej Pogačar took a record-equalling fifth win on Sunday, joining Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Induráin in the canon of the Tour’s most successful cyclists. Photograph: Geoffroy van der Hasselt/AFP/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Glasgow, Scotland Team Australia compete in the men’s 4000m team pursuit qualifying during the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games at Sir Chris Hoy velodrome. Photograph: Quinn Rooney/Getty Images Share View image in fullscreen Bray, England The green square and parched, dry and yellow grass on the cricket field of Maidenhead & Bray cricket club during a game in Bray. England is on track to record its highest ever number of heat-related deaths this summer after the UK Health Security Agency announced that an estimated 2,877 people had died in the May and June heatwaves. https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text: 1:15 Drought Record low water levels across Europe reveal mammoth skeletons and forgotten shipwrecks – video Water levels across several of Europe’s major waterways have dropped to exceptionally low levels, setting new records in some areas. Extreme heat exacerbated by the climate crisis is intensifying the drought hitting the continent as record-breaking heatwaves means the hot atmosphere is evaporating water from rivers, lakes, soils and plants quickly. The Danube has hit the lowest level of water in 30 years in several countries including Hungary, Serbia and Romania, and the Rhine has dropped to its lowest recorded level in some sections and is expected to drop further due to drought Climate crisis-driven heat ‘sucking soils dry’ as extreme drought hits Europe Source: Reuters Thu 30 Jul 2026 18.47 EDT Last modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 06.20 EDT Share Explore more on these topics Drought Europe Hungary Serbia England Climate crisis Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

The dried-up Danube in Budapest, Hungary. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Heat and drought have affected shipping, power plants and tourism across eastern Europe – as well as unearthing some surprises By Deborah Cole in Berlin and agencies Sat 1 Aug 2026 07.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google B aking temperatures and drought across large swathes of central and eastern Europe have driven water levels on the Danube and Rhine rivers to record lows in some areas, hitting shipping, energy production and tourism hard. View image in fullscreen Extreme conditions aggravated by the climate emergency left Europe’s waterways from the Netherlands to the Black Sea parched, triggering compounding crises. For the first time in their history, Hungary and Romania had to shut down atomic reactors normally cooled by the Danube. The largest nuclear power plant in Hungary, the 44-year-old Paks which supplies nearly half of the country’s electricity, has been cutting output since Monday. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen The Paks power plant’s cold-water intake channel from the Danube. The prime minister, Péter Magyar, said the Paks plant was operating at less than ​50% capacity and was expected ​to be ​completely powered down next week. The shutdown could extend for weeks as Danube water ⁠levels are expected to remain too ⁠low to ​restart ‌it. “An energy crisis situation could arise beginning Monday,” he posted on X. “Coordinated steps and restraint will be needed to avoid more severe consequences. We are counting on everyone!” Map of the Danube running across eastern Europe with two nuclear power plants detailed A malfunction at Hungary’s largest gas-fired power plant in Százhalombatta was worsening the grid shortage, he said. Hungarian authorities have asked citizens to reduce energy use in the peak evening hours, including refraining from charging EVs and switching off air conditioners, while carmakers and battery manufacturers have been ordered to cut power and water consumption. In Romania, authorities shut down a reactor unit at the Cernavodǎ power plant earlier in the week for safety reasons and announced a second would be switched off soon after. The prime minister, Ilie Bolojan, said the shutdowns could last for one to two weeks and also urged Romanians to reduce power consumption in the evenings. View image in fullscreen People swimming near a sunken German warship in Prahovo, Serbia . The Danube, which flows through 10 countries, has receded to unprecedented lows in some areas, exposing rocks, old shipwrecks, a second world war bomb and even the remains of an ancient woolly mammoth. A resident of Ryahovo village in northern Bulgaria discovered the bones of the giant ice age beast on the riverbed and specialists at the Regional History Museum in the nearby ‌town of Ruse arrived to investigate the rare find. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen Scientists examining the remains of an ancient mammoth on the dried-up riverbed. Last week, authorities in Budapest closed the Margaret Bridge after a wartime bomb was exposed at its base by the dropping water levels. The record low level of the Danube has forced Budapest cruise ships to dock upriver and sightseeing cruises to be cancelled. Cargo ship operations have ground to a near halt, according to Hungary’s ministry of transport and investment. View image in fullscreen Cattle sit on sand dunes visible after the Danube’s level fell substantially, near Calarasi, Romania. The river is expected to further ebb in the coming days, with no significant rain in the forecast and temperatures expected to exceed 38C across the region. From Slovakia and Hungary to Romania and Bulgaria farther east, ships on the Danube were unable to travel fully loaded along the waterway, and faced lengthy waits. At the Vidin-Calafat Bridge connecting Bulgaria and Romania, Bulgarians said they were out of work because the low water levels had trapped their boats onshore. View image in fullscreen View image in fullscreen A fisher tries to move his boat, blocked by algae on the bottom of the Danube, in front of the Calafat-Vidin Bridge. “It’s never dried up this much before,” Rossen Dobrev, a fisher, told Agence France-Presse. “Now we can even walk all the way to Romania.” Water levels on the Rhine in Germany also fell to near record lows on ⁠Friday, triggered by a heatwave and prolonged dry weather, the country’s WSV navigation agency said. Shallow water has forced reductions of cargo on ‌vessels to about 20% of their normal capacity. View image in fullscreen Three former vessels, including a sailing ship and an eel-fishing boat, connected by a bridge and now serving as a cafe at the old confluence of the Wupper and the Rhine. The Rhine is a crucial shipping artery ​for grains, minerals, ores, coal and oil products, including petrol, creating potential bottlenecks for companies in the EU’s top economy. Dutch officials said the Rhine had dropped to its lowest recorded level at the point where it flows into the Netherlands, and was due to recede further. The Netherlands has suffered from an officially recognised water shortage since mid-July, leading to use restrictions across most of the country, particularly in farming. In Serbia, hundreds of small boats and dozens of cargo ships were marooned on the dried-out riverbank near the northern city of Novi Sad. One houseboat owner, Radovan Segrt, who runs river excursions on his vessel, told the Associated Press that the water in the Danube had withdrawn about 15 to 20 metres from its shore. “The summer season is over now, as far as boat riding is concerned,” he said. http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/01/two-r.text: Two tankers have reported coming under attack near the Strait of Hormuz, a British maritime agency said on Saturday, as tensions between Washington and Tehran over the region continue to build.According to UKMTO, one vessel said it had been "struck by an unknown projectile" while northeast off the coast of Lima, Oman, causing damage to the engine room.No injuries have been reported so far, per the agency.Around three hours later, UKMTO said it had received a report of a second incident, this time northeast of Khasab in Oman."The Master of a tanker reports seeing a large splash and explosion in close proximity to the vessel," it said in a warning, adding that no damage to the ship had been reported at the time.The agency advised vessels in the region to proceed with caution and to dial in any suspicious activity.Authorities are investigating the incidents.The Strait of HormuzThe Strait of Hormuz, which connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea, is one of the world's most crucial oil and gas transit chokepoints, carrying roughly a quarter of the global seaborne oil trade.Tehran effectively closed the waterway following US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, and it has since become a key factor in the ongoing US-Iranian conflict - despite the "memorandum of understanding" agreed between the two sides in June.On Friday, the US military rejected claims that Iran had reclosed the Strait, saying it remained "open for commercial vessel transit.""Iran does not control it. Thousands of ships have sailed through the international waterway over the past four months," US Central Command (CENTCOM) said.The statement came as US President Donald Trump said he was "losing faith" in the prospect of a peace deal and threatened to hit Iran "very hard.""At some point, they're going to say, 'we just can't take it anymore,'" he added.US forces renewed strikes on Iran earlier this week after a brief pause, targeting what CENTCOM said were Iranian Revolutionary Guard command centers, maritime capabilities, missile and drone facilities, and coastal surveillance and defence sites."The strikes aimed to further diminish threats posed by Iran and its proxies to American forces, commercial shipping, and neighboring Gulf countries," CENTCOM said.The US had carried out 13 consecutive days of strikes on Iran earlier in July in an effort to "degrade Iran's ability to threaten commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz."In response, Tehran launched strikes on American military bases across the Middle East, targeting facilities in Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar.

http://www.euronews.com/2026/07/30/seven.text: Seven people were killed on Wednesday in a helicopter crash in Argentina's province of San Juan."With profound sorrow, we received the news of the helicopter accident that occurred in our province, in which seven people sadly lost their lives," San Juan Governor Marcelo Orrego wrote on X.Fatalities included firefighters, police officers and civil protection personnel, he said. The causes of the accident were under investigation and a rescue team had been deployed, emergency services stated.The Bell 412 aircraft had been training before heading to a neighbouring province to help put out days-long fires when it crashed in Ischigualasto natural park.The aircraft lost contact with control teams at 10:26 am, according to the Federal Emergency Agency (AFE).Another aircraft operating in the area managed to locate the crash site and alerted the authorities, who launched an emergency operation. The cause of the accident remains under investigation.Argentine Security Minister Alejandra Monteoliva expressed her condolences on X, writing "I stand with each of the families and their fellow officers in this moment of profound grief."San Juan's local government declared three days of mourning following the accident, during which the national and provincial flags will be flown at half-mast.As a consequence of the accident, the Ischigualasto Provincial Park announced on its social media accounts the suspension of all activities planned for Wednesday "for reasons beyond its control".

http://www.euronews.com/2026/07/30/drone.text: A drone struck a US-owned liquefied natural gas vessel at Egypt's Mediterranean port of Damietta on Wednesday, triggering a fire that spread to a second ship, in what would be the first attack on Egyptian soil since the war between Iran and the US began in February.Egypt's cabinet confirmed on Thursday morning that "preliminary investigations by the relevant authorities found that the incident was caused by a drone," making it the first official confirmation of the attack's nature.No side has claimed responsibility at this time, and an investigation remains ongoing.In the meantime, authorities were taking measures "to protect Egypt's interests and national security," the cabinet said.Egypt's Petroleum Ministry had earlier confirmed the fire without identifying the cause. Petroleum Minister Karim Badawi travelled to the port to oversee the response.The drone struck the Energos Winter, a Marshall Islands-flagged floating storage and regasification unit owned by US company New Fortress Energy, on its starboard side at approximately 3:20 pm CET, according to maritime security firm Ambrey and British firm Vanguard.The fire spread to the nearby Bermuda-flagged LNG tanker Gaslog Salem. Both crews were evacuated. The fire was brought under control and no injuries were reported. Both vessels were subsequently moved offshore for assessment.Tehran touts map of targetsEgyptian authorities and multiple maritime sources confirmed that Iranian state television had identified Damietta as a possible target for "retaliation against Ukrainian interests" two days earlier, following a Ukrainian strike on an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea over the weekend.The map shown on state-run TV described Damietta as "a gateway for gas exports to Europe." Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Tuesday that Iran "does not seek escalation" but was demanding "compensation" from Kyiv.Energy analytics firm Kpler said the attack disrupted operations at the terminal and forced both vessels to move offshore.Former head of the Damietta Port Authority, Major General Ayman Salah, said that the regasification process occurs at very high pressure and that any leak could cause a fire.The incident comes as the region enters one of its most volatile periods since the war began.On Wednesday, the IRGC launched ballistic missiles at US forces in Jordan, the US and Saudi Arabia struck Iran-linked militia sites across Iraq, and Yemen's Houthi group declared a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia, raising fears of the widest simultaneous regional escalation since the war began on 28 February.Egypt has so far been spared from attacks during the US-Iran war, maintaining relations with both Washington and Tehran.Egypt's Suez Canal, through which roughly 12% of global trade normally passes, has already seen a dramatic drop in traffic since the war began.It is now further imperilled by the reported plans by Yemen's Houthi group to impose a toll on passing cargo ships and threats of strikes on noncompliant vessels, which could severely reduce the traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb strait in the Red Sea.Egypt had previously been an LNG exporter — Damietta hosted one of the Arabic-speaking world's first LNG export terminals — but declining domestic gas production turned the country into a net importer.

http://www.euronews.com/2026/07/30/china.text: China has lodged an official complaint after New Zealand's foreign minister Winston Peters told a Chinese-born MP to "go back to your own country" during a heated parliamentary exchange in Wellington.Peters, the leader of the NZ First party, made the remarks on Wednesday after Green Party MP Lawrence Xu-Nan asked him, "Are you vaccinated?" during a debate over New Zealand's response to the Covid-19 pandemic.Xu-Nan was born in Tianjin, China, but grew up in New Zealand.Peters responded that the lawmaker had "come here five minutes ago" before telling him: "Go back to your own country.""This is called a democracy, unlike what you're used to. Go back to where you've come from, you loudmouth," Peters added.Speaking to the 1News channel on Thursday, Xu-nan said: "It's a little bit unbelievable to have a Minister for Foreign Affairs, I guess, scapegoating the migrant communities as a distraction to shift the blame away from all of the harm that this government is doing."China lodges complaintThe remarks prompted a rare intervention from China's ambassador to New Zealand, Wang Xiaolong, who wrote on X that he normally avoided commenting on domestic politics but that "sometimes, a statement says more about the person that makes it than anything or anybody else".The Chinese embassy in Wellington said on Thursday it had lodged a complaint with New Zealand's foreign ministry over what it described as "negative China-related remarks made by a certain politician".Peters has refused to back down, arguing his comments were a defence of democratic freedoms."We live in a democracy that includes free speech and rights," he wrote on X, adding that he would "not resile from that point".New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, whose National Party governs in coalition with NZ First, condemned Peters' remarks as "inappropriate attention-seeking".NZ First politicians have faced criticism over similar remarks before. Last year, Peters' deputy Shane Jones shouted "send the Mexicans home" at MP Francisco Hernandez, who was born in the Philippines.Mexico's ambassador, Alfredo Pérez Bravo, subsequently issued an official diplomatic communication to New Zealand's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, opting to raise the issue through diplomatic channels rather than publicly.Peters later withdrew his support for Jones' remarks, acknowledging that "in the heat of the moment" they "may have been expressed differently."

http://www.euronews.com/2026/07/30/frenc.text: Didier Gaspard Owen Maximilien, 19, was handed a SG$600 (€406) fine after admitting to posting to social media a video of himself putting a straw he had licked back into the dispenser of an orange juice vending machine.Maximilien, who is studying in Singapore, posted a video of himself executing the prank on Instagram with the caption "city is not safe".The clip went viral on Instagram shortly after the incident on March 12, triggering a backlash that led to his arrest in Singapore, which is known for its strict enforcement of public order and hygiene rules.Handing down the sentence, Judge Kelly Ho said given Maximilien's "age and nature of the offence", alternatives such as probation or a community-based sentence would not be imposed.Prosecutors agreed to the defence's proposal for a fine, saying the offence was at the "lower end" of its seriousness and while hygiene was compromised, no member of the public used the straw, so there "was no evidence of harm".They added that Maximilien "pleaded guilty at the earliest possible opportunity."In Singapore, public nuisance offenders face up to SG$2000 (€1353) fine and three months in jail."He is fully sorry for having caused all this trouble," Maximilien's defence counsel Kalidass Murugaiyan told the judge.iJooz vending machines are a common sight in shopping districts, selling freshly-squeezed orange juice for SG$2 (€1.35) a cup. The company said it replaced all 500 straws in the machine dispenser after the teenager's prank.Singapore is known for its no-nonsense approach to public stunts.Last year it deported an Australian man at the end of a nine-day jail term for rushing film star Ariana Grande during the Asian premiere of "Wicked: For Good".

https://newsroompanama.com/2026/07/18/fo.text: New York state regulators fined Swedish bank Swedbank $50 million for intentionally withholding critical information tied to the 2016 Panama Papers scandal. The New York State Department of Financial Services (DFS) found that the bank deliberately obscured its ties to high-risk offshore entities and excluded its Baltic subsidiaries from official inquiries in 2016 and 2018 to avoid exposing cross-border money laundering risks. Swedbank Fined $50 Million by New York Authorities Over Panama Papers Revelations Swedbank has agreed to pay a $50 million fine to New York’s state financial regulator to settle a money laundering case tied to the Panama Papers. The Swedish group reached the settlement with the New York State Department of Financial Services (DFS), which first launched the investigation in 2019. The probe was into the bank’s anti-money laundering and counterterrorism financing controls, and its disclosures to regulators between 2007 and 2019, according to a statement by Swedbank. The DFS had accused Swedbank of withholding information and misleading investigators during the probe into its ties with the Panamanian law firm, Mossack Fonseca. The Panama Papers, a 2016 cross-border journalistic expose led by ICIJ and Suddeutsche Zeitung, was based on a huge trove of leaked Mossack Fonseca documents. Among those documents was proof that customers of Swedbank’s Estonia subsidiary used Mossack Fonseca as a registered agent. Three years later, journalists from ICIJ’s Swedish partner SVT revealed that Swedbank may have withheld information from U.S. authorities over suspicious financial transactions, contrary to what the bank had claimed. Following the 2016 publication of the Panama Papers, DFS made two information requests to Swedbank asking about its relationship with Mossack Fonseca, related banks, institutions and individuals, the recent statement said. Authorities found that the bank failed to report on such relationships, failed to acknowledge the existence of European regulatory inquiries and withheld information relating to its subsidiaries in Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia. “Critically, the leak shed light on the failure of global financial institutions to follow legal requirements designed to ensure that their customers are not engaged in or facilitating fraud, money laundering, or other criminal acts,” the consent order reads. https://hungarytoday.hu/the-democratic-r.text: “The Democratic Rule of Law has Ceased to Exist” as President Signs Constitutional Amendment Tamás Sulyok signed the 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law, automatically ending his own term as President of the Republic tomorrow. With the amendment’s removal of almost all other checks and balances, Hungary will effectively cease to be a democracy. In addition to the removal of the President of the Republic and the President of the Constitutional Court, a term limit for members of parliament will take effect, barring most of the opposition in parliament from running in the 2030 parliamentary elections. In the video published on his social media platform, President Tamás Sulyok said that the Hungarian people are a wonderful people, a strong and great nation of Europe who have already endured numerous hardships, but in every struggle, have been able to rely on solid pillars. One such solid pillar stems from the development of Hungarian law, which rests on a thousand-year-old foundation. The rule of law means, above all, respect for the law—that is, the supremacy of the law over arbitrariness, and the supremacy of legal norms over individual decisions by public authorities—said the outgoing president. He stated that if the politicization of power circumvents the limits of the law, it will have unforeseeable consequences for our country.” In his view, this is a serious case in a constitutional sense and an unprecedented one in the 36 years of Hungarian democracy since the transition to democracy. Sulyok noted that the Hungarian National Assembly had voted to adopt the 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law. This amendment terminates the term of office of the incumbent President of the Republic with a single sentence. This sentence joins the ranks of those forced Gordian knots that will remain for posterity as grave and shameful historical examples of the abuse of political power,” he stated. Sulyok expressed the view that the primary responsibility of state institutions and the chief representatives of state power is mutual respect and the cooperation based on it. That is why he did not resign from the office of head of state. In his view, this means, above all, respect for human dignity in interpersonal relationships, and, in relations between institutions, respect for each other’s constitutional roles and powers. Only in this way can every state body fulfill its own constitutional role and mission. These principles also form the foundation of a civilized system of government based on the rule of law, in keeping with European culture. He believes that it is contrary to these principles for public authorities to seek to achieve their goals through threats, the exertion of pressure, and the circumvention of constitutional rules. “In response to messages demanding my resignation and threatening my removal, the protection of the constitutional order and the authority of the office of the head of state left me with only one course of action: to remain in office,” he stated. The 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law marked a breaking point in Hungarian constitutional democracy. By removing public officials—an act that openly violates the rule of law and the independence of institutions—and by imposing unprecedented restrictions on the right to vote, it sets a negative precedent that inflicts a deep wound on the constitutional values of democracy, the separation of powers, and the rule of law —emphasized Sulyok. He stated that the rule of law is fundamental to him, and that as president, he has always carried out his duties within the framework of the Fundamental Law and with full respect for it. As he noted, the foremost evidence of this is that the new ruling party has consistently viewed amending the Fundamental Law as the only way to remove him from office. Sulyok stated that we have reached a crossroads regarding a matter of national importance that transcends personal or political interests. In such a case, the president has two options: to fulfill his constitutional duty by signing the bill, or to refuse to sign it—which, however, would constitute a violation of the law. He announced that, under the current Fundamental Law, there is no constitutional remedy available against this amendment—which violates constitutional principles but was adopted by the National Assembly, as the body empowered to amend the Constitution, through a lawful procedure. “The sole responsibility for this decision lies with those who have the power to amend the Constitution.” Photo: Facebook Péter Magyar “I am fulfilling my obligation enshrined in the Fundamental Law after thoroughly weighing my legal options and my conscience. My signature is the final seal of my obligations as President of the Republic and of my complete and unconditional respect for the office of the President of the Republic under all circumstances. It is a sign that I have upheld Hungary’s Fundamental Law throughout and have not violated it,” he stated. He went on to add that it is also enduring proof that the fundamental values of a free society—the rule of law, democracy, and the principle of the separation of powers—have been trampled upon for the sake of power. The sole responsibility for this decision lies with those who have the power to amend the Constitution.” The democratic rule of law that emerged from the legacy of 1956 at the time of the regime change has thus ceased to exist —declared Sulyok. He went on to say that the legitimacy of the president of the Republic, which had remained unchanged since the transition to democracy, has also ceased to exist. Hungary’s next head of state will, in fact, replace a president who was removed through a process that violated constitutional values. He emphasized that the office of the president of the Republic will become subservient to the executive branch and politics; its role under public law will fade, and its fundamental function will cease to exist. Furthermore, it will no longer serve as any kind of check or balance. Those who stand firm in their faith and in the truth do not resort to violence, do not revile others, and do not humiliate others in their dignity. I believe that remaining human and humane, true to ourselves and to the truth, despite all attacks and under all circumstances, is the only path worth choosing. Let us cherish all that unites us; let us love Hungary—said the outgoing president in closing. Former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán reacted to the news with a post saying: Today, the last barrier has fallen. Tyranny is no longer a threat, but a reality. If this could be done to the President of the Republic, then tomorrow no one will be safe. May God protect Hungary!” The prime minister signaled stricter conflict-of-interest rules. http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27919.text: Big News Network.com 2nd LD Writethru: Hungarian president signs constitutional amendment ending own mandate BUDAPEST, July 18 (Xinhua) -- Hungarian President Tamas Sulyok on Saturday signed the country's 17th constitutional amendment, triggering the end of his mandate as head of state. Once the law is published in the official gazette, the termination of his mandate will take effect the following day. In a video statement, Sulyok said he had signed the amendment because he had "no constitutional means of acting against this amendment, which violates constitutional principles but was adopted by the National Assembly (parliament) ... through a lawful procedure." Prime Minister Peter Magyar welcomed the signing, saying it had "removed the last obstacle to implementing our joint decisions." He said he would consult parliamentary parties on a successor, adding that "the moral basis of the nomination can only come from the trust of society." Sulyok was elected by Hungary's then Fidesz-majority parliament in 2024 for a five-year term, with his mandate originally due to expire in March 2029. However, Magyar has repeatedly called on Sulyok to resign, accusing him of serving the interests of the previous Fidesz government. The constitutional amendment ending Sulyok's mandate was adopted by parliament earlier this week after Magyar's ruling party secured the two-thirds majority needed to amend the constitution. Under the constitution, parliament must elect a new president by secret ballot within 30 days. Any Hungarian citizen aged 35 or older is eligible for the office if nominated by at least one-fifth of lawmakers, or 40 members of parliament. Until a new president takes office, presidential duties will be exercised by Speaker of Parliament Agnes Forsthoffer. The new head of state will assume office on the eighth day after the election result is officially announced. Magyar has said he wants to nominate a candidate capable of representing the unity of the nation and winning support from opposition lawmakers, although he has not yet named a candidate. He has also said the latest constitutional amendment is intended as a temporary arrangement and that Hungary will eventually introduce direct presidential elections under a new constitution to be approved by referendum. 2nd LD Writethru: Hungarian president signs constitutional amendment ending own mandate 2nd LD Writethru: Hungarian president signs constitutional amendment ending own mandate Xinhua 19th July 2026, 04:15 GMT+11 BUDAPEST, July 18 (Xinhua) -- Hungarian President Tamas Sulyok on Saturday signed the country's 17th constitutional amendment, triggering the end of his mandate as head of state. Prime Minister Peter Magyar welcomed the signing, saying it had "removed the last obstacle to implementing our joint decisions." He said he would consult parliamentary parties on a successor, adding that "the moral basis of the nomination can only come from the trust of society." Sulyok was elected by Hungary's then Fidesz-majority parliament in 2024 for a five-year term, with his mandate originally due to expire in March 2029. However, Magyar has repeatedly called on Sulyok to resign, accusing him of serving the interests of the previous Fidesz government. The constitutional amendment ending Sulyok's mandate was adopted by parliament earlier this week after Magyar's ruling party secured the two-thirds majority needed to amend the constitution. Under the constitution, parliament must elect a new president by secret ballot within 30 days. Any Hungarian citizen aged 35 or older is eligible for the office if nominated by at least one-fifth of lawmakers, or 40 members of parliament. Until a new president takes office, presidential duties will be exercised by Speaker of Parliament Agnes Forsthoffer. The new head of state will assume office on the eighth day after the election result is officially announced. Magyar has said he wants to nominate a candidate capable of representing the unity of the nation and winning support from opposition lawmakers, although he has not yet named a candidate. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cpd7.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Sulyok said he had no constitutional recourse to challenge the amendment By Nick Thorpe ,Â Reporting from Hungary Â and Â Henry Moore Published 18 July 2026 Hungarian President TamÃ¡s Sulyok has agreed to step down, signing an amendment to the country's constitution which will end his presidency at midnight on Sunday. Prime Minister PÃ©ter Magyar's Tisza party had steamrolled the law change through parliament to oust Sulyok - widely seen as a loyalist of former prime minister Viktor OrbÃ¡n who lost power in April after 16 years. Sulyok had five days to sign the amendment or risk a protracted constitutional crisis and impeachment proceedings. He confirmed he would agree to the law change as the deadline passed on Saturday evening, but in a statement accused Magyar's government of violating the rule of law. He said the amendment marked a "breaking point in Hungarian constitutional democracy" and said the "core values of a free society... have been trampled underfoot for the sake of political power". It marks the latest and most dramatic move by the Tisza government, which saw Sulyok as a puppet of the former government and had pushed for his resignation. It has swept through major constitutional changes since winning a landslide victory in April. The 17th amendment, passed with an overwhelming majority on Monday , ends the president's term citing "serious loss of confidence" in him. It also removes the head of the Constitutional Court and forbids MPs who have served three terms from standing again - which applies to more than half the current deputies from OrbÃ¡n's Fidesz party. OrbÃ¡n had described the amendment as an act of tyranny and called for protests. Since the April election, Fidesz has been in free fall, reeling from the shock defeat. OrbÃ¡n himself has hardly been seen in public, and refused to take his seat in parliament. Image source, EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, Since his party swept to power in April, PÃ©ter Magyar (left) has repeatedly called on Sulyok (right) to resign In office from 2010 until 2026, Fidesz reshaped the Hungarian state to its own will, and filled supposedly independent state positions with party loyalists using its own two-thirds majority. The 141 Tisza deputies in parliament gave a standing ovation as the results of the vote passing the amendment were announced on Monday. After the vote, AndrÃ¡s Baka, former head of Hungary's Supreme Court, told the BBC: "I quite agree with the removal of the president." Hungary was governed by the rule of law from 1989 to 2010, he argued, after which Fidesz captured state institutions and created an authoritarian state. "And it is now very difficult to break up a sophisticated authoritarian regime... which was designed to survive even after electoral defeat," Baka said. http://www.jpost.com/history/article-902.text: In the spring of 1944, during the dark days of the Holocaust, 37 young men and women who had escaped the conflagration in Europe and come to Mandatory Palestine embarked on a series of dangerous missions, parachuting into Nazi-occupied Europe. Twelve were captured by the enemy. Five of the 12 returned from captivity, three were executed, and four were sent to concentration camps, never to return. The best-known of the group was Hannah Szenes, who was murdered by a pro-Nazi Hungarian firing squad in November 1944.What was the purpose of their missions, what did they accomplish, and why are they considered among the great heroes of the State of Israel? In this captivating work, Matti Friedman documents the efforts of four of the parachutists – Szenes, Enzo Sereni, Haim Hermesh, and Haviva Reick – from the spring of 1944 until the operation's dramatic conclusion that winter.In the introduction, Friedman writes, “Their actions changed nothing and yet somehow touched the fate of millions, including me. The strange gap between the mythic stature of the heroes and their scant accomplishments – this is the mystery that drew me to their story and kept me submerged in their world for years. “Understanding this country – an effort that has preoccupied me since I came here, like most of the parachutists themselves, as a teenager – requires figuring out who these people were and why they mattered so much.”To solve the mystery, Friedman tracked down yellowing documents in a Tel Aviv archive and traveled to the countries where the parachutists had journeyed – Italy, Hungary, Austria, Germany, and Slovakia – to piece together the story behind the mission.From Cairo to Tel AvivFriedman explains that the operation had two parallel command structures – the British officers of MI9 in Cairo and the Zionist leaders in Tel Aviv – who had recruited the volunteers from young escapees from Europe. Each, he writes, had their own motives in planning the missions.“The British,” writes Friedman, “think they're using Jewish parachutists, natives of occupied countries, for their war aims; the parachutists believe it's they who are using the British, and they sometimes refer to the entire MI9 operation as nothing more than a 'plane ticket.' The real mission is to save Jews.”Even among the Zionist leaders, he writes, there was no unanimity on the goals. At one meeting, militia commander Eliyahu Golomb told the recruits that their job was to reach surviving Jews and train them for combat. Another official said that their goal was to find Jewish refugees and help them stay alive until the end of the war. David Ben-Gurion presented his own version. The parachutists were to prepare survivors for mass immigration after the war, he declared.One of the recruits remembered leaving the meeting confused about the mission's objectives, but neither he nor anyone else dropped out of the program despite the lack of clarity.The volunteers underwent training in parachute jumping, and in early 1944, British army trucks took them from Tel Aviv to Cairo, where MI9 instructors taught them intelligence-gathering techniques and Morse code before they were flown to a liberated airfield in Italy, and then dropped into occupied Europe. Friedman is a skilled writer and tracks the missions of the four parachutists, their backgrounds, what motivated them, what they experienced when they landed in Europe, and ultimately what occurred. A significant portion of the book is devoted to Szenes's mission to reach her home city of Budapest.Of the four parachutists on whom he focuses, three were killed, and only Haim Hermesh returned. Friedman recounts the tragic fates of Szenes, Sereni, and Reick poignantly but with admirable restraint, which makes his retelling all the more meaningful.Ultimately, Friedman suggests, the true purpose of the parachutists' mission can be found in the words of the famous poem “Blessed is the Match” (Hebrew: “Ashrei hagafrur”) written by Szenes, which she handed to a fellow parachutist on a scrap of paper when they parted ways in a forest in Yugoslavia. The symbolism of lighting a flameLighting a flame, Friedman explains, symbolizes action.“What separates the Diaspora from the Land of Israel,” explains Friedman, “is action. The parachutists aren't commandos. They're storytellers. They've been sent to write, with their lives, a Zionist story about the war – a story that will lead others not to despair but to action. In this story, Jews will not be victims but heroes. This won't change the war, but it will change how people remember the war, and therefore change the future. When faced with tragedy, those who know the parachutists' story won't pull the covers over their heads, or bemoan the cruelty of fate, or wait for someone else to do something. They will look out into the night, grip the sides of the door, and jump.”Although Szenes and the others did not fully succeed in the mission as outlined by their British and Zionist superiors, they did succeed in this purpose – telling the Zionist story of the war and influencing people to take action. Today, no less than 32 streets in Israel are named after Hannah Szenes, and three kibbutzim – Yad Hanna, Lahavot Haviva, and Netzer Sereni – are named after the three heroes who were executed. Out of the Sky: Heroism and Rebirth in Nazi Europe is a compelling book that fills important gaps in the story of the parachutists and their impossible mission, while offering a deeper appreciation of true heroism.Out of the Sky: Heroism and Rebirth in Nazi EuropeBy Matti FriedmanSpiegel and Grau256 pages; $23

Those places were under the same afternoon alert while a flash flood warning for Rochester and several other places was set to last until 7 p.m. By 3 p.m., over 400 RG&E homes in Monroe County were without power. Earlier that day, the largest outage areas at 12:45 p.m. were East Rochester, Pittsford, Perinton and Penfield. Town of Byron storm The National Weather Service said the severe thunderstorm capable of producing a tornado was in the Town of Byron, about seven miles northeast of Batavia, and was moving east at about 35 mph. That placed the warning area beside the storm's path, not just in its center. The Rochester Pride Festival was canceled because of the storms. The Hilton Kiddie Parade was canceled and the Hilton carnival was postponed. - Advertisement - Saturday warning timeline There had also been a tornado warning in the Canandaigua area earlier on Saturday afternoon, and it ended at 1:45 p.m. That warning included Geneva, Canandaigua, Clifton Springs, Phelps, Bloomfield, Farmington, Gorham, East Bloomfield, Manchester and Shortsville. For residents in Rochester and the listed Monroe County communities, the immediate question was whether the warning would end on schedule at 3:15 p.m. or be extended as storms continued to move east.
