President Droupadi Murmu on Sunday embarked on a landmark three‑nation European tour covering Moldova, North Macedonia, and Romania, aimed at strengthening India’s bilateral cooperation in commerce, technology, agriculture, healthcare, and cultural exchanges.
The visit begins in Moldova on Monday, marking the first‑ever trip by an Indian Head of State to the Eastern European nation. President Murmu will hold talks with President Maia Sandu, Parliament Speaker Igor Grosu, and address a Business Forum, alongside interactions with the Indian diaspora. She will then travel to North Macedonia (July 21–22) for bilateral discussions with President Gordana Siljanovska‑Davkova, Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski, and the Assembly President. Her itinerary includes an address to the national parliament and participation in the India‑North Macedonia Business Forum. The final leg of the tour takes her to Romania (July 23–25), the first visit by an Indian President in over three decades. She will meet President Nicusor Dan, interim Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan, and parliamentary leaders, while also addressing the India‑Romania Business Forum and engaging with the local Indian community. MEA officials said the mission reflects India’s growing engagement with Central and Eastern Europe and complements its broader strategic partnership with the European Union. Significantly, Moldova, North Macedonia, and Romania had earlier denounced the Pahalgam terror attack, reaffirming solidarity with India against global terrorism.

http://www.jpost.com/jerusalem-report/ar.text: Sometimes you uncover a gem in the most surprising of places.I didn’t know what to expect in taking a bus to Tiberias for a one-night stay at the Dona Gracia Hotel and Museum. I hadn’t heard much about the influential Jewish woman before, and I was excited to learn more.Stepping into the hotel itself was like stepping through a time machine.The first floor looked like it belonged in a different century, with wooden furniture, a grand piano in the lobby, and heavy curtains concealing rooms at the back. The atmosphere felt intentionally curated, blending hospitality with storytelling. It set the tone for an experience that felt both historical and personal. Pleasant staff showed us to our room, and then we went out to explore for dinner.We ate at a local steakhouse called El Rancho and enjoyed a delicious meal. Afterwards, we walked along the beachfront, which was surprisingly empty. A light show began in the water with fountains forming shapes and colors. We watched it alone, wondering where the people were and what else the city had to offer.Back at the hotel, we discovered a small issue with our room. The staff were professional and resolved it within minutes, and we got a good night’s sleep.In the morning, the hotel gave us a coupon for a nearby cafe called CookieLiz. Breakfast felt generous, with spreads, eggs, drinks, and fresh bread. It was great to experience a local kosher place.Back at the hotel, we met the museum curator, Irit Ahdoot. She is dedicated to telling the story of Dona Gracia, whom she described as a female version of Theodor Herzl in the 16th century. I was surprised I had never learned about her before. Ahdoot’s storytelling was captivating and immersive. Dona Gracia rose to power in difficult circumstances and became one of the most influential figures of her time. In the 1500s, this was extraordinary. She recognized the danger facing European Jews and worked to create safety and opportunity long before modern movements. After becoming widowed, she took on full responsibility for her affairs. The story had a thrilling chapter in which she escaped pressure under Queen Mary of Hungary. Eventually, her efforts supported the establishment of Jewish life in Tiberias.The museum takes you back in time, with an Ottoman game table and a recreation of a hidden synagogue. It strongly conveys life during that period. It is a carefully designed space that blends historical artifacts with interactive storytelling. One highlight was dressing in 16th-century clothing and taking photos, which made the experience much more immersive.Ahdoot’s passion for the topic made the experience truly captivating. This getaway did not require a flight. If you want something unique by the waterfront, Tiberias is worth visiting. Overall, it left a lasting impression that stays with you long after you leave.■

https://www.kccu.org/u-s/2026-07-18/andr.text: On Air Now Playing KCCU U.S. Andrew and Tristan Tate arrested in Florida on charges of rape and sex trafficking NPR | By Robbie Griffiths Published July 18, 2026 at 7:57 PM CDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Listen • 2:19 Julia Demaree Nikhinson / AP Andrew Tate, right, and his brother Tristan arrive at an event on April 11 in Miami. Updated July 21, 2026 at 11:56 PM CDT LONDON – Influencer Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan have been arrested in Miami after British authorities issued 38 new charges against them, including allegations of rape and sex trafficking. The United Kingdom's Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) released a statement saying that the two men had been arrested by the U.S. Marshals Service on Saturday. The CPS said it was "seeking extradition" for the two brothers, aiming to bring them to Britain to face a total of 59 charges. The CPS said Andrew, 39, was being charged with seven further counts of rape and three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, as well as charges including indecent images of a child. The charges against Tristan, 38, include two counts of rape and three counts of sex trafficking. The CPS said the new charges bring the total number of alleged victims in the case to seven. Both Tate brothers are dual British-U.S. citizens. They were born in America, but spent much of their childhood and young adult life in the English town of Luton, Bedfordshire. The charges against them were largely collected by Bedfordshire Police, which previously put forward a file of evidence to the CPS. The new allegations are claimed to have taken place between July 2010 and August 2017. In a statement on Saturday, Assistant Chief Constable Karena Thomas from Bedfordshire Police said that the "complex investigation" had involved "national and international law enforcement". She went on: "We understand the interest that this case will generate, but we would urge the public not to speculate and to allow the legal process to be carried out correctly. "There is no place for male violence against women and girls, and we will continue to work tirelessly to support victims and investigate all reports made to us." On Sunday, Emily Williams, Deputy Chief of Public Affairs for the U.S. Marshals Service, told NPR in an email: "Yesterday, U.S. Marshals in the Southern District of Florida arrested Andrew and Tristan Tate pursuant to extradition proceedings. These arrests were made in accordance with the treaties and law enforcement agreements governing Justice Department extraditions." Andrew Tate was previously a champion kickboxer and reality television star, before becoming an influencer in the "manosphere", going into business with his brother Tristan. Andrew and Tristan moved to Romania, and in 2023, Romanian prosecutors filed a criminal indictment against them, accusing the brothers of crimes including violence, rape, and human-trafficking, as well as forcing women to take part in pornography. The two men spent several months under house arrest near Bucharest, in a case which Romanian prosecutors are still investigating. However, last year, the Tate brothers were allowed to leave Romania and travel to the United States. That was despite efforts by British authorities to have the two men extradited to the UK over earlier charges. Malcolm McHaffie, Head of the Special Crime Division at the CPS, said in a written statement: "We have decided to prosecute Andrew and Tristan Tate for further offences including rape, arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation and offences relating to indecent images of a child. McHaffie added that the Tate brothers have the right to a fair trial, and urged care from reporters and commentators not to share material that could "prejudice these proceedings". In a statement released on social media after their arrest, Joseph McBride, a lawyer who represents the Tate brothers, claimed that they were innocent, describing the arrests as a "political hit". "We are confident that once a competent judge sees the facts, and once the Department of Justice confronts this egregious abuse of its own authority, Andrew and Tristan Tate will walk free," McBride said. "America does not do Britain's political dirty work." (Photo: AFP) International News , Latest News July 19, 2026 Influencer Andrew Tate and brother arrested in Miami WASHINGTON, United States (AFP) — Radical social media influencer Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan were in custody in the US on Sunday, officials said, as Britain seeks their extradition to face new charges of rape, sex trafficking and assault. Karena Thomas, assistant chief constable of the United Kingdom’s (UK) Bedfordshire Police, said the pair had been detained “pending ongoing legal proceedings”. The US Marshals Service confirmed the arrests. US news outlet TMZ posted video of law enforcement officers placing the self-professed misogynist and his younger sibling in handcuffs and escorting them into waiting vehicles in Miami on Saturday. Asked by an onlooker if he had something to say, Tristan Tate did not respond, the footage posted on X showed. UK prosecutors, who are now due to seek the brothers’ extradition, said the arrests came after they brought forward 38 further charges against the pair. The Tate brothers now face 59 charges in total — 42 against Andrew and 17 against Tristan, British authorities said on Sunday. “We have decided to prosecute Andrew and Tristan Tate for further offences including rape, arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation and offences relating to indecent images of a child,” Malcolm McHaffie, head of UK’s Crown Prosecution Service’s (CPS) Special Crime Division, said in a statement. “The CPS has requested the extradition of the Tates from the US,” he said, adding that the latest charges stem from receipt of new evidence from Bedfordshire Police that bring the total number of alleged victims in the Tates case to seven. Earlier this year, police in Hertfordshire, north of London, said they were reopening a probe into rape and sexual assault allegations made by women against Andrew Tate between 2014 and 2015. They also face separate rape and human trafficking allegations brought by different women and investigated by Bedfordshire Police, which covers their hometown of Luton, also north of London. The Tate brothers are also accused of tax evasion and money laundering in the UK. Their attorney, Joseph McBride, said in a press release that the brothers “are innocent”. “We are confident that once a competent judge sees the facts, and once the Department of Justice confronts this egregious abuse of its own authority, Andrew and Tristan Tate will walk free,” McBride said. The Tates are dual British-US citizens who have been avid supporters of US President Donald Trump. Lawyer Matt Jury, of McCue Jury & Partners who represent four alleged British victims of Andrew Tate, said Tate was “now facing the real prospect of extradition to the UK after years of public campaigning by the four British women I represent”. “They have spent years fighting for action to be taken, and I now urge the authorities to ensure this case proceeds as quickly as possible. “Andrew and Tristan Tate are accused of some of the most serious offences, including multiple counts of rape and human trafficking. It is time they face justice,” he was quoted by the PA news agency as saying. In March 2025, the US state of Florida launched a criminal investigation against them. The status of that investigation is unclear. Andrew Tate is one of the most prominent proponents of the so-called “manosphere” network of communities, many of them online, that focus on traditional masculinity, anti-feminism and self-improvement. He promotes his divisive views, often incorporating alpha-male and aggressively misogynistic themes, to millions on social media including 10.8 million followers on X. In Romania, where they have been based in recent years, the Tates face allegations of trafficking minors, sexual intercourse with a minor and money laundering. https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/absolutel.text: Nadia Khomami Arts and culture correspondent Updated Fri, 24 July 2026 at 3:39 pm UTC 1 John Hajdu outside the Imperial War Museum in London. John is loaning his beloved teddy for the Childhood in War exhibition, which opens on 31 July.Photograph: Richard Ash/© IWM When John Hajdu was three, his parents gave him a teddy bear small enough to fit into his hands: 86 years later, it is the only surviving object from his childhood. The bear, which the 89-year-old simply calls “teddy”, stayed with him as his father was taken to a labour camp, his mother sent to a concentration camp, and he hid in a non-Jewish neighbour’s cupboard before being forced into the Budapest ghetto. From 31 July, teddy will go on public display for the first time as part of Childhood in War , a new exhibition at the Imperial War Museum, London, examining how conflict shapes children’s lives. Displayed in a recreated second world war bedroom, the bear sits among toys, books and personal possessions that ask visitors to consider what childhood looks like when play, education and family life are disrupted by war. The exhibition combines hundreds of objects with immersive environments, including a full-size railway carriage, a wartime classroom and a cold war living room and kitchen, alongside testimonies from children living through conflicts in places including Ukraine, Sudan and Afghanistan. For Hajdu, teddy represents a childhood interrupted. Before the war, his life was typical of a well-to-do, middle-class Jewish family. By 1944, after years of antisemitic persecution in Hungary, his father had been sent to a labour camp and Hajdu and his mother had been forced into a designated yellow-star house. Teddy did, and still does, mean so much to me. It was my only connection to a family life I barely remembered John Hajdu “We could only take with us what we could carry, and that meant just a few pieces of clothing and teddy,” he says. “There was absolutely no chance of being a kid. I had no other toys or books. We were only allowed out in the afternoon wearing the yellow star. I couldn’t meet other children. We weren’t allowed in parks, cinemas or swimming pools or cafes. I was completely isolated.” The exhibition explores exactly those everyday losses. A reconstructed classroom shows how war disrupts children’s education through objects from conflicts including the second world war, Northern Ireland, Afghanistan and the former Yugoslavia. There are comics warning children about landmines and unexploded ordnance. Visitors can also climb into an evacuee train carriage containing letters sent home and Kindertransport objects, including a red knitted jumper given to Jochewet Heidenstein by her parents before she and her sisters fled Berlin for Britain. In October 1944, Hajdu’s mother was arrested and taken to Mauthausen concentration camp in Austria. Believing she would never return, Hajdu’s aunt rushed him into the cupboard of a non-Jewish neighbour. Related: Children are the longest-lasting casualties of war “I had teddy in my pocket,” he says. “I was in complete darkness and had to keep completely quiet. It seemed like a very long time, which was an incredibly frightening experience for a seven-year-old … By that time I was able to comprehend what happened without fully understanding the enormity of the situation.” He later moved with his aunt into the Budapest ghetto, sharing a flat with more than 20 strangers. “There were no children. We survived on horse meat and bread. Dead bodies lay piled up on the streets, having died of cold, starvation or disease. I was always hungry. Again, I had teddy in my pocket.” The ghetto was liberated by Soviet troops in January 1945, just before retreating German forces planned to destroy it. Miraculously, Hajdu was reunited with both his parents. His mother survived Mauthausen after US troops liberated the camp, but returned with broken ribs, smashed teeth and lasting psychological scars. “I was convinced I’d never see my parents again,” he says. A decade later, after the Soviet suppression of the Hungarian uprising, Hajdu and his mother walked 40km (25 miles) and crossed an icy river under cover of darkness to reach Austria. They arrived in Britain in 1957 on a Red Cross train, with teddy travelling with them. Throughout the exhibition, stories such as Hajdu’s sit alongside contemporary accounts from children living through war today. Visitors can explore a 360-degree virtual tour of an underground school in Ukraine created by one of its pupils, read poems written by Ukrainian children for Unicef’s Poems for Peace project , and see drawings by children in Sudan that were later submitted as evidence of alleged war crimes to the international criminal court. A poem by a 15-year-old Afghan girl describes the moment the Taliban returned to power in Kabul in August 2021: “I witnessed how that day darkened not only Kabul’s sky, but also the dreams and hopes of so many.” The exhibition also examines how childhood can become politicised, with material from the Hitler Youth and Soviet Komsomol movements. “We wanted to talk about the impact of war on children’s lives,” says curator Fran Singleton. “With more conflicts in the news at the moment, it felt like the right time to create an exhibition that offers families a space to come together and discuss these important topics.” Related: ‘Into the arms of strangers’: child refugees of Nazi Germany remember For Hajdu, allowing teddy to leave his home for the first time has been surprisingly difficult. “Teddy did, and still does, mean so much to me. It was my only connection to a family life I barely remembered when I was three,” he says. “I find it difficult to look at the desk where he normally sits.” Now a grandfather of four, Hajdu spends much of his time speaking in schools about surviving the Holocaust. As the number of survivors dwindles, he hopes younger generations will continue telling these stories. “I tell them, ‘When you go home, talk to your grandparents and parents. Find out whether they’ve gone through traumas, whether it’s in Asia or Africa.’ “My small story is an example that you can survive. Unfortunately, people are suffering all over the world. We are getting older, and fewer and fewer Holocaust survivors are here to tell these stories. It’s absolutely vital that the younger generation takes on what we’re doing.” Show comments 1 Advertisement From Our Partners Advertisement Advertisement Express UK DWP confirms £0 BBC TV licence bill for state pensioners over 75 Express UK State pensioners over 65 handed £1,000 boost in July under Andy Burnham Mirror UK Five dead and dozens missing after horror inferno on ferry carrying 285 people The Guardian Kremlin connections: the Russia links to a £600m UK theme park Express UK Met Office names 32 areas facing heavy rain on Tuesday - full list Express UK Met Office issues ‘showers and thunderstorms' update for next week Advertisement Contact Feedback Help Cookie Policy EU Digital Services Act Terms and Privacy Policy Privacy Dashboard About Our Ads About Us Sitemap

https://www.express.co.uk/news/world/223.text: Home News World Brits are being urged to stop ignoring the risks and update old technology as soon as possible (Image: Getty) A chilling cybersecurity warning has been issued as experts reveal we are already locked in the middle of a silent, invisible global war - and everyday citizens are on the front line. The Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) has sounded the alarm, warning that Russian hackers are actively targeting critical industries and infrastructure, including communications networks, energy suppliers, financial services and the defence industry. Security officials have warned that it is no longer a question of whether a catastrophic breach will occur, but rather of when. Cyber criminals don't care about borders - they are going straight after the places that hurt us most, including local town halls, hospitals and the supermarkets we rely on. "It’s not about fearmongering. It’s about readiness," Lincoln Goldsmith, director of digital security firm Semperis , warned. "It’s not a case of if. It’s a case of when. You almost have to assume your security has already been breached ." Read our Privacy Policy Horror as mother, 22, charged with murder of toddler bound and left to suffocate Woman, 36, gang raped after being ‘kidnapped by taxi driver’ - one man arrested Russia is deliberately targeting nations that oppose its geopolitical actions, including members of the Five Eyes intelligence alliance (Image: Getty) According to security analysts, Russia is deliberately targeting nations that oppose its geopolitical actions, including members of the Five Eyes intelligence alliance - the UK, US, Australia, Canada and New Zealand . These state-funded cyber organisations possess massive computing power and resources, which they use to launch relentless, sophisticated campaigns against civilian infrastructure. Many people still think cyber warfare is confined to science fiction, but the real-world consequences are already proving to be devastating. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT In a terrifying incident in Florida , hackers infiltrated a local water treatment facility using remote-access software. A horrified employee watched his mouse move on its own across the screen, opening control panels to increase the sodium hydroxide concentration in the drinking water to toxic, lethal levels before the attack was manually stopped. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Automotive giant Jaguar Land Rover also fell victim to a complex attack that began through a single employee's insecure personal device. Once inside, the hackers gained the keys to advanced systems, completely shutting down smart factories and causing severe disruption across the entire supply chain. Hackers will actively hunt for weak links, such as old internet routers or an out-of-date computer (Image: Getty) Even more alarming are the direct attacks on public infrastructure. Russian intelligence hackers recently launched a coordinated assault on Poland's electricity grid by exploiting factory usernames and passwords on remote systems. The breach cut power to half a million citizens, leaving families completely unable to heat their homes during the depths of winter. Experts have warned that the rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has left an "exposed attack surface that has become scarily large". Everyday household items are now being used by hackers to sneak into our lives. From smart TVs and AI voice assistants to internet-connected kettles and fridges, we are filling our homes with gadgets that open a back door for criminals. If a hacker cannot crack a heavily protected company firewall, they will simply look for an easier target. This means they are actively hunting for weak links in your home, such as an old internet router or an out-of-date computer still running unsupported software like Windows 10 . The threat is now so severe that the Five Eyes intelligence alliance has ordered an urgent audit of all connected devices. While the Army and Navy guard our physical borders, ordinary people and local shops have been left to defend the digital front line. Security experts have warned we must stop ignoring the risks, update our old tech and think twice before connecting everyday household gadgets to the internet. https://www.katc.com/us-news/crime/socia.text: Influencer brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate were arrested Saturday in Miami after U.K. prosecutors said they brought further rape and sex trafficking charges against them.Britain's Crown Prosecution Service said the new charges relate to four further victims and were brought after authorities received evidence from Bedfordshire Police in southeastern England. The charges include rape, assault, trafficking and offenses relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.”The charges announced Saturday, which bring the total number of alleged victims in the U.K. to seven, are the latest in a long-running international legal saga involving the brothers that has spanned the U.S., Britain and Romania. The brothers have denied wrongdoing.Here are some things to know about the Tate brothers:Who the Tate Brothers areAndrew Tate, 39, and Tristan Tate, 38, are dual U.S.-British citizens known for their social media empire promoting wealth, male dominance and misogyny.Andrew Tate is a former professional kickboxer and self-described misogynist who has amassed more than 10 million followers, most of them boys and young men, on X. He has been banned from platforms like YouTube, TikTok and Instagram for violating hate speech guidelines.He also runs an online academy where he says he teaches young men how to get rich and attract women. Tristan Tate is also a former kickboxer.The brothers are avid supporters of U.S. President Donald Trump.What the Tates are charged withAndrew Tate and his brother have faced multiple charges in the U.K. and Romania, where they moved to in 2016.British prosecutors said the new charges relate to alleged offenses that took place between 2010 and 2017. They said Andrew Tate was charged with seven further counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, three counts of assault and 19 charges for offenses relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.FROM THE ARCHIVES | Police raid Andrew Tate's home in Romania as new allegations involving minors emergeTristan Tate was charged with one count of sexual assault, two counts of rape and three counts of arranging or facilitating sex trafficking.The Crown Prosecution Service said in a statement it “has requested the extradition of the Tates from the U.S. They have been arrested and await extradition proceedings to the U.K.”The Tates already face previous charges of rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other alleged victims in the U.K. between 2012 and 2015.In June, a U.K. High Court judge threw out a legal bid by the Tates to be told the names of their accusers.In Romania, the siblings were arrested in late 2022 along with two Romanian women. The four were accused of participating in criminal schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations and the Romanian case hasn’t gone forward because of legal and procedural problems.The case hasn’t been closed, and there is also a separate legal case against the brothers in Romania.Andrew Tate has repeatedly claimed that prosecutors in Romania have no evidence against him and that there is a political conspiracy to silence him.Why the Tates were in the U.S.British police previously sought the Tates' extradition to the U.K. once their legal proceedings in Romania concluded.But in February 2025 they were allowed to leave Romania after authorities lifted travel restrictions, and they flew to Florida on a private jet.Romania's foreign minister said at the time that a U.S. official in the Trump administration had expressed interest in the brothers’ legal case in Romania.Trump said he knew “nothing about” the case when asked if his administration pressured the Romania government to release the Tates.

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: A van driving around central London on 30 June 2021 to remind EU citizens living in the UK to register for settled status. Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen A van driving around central London on 30 June 2021 to remind EU citizens living in the UK to register for settled status. Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/Shutterstock Home Office EU citizens in UK get letters telling them post-Brexit residency rights were given ‘in error’ After years of building lives in UK, potentially hundreds of thousands of EU citizens are being told they have no right to remain Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent Sun 2 Aug 2026 08.42 EDT Last modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 09.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The UK Home Office has started stripping some EU citizens of their post-Brexit residency rights, in a move that has raised concerns about Britain’s compliance with its withdrawal agreement with Europe. The UK internal affairs authority has told at least 100 people that they were given residency rights “in error”, disrupting their lives just as they come to the end of their five-year “pre-settled status” and prepare to upgrade to the permanent “settled status”. A Portuguese woman working in the NHS and researching a PhD in Britain says her life has been turned upside down after being told by the Home Office she was granted post Brexit rights to live in the country “in error”. She was granted pre-settled status under the EU settlement scheme, similar to 1.3 million others who had been in the country for fewer than five years before the UK left the EU. She had expected that this would be upgraded to settled status without issue and was dismayed when the Home Office told her her status was a mistake. “I feel so overwhelmed, because this is going to influence so many spheres of my life,” said Gabriela, whose name has been changed to protect her identity. She said she was fearful of the hostile environment that may kick in if her legal right to stay in the UK expired. “I can lose my job, I maybe don’t have the right even to rent the property that I’m living in now, because of course I have to prove my right to live here to the landlord to rent a place. “My bank account might also be affected. I work in the NHS as well, I work with other surgeries as well, so I have three different contracts in different places and I don’t know how it’s going to be if this happens, It’s just very stressful.” Gabriela is one of more than 1 million EU citizens who were granted “pre-settled status” to remain legally in the UK because they had been in the country for fewer than five years before Brexit. The Home Office is now reviewing the cases of those who are required to apply to have their status upgraded to full “settled status”, including children, non-EEA citizens and anyone who arrived after 31 December 2020. It declined to say how many people it had written to, but through a freedom of information request the3million campaign group has been told that 95 people were contacted in March alone. Gabriela is Brazilian-Portuguese, however she did not have a Portuguese passport at the time of her application, something that is now being questioned by the Home Office. In a five page letter, the Home Office said: “It has come to our attention that you were granted pre-settled status without the evidence required to confirm that you meet the definition of ‘relevant EEA citizen” before midnight 31 December 2020, when the UK legally cut ties with the EU. “On the basis of the information and evidence that is currently available, it is therefore considered that your pre-settled status was granted in error,” it added. Gabriela said she had been totally open with the Home Office and had “not excluded anything” including the fact that her father is Portuguese, making her an EU citizen by birth. “Citizenship is by blood so it is not something I have changed since I was born,” she said. Monique Hawkins, acting chief executive of the3million, said the impact of the Home Office’s retrospective review was devastating for many. The group has knowledge of dozens of cases but fears there may be hundreds of thousands like Gabriela who will be hit by similar letters threatening removal from the country. “People applied to the EU settlement scheme in good faith and were granted status by the Home Office years ago. They acted on those decisions in good faith by building their lives in the UK and putting down roots. “We hear from people who are progressing in their jobs, from those whose children are in schools and have known no other country, and now, five years on, when they apply for settled status, they are being told that it was all a mistake. Imagine building a life somewhere and having it ripped out from under you like this.” Gabriela is appealing against the Home Office decision but the issue of “in error” cases has raised alarm bells at the Independent Monitoring Authority (IMA), the statutory body set up to monitor the implementation of the EU citizens chapter of the EU-UK withdrawal agreement (WA). In a statement , it said it “has raised concerns with the Home Office that the policy may be incompatible with the EU withdrawal agreement.” Hawkins said that under the WA, status “should only be removed if it is genuinely proportionate to do so”, but said “the Home Office is simply side-stepping that … entirely”. She said the approach was “completely unacceptable” and called on the Home Office to reconsider its policy. The Home Office said it had a “longstanding” policy not to routinely comment on individual cases. It added that individuals could apply to stay “under any immigration route available to them” if the status was granted in error and the individual was unable to prove it was “granted correctly” after being given all opportunities to do so. They also added that an individual granted PSS in error could make a further valid application for status, which, if refused, would give rise to a legal right of appeal. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: An army of volunteers have been gathering at beaches in the mornings and evenings to help with the cleanup. Photograph: Mark Pinder/The Guardian View image in fullscreen An army of volunteers have been gathering at beaches in the mornings and evenings to help with the cleanup. Photograph: Mark Pinder/The Guardian Tyne and Wear ‘There’s no nurdle fairy’: thousands mobilise to clean up plastic spillage in north-east England Volunteers painstakingly gather plastic pellets washing up on beaches after ship collision on 19 July Mark Brown North of England correspondent Sun 2 Aug 2026 09.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 09.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google “Y ou’ve got a local community that really cares about the coastline,” said Alice Laverty, reflecting on the huge army of volunteers who had taken to crisis-hit beaches in north-east England with passion and only the most basic tools. “They’ve all got a dustpan, a brush, a bucket, a kitchen sieve.” On beaches from Cambois in Northumberland to Seaburn on Wearside, up to 2,000 dedicated volunteers have been painstakingly sifting through sand to find tiny, lentil-sized pellets of plastic. The pellets, called nurdles, are being washed up on beaches after a ship collision on 19 July at the Port of Tyne, South Shields, led to a billion of them spilling into the water . Campaigners estimate there was up to 25 tonnes of them. View image in fullscreen The nurdles are tiny, lentil-sized pellets of plastic. Photograph: Mark Pinder/The Guardian The spillage has prompted anger and protests, and the north-east mayor, Kim McGuinness, has promised to make sure shipowners contribute to what she said was a “pollution emergency” . Since the collision, the nurdles have washed up on numerous beaches in the north-east. Some days, nurdle drifts have been like soup, visibly scarring the landscape. Other days, people have had to get down on their hands and knees to find them, but when they do, they’re there. Laverty, a Whitley Bay bookshop owner, was one of the first to respond. “I saw the horrendous pictures of millions of them floating down the Tyne and I went to the beach in the evening,” she said. “I was literally the only person on the beach with a dustpan and brush and I could see people looking at me going … what is she doing?” Volunteers sift beach sands for plastic nurdles - loop Helped by WhatsApp and social media, there is now a more organised army of volunteers gathering at beaches in the mornings and evenings to help with the cleanup. It is a race against the tides and the only way for volunteers to do it is by painstakingly sifting the sand or shaking seaweed. People have been drawing squares and cleaning the beach section by section. “It becomes quite addictive,” Laverty said. “I can’t walk past a nurdle without picking it up, and I reckon most Whitley Bay residents will be exactly the same.” She said a friend told her the story of Aphrodite punishing Psyche by mixing up different grains, seeds and lentils and setting her the impossible task of separating them by dawn. In the story, a sympathetic army of ants comes to the rescue. “Wouldn’t that be great,” she said. View image in fullscreen Alice Laverty: ‘I can’t walk past a nurdle without picking it up.’ Photograph: Mark Pinder/The Guardian The official advice from councils is not to handle the pellets, but Laverty said there was a greater cause. “There’s no nurdle fairy, this needs to be cleaned up now,” she said. “An official response with specialist equipment and trained staff takes time, and concerns about insurance and liability could further delay cleanup operations.” At Whitley Bay beach, the Guardian talked to other volunteers determined to do their bit. Helen Charlton, a business academic from Cramlington, said: “This is our home. I’m north-east born and bred and I’m incredibly proud of this region and I’m incredibly proud of the industry and commerce here as well. It’s not that we shouldn’t have shipping on the Tyne because we absolutely should. But the two have to coexist.” Lou Shackleton, a life and work coach from Whitley Bay, said the nurdles brought multiple dangers. “Everything is interconnected. The people that are fishing need the fish to be there and healthy. The seals need the fish. I heard a boat broke down yesterday because of nurdles affecting the engine. It’s the summer holidays, there’ll be people in the sea, kids playing. “I have a five-year-old, I don’t want him to be still finding nurdles on the beach in 10 years’ time.” View image in fullscreen Volunteers search for nurdles. Photograph: Mark Pinder/The Guardian Amy Ash, a user experience designer, has created a web app to help organise and mobilise the volunteers . “I surf, I swim, I’ve got two kids,” she said. “It is absolutely devastating that these things are on the beach. I really do not want this to be forgotten about.” As well as the sweepers and sifters, dozens of volunteers have been sewing together mesh bags for collecting the nurdles using scaffolding fabric. Nurdles are tiny disc-shaped plastic pellets that act as the raw material to manufacture most plastic products. Animals can easily mistake them for food with deadly consequences, campaigners say. The environmental charity Fidra , which works to end plastic and chemical pollution, says nurdles are a global problem. Last year it found plastic nurdles at 84% of the UK’s sites of special scientific interest . The Port of Tyne, HM Coastguard, the Environment Agency, local councils and specialist contractors are all involved in what has been called “a coordinated multi-agency effort” to clean up after the spill. By Sunday, about 3,000 volunteer hours had been logged and an estimated 285kg of nurdles had been recovered by the “people’s army”. An open letter is due to be sent on Monday calling for trained local teams to be allowed to help clear nurdles directly from the rivers, not just the beaches. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: President Donald Trump greets supporters after speaking at General Motors’ Milford Proving Grounds on July 27, 2026 in Milford, Michigan. Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images View image in fullscreen President Donald Trump greets supporters after speaking at General Motors’ Milford Proving Grounds on July 27, 2026 in Milford, Michigan. Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Trump tariffs Trump is determined to pursue his trade war – and he may be difficult to stop Eduardo Porter The president’s minions have trawled the statutes to restore roadblocks to trade. The invocation of Smoot-Hawley looks especially dangerous Sun 2 Aug 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 08.01 EDT Share Donald Trump may have found the killer weapon to punish countries at will: by imposing tariffs on their exports to the United States. The president has been looking for a new tool since February, when the supreme court struck down tariffs he slapped on virtually all of America’s trading partners based on the International Economic Emergency Powers Act, or IEEPA, on the spurious grounds that the US faced a variety of national emergencies. It’s become a parlor game among policy wonks to predict what new legal justification he would deploy to replace them. Well, it’s probably not what you think. The round-robin tariffs imposed on everybody last Friday, under the argument that America’s trading partners unfairly undercut US companies by importing things made with forced labor, has drawn a lot of attention. The blatantly specious accusation, sitting uneasily alongside America’s own state-sanctioned abuse of forced labor , underscored how low Trump will stoop to get his way on trade. But those tariffs, imposed under section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, do not provide the carte blanche Trump wants. Tariffs under this section are meant to retaliate against specific “acts, policies and practices” that are “unreasonable” and “burden or restrict” US companies. A blanket charge that every foreign country is enabling forced labor and thus hurting American business is unlikely to fly in court . The whole strategy can be challenged as “arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law” or as “unsupported by substantial evidence”. The truly menacing precedent comes from Trump’s decision, made the Monday before the worldwide forced labor tariffs came into play, to foist a 50% tariff on imports from Canada. The White House’s pretext is Canadian discrimination against American dairy, booze and cars, which, paradoxically, came about as retaliation against Trump’s original barrage of tariffs last year. Sly observers, however, have pointed to Trump’s threat to punish Canada for the forest-fire smoke that wafted into the US. Maybe the new duties are meant to soften Canada as talks get under way to renew the USMCA North American trade pact, or to convince Canadians to become America’s 51st state. Or just because “tariff” is a pretty word . The authority Trump invoked to attack Canada is ominous: section 338 of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930, which is the law that choked global trade in the 1930s and helped sink the world into the Great Depression. Section 338 is particularly dangerous because it offers cover for the president to slap trade levies on whatever country he wants under some fairly hazy arguments. Specifically, it grants the president authority to retaliate against countries that do anything to put the United States “at a disadvantage compared with the commerce of any foreign country”. As soon as the president decides this is going on, he is authorized to “declare such new or additional rate or rates of duty as he shall determine will offset such burden or disadvantage”. Until Trump, section 338 was never invoked to impose tariffs. It was mostly used as leverage, to guarantee that other countries treated American products the same as imports from anywhere else. If some country offered preferential access to a neighbor or ally, the US could demand the same terms, or else. This principle is now called “most favored nation treatment,” which is central to multinational trade rules enforced by the World Trade Organization. Trump doesn’t care about such niceties, though. He has a more destructive agenda in mind. And the statute appears to give him semantic wiggle room. He is determined to pursue his trade war. With such a sprawling mandate, he may be difficult to stop. America’s trading partners were elated in February when a 6-3 majority on the court, including two justices appointed by Trump, ruled against his use of the 1977 IEEPA to impose tariffs at will. It was close, though. The court has shown an almost unbelievable deference to the president. It didn’t object to Trump’s spurious invocation of national emergencies – a “public health crisis” due to illegal drugs from Canada, Mexico and China; trade deficits that “led to the hollowing out” of American manufacturing; something something because Brazil jailed its ex-president Jair Bolsonaro for plotting a coup. The justices merely objected to his use of the statute to impose taxes, which are the preserve of Congress. The executive has gotten away with similarly spurious arguments before. In 1975 President Richard Nixon was allowed to invoke the Trading with the Enemy Act of 1917 to slap tariffs on a zipper company from Japan, a country with which the US was not at war. Trump’s lawyers, in fact, argued before the supreme court that this precedent supported the president’s emergency powers to raise tariffs on anybody under IEEPA. Though Trump lost, his menace to the world remains. Since February his minions have trawled through legal statutes across American history to restore roadblocks to trade. Balance of payments crises don’t exist any more. Still, fresh from his supreme court loss, Trump imposed a 10% tariff on everybody by invoking section 122 of the 1974 act, which allows for tariffs to prevent such imbalances. The use of the law is so ridiculous that Trump’s own lawyers, in the IEEPA case, argued before the supreme court justices that section 122 could not be used as a substitute. In 1974, when the dollar’s exchange rate was fixed, a balance of payments crisis could happen when inflows of money from abroad couldn’t cover the trade deficit, forcing the government to sell foreign assets to plug the gap and preserve the exchange rate. These days the dollar floats. If too little money is coming in, it falls, making it cheaper and thus more attractive for foreigners to buy dollar assets, bringing things back into balance. Fortunately, the balance of payments tariffs had a statutory limit of 150 days. But Trump has tried other stuff too. Section 301 has been used many times before, including by Trump against China in his first term to penalize it for its industrial subsidies, which give its producers an unfair leg up. Trump has also relied on section 232 of the 1962 Trade Expansion Act to put levies on steel, aluminum, lumber, semiconductors and autos on specific grounds about protecting national security. None of these authorities, however, grant him the unrestrained blanket power that could be his under section 338. Let’s see what he does with it. Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/02/at-le.text: At least five people have died and 41 are still missing after an Indonesian ferry caught fire at sea, on Sunday. According according to Basarnas, Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency some passengers jumped overboard to escape the fire and were rescued by a nearby ship.Meanwhile, a total of 225 people onboard were rescued, and four other boats were on standby near the ferry, however they could not get close due to the risk posed by flammable material on the ferry, said the regional Surabaya Search and Rescue Agency.The ferry company had received a call from the ship's captain to report the fire as it sailed from Surabaya in East Java to Makassar in South Sulawesi.However, Basarnas said the captain had not been in contact after that, adding that a larger rescue operation was on its way from Surabaya, a six-hour journey from the site of the disaster.Muhammad Masyhud, a senior official at the Ministry of Transportation said in a statement: "Based on preliminary reports from the field, passengers are waiting to be evacuated by the vessels in the vicinity of the incident site."Adding, "the safety of passengers and crew is our top priority. We are continuously coordinating with all relevant parties to ensure that the evacuation process can proceed quickly, safely, and effectively".Indonesia, an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands, experiences marine accidents frequently, in some parts due to a lack of following of the safety standards and unpredictable weather.Last month at least four people died and 14 remained missing until search and rescue operations concluded after a ferry transporting more than 70 people sank while sailing near the small tropical island of Selayar south of the much larger Sulawesi.

https://www.dw.com/en/moscow-restaurant-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5I8hK Armed law enforcement officers have closed off the area to the public Image: Belkin Alexey/Russian Look/IMAGO Advertisement An explosion at a restaurant in central Moscow killed at least three people, including the suspected bomber on Saturday night, authorities said. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin described it as a "brutal terrorist attack." "Law enforcement agencies are investigating the circumstances of the incident. Those responsible for this crime will certainly be found and face the punishment they deserve," he said in an online post on Sunday. Russia's Anti-Terrorism Committee said a woman carrying "a homemade explosive device" tried to enter the restaurant on Kudrinskaya Square but was stopped by a security guard. The device exploded at the entrance, killing the woman, the guard and a restaurant patron. What do we know about the explosion? State news agency RIA Novosti reported that at least 21 other people were injured in the blast, which occurred shortly before 8 p.m. local time (5 p.m. UTC). The restaurant's website said the venue had been closed on Saturday for a private event. The explosion occurred at an Italian restaurant located in one of ​Moscow's seven Stalin-era skyscrapers Image: Sergei Vedyashkin/Moscow News Agency/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Heavily armed law enforcement officers sealed off the area and launched an investigation. Authorities did not immediately identify those they believed to be behind the attack. Russia has faced several attacks since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022. They blamed a ‌series of assassinations and attempted killings on Kyiv. Russian officials have yet to comment on any possible Ukrainian involvement into the Kudrinskaya Square blast. Russian general shot and badly wounded in Moscow To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Ukraine hits targets deep inside Russia overnight However, Ukraine used drones to attack other parts of Russia on Saturday evening and early on Sunday, including a bombing which targeted an apartment block and killed two in the city Engels, some 900 kilometers (560 miles) southeast of Moscow. Russia's Defense Ministry also said Kyiv struck a warehouse belonging to Wildberries, a major online retailer in Russia, with the Ukrainian drones hitting a site in the Samara Oblast, deep inside Russian territory. Regional Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said it was not immediately clear if there were any casualties. Russian officials also reported over a 100 Ukrainian strikes in the Belgorod Oblast, which borders Ukraine. They said Kyiv forces used artillery, rocket launchers, and drones, leaving 14 people injured. Over 200 Ukrainian drones have allegedly been shot down during the wave of attacks. Overall, Russia claimed 635 downed Ukrainian drones overnight. Meanwhile, at least one person was killed and seven wounded in the Russian attack on Ukraine's Kherson, with the attack involving artillery fire. In Dnipro, seven passengers were wounded in a drone strike on a minibus, with the regional military administrator Oleksandr Hanzha describing it as a "deliberate and cynical attack on civilians." At least nine people were killed and 33 injured in Russian strikes on Kyiv earlier this weekend. Edited by: Roshni Majumdar Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.dw.com/en/indonesia-at-least.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5I9BX A search and rescue operation was underway in Indonesia - such as this one near Bali in 2025 Image: Johannes P. Christo/REUTERS Advertisement At least five people have died and another 41 are missing after a ferry caught fire in Indonesia on Sunday morning, authorities have confirmed. The Mutiara Sentosa 2 ferrywas carrying a total of 271 passengers and crew members from Indonesia's second-largest city, Surabaya in East Java, across the Java Sea to Makassar in South Sulawesi. Search and rescue officials said 225 people had been rescued by Sunday afternoon but that an operation was still ongoing. Some passengers reportedly jumped overboard and were picked up by a nearby ship. Four other vessels were on standby nearby but could not approach because of the risk posed by flammable material on the ferry, officials said. What have Indonesian authorities said? "Based on preliminary reports from the field, passengers are waiting to be evacuated by the vessels in the vicinity of the incident site," said Muhammad Masyhud, a senior official at the Indonesian Ministry of Transportation. "The safety of passengers and crew is our top priority. We are continuously coordinating with all relevant parties to ensure that the evacuation process can proceed quickly, safely, and effectively," he added. The fire, the cause of which remains unclear, was reported by the ship's captain who, according to officials, has not been in contact since. Are shipping accidents common in Indonesia? Indonesia is an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands where marine accidents are a regular occurrence, due to a combination of unpredictable weather conditions and lax safety standards. Last month, a ferry transporting more than 70 people sank while sailing near Selayar, a small tropical island south of the much larger Sulawesi. At least four people were found dead, and 14 others remained missing until the end of the search operation. Edited by: Rana Taha Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.dw.com/en/poland-prime-minis.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5I8Dj Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Poland's image abroad was at stake Image: Lukasz Glowala/REUTERS Advertisement The Polish leader didn't mince his words. "We must wage a resolute fight against this violence, because thugs, hooligans, and this culture of violence are becoming increasingly brazen and insolent — and also because they have received political support," Donald Tusk said on Tuesday, before a Polish cabinet meeting in Warsaw. The liberal-conservative prime minister said he deplored the fact that "more and more such incidents" are taking place all over Poland . Tusk's comments came in response to an incident in Wroclaw two days earlier, in which three Polish men brutally beat up a young Ukrainian man and his girlfriend on the street. Cellphone videos show the attackers kicking the Ukrainian man as he lies on the ground. The woman was also hit, sustaining injuries to her neck and ear. The attack came after an argument in a shop; the attackers took exception to the couple's Ukrainian accents. Polish police acted swiftly: Two of the attackers, both of whom have previous convictions, are already in custody, and a third is being sought. Tusk warned that such incidents negatively impact Poland's image abroad. The country's reputation was greatly enhanced by its willingness to provide assistance after the start of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine . This could be destroyed, said Tusk, "if we allow thugs, hooligans and common criminals to beat and humiliate people just because they have a slightly different accent." Mood is turning against Ukrainians Poland provided military and humanitarian assistance to its neighbor from the very beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. It took in more than one million refugees from the war, and around 1.5 million Ukrainians are currently living in Poland. The majority of them work, pay taxes, and contribute to the Polish economy. Ukrainian refugees in a reception center in the Polish capital, Warsaw in April 2022, two months after the start of the war Image: Attila Husejnow/ZUMA Wire/IMAGO But four and a half years after the start of the war, the mood in Poland has changed. More and more often, Ukrainians are being verbally and physically attacked in public. Last Wednesday a Polish manager on a construction site in Skawina, near Krakow, was filmed aggressively insulting Ukrainian workers. In another incident on a local train near Warsaw, two drunken men shouted verbal abuse at a Ukrainian passenger. On July 11, a man on a bus in Bielsko-Biala insulted and threatened two Ukrainian girls who were trying to take a selfie. Even schoolchildren, including teenagers at a playground, have fallen victim to the new climate of hate. According to the police, 180 hate crimes against Ukrainians were recorded in the first six months of this year — a third more than in 2025. And on Friday (31.07.2026) the newspaper Gazeta Wyborcza warned that the internet is full of fake news about crimes Ukrainians are supposed to have committed against Poles. Award of honorary title considered a provocation Anti-Ukrainian slogans were already apparent during the presidential election campaign last year. But this May was a big turning point. The Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy prompted outrage in Poland with his decision to award a special unit of the Ukrainian army the honorary title of " Heroes of the UPA ." Poland holds the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) responsible for the mass murder of tens of thousands of Polish civilians in Volhynia between 1943 and 1945. Ukrainians, on the other hand, revere the soldiers of the UPA as heroes in the fight against the Sovietization of their country. Individual UPA units continued to fight against Soviet rule well into the 1950s. Memorial march in Krakow in July 2026 for victims of the Volhynia massacre committed by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army during WW2 Image: Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto/picture alliance Along with Polish opposition politicians, Tusk is also critical of Zelenskyy in the row about the UPA. However, he believes that the reactions on both sides are exaggerated and counterproductive. Poland's president Karol Nawrocki revoked the award of Poland's highest order to his Ukrainian counterpart, which had been made in 2023. Zelenskyy returned the award by courier to Warsaw. Avalanche of hate These demonstrative gestures by both leaders have set off an avalanche. The Polish internet is flooded with hatred for Ukraine. Przemyslaw Czarnek, the prime ministerial candidate of the leading opposition Law and Justice party (PiS), demanded that all military aid for Ukraine be stopped until Kyiv backs down in the row over the interpretation of history. Current opinion polls speak for themselves. According to a survey by the CBOS institute, for the first time since the start of the war a majority of respondents (54%) were opposed to taking in more Ukrainian refugees. Only 42% supported maintaining the policy to date. In 2022, at the start of the war, 94% of Poles wanted to offer sanctuary to refugees. Another poll, by the Opinia24 institute for the weekly newspaper Polityka, found that 44% were against providing further aid to Ukraine, and 41% in favor. 54% of respondents opposed Ukraine joining the EU. Only 33% supported Kyiv's desire to become part of the European Union. The Ukrainians who were attacked in Wroclaw spoke to the NEXTA Polska news service and urged their fellow countrymen to be careful while in Poland. They advised them to avoid any kind of conflict and to "speak less Ukrainian" in public, as a precaution. Tusk wants to de-escalate the row with Ukraine Poland's center-left government under prime minister Donald Tusk has emphatically condemned the anti-Ukrainian attacks. The Polish police and judiciary have also acted swiftly and decisively. After the incident in Wroclaw, Tusk urged President Nawrocki to "break his silence" and condemn the violence. So far, Poland's head of state still has not commented. During the presidential election campaign, Nawrocki, a former boxer, admitted that in his youth he took part in an organized brawl between fans of rival football clubs, violence he described as a form of "noble, masculine combat." Tusk agrees with the opposition 's criticism in the row about the UPA. All the same, he is trying to pour oil on troubled waters. On Wednesday, he met with the Ukrainian president Zelenskyy in private for the first time since the UPA crisis. "We also talked about the security challenges that, unfortunately, affect our people as well: it is important that Ukrainians who have left their homes because of the war and found refuge in Poland feel safe," Zelenskyy wrote afterwards on social media, and thanked Tusk. Continued support for Ukraine Polish-Ukrainian cooperation is vital for both countries, as demonstrated by an incident in eastern Poland in the early hours of Thursday (30.07.2026). During a massive Russian attack on Ukraine, a Russian rocket crossed into Polish airspace , landing in a field near a village around 90 kilometers inside the Polish border. The explosion left a crater ten meters wide. "I know it's not very popular these days to speak well of Ukraine," Tusk said after visiting the scene. Nonetheless, the Polish leader continued: "Poland's security directly depends on the effective actions of Ukrainian forces, including in the air." Tusk stated: "I know where the enemy stands," and added that, despite protests by the Polish opposition, he remains committed to supplying weapons to Ukraine . https://www.politico.eu/article/hungary-.text: Hungary faces “the most critical five days” ahead as a record drought in Central Europe has forced Budapest to shut down a nuclear power plant that generates 40 percent of the country’s electricity, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said Sunday. “As our electricity system will face an enormous strain, I ask everyone to pay even closer attention to each other from Monday,” Magyar said in a video appeal . The warning comes after Magyar announced over the weekend that the last operating reactor units at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant south of Budapest would be taken offline because of the continued drop in water levels in the Danube River, which the plant uses for cooling. Advertisement Advertisement “Due to the further drop in the Danube’s water level,” Magyar wrote Saturday , “tomorrow it will be completely shut down for the first time in 44 years." The Soviet-built Paks facility remains the backbone of the country’s power system. The loss of output has triggered national energy-saving measures and offers of support from regional neighbors . A prolonged outage would cripple Hungary’s electricity supply at a time when temperatures are forecast to rise above 40 degrees Celsius in Budapest next week amid an ongoing heatwave and drought across Europe. Magyar warned the shutdown could trigger an emergency at a time of high summer demand: “An energy crisis situation may arise from Monday. Coordinated steps and self-restraint will be needed to avoid more severe consequences.” The government has urged households and businesses to reduce electricity consumption during peak hours between 5 p.m. and 10 p.m., calling on people to limit their use of air conditioning and washing machines. Authorities have also prepared an emergency plan to temporarily restrict consumption at industrial facilities on a rotating basis, while increasing output from other power plants. The European Commission said Friday it was closely monitoring the situation and was prepared to convene an emergency meeting of its Electricity Coordination Group over the Paks shutdown. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c74g.text: Image source, Basarnas Image caption, KMP Mutiara Sentosa 2 ferry with thick plumes of smoke billowing from behind By Olivia Ireland Published 2 August 2026, 11:02 BST Updated 1 hour ago Five people have been found dead and 41 are missing after an Indonesian ferry carrying at least 250 people caught fire while at sea, officials say. The captain of the ship reported the fire - off Madura island - as the vessel sailed from the country's second-largest city, Surabaya in East Java, to Makassar in South Sulawesi, according to Basarnas, the National Search and Rescue Agency. Footage played by local Indonesian news outlet iNews shows large numbers of people in life jackets on what appears to be a lifeboat. Other clips show people climbing down from the ferry that has flames and plumes of smoke coming from the top of the vessel. Basarnas posted a video to its TikTok, with a statement saying at 08:24 (02:24 GMT) the Surabaya Search and Rescue office received information that passenger ship KMP Mutiara Sentosa 2 was on fire. "Based on information from the shipping company, the fire occurred at around 06:00-07:00 (00:00-01:00 GMT)." Later, Basarnas said it got confirmation the ferry "was almost entirely engulfed in flames" as "passengers held on in the ship's bridge and bow while awaiting rescue". It was unclear how the ferry caught fire, the statement said. In some of the footage, can be seen jumping into the sea, with crowds of people in life jackets gathering and lifebuoys being thrown to some before they are carried into a rescue ship. https://telex.hu/transtelex/2026/08/02/d.text: Menü Kereső Felrobbantanak egy Duna-parti sziklát, hogy így tereljenek több vizet a csernavodai atomerőműhöz Transtelex Alacsony vízállás a Dunán Corábiánál – Fotó: Daniel Mihăilescu / AFP Zsizsmann Erika (Transtelex) Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Ellenőrzött módon felrobbantanak vasárnap egy sziklát ott, ahol a Duna a Bala-ágra és az Ostrovi-ágra (Öreg-Duna) szétválik, hogy így tereljenek nagyobb vízmennyiséget a csernavodai atomerőműhöz. A Román Haditengerészet helyi idő szerint dél körül végezte az első tesztrobbantásokat az Antena3 CNN tudósítása szerint . A Duna jobb partján lévő Pârjoaia szikla egy gránitképződmény, amely a folyó két ágába jutó víz mennyiségét befolyásolja. A felrobbantása megosztja a közvéleményt, felmerült például, hogy a sürgősségi beavatkozás egyáltalán nem számol a helyiek szempontjaival, Valentin Coman újságíró arra hívta fel a figyelmet , hogy a hatóságok eddig egyáltalán nem foglalkoztak az olyan komoly infrastrukturális hiányosságokkal, mint például az, hogy Pârjoaia faluban például nincs bevezetve az ivóvíz, így a helyiek ki vannak szolgáltatva a kutak és források vízhozamának. Coman aggodalmát fejezte ki amiatt is, hogy a dobrudzsai kulturális örökség részét képező helyi templomot nem befolyásolja-e a robbantás. A romániai belügyminisztérium már pénteken közölte , hogy a Román Haditengerészet elkezdte a Duna felmérését az érintett területen, hogy előkészítsék a vízhozam átirányítását. A beavatkozás következő szakasza a Bala-ág részleges elzárása, amiről szintén szó volt már pénteken . A Pro Tv szombat este arról számolt be , hogy négy, kb. 70 méter hosszú és 3 méter magas uszályt töltenek meg kővel és süllyesztenek el, hogy így alakítsák ki azt a víz alatti küszöböt, amely csökkenti a Bala-ágba folyó vízmennyiséget, és az Öreg-Duna felé tereli a vízhozamot. Emellett az Alsó-Dunai Folyami Igazgatóság azon dolgozik, hogy egy méterrel mélyítsék az Öreg-Duna medrét, a csernavodai reaktorok hűtőmedencéjéhez vezető csatornát pedig kitisztítják. A kormány 7 millió lejt utalt ki a tartalékalapból a munkálatokra. Romeo Soare, az Alsó-Dunai Folyami Igazgatóság képviselője a ProTV-nek azt mondta, az atomerőmű körüli munkálatok hatása leghamarabb a következő hét közepén lesz érezhető. Sorin Rîndașu, a Román Vízügyi Igazgatóság vezérigazgató-helyettese szombaton arra figyelmeztetett az Agerpres szerint , hogy az atomerőmű még működő 2-es reaktora nagyjából négy-öt napig bírja még a jelenlegi körülmények között, ugyanis a Duna vízszintje Csernavoda térségében naponta mintegy 2-3 centimétert csökken. Rîndașu szerint azért van szükség a sürgősségi intézkedésekre, hogy megállítsák a vízszint csökkenését. A szakember arról is beszélt, hogy bár a Felső-Dunán, Ausztriában esők vannak, és a csapadék növelte a folyam mellékfolyóinak, és így a Dunának is a vízszintjét, hét napnak kell eltelnie, ameddig ez az ár az országhatárhoz ér, és további öt nap, ameddig eléri Csernavodát. A csernavodai atomerőmű 1-es reaktorát már kedden délelőtt leállították és leválasztották az országos energiarendszerről, csütörtökön pedig előbb azt közölték, hogy a 2-es reaktort is leállítják, majd mégis a működtetése mellett döntöttek . A csernavodai atomerőmű Románia villamosenergia-fogyasztásának közel 20 százalékát fedezi. Az 1-es blokk beépített teljesítménye 706,5 MW, a 2-es blokké 704,8 MW, így a két blokk egyidejű kiesése több mint 1400 MW termelőkapacitás elvesztését jelentheti az országos hálózat számára. Ilie Bolojan ügyvivő kormányfő péntek este a rendkívüli kormányülés után bejelentette, hogy országos energetikai válsághelyzetet hirdettek Romániában augusztusra a villamosenergia-termelés csökkenése miatt. A kormány felszólította az összes romániai erőművet, hogy maximális teljesítménnyel üzemeljenek, ezzel párhuzamosan az Országos Energiaszabályozó Hatóság (ANRE) és a Transelectrica sürgősségi eljárással hálózatra kapcsolja a már elkészült, de még engedélyre váró naperőműveket, szélerőműveket és tárolókapacitásokat. A sürgősségi intézkedések mellett Bolojan szerint leporolnák a Bala-ág elágazási térségének környezeti helyreállítását célzó projektet is, ami a csernavodai atomerőmű tervezett 3-as és 4-es reaktorai miatt is fontos lenne. A 150 millió eurós beruházás egyszer már eljutott a közbeszerzési eljárás meghirdetéséig, de ezt végül törölték. Bolojan pénteken önkéntes fogyasztáscsökkentésre kérte a lakosságot és a közintézményeket, különösen az esti órákban. Közölte, hogy a legnagyobb romániai ipari fogyasztókat már figyelmeztették a helyzetre, és hétfőn egyeztetnek velük a termelés tervezett korlátozásáról. https://english.republika.mk/world/orban.text: Overt tyranny has arrived in Hugary, said former Prime Minister Viktor Orban after the latest round of powergrab moves by Petar Magyar, who is forcing the President of the country Tamas Sulyok to resign. Magyar and his Tisza party carried out an unprecedented attack on the President, putting him in an undignified position and removed him from office. This has not happened in Hungary since the days of the darkest dictatorship. Sulyok is a victim of political violence. If you can do this to a President, there is no end to what you can do to an individual citizen. May God protect Hungary, said Orban. Tisza has a majority sufficient to amend the Constitution and is using it to force officials who are not loyal to the party out of office. http://www.jpost.com/travel/article-9029.text: Lithuania is one of my favorite countries in the world. I keep coming back, and every visit uncovers another charming town, fascinating story, or hidden gem - many of which I've shared on the GoTravel website. It's remarkably green, considerably more affordable than many of its Western European neighbors, and offers a welcome escape from the Israeli summer heat.There's another reason to plan your visit carefully. On the last Sunday of every month, dozens of museums, castles, and national heritage sites across Lithuania offer free admission. It's an easy way to save dozens of euros while exploring some of the country's most impressive cultural landmarks.1. Gediminas Tower, VilniusVisible from nearly every corner of the city, Gediminas Tower - together with a surviving section of the old defensive wall - is all that remains of the fortress that once protected medieval Vilnius. It makes an ideal first stop, whether you take the funicular from the northern side or take the short walking trail from the south. Inside, the tower presents engaging historical exhibits, while the hilltop rewards visitors with sweeping panoramic views of the Lithuanian capital.Money saved: €8.2. Palace of the Grand Dukes of Lithuania, VilniusJust a short walk away lies Cathedral Square and the Palace of the Grand Dukes of Lithuania. Just south of the palace lies Pilies Street - literally "Castle Street" - the Old Town's main pedestrian thoroughfare. The reconstructed palace traces the history of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania through grand ceremonial halls, archaeological discoveries, and thoughtfully curated exhibitions.Money saved: €6–10.3. Bastion of the Vilnius Defence WallAfter exploring Vilnius' atmospheric Old Town, the Gate of Dawn, and the nearby market, continue on to one of the city's best-preserved fortifications: The Bastion of the Vilnius Defence Wall. The site features underground tunnels and exhibitions that explore the city's military past.Money saved: €6.4. Energy and Technology Museum, VilniusDirectly across the river from Gediminas Tower is an interactive museum housed in Vilnius' first municipal power plant, built in 1903. The museum combines the original industrial machinery and architecture with hands-on exhibits covering energy, engineering, transport, and technology, making it an engaging visit for both adults and children.Money saved: €9.5. National Gallery of Art, VilniusArt enthusiasts should also make time for the National Gallery of Art, located a short distance away. As Lithuania's leading museum of modern and contemporary art, it showcases paintings, sculptures, photography, prints, installations, and video works that trace the evolution of Lithuanian artistic expression.Money saved: €8.6. Trakai CastleAround 30 minutes from Vilnius stands Trakai Castle, the iconic island fortress set amid the waters of Lake Galvė and one of Lithuania's most recognizable landmarks. While you're there, consider taking a boat trip among the lake's many small islands. On the last Sunday of every month, admission to the castle museum is free.Money saved: €12.7. Open-Air Museum of LithuaniaOn the drive to Kaunas, Lithuania's second-largest city, it's worth stopping at the Open-Air Museum of Lithuania near the shores of the Kaunas Reservoir. The museum stands on the site connected to the former town of Rumšiškės, whose residents were relocated after the reservoir was created. Today, it is one of Europe's largest open-air museums, featuring dozens of traditional wooden homes, farmsteads, windmills, and churches relocated from every region of Lithuania.Money saved: €12.8. Ninth Fort, near KaunasThe Ninth Fort is one of eight defensive forts constructed around Kaunas in the late 19th century. It is best known for its tragic role during the Holocaust, when tens of thousands of people - most of them Lithuanian Jews, along with deportees from other European countries - were imprisoned and murdered there.Today, the site houses a museum with exhibitions covering the Soviet and Nazi occupations, as well as the Holocaust, alongside a monumental memorial considered one of Europe's most striking Holocaust monuments. On the last Sunday of every month, admission to the museum and its exhibitions is free, although guided tours of the underground sections require advance booking and an additional fee.Money saved: €8.The final stop may be a sobering one, but the journey back between Lithuania's two largest cities - just an hour and a half through forests, fields, and seemingly endless greenery - serves as a reminder of why this country leaves such a lasting impression. It is a landscape that refreshes the senses long after the trip has ended.About the author:Carmit Weiss is the director of the GoTravel travel website, one of the most comprehensive and trusted Hebrew-language resources for travelers exploring destinations around the world.

https://www.rollingstone.com/culture/cul.text: By Daniel Kreps Daniel Kreps Contact Daniel Kreps on X Contact Daniel Kreps by Email View all posts by Daniel Kreps July 19, 2026 Tristan and Andrew Tate Andrei Pungovschi/Getty Images Andrew and Tristan Tate were arrested in Miami Saturday as British authorities sought their extradition on new charges of rape, sex trafficking, and “offenses relating to indecent images of a child.” The sibling social media influencers were taken into custody by the U.S. Marshals on a sealed warrant that the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) revealed Sunday morning. “We have decided to prosecute Andrew and Tristan Tate for further offenses including rape, arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation and offenses relating to indecent images of a child,” Malcolm McHaffie, Head of the Special Crime Division at the Crown Prosecution Service, said in a statement. “These charging decisions followed receipt of a further file of evidence from Bedfordshire Police and bring the total number of alleged victims in this case to seven. The CPS has requested the extradition of the Tates from the US. They have been arrested and await extradition proceedings to the UK.” In May 2025, the CPS charged Andrew and Tristan Tate with 11 and 10 counts respectively — including three each for rape — based on accusations from three victims in the U.K. The additional charges stem from allegations from a fourth victim. “The CPS has decided to prosecute Andrew Tate , 39, with seven further counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, three counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and 19 additional charges for offenses relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography,” the CPS said Sunday of the additional charges. “The CPS has decided to prosecute Tristan Tate, 38, with one count of sexual assault, two counts of rape and three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation.” In total, the brothers now face 59 charges combined. The Tate brothers’ lawyer Joseph McBride denied the allegations in a statement to the Associated Press and accused the U.K. of “filth and slander” in response to a defamation lawsuit the brothers filed against the U.K. government.
