https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Matthew Roberts, a 27-year-old Bundjalung, Yaegl and Gamilaroi man, took his life inside Lithgow correctional centre on 7 July after being remanded in custody in March. Composite: Guardian Design/Supplied View image in fullscreen Matthew Roberts, a 27-year-old Bundjalung, Yaegl and Gamilaroi man, took his life inside Lithgow correctional centre on 7 July after being remanded in custody in March. Composite: Guardian Design/Supplied Indigenous Australians A record number of First Nations people died in NSW prison custody last year. Advocates fear this year will be worse Exclusive: Karlene Whitton says her son Matthew Roberts took his own life three months into his jail term. ‘I keep picturing it every night’ Warning: This article contains images and names of Indigenous Australians who have died Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Jordyn Beazley Sun 2 Aug 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google First Nations advocates warn that prisons in New South Wales could exceed the record number of Indigenous deaths in custody set last year , after two men died this month. Matthew Roberts, a 27-year-old Bundjalung, Yaegl and Gamilaroi man and father of two young boys, took his life inside Lithgow correctional centre on 7 July after he was remanded in custody in March. Another First Nations man, 21, died a week later at Clarence correctional centre. “I’m in shock, I keep picturing it every night,” Roberts’ mother, Karlene Whitton, said. Whitton said Roberts had been on suicide watch during a previous period he spent in prison some years ago. On the night he died, she said he told her over the phone that he wanted to end his life. “He hung up and said ‘I love you, Mum’, and I started crying and thinking ‘oh, please don’t!’” she said. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Asked what preventive measures were taken to support Roberts, a spokesperson for Corrective Services NSW said: “The intersection between mental health and the justice system is complex. “Many individuals enter custody with significant and longstanding needs. Corrective Services NSW works with Justice Health to deliver mental health care to people in custody, with a strong focus on safety for those in our care, our staff and the broader community,” they added. “Given this matter is being investigated and will be considered by the coroner, we can’t provide further comment at this stage.” The Roberts family are being supported by the Dhadjowa Foundation, which is helping them fundraise for his funeral. The foundation was started by April Day, whose mother, Tanya, a Yorta Yorta woman, died in custody in Victoria 2017. Man dies in Sydney prison unit that watchdog wanted shut down because it ‘cannot provide a safe environment’ Read more “Right now, our focus has been supporting the family to lay Matthew to rest and helping them navigate a system that no grieving family should have to face alone,” Day said. “No family should have to fundraise to bury their loved one, especially when they have died in the care of the state.” Whitton said her son was “a real joy”. “He was always happy, he loved his babies, he loved his niece, he loved all of his three nephews,” she said. “He played football, he was into sports, I’ve got trophies of his, he played rugby union. He had a lot of friends.” ‘Shameful’ record Clarence correctional centre, which is privately run by British multinational Serco, issued a statement extending its sympathies to the family of the man who died there on 15 July, and to “the wider Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community”, but has not released information about his cause of death. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion On Monday an 18-year-old woman died at Dame Phyllis Frost centre in Victoria. At least seven First Nations people have died in custody so far in 2026 amid a record number of people in prison, despite crime rates largely remaining stable over the past two years . Twelve First Nations people died in NSW prisons in 2025, a new record for the state. Of the 39 total deaths in Corrective Services custody, almost one in four were described as self-harm . The prison population – which is correlated to the number of deaths in custody – grew more in the four months to March 2026 than in the previous four years, Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research (Bocsar) data released in May showed. Some 41% of those who entered prison during this period were First Nations people, and more than one-third of the prison population at the time of the Boscar report in March were Indigenous, the highest proportion on record. Sharif Deen, the acting chief executive of the NSW and ACT Aboriginal Legal Service, said the state was in the middle of “a deaths in custody crisis” and she worried it may exceed the “shameful” record set last year. “This tragedy is being fuelled by an unprecedented increase in the number of Aboriginal adults being forced into prisons and police cells,” she said. “We are terrified about the consequences for our clients.” Explore more on these topics Indigenous Australians Deaths in custody New South Wales Prisons news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Australia World AU politics Environment Climate crisis Indigenous Australia Immigration Media Business Health Science Tech Podcasts Newsletters

Brisbane’s median price has fallen about $8,000 since May, bringing an end to a historic 40-month incline. Photograph: Darren England/AAP View image in fullscreen Brisbane’s median price has fallen about $8,000 since May, bringing an end to a historic 40-month incline. Photograph: Darren England/AAP Housing House prices slide across Australia as Middle East conflict and tax changes begin to bite Cotality data shows a drop in Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth, as nation’s median home price falls about $19,000 below its March peak Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Luca Ittimani Sun 2 Aug 2026 10.01 EDT Last modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 10.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google House prices have fallen in Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth as the market downturn spreads across Australia. New Cotality data, released on Monday, showed prices have fallen across most of the nation since May. Brisbane’s median price has fallen about $8,000 since May, to equal its March level of $1.1m. The city’s dwelling prices had increased for an historic 40 consecutive months, since February 2023, until they fell in June. Fines, indefinite motel stays and uncertainty: how a homeless camp exposed regional Australia’s housing crisis Read more Adelaide and Perth median home prices have each fallen about $4,000 below their record highs set in May, at $944,000 and $1.03m respectively. In June, regional Australia’s home values fell overall for the first time since January 2023. Regional home values fell or stayed flat in every state in July. Nationally, the median home price is now $928,000 – about $19,000 below its March peak. Sydney, Melbourne and Canberra median prices have respectively fallen $69,000, $39,000 and $22,000 since February. Prices in Sydney and Melbourne are still higher than they were in January 2025 and in Canberra are above where they were in September 2025. Prices are still higher than January 2025 The Reserve Bank has reported fewer than 1% of borrowers have fallen into negative equity, with home values worth less than their loans, while an even smaller share are unable to make repayments. The housing market has slowed since February, when the Reserve Bank of Australia began to hike interest rates and the US war on Iran broke out. Housing demand has fallen further since the May federal budget trimmed property investors’ tax concessions. Capital gains tax changes are already having an impact on wealth inequality – and vested interests are running scared | Greg Jericho Read more NAB on Thursday reported a 15% fall in home loan applications from the first three months of 2026 to the three months to June. Westpac, Equifax and Loan Market have independently reported falling mortgage demand. The RBA governor, Michele Bullock, speaking at an Anika Foundation lunch on Wednesday, said she was surprised by the slump in house prices and housing demand since May. Bullock said interest rates were only “a bit” restrictive, attributing the slump to falling buyer demand. “I expect that things will settle down,” Bullock said. “People will get used to the new rules. Hopefully the conflict overseas will die down, and they’ll get a bit more confidence. Prices might lower a bit. People might feel more confident to come back into the market.” Buyers and sellers are already showing signs of adjustment, with auction clearance rates edging up from from their June low of 47.4% to reach 53.6% at the weekend, according to Cotality’s preliminary data. The property research company reported the number of new listings had declined over July as sellers held off going to market to wait out weak conditions. The RBA is not expected to raise interest rates when its board next meets on 11 August. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Elisabeth-Jane Ross is believed to have died between five and seven days before her body was found on 18 July. View image in fullscreen Elisabeth-Jane Ross is believed to have died between five and seven days before her body was found on 18 July. Greece Man arrested after Scottish woman found dead inside suitcase in Athens Greek police say 26-year-old Afghan national is believed to have left Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s body in derelict building Helena Smith in Athens Sun 2 Aug 2026 14.29 EDT First published on Sun 2 Aug 2026 10.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Greek authorities have arrested an Afghan national in connection with the death of a Scottish woman whose body was found in a suitcase in an abandoned building in central Athens. Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, a charity worker described as an “angel full of innocence and goodness” by friends, had been in Greece for almost three weeks when she is believed to have died. Police sources said the suspect was a 26-year-old Afghan citizen who had allegedly confessed to the crime. He had been brought in for questioning by Greece’s homicide division last Thursday, two days after Ross’s body was publicly identified. A statement released by police on Sunday said: “A criminal file has been opened against a 26-year-old foreign national for intentional homicide, robbery and violation of the law [regarding] weapons.” Explaining the accusation of ownership of illegal weapons, security officials said “various arms – some real, some fake” had been discovered in the suspect’s home, also thought to be in the downtown area of Kypseli where the body was discovered. He is expected to be charged on Monday. Throughout the investigation, Greek authorities had worked closely with the UK’s National Crime Agency (NCA) and Police Scotland, according to the statement. Ross, who had strong links with the charity sector in Greece, is the daughter of a prominent lawyer in Edinburgh, where she also lived. She was reported to have friends in Kypseli, where her body was discovered on 18 July by a homeless man in what had once been a car park. Wrapped in cloth, it had been placed in a suitcase left in a decrepit, rubbish-strewn building at the site. Sources told the Guardian that the suspect’s alleged use of credit cards that belonged to Ross had contributed to police identifying him. “He was caught on camera withdrawing money with the cards from various ATMs,” one said. “The credit cards belonged to Ms Ross. That played a big role in leading us to him.” For days, investigators were unable to make headway, citing the lack of fingerprints or DNA on the suitcase. Adding to the mystery was the discovery that her mobile phone had been used until the time when the body was publicly identified last week. Police had described text messages sent to her father and other members of her family as deliberately misleading. The messages had spoken of her “need to be alone”. The Briton’s “dispersed movements” in the days leading up to her death had made the quest to track her killer even harder. After leaving the home of close friends in Keratsini, a suburb close to the port of Piraeus, where she had stayed for two weeks after flying to Greece, she had gone her own way, renting an apartment in the district of Exarchia in downtown Athens. Greek media outlets reported the suspect had been found in possession of the keys to the rental apartment and that he was “the partner” of one of the Briton’s friends. “As confirmed, the victim arrived in the country on June 26 and stayed at the home of friends until July 10, from where she departed to an unknown [address],” the police statement said. The homicide division said it had made the announcement after amassing evidence that proved the Afghan had “placed the body in the case and carried it to the abandoned car park” in Kypseli. Analysis of CCTV footage had played a role. “The subsequent preliminary investigation … using investigative material and digital analysis of video footage, proved the involvement of the 26-year-old foreign national in the incident. [He] was brought in [for questioning] on 30 July and confessed to his actions,” the statement said. It remains unknown how Ross died. Media reports quoted the suspect as telling police that when he visited the flat in Exarchia he had discovered her lifeless body in the bathroom. An initial on-site postmortem showed there were no evident signs of injury or struggle on the Briton’s body but proved inconclusive because of advanced decomposition. Authorities have fast-tracked toxicological tests and analysis of vital organ tissues to determine the cause of death. Grigoris Leon, who heads the Hellenic Society of Forensic Medicine, told the Guardian that examination of the lungs and eyes would help provide answers and determine “whether she had died a natural death”. As tributes have poured in, flowers have been left beside the abandoned lot in Kypseli. One note read: “Here lies an angel.” One friend in Edinburgh agreed with that, saying: “We have lost an angel, an angel full of innocence and goodness who only wanted to help people wherever she went.”The UK Foreign Office previously said: “Our thoughts are with Elisabeth’s family during this difficult time. We are providing consular support and are in contact with the local authorities.” A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “We are aware of the death of a Scottish woman in Athens and are liaising with authorities in Greece. Officers are providing support to her family in Scotland.” Explore more on these topics Greece Scotland Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

Firefighters battle a wildfire near Porto Germeno, north-west of Athens, on Sunday. Photograph: Michael Varaklas/AP View image in fullscreen Firefighters battle a wildfire near Porto Germeno, north-west of Athens, on Sunday. Photograph: Michael Varaklas/AP Greece Two helicopters collide outside Athens as Greece battles to control wildfires Fire department says two-person crew of one aircraft killed in incident during gale-force winds to west of capital Helena Smith in Athens and agencies Sun 2 Aug 2026 13.36 EDT First published on Sun 2 Aug 2026 09.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two firefighting helicopters have collided west of Athens, killing the two-person crew of one of the aircraft, as efforts to control a massive wildfire barrelling towards the outskirts of the Greek capital intensified. Gale-force winds that have pushed flames towards settlements on Athens’ western fringes were caught on video on Sunday downing one of the helicopters. “The pilots ... were taken unconscious to hospital, where their death was confirmed,” said the fire department’s director of communications, Vassilis Vathrakogiannis. The Greek prime minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis said the two dead were a Dane and a Greek. The two crew members of the second helicopter were rescued. As Europe’s wildfire crisis fractured along different routes, and in further proof of the destructive force of climate-driven wildfires across the continent, the blazes ripped through Greece’s tinder-dry landscape, up mountain slopes and down to the sea, before encroaching on the capital. Warning of “extremely difficult” days ahead, Mitsotakis underlined the threat posed by gusts that in recent days have exceeded 78mph (125km/h). “When the winds blow with such force, even the dozens of aircraft we have at our disposal cannot operate safely,” he wrote on social media. More than 100 homes were destroyed overnight in fires that broke out around the popular coastal village of Porto Germeno, about 45 miles (70km) north-west of Athens. By Sunday, more than 500 firefighters and forest commandos had been dispatched to keep the flames at bay. View image in fullscreen A firefighting helicopter drops water over a forest near Porto Germeno, north-west of Athens, on Sunday. Photograph: Michael Varaklas/AP The eastern Mediterranean, no stranger to wildfires, has had a relatively calm summer to date, leaving Greeks to watch in horror as the blazes have hit farther west. As the advance of wildfires in Spain was finally curbed and officials in France announced that a mega-fire – four times the size of Paris – had begun to be contained, the blazes in Greece have prompted mass evacuations and devastated huge swathes of land from Crete to the southern Peloponnese, the Ionian isle of Cephalonia and islands across the Aegean. Last week three Greek firefighters died from injuries sustained while they fought blazes. Extreme winds have been a blessing – in bringing down summer temperatures – but also a curse, with their-gale force strength obstructing firefighting efforts. Greece’s civil protection minister, Evangelos Tournas, a retired air force general, said at the weekend that the fire department had been “pushed to its limits”. He said high winds had created “extremely difficult conditions resulting in many cases where aircraft either cannot draw water or cannot carry out drops due to extreme turbulence”. View image in fullscreen People using olive branches to beat back the flames in the Megara valley, in western Attica, Greece, on Sunday. Photograph: Louisa Gouliamaki/Reuters France’s largest wildfire remained contained after 224,000 people were forced to flee in what may have been the largest peacetime evacuation in French history. But active pockets still burned across 160 sq miles (420 sq km) of devastated forest. Thousands remained unable to return home, and nearly 3,000 firefighters were deployed against the Gironde mega-fire and a second blaze in Provence that had stopped advancing but remained uncontained. “The fire is now fixed, which does not mean that the fire is extinguished,” the Gironde prefecture said on Sunday, using the French firefighting term for a blaze whose advance has been stopped and whose perimeter has been contained. The region remained under France’s highest red forest fire alert. Dry conditions and soaring temperatures around Bordeaux, combined with afternoon winds, created a continued risk of renewed flames. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day Preview latest after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen A deer in the forest in Le Temple, Gironde. Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters Additional firefighters from Ukraine, Lithuania and French Polynesia were expected on Sunday and Monday to reinforce the operation. Weather tracker: Why Europe’s wildfires are proving so fierce and difficult to stop Read more Hundreds of miles away, nearly 1,500 firefighters were battling a separate fire in the south-eastern Var department that tore through roughly 7 sq miles in little more than a day. Authorities said the fire in the Gros Bessillon hills was stabilised on Sunday morning, meaning its perimeter had not expanded overnight. But unlike the Gironde fire, it had not yet been declared contained. Firefighting aircraft supported crews working to keep the flames away from villages among the vineyards, olive groves and wooded hills of the region known as Green Provence. About 2,500 people were evacuated as the fire threatened communities. The blaze was the fourth major fire to strike the central Var since 19 July. A separate, smaller fire near Brignoles earlier in the week forced the Hollywood actor George Clooney and his family, along with about 700 other residents , to evacuate before it was brought under control. View image in fullscreen Smoke above Montfort-sur-Argens, near Correns, in Var, on Saturday. Photograph: Manon Cruz/Reuters The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said France’s wildfires were generally under control but cautioned that conditions remained highly changeable. He announced that a national coordinator attached to the prime minister’s office would oversee reconstruction in fire-ravaged areas. More than 450 sq miles have burned across France since the beginning of the year. Fires in France and Spain alone have driven roughly a third of a million people from homes and holiday sites, emptied communities at the height of the summer and stretched firefighters, aircraft and emergency services across simultaneous disasters. The crisis is unfolding on the world’s fastest-warming continent. Europe has heated at more than twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service. Higher temperatures and prolonged drought leave forests and scrubland drier and more combustible, allowing fires to spread faster and burn more intensely. Human-caused climate breakdown doubled the likelihood of the extreme fire conditions that fuelled the French blazes, scientists at World Weather Attribution calculated in a rapid analysis on Thursday while the fires were still burning. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Andy Burnham promises to be relentless in tackling small boat crossings – video Immigration and asylum Burnham to be ‘relentless’ on small boat crossings after Ceuta crisis Prime minister says UK needs to ‘bring back that control’ and safe routes for refugees are necessary to tackle trafficking Alexandra Topping Political correspondent Sun 2 Aug 2026 14.16 EDT Last modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 14.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Andy Burnham has pledged to be “relentless” in tackling small boat crossings after tens of thousands of migrants entered the Spanish territory of Ceuta, and he said “safe routes” for refugees were necessary to tackle trafficking gangs. Speaking during a visit to Dover, the prime minister said he had been assured by the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, that approximately 98% of the estimated 50,000 people who entered Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta last week had now been returned to Morocco. But while that dealt “substantially” with the immediate issue, “of course there’s a broader issue about the Schengen area and our relationship with it”, he said, adding: “I would want to be in regular dialogue with the EU on those issues”. Asked if he wanted to change the tone of the debate on the issue by stressing the need for safe routes, he said the UK had to “deal with the issue rather than play politics with the issue” and make changes that would reassure the public. “The public don’t like the idea that the border looks like it’s not controlled. We need to bring back that control, but also we need to offer support for people who genuinely need it,” he said. “It’s about changing the whole approach, and slowly but surely we are putting in place those building blocks of a very different approach to this issue.” Last Wednesday was the busiest day for small boat crossings across the Channel so far this year, with 752 people arriving in the UK. Official provisional figures suggest 14,526 have entered the UK so far this year. This is 43% lower than the number recorded by this time last year (25,436) and down 14% on the same period in 2024 (16,903). “Progress is being made but we’re not complacent,” Burnham said. He said the number of National Crime Agency officers tackling organised immigration crime had more than doubled since the start of 2025, from 376 to almost 800. On Sunday the latest figures showed that more than 2,000 people had crossed the Channel in small boats since Burnham became prime minister. Home Office numbers showed 326 people arrived on Saturday in four boats, bringing the number up to 2,057 since he took over from Keir Starmer on 20 July. There were 1,962 crossings in the same period last year. On a separate visit to the National Crime Agency headquarters in Stratford, Shabana Mahmood said the government’s work to tackle small boat crossings were beginning to “bear fruit”. The home secretary has faced fierce opposition within the ranks of the Labour party over proposed immigration measures including doubling the time it takes to qualify for indefinite leave to remain from five to 10 years. But she said reform was needed “to address the pull factors that draw people into boats in the Channel”, adding: “I want to change the calculus. I want them to change their mind about whether they get on the boat in the first place.” She rejected calls to copy Spain’s response to the influx into Ceuta, in which tens of thousands of people have been returned to Morocco without processing any asylum claims. That was possible because Morocco and Spain share a land border and have an agreement in place. Mahmood said people smuggling and the shared waters of the Channel made things “trickier in many ways”. At least 72 people died trying to reach Ceuta, some of them drowning and others being crushed when attempting to climb the border fence. Sánchez called the huge influx “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity”. The surge of people, which took place over the course of just 24 hours from Thursday, overwhelmed the city of 85,000 people, triggered a political crisis for Madrid and led to an angry reaction from some EU countries, including calls for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone. On Saturday, Spanish police installed a 500-metre (1,640ft) floating barrier off its border ‌with Morocco to prevent others from making their way around the border. But Spain’s leftwing government has continued to come under pressure from right and centre-right governments already angry at its plan to regularise about 500,000 immigrants living in Spain . EU ministers have convened emergency talks for Tuesday . The leaders of 22 EU countries have demanded an emergency response, citing the need to prevent further uncontrolled crossings. The summit was called during a “sobering” meeting of officials representing EU member states and Frontex border agency experts on Saturday, as EU leaders sought to heal divisions in the bloc and restore a unified approach to migration. Isabelle Rose Welsh was the victim of a ‘sadistic’ campaign of abuse, the judge said. Photograph: Cleveland police/PA Police Cleveland police failed to arrest man who later killed two-year-old girl Harrison Simpson was subject of arrest warrant for breach of court order 18 months before killing girlfriend’s daughter Neha Gohil and PA Media Sun 2 Aug 2026 12.47 EDT Last modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 13.07 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Cleveland police failed to arrest a paedophile for breaching a non-molestation order, 18 months before he sexually assaulted and murdered and his girlfriend’s two-year-old daughter, a court heard. Isabelle Welsh died on 14 September 2025 after what police described as a “campaign of violence” against her. The two-year-old collapsed at her home in Teesside after weeks of abuse that left her covered in bruises and with 21 broken bones. The toddler’s mother, Alexandra Walker, 26, and Walker’s boyfriend, Harrison Simpson, 22, were convicted of murder and child cruelty on Thursday after a trial at Teesside crown court. View image in fullscreen Alexandra Walker and Harrison Simpson. Photograph: Cleveland police/PA Simpson was also convicted of sexually assaulting Isabelle before her death. Walker was cleared of that charge. The pair were jailed for life, with minimum terms of 28 years and six months for Simpson and 22 years for Walker, both minus time spent on remand. Cleveland police admitted that officers failed to execute a warrant issued by Teesside magistrates court for Simpson’s arrest in March 2024, according to the Sunday Times. Simpson had failed to attend court for breaching a non-molestation order, which is an injunction designed to protect victims of domestic abuse, when the warrant was issued in March 2024. It is understood the non-molestation order was in place after reports Simpson had harassed and threatened a woman. Cleveland police said in a statement: “Multiple inquiries and arrest attempts were carried out to try to locate and arrest him, but these proved unsuccessful.” It added: “We recognise the time Simpson had an outstanding arrest warrant is far from adequate. A review of this was immediately conducted upon his arrest for murder. “This review, along with a determination to continually improve our processes around suspect management, has led to a number of recent changes, such as ongoing improved visibility across the force around outstanding warrants, a comprehensive data system which tracks all outstanding warrants, and stringent oversight including a governance group led by a superintendent.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Preview latest after newsletter promotion At the sentencing, Justice Norton said Isabelle’s murder was “distressing” and said the two-year-old had endured a “sadistic” campaign of abuse. “Any death is a tragedy. The death of a very young child at the hands of those who should have cared for, protected, and loved her – as she no doubt loved them – is particularly distressing for all involved,” the judge said. A statement by the family of Isabelle Welsh previously said: “Isabelle should have had her whole life ahead of her, but she was taken from us in the most heartbreaking way. She was so loved and our lives will never be the same without her.” The senior investigating officer Det Ch Insp Steve Chatterton said the case was one of the worst he had dealt with. “The pain and suffering she experienced at the hands of Walker and Simpson was sickening,” he said. Photograph: Jack Taylor/PA View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham has paused the early release scheme initiated under his Labour predecessor but still faces pressure to act on prison overcrowding. Photograph: Jack Taylor/PA Prisons and probation Burnham to focus on keeping child rapists in prison as release scheme talks enter final day Review goes down to the wire after ministers speak with victims’ representatives and support services Alexandra Topping Political correspondent Sun 2 Aug 2026 12.27 EDT First published on Sun 2 Aug 2026 11.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Andy Burnham is focused on preventing the release of child sexual abuse perpetrators as part of the government’s early release scheme, as urgent talks on which serious criminals could be exempted go down to the wire. Government ministers are understood to have 24 hours to assess which criminals can be released early to free up prison space, with every exemption weighed up against the threat of the criminal justice system’s collapse. The prime minister halted controversial plans to release thousands of killers, rapists and sex offenders from prison in September, intended to ease critical prison overcrowding, during his second week in the role. He is keen to make as many exceptions as the small headroom in the prison estate will allow, the Guardian understands. Burnham wants to keep child rapists and other perpetrators of serious sexual abuse from being released early after ministers heard the concerns of victims’ representatives and support services who warned that a failure to put in place safeguards for abuse victims would put them at particular risk . A review of the scheme is expected to conclude by the end of Monday to give the Prison Service time to prepare, with a final decision on exemptions still to be made. But ministers are keenly aware that if no action is taken, prisons will run out of space, while exempting some criminals is likely to lead to further calls for others to also be kept behind bars, sources told the Guardian. The former justice secretary David Lammy, who brought forward the act that paved the way for the releases, previously warned that failing to implement it could leave no capacity across jails in England and Wales in November. The new justice secretary, appointed by Burnham on 20 July, is Alex Norris. The early release scheme – accompanied by a significant expansion in electronic tagging of offenders – is still expected to take place this autumn with an initial group of about 700, despite warnings by probation officers of potential chaos . It is likely to cause a headache for the new prime minister as he faces the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, in the House of Commons for the first time. A government source said: “If we don’t take any action, we will run out of room – it’s not sustainable at all.” It comes after the family of PC Andrew Harper expressed outrage that his killers may be eligible for early release. His mother, Debbie Adlam, said the proposed inclusion of two of her son’s killers – Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers – was “another letdown” for their family. View image in fullscreen PC Andrew Harper sustained fatal injuries while responding to a reported burglary in Sulhamstead, Berkshire, in August 2019. Photograph: Thames Valley police/PA New sentencing laws were passed under Keir Starmer’s government to ease a looming prison overcrowding crisis that ministers said could seize up the criminal justice system . Victims’ advocates are concerned that high prisoner numbers will limit the number of serious criminals who could be exempted. The former safeguarding minister Jess Phillips, a vocal critic of the scheme , said it was right that exemptions were being considered but there needed to be “a whole system change with how victims and risk is managed as the sentencing review goes forward”, which had to be carried out with victims’ agencies, probation officers and police. Under the Sentencing Act 2026 , which passed in January, from September some serious offenders will be eligible for release halfway through their sentences rather than two-thirds of the way through. Those convicted of less serious crimes can be freed after serving a third of their sentence instead of 40%. The new law also restricts the use of short-term prison stays, which will be replaced with probation and community orders – a move that some critics have said will put pressure on an already overburdened probation service. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Preview latest after newsletter promotion Will Burnham fix our barbaric prisons – or cave to rightwing populism? The answer is a tragedy | Simon Jenkins Read more Phillips said any review needed to examine not only the early release scheme but the presumption against short sentences. “Exemptions are an immediate safety crisis, but real in-depth work to make the situation better forever and be one based on risk and rehabilitation must be done,” she said. Claire Waxman, the victims’ commissioner for England and Wales, met Norris on Wednesday, and she told the Telegraph she welcomed his acknowledgment that victims had been let down and she was “cautiously more hopeful” about progress on answering her concerns. But prison reform groups, government officials and politicians reacted angrily to Burnham’s decision to pause the scheme, warning that abandoning measures to ease jail overcrowding could lead to the criminal justice system “collapsing under its own weight”. Ciara Bergman, the chief executive of Rape Crisis England and Wales, said centres had been supporting scores of victims through the “distress and terror of finding out that their rapists and abusers were due to be released … or in some cases already had been”. She said: “Victim-survivors should never have been put in this situation, not least because so little is known about the factors which make some more like to offend than others, and how sexual violence offenders can effectively be managed and monitored in the community.” A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said it was taking action to fix the prisons crisis, “caused by 14 years of Conservative neglect”. “We are pulling every lever to protect the public and cut crime,” they said, pointing to the building of new prisons, expanding tagging, strengthening community punishment and giving victims a say in offenders’ licence conditions. “We have paused changes due to start in September to conduct an urgent review to make sure we get this policy right for victims without running out of prison spaces.” Explore more on these topics Prisons and probation UK criminal justice Andy Burnham Labour news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Prisoner early release scheme paused by Andy Burnham may still go ahead Mahmood and Streeting accused of making ‘cheap jokes’ about prisoner early release scheme Expansion of electronic tagging in England and Wales will put public at risk, watchdog warns Ministers warned not to scapegoat prison staff over mistaken release of Hadush Kebatu Education cuts in prisons ultimately endanger the public, watchdog says Robert Jenrick’s call to arm prison officers is ‘nonsense’, governors say Prisons minister vows to end ‘toxic’ cover-up culture in England and Wales Staffordshire prison locked down after third violent incident in weeks UK prison officers to demand electric stun guns for dangerous jails Ban inmates from cooking after Hashem Abedi assault, says prison union Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-hits-targe.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5I9h4 Ukraine is taking the war 'back to where it came from' with drone strikes deep inside Russia, said President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday Image: REUTERS Advertisement Ukrainian drones rained down on numerous military, energy and civilian infrastructure sites deep inside Russia on Sunday, killing at least eight people overnight. Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces downed 635 drones over the course of the attacks. Two people were killed in the city of Engels on the Volga River when drones hit residential buildings. Another apartment complex in nearby Saratov City was also damaged. Three people were reported killed and two injured in the Udmurtia region (1,300 kilometers from Ukraine ), and another three killed and five injured in Belgorod according to local officials. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday said Kyiv had targeted an oil refinery in Saratov and a military base that is home to Russian long-range bombers in Engels. Zelenskyy said the attacks were his country's answer to Russian aggression and thanked Ukrainian forces for taking the war "back to where it came from." Kyiv said fires had damaged both sites and that its forces had also struck an oil depot in the western Kaluga region. Unverified video uploaded to social media sites purported to show fires burning at the Saratov oil facility. Why is Ukraine targeting Wildberries warehouses? Ukraine again targeted the online retailer Wildberries in its attacks, striking a logistics warehouse in Samara — more than 800 kilometers (500 miles) from Ukraine's front-line positions. Sunday's attacks on Wildberries were just the latest onslaught on the retail giant , which Kyiv says aids Russia's military. Kyiv has attacked nearly a dozen Wildberries warehouses since July 18. No casualties were reported at the facility and local management said that a fire at the site had been brought under control. Although the number of drones that Russia claims to have downed cannot be confirmed, the figure is indicative of the scale of Kyiv's effort to strike Russia deep inside its own territory as it defends itself against an army that launched a full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022. The Wildberries attacks are seen as an attempt to bring President Vladimir Putin 's war home to Russia's citizens, applying pressure to the country's already anaemic economy in hopes of finally ending Moscow's ongoing invasion . Skip next section Far-right politicians call for migrant expulsions, security reinforcement 08/02/2026 August 2, 2026 Far-right politicians call for migrant expulsions, security reinforcement Abascal called for the border with Morocco to be closed immediately Image: Gabriela Sardá Núñez/Europa Press/IMAGO The border crisis in Ceuta has sparked debates in Spain and across Europe about the Spanish government's migration policy. Many governments in Europe have sought to curb immigration, but Spain has pursued a different approach, recently announcing a plan to provide legal status to up to 500,000 undocumented migrants. Pedro Sanchez and his Socialist government have been heavily criticized this week by politicians from Spain's right and far-right parties. The leader of the opposition, the conservative People's Party's Alberto Nunez Feijoo, has traveled to the exclave, where he slammed Sanchez for failing to prevent the border rush. The leader of the far-right Vox party, Santiago Abascal, who was also in Ceuta on Sunday, blamed the Socialist government for the migrant surge, which he described as "an invasion." He said the surge was an "act of war" and an "attack on the sovereignty and security of Spaniards." Abascal also said Sanchez was "a danger" to the country, and called for the EU-Morocco agreement, which functions as a partial free trade area, to be scrapped. Far-right influencer and Member of the European Parliament Alvise Perez called for migrants to be expelled during a confrontation with a crowd of rival protesters in Ceuta. Much of the city's population is of Moroccan descent. Perez had to shelter in a bar before being escorted away by police. Sanchez and his government have also been criticized by other right-wing politicians in Europe, most notably Italy's Interior Minister Antonio Tajani. Italy has suspended free movement with Spain, even though both are part of the Schengen Area. https://p.dw.com/p/5I9jz Skip next section Most migrants return but Ceuta still on edge as death toll climbs to 72 08/02/2026 August 2, 2026 Most migrants return but Ceuta still on edge as death toll climbs to 72 Karl Sexton | Jenipher Camino Gonzalez Editor Between 50,000 and 60,000 mostly male migrants broke into Ceuta this week Image: Henry Nicholls/AFP Relative calm had returned to Ceuta on Sunday, but the city remained on edge following the deadly border rush. Local officials have warned that the city's recovery has just begun, while right-wing politicians are blaming the Socialist government in Madrid for chaotic scenes that unfolded this week in the Spanish North African exclave. Spanish Civil Guard ships were searching the waters around the city on Sunday for more bodies after between 50,000 and 60,000 migrants breached the border with Morocco. Nearly all of them had walked back to the Moroccan side of the border by Sunday, according to officials in Ceuta, normally home to around 84,000 people. At least 72 people died during the crush on Thursday and Friday, the Spanish government representative in Ceuta, Miguel Angel Perez, said. Some drowned, while others were killed in a stampede at a breakwater barrier and a border fence. Perez added that medical services have treated more than 1,000 people. He said while the situation in the exclave had improved significantly, work remained to be done for the city to return to normal. On Saturday, authorities installed a 500-meter (1,600-foot) floating barrier in the waters off Ceuta to boost border security, as well as reinforcing police and army patrols. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c141.text: Figure caption, Watch: Moment before helicopters collide while tackling Greece wildfires By Paulin Kola Â and Â Nikos Papanikolaou Published 2 August 2026, 16:21 BST Updated 1 hour ago Two crew members have been killed after two helicopters collided mid-air in Greece as they were battling wildfires, local authorities say. The two fatalities were a Danish pilot and a Greek fire service liaison officer. A British pilot and another Greek coordinator on the second helicopter survived. Video of the incident some 65 km (42 miles) west of the capital Athens, shows one of the Bell helicopters hitting the propellers of the other, which bursts into flames. Both fell into a ravine. Several fires have broken out in Greece this week, prompting mass evacuations. Several other European nations have suffered devastating wildfires after a succession of prolonged heatwaves. According to the Greek Fire Service, the two leased Bell helicopters collided while taking part in efforts to tackle a large wildfire burning on the Attica-Boeotia border. The crew members of one aircraft were rescued alive, while the second crew were recovered unconscious and later pronounced dead. Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis expressed his "deepest sorrow" over the accident. In a post on X, he said the loss of the Greek coordinator and Danish pilot "fills us all with grief". He also sent condolences to their families. According to protocol, all Bell helicopters across the country have been grounded, a source from the Ministry of Civil Protection told the BBC. The source added that the second Bell helicopter involved in the collision made an emergency landing in an area of low vegetation. "The two people on board, a British pilot and a Greek fire service liaison officer â escaped with minor injuries," the source said. "Both remained conscious and have been admitted to hospital, where they will remain under observation for 24 hours as a precaution." Erickson Air-Crane and Chinook helicopters, as well as Canadair water-bombing aircraft are continuing to carry out firefighting efforts. Early this week, France and Spain battled huge fires - two of the main ones were close to Madrid and Bordeaux respectively. Those have now been contained, though they are still burning. Some 300,000 people who were evacuated have started to return to their homes. In Greece, media reports describe "a titanic battle" along a swathe of territory that includes Porto Germeno, Psatha, Fokida, Megara and Kefalonia, where more than 500 firefighters have been struggling to bring the situation under control over the past 72 hours. Most wildfires are sparked by people, whether intentionally or accidentally, but climate change is making the conditions for them more common. Last winter was mild and wet, encouraging vegetation growth, which has then dried out in successive hot spells, generating fuel for wildfires. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czjl.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Officials say two people were killed in the attack on Gaza City By Jamie Whitehead Published 2 August 2026, 15:46 BST Updated 3 hours ago At least 13 people, including several children, have been killed in the latest strikes on Gaza, Palestinian officials have said. Gaza's Civil Defence Authority said Israeli military aircraft carried out the attacks on Gaza City, Khan Younis and Deir el-Balah. It was the second successive night of Israeli strikes on the territory, and it comes days after Hamas accepted a disarmament plan, which would see the Palestinian group hand over its weapons to US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace. A spokesperson for the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), said it was targeting military operatives in Gaza, and two Hamas militants were killed. The Israeli Energy Minister, Eli Cohen, said on Sunday that no deal had been reached to stop attacks on the Gaza Strip, a territory now under 70% Israeli control. Cohen added that he saw a need for the strip to be placed under the full control of Israel if Hamas did not disarm - despite the Board of Peace plan for Israel to pull out of the territory - the Reuters news agency reported. In a post on X on Sunday, the IDF said it had killed two Hamas commanders, one from the elite Nukbha force, and one from the Maghazi Battalion. The IDF also said killed another Hamas militant from the Jabalia Battalion in northern Gaza in a separate attack last week. It said all three were planning to attack Israeli targets. Palestinian health officials said two people, including a child, were killed in a strike on a residential building in Gaza City, while another person was killed near Jabalia in northern Gaza. A father, mother and their nine-year-old son were killed after a strike on a house in Khan Younis, and a man and woman died after their apartment block was struck in Deir el-Balah. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed since a supposed ceasefire came into effect last October. Image source, Reuters Image caption, In Deir al-Balah, residents assess the damage of the strikes Last week, President Trump said the Board of Peace had reached an agreement for the "complete disarmament" of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza. On Friday Trump insisted that Israel was "very happy" with the proposed agreement, describing it as a "big step for the Middle East". But Israel remains deeply sceptical about Hamas' willingness to give up its weapons or its control in Gaza. Far-right Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir dismissed the draft as "not acceptable". It is part of the second phase of a US-brokered Gaza ceasefire plan that aims to end the war in Gaza. The 20-point plan, unveiled in September last year, included the creation of the Board of Peace to oversee the agreement's implementation, as well as the disarmament of Hamas, withdrawal of Israeli troops and reconstruction of Gaza. A 15-point road map was also published on Friday, which sets out the final steps for implementing the agreement. What's in the Gaza peace deal roadmap? Published 2 days ago Bowen: Plan for Hamas to disarm faces big obstacles, yet it offers rare hope for Gaza Published 2 days ago The roadmap, which has not yet been implemented, states: "A process shall begin to inventory and store heavy weapons, military production sites, weapons depots, and tunnels". It says this is conditional on Israel meeting its commitments under the initial ceasefire agreement. How the weapons would be handed over to the Board of Peace is not yet clear, although it is believed that all heavy weapons and other military hardware would be moved into storage and managed by the Palestinian National Committee - a group of independent technocrats to which Hamas has agreed to hand over power. The committee has so far been working from Cairo and has not entered Gaza. Israel has destroyed more than 1,500 buildings in areas of Gaza that have remained under its control since the ceasefire, satellite images seen by BBC Verify last November showed. The actual number is likely much higher, with imagery unavailable for some areas. According to UN estimates, around 60 million tonnes of debris has been generated since October 2023. Hamas - proscribed by the UK government as a terror organisation - has governed the Gaza Strip since 2007. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c998.text: Image source, Zelenskiy / Official Image caption, President Zelensky described the latest Ukrainian strikes as "our long-range sanctions" against Russian facilities he says finance Moscow's war By Jaroslav Lukiv Published 3 hours ago Ukraine has said it carried out overnight strikes deep inside Russia, hitting a major oil refinery and an airfield that houses Russian strategic aviation. President Volodymyr Zelensky said the Engels airfield and the refinery, both in the Saratov region some 600km (373miles) from Ukraine's border, were hit. An oil depot was also struck in Kaluga region and a drone launch site in Bryansk. Russia said eight people were killed in the Ukrainian strikes, and 635 drones shot down or intercepted. It also reported yet another strike on a warehouse of Russia's biggest online retailer Wildberries. Meanwhile, Moscow said its forces attacked overnight two Ukrainian ports and two vessels in the Black Sea. Later on Sunday, Ukraine said one person was killed in a Russian strike on a postal terminal near the north-eastern city of Kharkiv. Both Russia and Ukraine have recently intensified attacks focusing on major cities, energy facilities and warehouses, as the vast front line remains virtually static and US-led mediation attempts to end the war have shown no breakthrough. Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Trump now 'not sure' about letting Ukraine build Patriot missiles Published 1 day ago Nine killed in strikes on Kyiv, as Ukraine sinks Russian container ship Published 1 day ago In Sunday's post on social media, President Zelensky described the latest Ukrainian strikes as "our long-range sanctions" against Russian facilities that he says finance Moscow's war. He said the Engels airfield and Saratov oil refinery were "strategic facilities". The Ukrainian military said in a separate statement that its attack triggered a blaze at the airfield - one of the main bases of Russia's strategic aviation. It said Tu-95MC and Tu-160 bombers were regularly using Engels to launch missile strikes against Ukraine. Saratov regional Governor Roman Busargin admitted that "a drone attack caused damage to civilian infrastructure in Saratov and Engels". He later said that two people were killed. Separately, three people were reported killed in a Ukrainian drone attack on a civilian vehicle in Russia's Udmurtia region, and another three in the Belgorod region bordering Ukraine. Image source, Rozetka Image caption, Ukraine's major online retailer Rozetka said its largest warehouse was hit by Russian drones overnight In the Samara region, Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev described a strike on a Wildberries warehouse that caused a fire as "yet another terrorist act" by Ukraine. The governor reported no casualties in the overnight attack. In recent weeks, Ukraine has hit a number of Wildberries logistics hubs, describing them as legitimate targets providing the Russian military with drone components, navigation equipment and other gear. Wildberries - often described as Russia's Amazon - employs some 48,000 people. Ukraine's attacks are reported to have had a serious impact on the Russian economy, especially on hundreds of small and mid-sized businesses using the retailer. Meanwhile, Russia has been recently targeting warehouses of Ukraine's Nova Poshta postal company and major online retailers like Rozetka. Rozetka said its largest warehouse was hit overnight by Russian drones, but reported no injuries. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/c1719p.text: At the scene of deadly Moscow bomb blast At the scene of deadly Moscow bomb blast Close At least three people have been killed and 21 injured after a homemade explosive device was detonated at an Italian restaurant in Moscow, Russian state media reports, quoting security officials. The blast happened at about 20:00 local time (17:00 GMT) on Kudrinskaya square near the city centre. The National Anti-Terrorist Committee said a woman carrying the explosives tried to enter the restaurant, which was holding a private event, but was stopped by a security guard. The BBC's Russia editor Steve Rosenberg reports from the scene in Moscow, where the explosion happened. Washington State Governor Bob Ferguson declared a statewide emergency and burn ban on Saturday morning. "Our state is facing a very serious situation with multiple fires, and our hearts go out to Washingtonians who are losing their homes", Ferguson said. According to officials, no injuries or fatalities have been reported. Spokane is the state's second most populous city. https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/08/02/a-bu.text: Menü Kereső A bucsai mészárlás felelőse lehetett a moszkvai éttermi robbantás célpontja Külföld Nyilas Gergely Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom A bucsai mészárlásért Ukrajna szerint felelősnek tartott tábornok lehetett a célpontja annak a robbantásnak , amelyet egy moszkvai étteremben hajtottak végre szombat este. Orosz források szerint a merényletnek 21 sérült mellett három, ukrán lapok szerint öt halálos áldozata van, köztük egy biztonsági őr, valamint az a nő, aki a gyanú szerint a helyszínre vitte a bombát, de az őr nem engedte be. A feltételezések szerint ő nem feltétlenül tudta, hogy mi van a bevitelre szánt dobozban: a repeszekkel teli bombát távirányítással robbantották fel. Az Oroszországból külföldre kényszerített Meduza szerint Alekszandr Csajko lehetett a merénylet célpontja, aki születésnapját ünnepelhette a Balzi Rossi nevű belvárosi étteremben. Erről egy ukrán Telegram-csatorna is beszámolt egy rövid videót mutatva a születésnapi előkészületekről. Az bizonyos, hogy egy exkluzív, zárt rendezvényt tartottak, amelyet feltűnően sokan őriztek. Csajko a múlt héten lett 55 éves, de mást is ünnepelhetett: idén májusban nevezték ki a 2015-ben létrehozott Légi és Űrerők (VKSZ) parancsnokává. Csajkónak azonban sokkal közvetlenebb szerepe is volt az elmúlt négy és fél évben az Oroszország által Ukrajna ellen indított háborúban. 2022-ben ő volt a Keleti Katonai Körzet vezetője, az ehhez tartozó egységek szállták meg a háború első napjaiban Kijev több elővárosát, többek között Bucsát, ahol az orosz katonák bizonyíthatóan több száz civilt öltek meg . A mostani kinevezéséig a vezérkari főnök helyetteseként is szolgált Csajko az EU szankciós listáján is szerepel. Az éttermi rendezvényen a hírek szerint több magas rangú katonai, hírszerzési tiszt is részt vett, de arról, hogy a vendégek közül kik sérültek meg, nincsen nyilvános információ. A Kincstár informatikai szakértői az észlelést követően haladéktalanul leválasztották a fertőzéssel érintett szervereket, és megtették a szükséges intézkedéseket a további károk elkerülése érdekében – közölte a Telex érdeklődésére a Magyar Államkincstár. A jelenlegi információk alapján az incidens során adatvesztés nem történt, az incidens nem érinti a Kincstár által kezelt ügyféladatokat. Az incidens következtében egyes belső felhasználók, munkatársak számítógépén lévő állományok titkosítottá váltak. A szakértők jelenlegi információi szerint a támadás orosz szerverekről történt. Az esemény teljes körű kivizsgálása a Nemzeti Kiberbiztonsági Intézet szakértőinek közreműködésével zajlik, összehangoltan dolgoznak a támadás elhárításán és a biztonságos működés mielőbbi helyreállításán. Az incidens bejelentése a Nemzeti Adatvédelmi és Információszabadság Hatóság (NAIH) felé megtörtént. https://english.radio.cz/osoblazka-a-nar.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Osoblažka: A narrow-gauge railway through a magical corner of Czechia, straight out of a fairy-tale Facebook Twitter It's one of Czechia's best-kept secrets: a narrow-gauge railway that snakes through a fairy-tale landscape in the country's far northeast. We took a ride on the Osoblažka to find out what makes it so special. All aboard! Finding Osoblaha on a map of Czechia is no easy task. The village of around one thousand people lies in a former Moravian enclave within Silesia. Nearly destroyed during the final battles of World War II and later affected by the expulsion of its German population, the region became one of the country's most remote corners - geographically and in the public’s imagination. Yet today, its historic narrow-gauge railway has turned it into an unforgettable summer destination. Wait for the green light! "If you're travelling with us for the first time, please don't touch the door handle until the green light comes on!" Driver Lukáš Weiss reminds the passengers before the last Friday evening train departs from Třemešná on its winding 20-kilometre journey to Osoblaha. Although the railway's vintage carriages are decades old, safety has improved significantly, including locking the old-style door handles while the train is moving. Once everyone is aboard, Lukáš rushes to the locomotive. His shift begins early in the morning and doesn't end until after he spends the night at Osoblaha station and drives the first train back the following day. "I’m not looking too good," he says. Standing in the sweltering locomotive cab, he smiles apologetically at the sweat soaking through his red uniform shirt. As the train rolls through the countryside, he points out the wildlife outside. "There's a roe deer running on the left, but that's a fallow deer on the right! We often see cranes here too. It's beautiful around here." A railway revived the region The Osoblaha region remains refreshingly untouched: no crowds, no teeming car parks, no overpriced ice cream or tourist traps. Visitors are welcomed by a more serene life. They may find a unique Jewish cemetery, a regional museum, and the Osoblažka itself - a narrow-gauge railway that has been running since December 1898. Nicknamed the "Railway of One Hundred Tuns," it actually winds through even more bends than that. More than just a tourist-train For local resident Anna Žigová, travelling home with her three granddaughters from Krnov, the train is part of everyday life. "Sometimes we take the bus, sometimes the train, but this is much better for the children," she says as the girls watch the countryside pass by in the evening sun. The railway brings together locals, commuters, tourists, railway enthusiasts and families. On board, passengers can even buy refreshments. "Would you like a coffee with a wafer? Or perhaps a non-alcoholic beer?" steward Michal Majetny asks as he walks through the train; a pleasant and unexpected service on such a small regional railway. A labour of love "Where do all the passengers come from?" conductor Roman Vrábel ponders. "During the school year it's children going to school and people commuting to work. In summer there are mainly tourists. And when the steam train is running, some people travel one way on the steam service and return on this diesel train." Roman normally works as a dispatcher at Ostrava's main railway station, but spends his free time working on the Osoblažka. "Yes, I earn a little extra, but above all I enjoy it. I like people." His new colleague Rostislav is making an even bigger career change, leaving teaching behind to train as a locomotive driver after moving into Bohušov station. Meanwhile, the volunteers running the historic steam trains and those operating the regular passenger service work seamlessly together. "When the organisation decided to take over regular passenger services from Czech Railways for local people and tourists, they simply asked those of us working on the steam trains whether we'd join them," says operations manager Pavel Schreier, who is spending the day shovelling ash from a steam locomotive. "The answer was obvious." Like the peaceful countryside it passes through, the Osoblažka has a quiet charm of its own. Free from crowds and commercial attractions, this little railway has become one of Czechia's most beautiful and unique summer journeys. https://lasvegassun.com/news/2026/jul/19.text: What to know about the Tate brothers, social media influencers facing rape and trafficking charges Published Sunday, July 19, 2026 | 4:48 a.m. Updated Monday, July 20, 2026 | 1:07 p.m. LONDON (AP) — Influencer brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate appeared before a federal magistrate Monday in Miami for the first time since prosecutors in the United Kingdom brought new rape and sex trafficking charges against them. Their lawyer said the brothers will fight extradition to the U.K. and suggested their arrest in Miami was politically motivated without explaining why. A U.S. district judge will consider in the weeks ahead whether they meet the conditions for extradition. U.S. Magistrate Lauren Louis set another hearing for July 27. The brothers have denied wrongdoing. Here are some things to know about the Tate brothers: Who the Tate Brothers are Andrew Tate, 39, and Tristan Tate, 38, are dual U.S.-British citizens known for their social media empire promoting wealth, male dominance and misogyny. Andrew Tate is a former professional kickboxer and self-described misogynist who has amassed more than 10 million followers, most of them boys and young men, on X. He has been banned from platforms like YouTube, TikTok and Instagram for violating hate speech guidelines. He also runs an online academy where he says he teaches young men how to get rich and attract women. Tristan Tate is also a former kickboxer. The brothers are avid supporters of U.S. President Donald Trump. What the Tates are charged with Andrew Tate and his brother have faced multiple charges in the U.K. and Romania , where they lived from 2016 to 2025. British prosecutors said the new charges relate to alleged offenses that took place between 2010 and 2017. They said Andrew Tate was charged with seven further counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, three counts of assault and 19 charges for offenses relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography. Tristan Tate was charged with one count of sexual assault, two counts of rape and three counts of arranging or facilitating sex trafficking. The Crown Prosecution Service said in a statement it “has requested the extradition of the Tates from the U.S. They have been arrested and await extradition proceedings to the U.K.” The Tates already face previous charges of rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other alleged victims in the U.K. between 2012 and 2015. In June, a U.K. High Court judge threw out a legal bid by the Tates to be told the names of their accusers. In Romania, the siblings were arrested in late 2022 along with two Romanian women. The four were accused of participating in criminal schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations and the Romanian case hasn’t gone forward because of legal and procedural problems. The case hasn’t been closed, and there is also a separate legal case against the brothers in Romania. Andrew Tate has repeatedly claimed that prosecutors in Romania have no evidence against him and that there is a political conspiracy to silence him. How the extradition process could work The brothers appeared Monday before a magistrate judge in Miami, where they were being held in federal detention. Bail is rarely granted to those held for international extradition, and their lawyer said he expects they will remain jailed for the time being. In the coming weeks, a U.S. district judge will consider whether they meet the conditions for extradition. The ultimate decision about whether to order the extradition will fall to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. While the State Department has some discretion to deny extradition requests from the U.K., it has granted nearly every British request since ratifying a strengthened extradition treaty in 2007. One exception came during Trump’s first term, when the U.S. declined an extradition request for the wife of a former American diplomat involved in a fatal crash in England , citing diplomatic immunity. The rejection prompted an international outcry. Why the Tates were in the U.S. British police previously sought the Tates' extradition to the U.K. once their legal proceedings in Romania concluded. But in February 2025 they were allowed to leave Romania after authorities lifted travel restrictions, and they flew to Florida on a private jet. Romania's foreign minister said at the time that a U.S. official in the Trump administration had expressed interest in the brothers’ legal case in Romania. Trump said he knew “nothing about” the case when asked if his administration pressured the Romania government to release the Tates. https://www.lahainanews.com/wire/?catego.text: Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate arrested in Miami, US Marshals Service tells AP By AP | Jul 19, 2026 FILE - Andrew Tate, right, and his brother Tristan arrive an event, April 11, 2026, in Miami. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson, Pool, File) By ALANNA DURKIN RICHER Associated Press Influencer brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate, whose social media empire promoting wealth, male dominance and misogyny has made them among the world’s most polarizing internet personalities, were arrested Saturday in Miami as British authorities sought their extradition on rape and sex trafficking charges. The brothers were taken into custody by the U.S. Marshals Service on a sealed warrant, agency spokesperson Brady McCarron told The Associated Press, placing the United States at the center of an international legal saga that has stretched from Romania to Britain. Britain is seeking their extradition on rape and trafficking charges British prosecutors announced Saturday that they were seeking the brothers’ extradition on charges alleging they raped and trafficked women between 2010 and 2017. The dual U.S. and British citizens moved to Romania in 2016. They were arrested there in 2022, accused of participating in schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations and the Romanian case hasn’t gone forward because of legal and procedural problems. Last year, they were allowed to leave Romania and flew to Florida on a private jet. The brothers are expected to appear in Miami’s federal court early next week, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke to on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive law enforcement operations. The pending charges in the United Kingdom accused the brothers of abusing women in an area north of London, where they grew up. Their lawyers had said they denied the allegations. Joseph McBride, an attorney representing the Tate brothers, said in a phone interview Saturday evening that he has not been able to speak with his clients but called the new charges out of the U.K. “filth and slander” intended to derail defamation lawsuits filed by the brothers in the U.S. “They’re pulling out all the stops to make sure these guys never get their day in court,” McBride said. “We are confident that once a competent judge sees the facts, and once the Department of Justice confronts this egregious abuse of its own authority, Andrew and Tristan Tate will walk free. America does not do Britain’s political dirty work.” Tate has been banned from social media platforms for hate speech Andrew Tate, 39, first reached a mainstream audience as a contestant on the U.K. reality television show “Big Brother” in 2016. He was removed from the show when a video surfaced that appeared to show Tate assaulting a woman. He and his brother Tristan Tate, 38, are vocal supporters of U.S. President Donald Trump. Andrew Tate has amassed over 10 million followers on X but has been banned from platforms like YouTube, TikTok and Instagram for violating hate speech guidelines. His most widely condemned rhetoric includes comments that women who are sexually assaulted should bear some responsibility for their attacks, graphic descriptions of how he might attack women and criticisms of people who seek treatment for mental illness. The Tate brothers have consistently denied allegations of abuse and human trafficking, claiming that violent and misogynistic statements have been taken out of context or were intended as jokes. In a statement Saturday, the U.K.’s Crown Prosecution Services said that in addition to the charges publicly announced against the brothers in 2025, involving alleged crimes against three women, it was bringing a total of 38 new charges related to “four further victims.” Both brothers are accused of rape and human trafficking. Andrew Tate faces an additional charge of profiting from prostitution, and 19 charges “for offences relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography,” according to U.K. authorities. “There is no place for male violence against women and girls, and we will continue to work tirelessly to support victims and investigate all reports made to us,” said Karena Thomas, an assistant chief constable of the Bedfordshire Police, which investigated the case. ___ Associated Press writer Savannah Peters in Santa Fe, New Mexico contributed to this report. https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/20/nato-rus.text: Russia has carried out a wave of ballistic missile and drone strikes on Ukraine, killing at least eight people and injuring dozens. Ukrainian drone attacks destroyed two warehouses in Russia and an oil depot, in the deadliest strikes inside Russia in over two years. NATO's military committee chief said the alliance is prepared for any Russian move including "touching Poland or the Baltic states." Russia launched one of its largest ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv, while Ukrainian drones carried out their deadliest strikes inside Russia in more than two years — stoking fears of wider escalation and further strains on oil supplies. Russia has carried out a wave of ballistic missile and drone strikes on Ukraine, killing at least eight people and injuring dozens, Ukrainian officials said Sunday. At least one person was killed, and 15 were wounded in Kyiv, where residential buildings, warehouses, a supermarket, and a dormitory were damaged, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram on Sunday. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the raid on Kyiv was "one of the most massive ballistic attacks" since Russia launched a full-blown war against the country in 2022. Separately, three more people were reportedly killed during Russian strikes in the northeastern Kharkiv region on Sunday, as Ukraine's Air Force said it intercepted 18 missiles and 108 of 126 drones, with the salvo including 25 ballistic missiles. The missile barrage came after Ukrainian drone attacks on Saturday destroyed two warehouses belonging to Wildberries, Russia's largest online retailer, and an oil depot, reportedly killing at least nine people and injuring more than 80 , the deadliest Ukrainian strikes inside Russia in over two years. Russia's Defense Ministry said 379 drones were downed across 19 regions. Zelenskyy described the facilities targeted as used by Russia to supply "sanctioned components for drone production and navigation equipment." The tit-for-tat strikes mark a sharp escalation in a campaign that has increasingly targeted Russia's energy complex. Ukrainian naval drones hit two large Russia-linked crude tankers , the Louise 1 and Banda, in the Black Sea last week — a waterway that accounts for more than 20% of Russia's seaborne crude flows. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, chair of the NATO Military Committee, said in an interview with the Kyiv Independent published on Saturday that the defense alliance is prepared for any Russian move against its eastern flank. Baltic states, such as Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, and Poland have stepped up defenses of critical infrastructure and transport systems as warnings mount of potential Russian attacks. Moscow "would lose a lot, much more than what they could gain, just by touching Poland or the Baltic states. And we are ready," the alliance's military chief told the Ukrainian news outlet on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Ankara on July 7. Cavo Dragone said that the alliance's first objective remains a ceasefire and negotiations toward "a long-lasting peace for Ukraine," while acknowledging allied stockpiles are being drawn down and pointing to joint ventures with Ukraine's defense industry as a way to sustain support. Kyiv, meanwhile, has pressed for more air defense aid. "Protection against ballistic missiles is our constant and top priority right now," Zelenskyy said, adding that interceptors are needed every day. The U.S. and Ukraine have reached a political agreement on licenses to produce Patriot interceptor missiles, he said last week, adding that he hoped production could begin by the end of the year. Any hit to Russia's crude exports could compound a market already strained by the U.S.-Iran conflict and disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, analysts say. Renewed hostilities in the Gulf region pushed the Brent futures contract above $90 a barrel on Monday, as investors braced for a return to all-out war. "Any reduction in Russian crude exports could push prices far higher than $100," Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates, told CNBC last week .
