Photograph: Marty Melville/Reuters New Zealand New Zealand legislation making English an official language ridiculed as ‘pathetic’ Passing of bill gives English same status as Māori and sign language but, with it already spoken by 95% of country, critics call it ‘a pointless exercise’ Eva Corlett in Wellington Mon 3 Aug 2026 00.06 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 02.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Legislation recognising English as an official language of New Zealand has been passed by parliament, prompting derision from linguists and legal experts and a now-viral broadside from a Māori MP who called it “pathetic”. The English language bill became law on 30 July giving English, which is spoken by 95% of the country, the same official status as te reo Māori (Māori language) and New Zealand sign language. The bill formed part of a coalition deal between the centre-right National party and the minor populist New Zealand First party, whose leader, Winston Peters, has long opposed affirmative initiatives for Māori. National needed to strike deals with New Zealand First and another minor party, Act, in order to govern. Why is the New Zealand government cutting Māori words from some school books? Read more Ministry of justice officials had recommended that lawmakers should not pass the bill, because there was “no evidence to support concerns about the use or status of English as an official language”. Te reo Māori and New Zealand sign language had become official to protect linguistic minorities, they said. However, the coalition government and the major opposition Labour party voted in favour of the bill, with minor opposition parties the Greens and Te Pāti Māori against. During the debate, Green MP Tamatha Paul said the bill was “a pathetic waste of the responsibility of this house”, in a speech that has generated millions of views online. Paul said the coalition government were “snowflakes” who saw the word Aotearoa – the Māori name for New Zealand – and “shiver in their boots”. Speaking on behalf of New Zealand First during the final reading, MP Casey Costello denied the law was trivial or unnecessary. “This is a practical measure. It aligns the statute book with longstanding practice, and provides a clear statement about the status of English within New Zealand’s official framework,” Costello told the house. Peters, who is also the foreign affairs minister, has previously argued the bill was necessary because the use of Māori in public services was causing confusion. Labour, meanwhile, has previously said it was against the law but had voted in its favour in order to move on from a “needless culture war”. New Zealand coalition votes to make English an official language as critics decry ‘cynical’ bill Read more Dr Sidney Wong, a linguist and post-doctoral fellow at crown research centre Te Pūnaha Matatini, said official language status was given to languages in need of protection and services, but English was not under any threat. “The main reason why this bill was put in place was based on ideology – there was this perception that English was under threat, that it doesn’t have the prestige, and it needs that sort of legislative protection. But it doesn’t need that,” he told the Guardian. Wong said if the government was really interested in protecting English, it would be funding research into the way New Zealanders spoke English, but the law did not address this. “That’s where the money should be going. Not spending time on this 70-word legislation that’s not going to benefit anyone.” Dr Dean Knight, a law professor at Victoria University of Wellington, said the legislation was “a pointless exercise” that made no difference legally or practically as English was already the dominant language. “Folk who got excited by this performative law-making will be disappointed to learn that, despite the dog-whistling and claims from its promoters within parliament, it does not mandate priority to the English language in government communications and elsewhere,” he said. “Like before, Aotearoa New Zealand will continue to have three official languages.” Explore more on these topics New Zealand New Zealand politics Māori Winston Peters Asia Pacific Language news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Russotwins/Alamy Bird flu Suspected mass bird flu deaths found in second state as Murray Watt warns ‘this is the beginning’ Environment minister says Australia has ‘long and difficult journey’ and says more mass mortality events likely Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Lisa Cox and Petra Stock Mon 3 Aug 2026 05.13 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 05.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Aerial surveillance has detected mass bird deaths in a second Australian state in another suspected escalation of the spread of deadly H5 bird flu . The environment minister, Murray Watt, said on Monday Australia had begun “a long and difficult journey” as CSIRO analysis confirmed Australia’s first mass mortality event at Baudin Rocks off South Australia’s coast. Hours later, Victorian authorities said aerial observations had identified a “cluster” of dead and sick greater crested terns in the Glenelg River estuary near Nelson and across Lawrence Rocks, in the state’s south-west, over the weekend. If samples taken from the Victorian birds return positive results, it would be Australia’s second confirmed mortality event from the deadly disease that has devastated wildlife populations globally. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “I want to level with people: this is the beginning of what is likely to be a long, difficult journey in terms of the impacts on wildlife,” Watt said on Monday. Aerial surveillance over Baudin Rocks identified about 50 dead and 30 sicks birds, the South Australian government said on the weekend. Samples taken from five greater crested terns and a silver gull were sent to the CSIRO’s Centre for Disease Preparedness and confirmed positive on Monday. “The reality is, you can’t stop native and wild birds flying around, and you can’t stop wild animals moving around, and that will mean more mass mortality events like the one we have now seen,” Watt said. View image in fullscreen Federal environment minister Murray Watt. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP “What we can do, and what we have been doing, is build up the resilience of the populations of our native birds and mammals.” In Victoria, the state’s chief veterinary officer, Dr Graeme Cooke, said aerial surveillance had made observations that were “consistent with what was recently reported in South Australia”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion First Australian mass mortality event suspected as deadly bird flu virus rapidly escalates among native birds Read more Speaking to media on Monday afternoon, Cooke said aerial and ground surveillance in the south-west, near Portland and Nelson, in the past few days showed “a clear increase in the number of dead terns along that part of the coast”. “Last week we talked about individual detections; the first cases of the H5 bird flu in Victoria. We are now seeing a change as the disease spreads out and has further impacts,” he said. The region is home to an important breeding colony of Australasian gannets as well as seal colonies and the Glenelg estuary and Discovery Bay, an internationally significant wetland site. South Australia’s environment minister, Emily Bourke, said she was also concerned about a confirmed case of H5 bird flu in a petrel found in the Coorong, one of several new locations where the deadly disease has been detected in the state. The migratory petrel was one of 18 new cases in SA confirmed by CSIRO on Monday, which included the samples from six birds at Baudin Rocks. The new cases included a silver gull in Glenelg, two greater crested terns at Troubridge Island, a silver gull at Southend, a greater crested tern at Monarto and six greater crested terns on Pages Islands. The Coorong is a large area that is home to internationally significant wetlands that support populations of waterbirds and migratory species. “That confirmed location is of concern because it is where waterbirds are also located,” Bourke said “So it’s going from seabirds, but also potentially now into where we know a lot of waterbirds are nesting and using this space as a safe haven.” Explore more on these topics Bird flu Victoria New South Wales Birds Wildlife news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Seven suspected new bird flu cases are ‘evidence of spread’ into Australian wildlife, experts warn Deadly H5 bird flu found in local Australian seabird for first time Bird flu?! Photograph: Barry Iverson/Alamy Oil Oil prices plunge and Europe’s stock markets rally after Trump calls off Iran strikes Brent crude drops by 5% after US president said talks on Middle East peace deal would resume Business live – latest updates Julia Kollewe Mon 3 Aug 2026 04.44 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 05.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Crude oil prices fell sharply and European stock markets rallied on Monday after Donald Trump cancelled planned strikes on Iran to focus on negotiations for a peace deal. Brent crude was trading 5% lower at $83.50 a barrel by mid-morning, after falling as low as $81.55 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate dropped more than $5 to $79.47 a barrel. Both global oil benchmarks jumped more than 20% in July after fighting between the US and Iran resumed, and as attacks on several tankers in the strait of Hormuz revived fears for the safety of vessels transiting the important shipping passage. UK economy faces recession if strait of Hormuz remains closed, EY warns - business live Read more Trump said late on Saturday on his Truth Social platform that Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked for time to complete a deal that would lead to “the Immediate, Complete and Total” reopening of the strait and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat”. On Sunday, he said talks with Tehran would start on Monday . Kathleen Brooks, the research director of the broker XTB, said the drop in oil prices should help support markets. “This will ease inflation fears and could also act as a dampener on bond yields, which rose sharply last week, especially at the long end, where 30-year US Treasury yields jumped to their highest level for 19 years ,” she added. In a positive start to August, European shares edged higher. The pan-European Stoxx 600 index rose 0.4%. Energy stocks declined 2%, while travel and leisure shares gained 2.1%. Tony Sycamore, a market analyst at the investment platform IG, said: “The bigger focus is whether this week turns into a rinse and repeat of last week – with hopes of a deal collapsing as Iran digs in its heels and continues to leverage its control over the strait, potentially through an attack on a US base or a tanker transiting the waterway.” Two tankers laden with Saudi oil crossed the Bab el-Mandeb strait out of the Red Sea over the weekend, while traffic in the strait of Hormuz slowed after reports of vessel attacks, according to shipping data. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre has reported three more tanker attacks since Saturday. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Preview latest after newsletter promotion On Sunday, the oil cartel Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies, known as Opec+, agreed to increase oil production by about 188,000 barrels a day from September, unwinding output cuts. However, because of the export disruptions from the Gulf, Russia and Kazakhstancaused by the Iran and Ukraine wars, production increases by Opec+ have had little impact on prices. Elsewhere in the markets, the Japanese yen hit a three-month high after Tokyo and Washington launched a joint operation to support the currency. Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Donald Trump Blanche formally rescinds Trump’s $1.8bn ‘anti-weaponization fund’ ahead of nomination hearing Todd Blanche issues formal order terminating measure widely derided as a ‘slush fund’, in move that could clear path for his nomination as attorney general Associated Press Mon 3 Aug 2026 00.46 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Acting US attorney general Todd Blanche issued a formal order late on Sunday terminating Donald Trump’s $1.8bn “anti-weaponization fund” to compensate his political allies, a move that follows weeks of negotiations with two Republican senators who were blocking his nomination to become attorney general. While Blanche has repeatedly said publicly that the fund was dead, the justice department had resisted formally confirming that in writing. That had drawn concern from lawmakers that it could be revived in some form, especially after Trump expressed continued support for the idea. A spokesperson for Texas Senator John Cornyn, one of the senators holding up Blanche’s nomination, confirmed the agreement. The other GOP senator, North Carolina Senator Thom Tillis, did not have immediate comment. The announcement comes ahead of a Senate judiciary committee vote on Blanche, which is scheduled for Tuesday. Trump vows to push $1.8bn slush fund as Senate committee set to reconsider AG nomination Read more “My team and I have met with committee members and Senators over the past several weeks and addressed any concerns or outstanding questions,” Blanche said in a post on X. “We have enjoyed good faith discussions, and as a result issue the following order.” The order says that “although the acting attorney general has repeatedly advised Congress through testimony, including under oath, as well as in written responses, that the Fund is not moving forward, and the Department has repeatedly represented to district courts that the Fund is not moving forward, today’s Order officially rescinds the May 18, 2026 Order.” The document released by Blanche on Sunday night also limits the scope of another provision of the settlement that provided broad immunity for Trump and members of his family from tax audits . It clarifies that the tax audit immunity agreement “applies only retroactively” to claims open at the time of the settlement and does not protect the president from examination of future tax filings. The two sides have been negotiating for weeks, but Trump has said repeatedly during the talks that he thinks the fund should go forward . Earlier on Sunday evening, Trump said that people who had faced charges from the January 6 attack on the Capitol and could have benefited from the fund had “their lives destroyed”. “This would be a reimbursement for the pain that they suffered,” Trump said. “A lot of people like it.” Explore more on these topics Donald Trump Trump administration US politics news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Composite: Getty and Shutterstock Hungary Hide the Pain Harold and Rubik’s Cube creator among social media’s picks for Hungarian president Newly elected Tisza party asked public to put forward names, which have ranged from the sensible to the bizarre Lili Rutai in Budapest Mon 3 Aug 2026 02.10 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 02.11 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Eszter Jámbor, a 46-year-old content creator who focuses on sex education, had a different kind of question for her Instagram followers last week: who did they think should be Hungary’s next president? The suggestions ranged from reality TV stars to bodybuilders and the Victoria’s Secret model Barbara Palvin. But another anonymous online poll asking Hungarians the same question revealed the most popular candidate to be András Arató, a retired electrical engineer who found global online fame as a meme: Hide the Pain Harold. Katalin Karikó, the Nobel-winning biochemist, and Ernő Rubik, the inventor of the Rubik’s cube, were also popular choices. “Obviously, politics are serious, but there’s also room for a bit of humour, for that sense of freedom that a part of Hungary is now feeling after the past 16 years,” said Jámbor. Since ousting its rightwing populist leader Viktor Orbán in a milestone election earlier this year, the central European country has been living through a period of rapid political change. The man who succeeded Orbán, Péter Magyar , has begun enacting some of the reforms he promised on the campaign trail: taking “propaganda broadcasts” on public media off air and removing Orbán’s allies from the heads of the prosecution, police and military. Perhaps the biggest fight, however, was the one Magyar picked with the then president, Tamás Sulyok, who was forced to sign a constitutional amendment ending his own term in July. After Sulyok, who was appointed by Orbán’s Fidesz party, left his post, the new prime minister called for suggestions. “Let’s make a decision together,” he said in a Facebook video. View image in fullscreen Péter Magyar speaking in front of EU and Hungarian flags. Photograph: Robert Hegedus/MTI/AP Lawmakers from the ruling Tisza party will elect the new president in parliament, but Magyar encouraged “public figures, NGOs and civilians” to put forward names. Less than 24 hours after opening the discussion, however, Magyar said he had nominated the chess grandmaster Judit Polgár for the role. The move prompted a popular backlash criticising his hastiness and Polgár, subject of the Netflix documentary Queen of Chess, turned him down . Magyar apologised for the “miscommunication”, but polls in the aftermath showed his party’s popularity down by 3%. “The process is still imperfect,” says Imre Ónádi, a 55-year-old architect who created a Facebook page and group to support the candidacy of the conservative politician Péter Márki-Zay, who unsuccessfully ran against Orbán in the 2022 general election. Ónádi welcomed Polgár’s refusal “not because she isn’t the right person, but because her nomination was announced without discussion”. He thought Magyar’s apology was a good sign. “It seems they take into account what the population says. That’s democracy, after all,” he added. For now, emboldened by the grassroots success of the Tisza party in the April election but lacking any official channel for recommendations, that discussion is happening in social media posts, online polls and open letters. However, it is unclear whether these popular recommendations are reaching Tisza and how the administration intends to handle them. While the government has set up an online consultation space to discuss an update on traffic regulations, there is no official channel for presidential recommendations, despite Magyar’s encouraging words. “I have a political fever,” said Jámbor, undeterred. “I’ve been voting since I was 18. But I finally feel like I have a say in what happens in the country.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day Preview latest after newsletter promotion ‘Attack on civil society’: why Viktor Orbán’s favourite thinktank is in crisis Read more Any Hungarian over the age of 35 with voting rights can become president, but Magyar has said his candidate must be independent of political parties. He has met two popular contenders: the well-known historian Ignác Romsics and Botond Fülöp, a lawyer who uncovered the child abuse pardon scandal that ended the presidency of Katalin Novák in 2024 . It is expected that Tisza’s 141 parliamentarians will propose and swear in a candidate before 19 August. Technically, Fidesz, which has 44 members of parliament, could nominate its own candidate, but the party has said it will not take part in the election as it believes Sulyok’s dismissal was unlawful. No other party has enough MPs to nominate someone for the position. Amnesty International Hungary believed that the removal of Sulyok was justified, said Áron Demeter, the head of communications and campaigns in the organisation’s Budapest office. “But we could debate Tisza’s method,” he added, arguing that the government could have pursued impeachment to remove the president instead of pushing through an amendment to the constitution. With its so-called supermajority in parliament, Tisza “shouldn’t do the same things Fidesz did, with the same tools, just because their goal is nobler”, Demeter said. Photograph: True Story Movies Review Atlas of Disappearance review – forensic quest for thousands of forgotten victims of the Spanish civil war Researchers employ technology in a bid to identify and retrieve remains in Spain’s Valley of the Fallen, in Manuel Correa’s emotional documentary Phuong Le Mon 3 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 02.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google P erched on the Sierra de Guadarrama mountain range overlooking Madrid is the Valle de los Caídos , a colossal memorial site constructed under the Franco regime. Supposedly a symbol of atonement and reconciliation, it has been criticised as an emblem of fascist glorification; it was where Franco was buried until his exhumation in 2019 . There are, however, tens of thousands more bodies are trapped inside; in the aftermath of the White Terror, the corpses of those executed under the dictatorship were clandestinely removed from mass graves and deposited in the monument’s crypt. Both thought-provoking and heartwrenching, Manuel Correa’s documentary follows three grieving families and their fight to rescue their loved ones from this horrifying limbo. Here, architecture emerges as a means of oppression. Through examining various construction blueprints, the film lays bare how the crypt was specifically designed for maximum inaccessibility. The bodies of the victims were meant to languish, hidden away, in perpetuity, as does the evidence of the dictatorship’s barbarity. To combat these efforts to bury history, Correa founded the Office of Documentary Research, where activists, geographers, and architects wade through the fog of secrecy with state-of-the-art technology. View image in fullscreen Rows of numbered niches containing unknown remains. Photograph: True Story In their hands, architectural tools are a path to liberation, as activists use forensic devices to counteract governmental delays in exhumation and retrieval. Using digital maps and 3D renderings, the clinical presentation of their work makes for a staggering contrast to the emotional testimonies of the victim’s relatives; both are driven by an unalterable sense of justice. The film ends on the evocative image of water seeping through the crevices of the Valle de los Caídos, causing internal structural damage. Monuments might crumble to the ground, but the memories of the perished will live on forever. Photograph: Peter Turnley/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A soldier in Red Square, Moscow, during the attempted coup in 1991. Photograph: Peter Turnley/Getty Images Book of the day History books Review The August Coup by Robert Service review – the drink-soaked collapse of the Soviet Union This brilliant account of attempts by the old guard to take back control captures the ludicrousness of it all beautifully John Simpson Mon 3 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google M arxist-Leninist rule in Russia lasted 74 years, and in August 1991 it effectively collapsed in just three days: clear evidence of how hollowed out it had become. In the period that followed, Russia tried parliamentary democracy and unalloyed capitalism, then sank back into autocracy. Now it’s struggling under a wholly unnecessary war against its neighbour and former possession, Ukraine. Why did the system of Lenin, Stalin, Khrushchev and Brezhnev vanish so fast, without a fight? Because that’s how regimes fall in Russia: look at tsarism in 1917. (It almost happened again in June 2023, when the warlord Yevgeny Prigozhin’s men marched on Moscow largely unopposed; Vladimir Putin might have gone the way of Nicholas II had he not made some pretty wholesale promises to Prigozhin, then allegedly blown him up two months later.) Mikhail Gorbachev came to power in 1985 with the intention of saving the USSR. Instead, he oversaw its death. He was a charming, decent man but no visionary, and the two medicines he brought to the patient’s bedside, perestroika (restructuring) and glasnost (openness), proved to be wholly ineffective. The brief coup of August 1991 against him, headed by Vladimir Kryuchkov, the boss of the KGB, was the kneejerk response of a bureaucracy that knew things were going wrong but had absolutely no idea what to do about it. It failed quickly, and Gorbachev was back at his desk within days, but the coup had damaged him fatally. Four months later, at the end of 1991, he was bundled out of power by the tough, brutal, boozy muzhik, Boris Yeltsin. Robert Service, author of The August Coup , is the English-speaking world’s foremost historian of 20th-century Russia and Bolshevism. His biographies of the three major Soviet leaders, Lenin, Stalin and Trotsky, are outstanding, even in that crowded field. In writing about the death of the system that these prodigies and monsters helped to create, Service has displayed a remarkable grasp of the vast sources, and a delightfully clear writing style which makes even the complexities of Soviet bureaucracy easy to understand. Compared with his earlier subjects, the story of the coup against Gorbachev and the collapse of the USSR is moderately simple; but Service guides the reader through the chaos of the collapsing system and the machinations of the coup leaders with ease and grace. The acting president, Gennady Yanayev, was supposedly in charge, but he had been drinking solidly for an entire day After the fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989 and the loss of the various Soviet satrapies in eastern and central Europe , the USSR was falling apart, and Gorbachev, as its president, was shedding power and influence. No one knew how many Soviet republics would break away, and Gorbachev’s plan for running the rump of the union was bitterly contested. Yeltsin was the president of the Russian Republic, the largest, richest and most effective part of the old USSR. The two men were in angry contention. The coup leaders didn’t support either of them: they wanted to go back to a system which would restore as much Soviet power as possible. The assumption at the time was that the KGB had led the coup to protect its own interests, but Service demonstrates that Kryuchkov, the KGB boss, was much more concerned about the overall collapse of the Soviet system. And anyway, many KGB officers refused to join the coup. I was lucky enough to be in Moscow during those extraordinary days. Service captures the ludicrousness of it all beautifully. The coup leaders lost their faith in what they were doing almost immediately, and many of them didn’t have much to begin with. They argued, betrayed each other, or were paralysed by fear or torpor. Most of the people involved left some account of what happened, so the records available to Service were particularly rich. He provides us with a graphic description of the fatal press conference that the plotters gave at 5pm on the first day of the coup. The acting president, Gennady Yanayev, was supposedly in charge, but he had been drinking solidly for an entire day and his hands were visibly shaking. The press conference was broadcast live on state television, so everyone could see the condition he was in. After that, failure was certain. The basic reason it collapsed, though, was that the plotters didn’t manage to get hold of Yeltsin. It was easy enough to imprison Gorbachev at his palatial residence, Zarya, on the Crimean coast, where he was holidaying with his wife Raisa and their daughter; but Yeltsin remained free, and had use of the Russian republic’s Moscow headquarters, known as the White House. You might expect communist plotters to be good at cutting communications and taking over the media, but no one stopped Yeltsin from phoning allies and friends around Russia and across the world. Nor did they try to prevent him making his famous speech from a tank in front of the White House, condemning the coup and pledging to support democracy. It was a good speech, and the television coverage of it was seen worldwide. Again, no one pulled the plugs. Journalists like me were able to broadcast live throughout the coup. Yeltsin stayed inside the White House, mostly protected by a small crowd of unarmed demonstrators whose numbers dropped as the first night wore on and the rain came down. Yet Yeltsin suffered from the same weaknesses as many of the plotters. In the lobby of the White House I begged to be allowed to go up to his office and interview him, but was told he was too busy speaking to world leaders and organising the opposition. Later, the former Soviet foreign minister Eduard Shevardnadze arrived to see him. When he came out of the building an hour afterwards, he announced that Yeltsin had told him he would defend Russia’s freedom to the last drop of blood in his body. Stirring stuff. Three years later I reminisced with Shevardnadze about it all. He laughed. “When I got into Yeltsin’s office, he was lying unconscious on the floor with a couple of empty vodka bottles beside him.” But what about him fighting to his last drop of blood? “What do you think would have happened if I’d come out and told you I couldn’t speak to Yeltsin because he was dead drunk?” Such was the chaos and absurdity surrounding the death of the Soviet Union. In the days that followed no one had any idea where authority lay. The famously brave and entrepreneurial cameraman Rory Peck and I marched into KGB headquarters, the Lubyanka, and filmed in Kryuchkov’s own office. After that we even filmed among the ultra-secret KGB files. The next day Rory offered to buy the contents of the Central Museum of the Revolution for a million dollars. Only the fact that the official in charge couldn’t find a bank prepared to accept that much cash stopped the deal going through. We tend to forget the details of this pivotal episode. Perhaps Russia’s troubled history since 1991 has wiped them from our memories. Now Service has brought his magnificent grasp of Soviet history to the task of chronicling the ludicrous way it ended: not with a bang, but with the clink of vodka bottles. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Ireland was first alerted to the threat when the Russian spy ship Yantar visited Irish and UK waters in 2024. Photograph: Royal Navy/PA View image in fullscreen Ireland was first alerted to the threat when the Russian spy ship Yantar visited Irish and UK waters in 2024. Photograph: Royal Navy/PA Ireland Is Ireland’s unprotected ocean the weak link in European defence? Russian presence in Irish waters underscores the fact that, rather than being out of sight and out of mind, the country is on the frontline Jennifer Rankin in Cork and Brussels Mon 3 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 05.21 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google For a long time, Ireland paid little attention to its surrounding seas, a vast maritime area, 10 times the size of the land. Alarm bells began ringing only when a Russian spy ship, the Yantar, began visiting Irish waters. The vessel, ostensibly a research ship, is believed to be capable of attaching spy equipment to undersea cables and has advertised its presence. While loitering in the Irish Sea in 2024 , the ship remained over a gas pipeline connecting Ireland and the UK and turned on its transponder, as if broadcasting its proximity to critical infrastructure. In recent weeks, Irish officials have also noticed a rise in Russian shadow fleet vessels traversing the north Atlantic in order to circumvent British and French waters, where controls have been stepped up. For officials, the Russian presence in or near Irish waters underscores that Ireland, which has long viewed itself as protected by geography – out of sight and out of mind – is really on the frontline. And the threat is broad. Irish waters are busy: dense with shipping lanes, gas pipelines and transatlantic internet cables, which helped lure US tech companies to make Ireland their European headquarters. Nearly 75% of transatlantic subsea cables pass through or close to Ireland’s exclusive economic zone , the 200-nautical mile space where it has sovereign rights over natural resources, which is seven times greater than the land mass. It has more limited jurisdiction over an even broader area. Map of Ireland and Britain showing Ireland’s exclusive economic zone. When Ireland took charge of the EU’s rotating presidency last month, it had a message. While its totemic neutrality is not up for debate, the days of Ireland’s slumber on defence are over. Security is listed as a priority of Ireland’s six months chairing the Council of the EU. Ireland would be working with other European nations “on shared objectives and priorities in defending our critical infrastructure, and making sure that we are focused on security more broadly”, Ireland’s foreign minister, Helen McEntee, told reporters last month. “We are not immune to any threat.” That sounds unremarkable, but signals a reassessment of Ireland’s approach to defence. In February, McEntee published Ireland’s first ever maritime strategy, which aims to end Ireland’s “sea blindness” – the sense that security was purely about the land. Officially, it aims to ensure Ireland can defend its maritime domain, including critical undersea infrastructure. View image in fullscreen ‘We are not immune to any threat,’ said Helen McEntee, the foreign minister, who has published Ireland’s first maritime strategy. Photograph: Bryan Meade/EPA There is still a long way to go. “We are dependent on the goodwill of friends and neighbours,” said the retired Irish naval officer Caoimhín Mac Unfraidh. “But it wasn’t always the case and it won’t always be the case.” During a 29-year career in the Irish Naval Service, Mac Unfraidh commanded two ships, the LÉ Orla and the LÉ Eithne. Both were decommissioned in 2022 along with a third vessel. He described the maritime strategy as “a good effort”, but feared spending remained “minimalist”, despite pledges for sonar and radar equipment. “What is needed is that sort of overarching vision for a maritime nation to have a navy worthy of its name. And that means new ships, with new capabilities, recruitment campaigns and the establishment of several more bases.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Preview latest after newsletter promotion UK signs ‘rebooted’ defence agreement to protect Irish waters Read more In 2025, Ireland’s government confirmed only two ships were in operation out of a fleet of eight, partly because of a staffing crisis. The broader neglect of the military was highlighted earlier this month, when Volodymyr Zelenskyy turned down an offer from Dublin to send 27 light-armoured combat vehicles to Ukraine. “The cost of restoring them is higher than the value they would provide,” the Ukrainian president said. Irish government officials stress that Ireland has pledged €1.7bn (£1.4bn) in defence capital spending for 2026-30, a 55% increase on the previous period. And the government believes it has turned a corner on naval recruitment, with an increase in new joiners leading to a 12% increase in personnel in 2025, compared with the previous year. But Ireland remains the lowest defence spender in the EU, at a time when other countries are sharply increasing budgets. In 2024, Ireland spent just 0.2% of its gross domestic product on defence, far behind the 1.3% EU average and notably lower than neutral Austria (0.6%). EU officials have offered sotto voce criticism. The former European Commission vice-president Margrethe Vestager, who was responsible for tech policy, warned Ireland in 2022 that it had a responsibility for the maritime zone: “No one can be a weak link of our chain of protection.” In 2025 a former Estonian president, Toomas Hendrik Ilves, excoriated Ireland’s then president Michael Higgins after he criticised Nato’s “appalling” appeal for higher spending in response to the Russian threat. “Do these people have any sense of self-awareness, their privileged geography or the appropriateness of even commenting as the beneficiary of implicit Nato security?” Ilves said. View image in fullscreen Members of the Irish navy form a guard of honour for the arrival of Pope Francis in Dublin, August 2018. The Irish Naval Service was formed in 1946. Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Reuters Despite being an island nation, the sea was nobody’s political priority. Ireland gained independence in 1922, but the British retained control of Irish waters until 1938. Ireland did not have a fully fledged navy until 1946. Eoin McNamara, at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs, observes: “National security tends to be very divisive politically in Ireland, without bringing a whole lot of political reward, aka votes.” Last year, the Nato-critical leftwinger Catherine Connolly won a landslide to become Ireland’s president. During her campaign she compared Germany’s military spending to the 1930s and said she was concerned about arms spending and the “militarisation” of the EU. Meanwhile, people see the cost of living, housing and immigration as the most important issues facing Ireland, according to a recent poll from More in Common . Foreign and security issues were barely on the radar: 5% cited the war in Ukraine and 4% defence. “There is a lot of momentum from public opinion to focus on these bread-and-butter domestic issues,” McNamara said. Defence, he said, was “the insurance policy of the economy”, alluding to the profound economic shock posed by disruption to internet or energy cables. “I don’t think that has reached public opinion yet.” Explore more on these topics Ireland European Union Europe Russia Nato features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/03/cuba-.text: Cuba's power grid failed on Sunday, causing another nationwide blackout, a state energy company said in a social media post.As the lights suddenly turned off across the capital Havana, residents who were sat outside to get some respite from the summer heat audibly groaned en masse.Cuba has been suffering rolling power cuts due to ageing equipment and a US energy embargo that halted regular deliveries of fuel for power stations.State-run UNE said there was a "total disconnection" of the national electricity system, plunging the country, including the capital, into abrupt darkness.This is just the latest in a series of total collapses of the electricity grid.Just 24 hours ago, the whole west of the country went dark.The power cuts have made normal life almost impossible, with each outage also meaning that water supplies trickle away and ceiling fans slow to a halt.It is a growing strain for a society used to adversity but now stuck in a months-long crisis that has no obvious end in sight.Residents in the worst-affected areas have vented their frustrations by setting piles on trash on fire or banging on pots and pans.The Ministry of Energy said that protocols to reactivate the grid were underway.Washington has authorised the arrival of only one Russian tanker, carrying 100,000 tons of crude, which came in March. Those reserves have since been exhausted.In addition to enacting an oil blockade, the Trump administration has ramped up sanctions against Cuban state-owned businesses, prompting many foreign firms to suspend operations in the country.The United States has also indicted former president Raúl Castro, brother of revolutionary leader Fidel Castro, over the downing of two civilian planes three decades ago.Talks between Havana and Washington appear to have made little in the way of progress.Havana has enacted a series of free-market reforms to give the economy a boost.

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/03/myanm.text: Myanmar's detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi met with the nation's Red Cross representative on Monday, the president's office said, the first publicised meeting between her and a foreign official since she was ousted in a 2021 military coup.The military deposed Suu Kyi in February 2021, jailing the Nobel Peace Prize laureate and triggering an ongoing civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people on all sides.The coup leader and former junta chief, Min Aung Hlaing, was installed as civilian president in April following highly restricted elections.Later that month, Suu Kyi, now 81, was moved to house arrest after Min Aung Hlaing said he had commuted the rest of her sentence.She was detained on a host of charges which rights groups say were concocted to sideline her and her popular National League for Democracy party.The president's office said in a statement that Arnaud de Baecque, the Resident Representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) to Myanmar, met with Suu Kyi on Monday morning.In photos released by the president's office, Suu Kyi is seen shaking hands with a man who appears to be de Baecque.Another image shows Suu Kyi cutting a birthday cake, and yet another shows the cake with text reading: "Happy Birthday Aunty Suu."The images could not be immediately verified by the AFP news agency but AI tools found no instances of fabrication."We are happy to see her photo like this if it's really her meeting with the ICRC. We can know now that she's alive," a veteran politician of her party told AFP on condition of anonymity."However, Aunty should be released immediately as she's being detained unlawfully," the politician said.Proof of lifeAuthorities have not disclosed the exact location of Suu Kyi's detention in the capital Naypyidaw, nor how many years of her sentence remain.Her son, Kim Aris, a British national, has sought independently verified proof of his mother's life after she was transferred to house arrest.He says he has not heard from his mother, who remains massively popular inside Myanmar.Since the coup, Myanmar has been largely ostracised by the international community, and the 11-nation Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) has excluded the country's leadership from high-level summits.But neighbour Thailand has been leading an effort to bring the once pariah state back in the diplomatic fold, both bilaterally and through the regional bloc.Since his change in position, Min Aung Hlaing has travelled to India, China and ASEAN member Laos, and he is scheduled to make an official visit to Thailand this week.Despite the diplomatic outreach, the continued detention of Suu Kyi remains a major sticking point for some nations.The ASEAN bloc has pressed for its special envoy to meet Suu Kyi, but so far Myanmar has refused.Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told reporters last month that Myanmar's Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe had assured his regional counterparts during a trip to Thailand that Suu Kyi was "in good health.""We have been told she has been taken care of well but it needs to be proved," Sihasak added.

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/03/trump.text: Iran's foreign ministry said on Monday there were currently no negotiations with the United States but talks were under way with Oman over the management of the Strait of Hormuz."We are not currently negotiating with the United States. Our negotiations are with Oman to secure passage through the Strait of Hormuz," said foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei during a weekly press briefing.That statement contradicts US President Donald Trump who said that new negotiations with Iran would begin on Monday after he decided to hold off on striking the Islamic republic to pursue a deal to end the war entering its sixth month.Trump told reporters on Sunday that the talks would cover the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies that has become a sticking point in the conflict, and the denuclearisation of Iran.For its part, Iran said it was nearing a deal with Oman over a new route through the strait, where a tanker reported an explosion nearby on Sunday, underscoring the continued volatility of the strategic waterway.Oil prices fell on Monday at the opening of Asian trade after Trump announced the new negotiations, with West Texas Intermediate dropping 4.7% to $80.72 (€69.99) per barrel.Washington and Tehran have been at war since 28 February, when the US and Israel launched surprise strikes against Iran, though months of on-off diplomacy have led to periods of relative calm.Following a return to strikes last month, fears had mounted that the fighting could escalate once again. Trump had threatened to hit Iran "very hard" and was reportedly considering renewed attacks including against energy infrastructure, with US embassies across the region on alert.Trump pulled back from that threat on Saturday, saying the "perimeters" of a deal were there."Now what we're doing is we're talking to them in the form of a negotiation. It begins tomorrow afternoon," Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One on Sunday, without providing details of the venue or participants in the talks.The US president said he had been asked by Iran as well as US partners Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar to hold off on the strikes, which he claimed would have been "the biggest attack since World War II."Iranian media denied that Tehran had asked Trump not to strike.A previous ceasefire deal that included the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz fell through and Iran has since tightened its control over the waterway.The US president said at the start of the conflict that the war was necessary to deal with Iran's nuclear programme. Western nations accuse Iran of seeking a bomb, though Tehran insists the programme is entirely civilian in nature.'Exchange of views'Iranian lawmaker Hassan Ghashghavi, spokesman for the parliament's national security commission, said on Sunday that mediators were trying to revive the US-Iran memorandum of understanding that was agreed in June.That agreement was not intended as a final peace deal, but as a stepping stone to negotiations on a comprehensive agreement, though it did include provisions on Hormuz."They know that the main issue and, in fact, the key to the matter right now is the issue of the Strait of Hormuz, so yes, there is an exchange of views," Ghashghavi said.Posting on X, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said: "We must strive to compel the enemy to remain committed to what it has signed."Deal with Oman?Before the war, there was free passage for all vessels through the Strait of Hormuz, but Iran closed the strait during the war and now insists on retaining control and charging tolls, something the US rejects.That dispute sparked the return to strikes last month, as Tehran refused to let ships travel any route other than one which hugs the Iranian coast.On Sunday, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei told state television that a deal was close with Oman, which sits on the other side of the strait, over a new route through it."We are now going to reach an understanding on a route acceptable to both sides, neither the northern route nor the southern route, but one that respects the sovereign rights of both sides and safeguards our national interests and security," he said.He insisted though that such an agreement did not mean the reopening of the strait.Maritime trade tracking firm Kpler said on Friday that traffic through Hormuz had dropped sharply.On Sunday, a tanker off the coast of Oman reported hearing an explosion near the vessel, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) Centre reported, adding that the vessel and crew were all safe.

https://www.dw.com/en/myanmar-aung-san-s.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IAOK An image released by Myanmar's junta appears to show Aung San Suu Kyi shaking hands with a Red Cross representative Image: picture alliance/dpa/Myanmar President Office via AP Advertisement Myanmar's detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi met with a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross on Monday, marking one of the only publicly confirmed contacts between the 81-year-old Nobel laureate and an outside party since the military ousted her government in February 2021. The meeting, held in the capital Naypyitaw with ICRC resident representative Arnaud de Baecque, was announced by Myanmar's military-backed government, which released four photographs of the encounter. What do we know about the meeting? Two images show Suu Kyi shaking hands with and meeting de Baecque in a sparsely furnished room. The government did not disclose further details of what was discussed. The former leader met with an ICRC representative in Naypyidaw Image: Myanmar Government spokesperson/Handout/REUTERS Two other photos offer a rare glimpse into her circumstances: Suu Kyi is shown cutting a pink birthday cake in what appears to be her residence, with a clothes rack and storage boxes visible in the background. The cake's inscription — "Happy Birthday Aunty Suu" — suggests the images may have been taken around her 81st birthday in June. While it could not be independently verified when or where the photos were taken, AFP said AI analysis found no signs the images were fabricated. One of the images shared by Myanmar's government showcases a cake. Image: Myanmar President Office/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance When was Aung San Suu Kyi last seen in public? Suu Kyi has had no confirmed public sightings since her 2021 detention, and her exact whereabouts and details about her health have been difficult to determine. She is serving a 27-year sentence on charges her allies say were politically motivated. In late April, following elections that installed former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing as president , authorities said her sentence had been commuted by one-sixth as part of a broader prisoner amnesty and that she had been moved from prison to house arrest. Despite that shift, the new administration has largely resisted outside access to her. A May request from the Philippines, on behalf of the regional Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) bloc, to allow a special envoy to visit Suu Kyi was turned down. Pressure for access has been building from other ASEAN members as part of broader efforts to resolve Myanmar's political crisis, now compounded by a civil war that followed the coup. Suu Kyi's younger son, Kim Aris, who lives in London, has led an online campaign with Myanmar democracy activists demanding proof that his mother is alive and in good health, saying he has gone years without hearing from her. Myanmar's junta said in December that she was "in good health." The ICRC did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the meeting, according to Reuters. https://www.dw.com/en/fact-check-russian.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5I5eL A major disinformation campaign in the run-up to the elections is misusing the logos of established German media outlets and fabricating scandals involving German politicians Image: X Advertisement Eric Stehr was unsure what to think when he first saw fake videos about himself. He describes his reaction as "mixed feelings," somewhere between amusement and concern, laughter, and helplessness. "I don't want something like that online," he told DW. "But at the same time, I know there's nothing I can do about it." A German student, Stehr is running for the state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt as a candidate for the socialist Left party. Being second on the party list, he has a good chance of winning a seat in the election on September 6. But social media posts about him have falsely claimed that: He murdered his grandmother to inherit her apartment ( archived video on archive.org ) He killed a webcam model out of jealousy ( archived video on archive.org ) He organized underground LGBTQ+ sex parties at a German university ( archived video on archive.org ) He helped Bauhaus University Weimar give better grades to students from western Germany ( archived video on archive.org ) The false reports have been cleverly designed so that they appear to come from major German media outlets, including the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung , Stern TV , ARD and Spiegel TV . But the videos are as false as the allegations they make. Fake videos on X are making false allegations against Stehr, the Left Party candidate running in the Saxony-Anhalt state election Image: Screenshot: X.com A spokesperson for the police confirmed to DW that Stehr is not under investigation and has not been suspected of murder. Meanwhile, a Bauhaus University Weimar spokesperson confirmed to DW that there are no reports of alleged university sex parties or an alleged grading scandal. More than 180 fake posts ahead of elections According to DW Fact Check findings, the videos are part of the Russian influence operation known as Matryoshka, also referred to as Operation Overload. DW Fact Check has identified more than 180 fake posts on X, Bluesky and TikTok ahead of the upcoming elections. The data comes from a detailed archive maintained by the anonymous investigative collective Antibot4Navalny , which was originally founded to expose disinformation targeting late Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny and now tracks Russian influence operations online. DW reviewed several fake posts published since June 24. Notably, the campaign operates only on weekdays, with disinformation activity dropping off on weekends. Many of the posts target candidates running in the upcoming German elections in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania , Lower Saxony and Berlin , all scheduled for September. The votes are seen as an indicator of Germany's political mood and a test for the country's recently reshuffled federal government. Operation Matryoshka reaches new level Observers were not surprised to see Germany become a target of the campaign, but the scale of the operation has raised concerns. "This influence campaign has been active across multiple platforms since September 2023," said Julia Smirnova, researcher at the Berlin-based Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy (CeMAS). "Its targets have included Germany's federal election, elections in Moldova and Armenia, and the Olympic Games in France." Operation Matryoshka, named after the traditional Russian nesting dolls, seeks to manipulate public opinion through fabricated media content Image: Sascha Steinach/IMAGO What is new, Smirnova said, is the focus on relatively obscure individual candidates in local elections. "It is unusual for Russian influence campaigns to target specific candidates in regional elections." According to her observations, candidates from all parties have been targeted, except for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) . "What we're seeing now ahead of the state elections is a continuation of Russia's long-term strategy: Supporting parties perceived as more Russia-friendly while discrediting other parties and candidates," said Smirnova. Pablo Maristany de las Casas, a specialist in foreign information manipulation and interference campaigns at the London-based Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD), sees similar patterns. Like Smirnova, he says the narratives mirror earlier Russian influence operations. The messages, he argues, are once again "pro-Russian, anti-German and anti-EU." Who is behind Operation Matryoshka? While no definitive link to the Russian state has yet been established, there is evidence that Russian-speakers are behind some of the posts, according to Maristany de las Casas. For example, a Spanish-language post on X was found to contain a revealing clue: The post, which targeted candidates Lydia Hüskens and Andreas Silbersack of the Free Democratic Party (FDP), abbreviated their party's name as "SvDP," which would the Russian version: Svobodnaya Demokraticheskaya Partiya . A revealing clue lies in the abbreviation: in this post, the Free Democratic Party is referred to by the Russian abbreviation "SvDP" Image: X The OSINT research group Gnida Project , which investigates Russian disinformation campaigns, has previously linked Matryoshka to Russian actors. According to its findings, the operation is technically and operationally connected to Storm-1516, a well-known unit reportedly controlled by Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, and which was also active in the lead-up to Germany's federal election in 2025 . For Smirnova, the evidence points strongly in one direction. "With a very high degree of probability, this is a Russian campaign carried out on behalf of the presidential administration," she said, before adding that such operations are often executed by private companies specializing in digital marketing and political influence campaigns. How can Matryoshka fakes be distinguished from real media reports? The fake videos are professionally produced, but small inconsistencies often reveal that they are imitating established media brands. Key questions can help identify manipulated content: Is the video published on an official account belonging to the media outlet? Do the design and typography match the outlet's actual branding? Where does the footage come from, and does it support the story being told? Does the video present any verifiable evidence for its claims? In the current wave of fakes, these questions quickly expose a familiar pattern: Fabricated stories, stolen footage, cloned logos, and imperfect copies of genuine video formats. Many of the discrepancies become apparent only upon closer inspection. What narratives are being spread ahead of the elections? The campaign's messaging broadly falls into two categories. Discrediting candidates: In one case DW spotted a video about Berlin Mayor Kai Wegner ( archived video on archive.org ) of the Christian Democrats (CDU), in which he is falsely accused of murdering a professional tennis player. The voice of the video is AI-generated and no evidence is provided. Berlin police confirmed to DW that no professional tennis player had recently been killed in the city and that there are no investigations involving Wegner. Videos promoting a wide range of false narratives are posted on X, as in the case of the fake video about Berlin Mayor Kai Wegner Candidates from the CDU, the Social Democrats (SPD), Greens, the Left Party, and the FDP have also been targeted with false allegations of corruption, drug use, and, in dozens of cases, fabricated sex scandals. Deepening divisions between eastern and western Germans: One fake video masquerading as a Eurostat report ( archived video on archive.org ) claims that a large majority of western Germans consider reunification a "historic mistake." The supposed survey is not described in any detail, and no evidence of its existence can be found. In a statement to DW, Eurostat said: "This is a fake video. Eurostat did not produce it. Eurostat did not conduct the "survey" mentioned in the video." In fact, genuine polling paints a different picture of western Germans sentiments: According to an ARD DeutschlandTrend survey from October 2025, 64% of respondents in western Germany said they were satisfied with the state of German reunification. The campaign is also promoting a narrative of a supposedly deepening divide between eastern and western Germans Image: X Numerous other posts claim that eastern Germans face systematic discrimination, that eastern Germany receives less investment in security and infrastructure, or even that experts predict a new division of Germany by 2030. One video goes so far as to claim there are plans to build a new Berlin Wall. None of these claims are true. Some posts even use the hashtag #TimeToDivideGermany. "The goal is to pit eastern and western Germans against one another, or to suggest that people in eastern Germany are despised, hated, or discriminated against by western Germans," Smirnova said. "It is also about harming specific politicians through false accusations." How effective is the disinformation campaign? The operation remains active, with new fake content appearing regularly, but experts interviewed by DW say the campaign's impact appears limited so far. "The impact is really not that significant, as we can see from this artificial amplification of content," Maristany de las Casas said. Many posts receive tens of thousands of views, sometimes more than 100,000, yet generate little genuine engagement. Comments, shares, and other interactions remain relatively low, and previous research suggests that disinformation campaigns such as Matryoshka/Overload have achieved only modest influence . Another reason may be platform moderation. Unlike X, platforms such as Bluesky and TikTok often remove the content relatively quickly. Eric Stehr, however, does not want to rely on that. He plans to file a criminal complaint over the fake videos. His attempt to have one of the videos removed from X was unsuccessful, he said, because the platform said it "saw no reason to take it down," and for now, the disinformation campaign targeting German politicians continues. Additional reporting by Asya Lokina , Aldo Sanchez Vera and Anwar Ashraf. https://www.dw.com/en/cuba-suffers-yet-a.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IABt Cuba has suffered several recent blackouts like this one on July 14 Image: REUTERS Advertisement Cuba 's state-owned grid operator said the island's power system collapsed late on Sunday, the latest in a series of rolling power cuts caused by aging infrastructure and a US energy embargo . The outage comes on the heels of three nationwide power outages last month. Cuba faces most severe energy crisis in decades To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What do we know about Cuba's latest blackout? The state-run utility UNE said there was a "total disconnection" of the national electricity system, which means the entire country of 10 million people, including the capital, Havana, has been plunged into darkness. The Ministry of Energy said that protocols to reactivate the grid were underway. The series of outages afflicting the island in recent times have also affected water supplies and cooling systems, making normal life extremely difficult. Normal life on Cuba has been made almost impossible by the outages (photo from July 14) Image: picture alliance / ZUMAPRESS.com Cuba, which relies largely on aging oil-fired power plants, lost access to fuel from its previous primary supplier, Venezuela, after US President Donald Trump imposed an oil blockade following Washington's ouster and capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro on January 3 . Imports from Mexico , which subsequently became Cuba's key supplier of oil, have also ceased under US pressure. Supplies brought by a single Russian tanker in March with Washington's authorization have been exhausted. Cuba has also been under a broader US embargo for decades. Why the US won't leave Cuba alone To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Stepped-up US campaign against Cuba Cuba is also facing other pressure from the US, including ramped-up sanctions against Cuban state-owned businesses imposed by the Trump administration. These have led to a number of foreign companies suspending their operations in the island. Washington has also indicted former President Raul Castro over the downing of two civilian planes 30 years ago, in which three US citizens and a US resident died. The US redesignated the communist island as a "state sponsor of terrorism" for a third time in 2025, shortly after former President Joe Biden moved to have it deleted from the list. Trump has even made scarcely veiled threats to take over the island . Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1e1.text: Image source, Myanmar Military Information Committee Image caption, Suu Kyi's son has mounted an international campaign demanding proof of life for the democracy icon By Jonathan Head South East Asia correspondent Published 2 hours ago Detained Burmese leader Aung San Suu Kyi has been allowed to meet a delegation from the International Committee of the Red Cross, the first confirmed outside contact with her since a letter to her son two and a half years ago. In photographs of the meeting released by the military government Suu Kyi appeared to be healthy. She was detained shortly after the armed forces deposed her government in 2021, and sentenced to 33 years in jail on what are widely viewed as trumped-up charges, though her sentence has been reduced and she has been moved to house arrest . Despite repeated assurances from the military that Suu Kyi is alive and well, they have never provided any convincing evidence of this. Her son Kim Aris has in recent months mounted an international campaign demanding proof of life for the 81-year-old democracy icon. Now a delegation from the ICRC has been allowed to meet her â her first confirmed meeting with anyone outside the government for nearly four years. Photographs released of her with the ICRC team show Suu Kyi looking relaxed and well, although no details of her state of health have been given, nor of what they talked about. Image source, Myanmar Military Information Committee Image caption, Aung San Suu Kyi was recently moved to house arrest The Myanmar government, still headed by coup leader Min Aung Hlaing and dominated by the military despite an election held earlier this year, is trying to end its diplomatic isolation in a series of official visits to neighbouring countries. Among the top demands being made of Myanmar's military leadership is that they end the aerial bombardment of opposition-held areas, start negotiations to end the civil war, and release Aung San Suu Kyi. They have so far rejected those calls, but the publication of this morning's meeting suggests they may be willing to accede to the last demand. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c24m.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Two store employees were killed after a blast tore through the earthquake-hit Aeon Mall in Kumamoto By Koh Ewe Published 52 minutes ago Two workers who died in a shopping mall explosion that followed a powerful earthquake in Japan last week were asked by a boss to re-enter the building to secure cash. Their employer, general goods store Habita, has apologised for the "loss of two precious lives". The two were among 38 people who died in the magnitude 6.8 earthquake in Kumamoto prefecture on 28 July. Seven of the fatalities were from Aeon Mall. "The instructions given at the time were inappropriate, and I truly regret them," Habita sales director Goji Yuse said, NHK reported. One of two workers has been named as 22-year-old Kurumi Otake. The identity of the other deceased employee has not been made public. Otake's family told local media that she ran into a relative outside the Aeon Mall after the earthquake. She told the relative that she had to go back in because her company had asked her to move money from the cash register into a safe. This was confirmed by two company representatives, who attended Otake'a wake on Sunday and apologised to her family. He added that the company was considering how to proceed with the matter, NHK reported. "Looking back now, it was not worth a life," Yuse told reporters at the wake, Kyodo reported. Otake's relative described her as someone with a "strong sense of justice". She had supported her mother after her father died three years ago, Asahi Shimbun reported. "If she hadn't gone back inside the store at that time, Kurumi would still be with her family today," the relative said. While most people in Aeon mall had evacuated shortly after the earthquake, some employees were still in the building about an hour later, when an explosion ripped through the mall. "My daughter is not coming back," local media reported her mother as saying. Habita, founded in 1976 and operates more than ten stores across several prefectures. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgew.text: Figure caption, Watch: Malaysian boy goes on trial for allegedly murdering girl at school By Tessa Wong Published 7 hours ago A teenage boy in Malaysia is on trial for allegedly killing a female schoolmate, in a high-profile case that has sparked debate about the effects of social media on children. The boy is accused of murdering 16-year-old Yap Shing Xuen last October. The girl was found fatally stabbed multiple times in a toilet at their secondary school on the outskirts of the capital Kuala Lumpur. The boy, who was 14 at the time, has pleaded not guilty. If convicted, he could spend decades in prison. Police previously said they suspected social media could have influenced the boy. Image source, Aaple Wong Image caption, Yap Shing Xuen was found fatally stabbed multiple times in her school's toilet Police also confirmed a note was found on him at the time of his arrest. Reports about the note's alleged content have fueled the wider discussion about the role of social media. Under Malaysian law, the boy cannot be publicly identified as he is still a minor. His young age also means he will not face the death penalty if found guilty. However he could still face 30 to 40 years in jail, and he could also be flogged. The age of criminal responsibility in Malaysia is 10 years old. The case has profoundly shocked the country and triggered a nationwide conversation about the negative effects of social media on children, particularly exposure to the manosphere and incel culture. Some have compared the case to the Netflix series Adolescence, which explores similar themes involving teenage boys, online radicalisation and violence. Last year Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim was asked about the case as well as other recent cases of violence in schools. He was quoted by local media as saying that "almost all of these issues stem from the use of mobile phones and social media", and vowed to look into stricter measures. Authorities have since put in place new rules which they say will protect children and reduce their exposure to harmful online content. Since June, Malaysia has banned all children under the age of 16 from having accounts on major social media platforms. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c07r.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Students and staff at Purja's former school lit candles in commemoration of him By Koh Ewe Published 3 hours ago Tributes are pouring out across Nepal after an avalanche killed all 10 members of an expedition on Pakistan's Broad Peak, six of whom were Nepalese. Among them was Nirmal Purja, also known as Nims, a British-Nepali climber most known for climbing the world's 14 tallest peaks in just over six months. His death has sent shockwaves through the global mountaineering community and through Nepal, where he is a celebrated figure for giving a spotlight to Nepali climbing guides. Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah was among those who paid tribute, saying his "history of courage, dedication and contribution will always remain inspiring". In a moving tribute on Facebook, Purja's brother Kamal wrote: "I feel as though I have lost my whole world. My brother was not only my younger brother - he was my heart." "Although our hearts are broken, we are incredibly proud of you. Your legacy will live forever," he added. At the Small Heaven School in Chitwan district, near Kathmandu, which Purja had once attended, students and staff lit candles and mourned his death. Sarbagya Paudel, one of the students at the vigil, said Purja's "bravery has set a great example for our school. Not only has he made our school proud, but he has also brought pride to Nepal". Purja is still fondly remembered by those who had known him from his schooling days. Shailendra Baral, his school hostel supervisor, told AFP that as a young boy Purja had been "fearless and committed to achieving something". "He was honest and an obedient student, which made us happy. We found courage in him even when he was a child." Bahadur Panta, Purja's school friend, said he had prayed for the mountaineer through "sleepless nights" after news broke of his disappearance. "It was not only me and my friends. I think people all over the world who knew him... prayed for him. But it was his fate, no one could avoid it," he told AFP. Social media was also awash with tributes to Purja, with many saying that Nepal was in mourning and that the country had lost a "legend" and "many great climbers". "Their legacy will live on," said one comment. Purja was catapulted into international stardom after his journey was documented in a 2021 Netflix documentary. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Bahadur Panta was a friend of Purja's in school Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, He was among dozens that gathered at the Small Heaven school in Chitwan Among his 10-member expedition on Broad Peak, there were six Nepali climbers. The other four climbers were from the US, China, Oman, Pakistan. They had gone missing after being caught in an avalanche last Thursday on the 8,047m (26,400ft) peak. Broad Peak is regarded as one of the more challenging mountains for climbers. The first successful ascent was in 1957, when an Austrian expedition reached the summit. Since then, many more have climbed the mountain, but dozens have lost their lives. Purja served in the British military for 16 years, 10 of which were spent in the special forces, and he was awarded an MBE by the late Queen in 2018 for his achievements in extreme high-altitude mountaineering. Purja, who lived with his wife and three-year-old daughter in Hampshire in southern England, said he was also the first Gurkha to climb Everest while serving in the British military. But as he became more famous, troubling allegations emerged about his conduct. In 2024, a New York Times article detailed sexual allegations two women made against Purja. One alleged that he had sexually assaulted her in a hotel room in 2023 and another said he had grabbed and propositioned her while guiding her on an expedition to K2 in 2022. He denied these claims through his lawyer. Body of mountaineer Nirmal Purja recovered after Pakistan avalanche Published 23 hours ago Who is Nirmal Purja, the famed mountaineer killed in Broad Peak avalanche? Published 20 hours ago But while Purja may be the most recognisable face, he was not the only famed climber in the disaster-hit expedition on Broad Peak. The 10-member team also consisted of big names in Nepal's climbing community. There was Pur Bahadur Gurung - also known as Yukta - who summitted Everest 10 times. In 2024, he was part of the team that discovered a century-old shoe on the world's tallest peak, believed to be that of British climber Andrew Irvine, who vanished on Everest with George Mallory in 1924. "Standing with you on the summit of Mount Everest is a memory I will cherish forever," fellow mountaineer and guide Uttam Lapraki wrote in a tribute to Yukta on social media. "The Himalayas have lost one of their finest sons, but your courage, kindness, and legacy will continue to inspire generations of climbers." Another member of the team, Kili Pemba Sherpa, was part of a historic 2021 expedition that summitted K2, the world's second-highest peak, in winter. That expedition was made up of all Nepali climbers, including Purja. Imagine Nepal, an expedition company where Kili Pemba worked as a guide, wrote on Instagram that he had "stood with us from the very beginning, from the days we first started climbing together". "He was humble in every way and never tired of helping climbers when they needed him. He was a foundation of our team and a part of every summit we have ever celebrated."
