https://www.politico.eu/article/volodymy.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has appointed Kyiv’s chief negotiator and former Defense Minister Rustem Umerov as head of the country’s Foreign Intelligence Service, according to a decree published by the presidential office on Monday. Umerov’s current position as secretary of the National Security and Defense Council will be taken over by Ihor Klymenko, who was serving as minister of internal affairs, as announced in a separate presidential decree. Klymenko had been considered by lawmakers the leading candidate to replace ousted Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov. Umerov’s appointment comes as part of a broader reshuffle of Ukraine’s security leadership that Zelenskyy announced in July. The overhaul included the dismissals of Fedorov , Commander-in-Chief Gen. Oleksandr Syrskyi and others. Ukraine needed “more strength” in its wartime leadership, said Zelenskyy. Umerov will now be in charge of a broader portfolio including “diplomacy, defense, negotiations with the U.S. and other designated partners, as well as talks on ending the war,” according to Zelenskyy’s announcement . A key participant in Ukraine-Russia negotiations, Umerov will also continue overseeing work on the EU–Ukraine Drone Deal. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.politico.eu/article/paris-co.text: A Paris court on Monday rejected Russian television star Xenia Fedorova’s appeal against a ruling that she must leave the country, a week after French authorities accused her of acting as “a conduit for disinformation campaigns” orchestrated by Moscow to “destabilize public order.” The former head of Kremlin-backed RT France, who has been under house arrest in Paris since Wednesday, challenged three government measures: the expulsion order, a requirement that she remain in Paris and report to police daily, and a six-month asset freeze. But an administrative court ruled she had failed to demonstrate any of these measures caused her immediate and serious harm. The former RT France chief was a regular commentator on media platforms owned by conservative French billionaire Vincent Bolloré — including CNews and Europe 1 — where her Russia-friendly views on Ukraine, NATO and European security had come under growing scrutiny ahead of the country’s 2027 presidential election. Advertisement Advertisement Fedorova on Friday took to social media to reject the allegations, accusing President Emmanuel Macron’s government of “political pressure” and “censorship of opinions that do not align with the official narrative”, insisting she had merely exercised her right to express her views after living in France for nearly a decade. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez defended the expulsion last week, saying Fedorova “simply relays Russian propaganda” that seeks “to undermine the democratic functioning of France,” while Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot has described her as “a proven propagandist, who serves as a relay for Kremlin disinformation.” Monday’s ruling only concerned Fedorova’s request to suspend the measures, not the merits of the expulsion order itself.

https://www.politico.eu/article/ursula-v.text: BRUSSELS — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen sought to smooth over tensions with Spain after Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez accused many of his fellow EU leaders of exploiting the migration crisis in Ceuta to attack his government. In a letter sent to Sánchez on Monday, von der Leyen praised Spain’s handling of the influx of migrants from Morocco into its North African exclave. Her response came after Sánchez wrote to her over the weekend , condemning leaders who “have chosen to attack Spain and to call for its temporary exclusion from the Schengen Area.” Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Thursday was the first to propose Spain be suspended from the 29-country Schengen zone in which internal border controls have largely been abolished. Italy and France both imposed restrictions on free movement last week. Advertisement Advertisement Around 50,000 people crossed into Ceuta from Morocco last week, with dozens dying in the attempt. Almost all those who entered have since returned to Morocco. Von der Leyen on Monday praised the “swift handling” of returns by Spanish and Moroccan authorities, saying they had “successfully prevent[ed] illegal movement onwards to mainland Spain and Europe.” The exchange followed a joint letter from 22 EU leaders at the weekend calling for an emergency meeting of interior ministers and a tougher, coordinated response to the crisis. That meeting will take place on Tuesday, with EU ambassadors discussing the situation on Monday afternoon. The intervention by EU leaders opened a new political fight over Spain’s migration policy, including Madrid’s plan to regularize more than 1 million undocumented migrants. Some governments argued that the measure created a “pull factor” by encouraging people to believe that irregular entry could eventually lead to legal residency. Sánchez rejected that criticism in his letter, accusing some EU countries of responding in a “selfish,” “polarizing” and unlawful manner. He argued that Spain needed European solidarity rather than blame after the deaths and the strain placed on Ceuta’s authorities. The Spanish government refused to comment for this article. Von der Leyen’s letter offered that solidarity while making clear that the crisis would also have to prompt stronger EU action. Advertisement Advertisement “Migration is a European challenge that requires a European response,” she wrote. “And in this, solidarity is fundamental.” The Commission, she said, had offered Spain financial and operational support, with Frontex, Europol and the EU asylum agency ready to assist. Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner on Friday told Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska that the bloc was willing to “increase support for Spain” to “control the situation,” and to deploy members of Frontex, the EU agency that supports member countries in monitoring and managing the EU’s external borders, to Ceuta. Frontex currently has staff deployed in Ceuta, as well as on the Canary Islands and parts of the Andalusian coastline. An official watches as people gather at the border between Morocco and Spain on July 31, 2026. | Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP via Getty Images Madrid has repeatedly declined to request that the agency’s presence in Spain be increased, insisting that border control falls under the jurisdiction of national authorities. Following a surge in migrant arrivals to Ceuta in 2021, and an increase in arrivals to the Canary Islands in 2024, Spain’s interior ministry rejected calls to ask for Frontex’s support, insisting it had sufficient resources to manage the situation. ‘We must do more’ Von der Leyen said the incident had exposed weaknesses in the bloc’s border management. “It is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points,” the Commission president wrote, including through “vigilant monitoring and the use of physical barriers where needed.” She outlined five priorities: preventing irregular migration through stronger cooperation with partner countries, reinforcing the EU’s external borders, establishing early-warning systems, dismantling smuggling networks, and improving returns. Advertisement Advertisement Morocco, she said, remained an “important strategic partner” in combating migrant smuggling and irregular migration. The EU should work with Rabat and Madrid to improve early-warning systems around Ceuta and Melilla, as well as technical and financial support for Morocco, she said. Von der Leyen also endorsed the emergency meeting of the EU’s justice and home affairs ministers on Tuesday, describing it as a first step toward a collective response. The ministers should agree on a way forward before EU leaders assess the measures at their next European Council meeting, she said. “Spain and its people can count on the enduring support of the Commission,” von der Leyen concluded.

https://www.politico.eu/article/spain-mo.text: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez described last week’s sudden influx of 50,000 migrants into the exclave of Ceuta in North Africa as an “ attack ,” but has been careful to accuse people smugglers rather than the Moroccan authorities of orchestrating it. That diplomatic position from Madrid is coming under pressure, however, from Spanish politicians from both the right and left, who argue that Rabat has questions to answer about the cross-border surge, in which 88 people died . From the moment massive numbers of people began to enter the city last Thursday, Spanish Civil Guard forces reported that Moroccan gendarmes who normally assist in securing the border had inexplicably left their posts. Advertisement Advertisement That led many to suspect that such a large flow of people could hardly be masterminded without the acquiescence of Morocco, which claims the Spanish cities of Ceuta and Melilla as occupied territories. Diplomatic speculation has also centered on whether Rabat could be flexing its muscles over Spain’s recent rapprochement with Algeria, which supports self-determination in Western Sahara — a territory claimed by Morocco. “Let’s call things by their name: Morocco is using human beings to attack our sovereignty,” said Eduardo Rubiño, lawmaker with the Sánchez-allied, left-wing Más Madrid party. Ceuta Mayor Juan Jesús Vivas from the conservative People’s Party on Monday said the situation could not be characterized as “a migration crisis” because “people have the perception that this, if not orchestrated, was encouraged or permitted” by Moroccan authorities. Vivas conceded that Madrid had to do its utmost to continue working with Rabat, but also told Spanish newspaper El País that “Morocco has shown us that it is not reliable.” Since the outset of the crisis, Spain’s Socialist-led government has prioritized smooth relations with Morocco, which will prove critical to resolving the crisis, rather than pinning the blame on Rabat. Advertisement Advertisement A spokesperson for Spain’s foreign ministry insisted “the relationship with Morocco is excellent, and coordination on migration and other issues remains very strong.” While visiting Ceuta on Friday, Sánchez characterized the crisis as “an attack, a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity,” but made no attempt to link Rabat to the operation, which he attributed to “mafias that traffic in human beings.” Instead, he described Morocco as “an ally” and thanked Rabat for its help in repatriating the people who had entered the exclave without authorization. Political liability Moroccan authorities avoided addressing the Ceuta crisis until late on Sunday evening, when Interior Ministry Spokesperson Rachid El Khalfi delivered a statement blaming the sudden influx of migrants on social media posts “which aimed to create the illusion of easy access to the European space without legal consequences.” “The Kingdom of Morocco will continue to be, as it has always been with its partners, a reliable and responsible partner, firmly committed to strengthening international cooperation and coordination in the fight against irregular migration and human trafficking,” El Khalfi said. Spanish opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who heads the center-right People’s Party, this weekend demanded a clarification of “what failed in co-operation with Morocco” and said that Spain had a right to demand that Rabat deliver on its obligations on border security. Advertisement Advertisement He said he wished Spain to “have a relationship of good neighborliness, cooperation, and mutual respect with Morocco,” but that “there are things that shouldn’t be done, and if they are, they must be met with a strong response.” Still, the People’s Party has focused its broader political strategy on the Sánchez government’s failure to anticipate the sudden influx of migrants, rather than focusing on Morocco. Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska this weekend claimed the country’s National Intelligence Center, which handles both foreign and domestic intelligence and counterintelligence under the Ministry of Defense, had failed to warn Madrid of any developments on the border. But intelligence sources quoted by Spain’s Cadena Ser radio network on Monday said that in the lead-up to last week’s crisis, the interior ministry had been warned that a mass entry into Ceuta could take place at any moment. Moreover, Spanish media reported that in July the ministry’s own Office for Refugees and Asylum warned that the growing number of migrants swimming to Ceuta could soon overwhelm the exclave. “Sánchez and his government lie — as they always do,” People’s Party spokesperson Ester Muñoz said . “The government was warned by its intelligence services and did nothing.” Brussels brawl Madrid’s inability to anticipate the crisis will be under scrutiny at an emergency meeting of the EU’s ambassadors on Monday, and at a separate extraordinary summit of the bloc’s interior ministers scheduled for Tuesday. Advertisement Advertisement Over the past five days, a plethora of EU leaders and far-right parties have slammed Spain for losing control of one of the bloc’s external borders and effectively bringing the Ceuta crisis upon itself by moving to grant legal status to 1.2 million unauthorized migrants . In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, European Council President António Costa and Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin, 22 of the bloc’s leaders on Saturday called for EU-level oversight on national policies “that can serve as pull factors.” Ahead of Monday’s meeting of EU ambassadors, Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares pushed back against Madrid’s critics in other European capitals and said his country would “demand solidarity from all the States of the European Union.” “Spain currently has the lowest number of irregular entries on the Mediterranean route,” Albares said during an interview on Spanish state broadcaster TVE. Rather than question Madrid’s efforts, he insisted that the EU’s role was to support and assist Spain in the defense of “the only two European and Spanish cities that share a land border with Africa.” At the same time that he chided critical member countries for their attitude, Spain’s foreign minister praised Rabat for its help in resolving the crisis. “From the very beginning, Morocco offered its cooperation to try to prevent this flow of people and, above all, to ensure their immediate return, as is happening,” he said. “The vast majority of those who entered are already back in Morocco, and Morocco continues to offer this cooperation so that every last person who entered Ceuta returns to Morocco.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.politico.eu/article/france-c.text: PARIS — The French government will need to green light attempts by non-European investors to acquire more than 10 percent of shares in French companies “operating in a sensitive sector” and listed on a stock market outside the EU, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said. “Against a backdrop of heightened geopolitical tensions, we are strengthening oversight of foreign investments in sensitive sectors,” the French leader wrote on X on Sunday. “Our responsibility is twofold: to support the growth of French businesses while safeguarding our strategic interests.” The threshold will apply to government-designated sectors including defense, critical infrastructure and key technologies. Advertisement Advertisement Earlier this year, Lecornu asked three parliamentarians from his center-right coalition to report on France’s economic security. Obtained by POLITICO , the document called for a “radical change in posture” and urged the government to take “a holistic approach” to protecting strategic assets, securing critical supply chains, reducing dependencies and strengthening technological sovereignty. In a press release on the threshold change, Lecornu’s office said the government would give its response on any proposed foreign investments within 10 days of notification to “avoid placing an undue burden on companies’ ability to raise capital in financial markets.” The move is intended to “guard against opportunistic acquisitions by non-EU investors in French companies listed outside the EU that could pose risks to national security,” the statement noted. France had previously set up a screening process for planned acquisitions of over 10 percent of shares in French companies listed on European markets during Covid-19, with the stated aim of “protecting strategic companies” in a time of crisis. The measure was later made permanent and is now being extended to French companies listed outside the EU. The new rules will come into effect in the coming days. Other EU countries, such as Germany and Spain , have similar foreign investment screening regimes that apply a 10 percent threshold to acquisitions in certain strategic sectors. Paul de Villepin contributed to this report. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.politico.eu/article/donald-t.text: Iran said Monday there are currently no direct talks with the United States, after President Donald Trump said negotiations would resume. Speaking at his weekly news conference, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran’s current negotiations are limited to Oman and focused on reopening the Strait of Hormuz. “Our negotiations are with Oman. We are focused on an understanding on a route that will ensure the safe passage of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz,” Baghaei said at a news conference, according to Iran’s state news agency IRNA. He added that “the focus of the negotiations with Oman will be on this issue,” while “the issues related to Iran and the United States should be examined in the next stages to see where the situation will go.” Advertisement Advertisement U.S. President Donald Trump said negotiations with Iran would resume Monday, after scrapping a planned military strike over the weekend. Speaking on Sunday, the American leader also refused to set a deadline for reaching a broader deal with Tehran. “They knew the extent of the attack because they saw it forming. Now what we’re doing is we’re talking to them in the form of a negotiation. It begins tomorrow afternoon, and we’ll see,” said Trump, talking to reporters aboard Air Force One. Asked whether he had imposed a deadline, the U.S. president responded : “Would I rather make a deal? I’m not looking to kill people because people die, a lot of people die, and we don’t want that.” Trump’s remarks came on the heels of his early Sunday announcement on Truth Social that the U.S. was shelving a “massive attack,” after Iran and several Middle Eastern countries asked Washington to pause military action while negotiators worked toward an agreement. He said the framework under discussion included the “Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT” and an end to Iran’s nuclear threat, adding that Israel had also agreed to pause strikes. Baghaei stated there would be “no significant change” in the situation in the Strait of Hormuz as long as Iran remained under what he described as U.S. military pressure.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c235.text: Figure caption, "I think there's a deal" - Trump on calling off Iran strikes By Bernd Debusmann Jr ,Â White House reporter ,Â Reporting from Air Force One Â and Â James Chater Published 3 August 2026, 01:11 BST Updated 7 minutes ago Iran says it is negotiating with Oman to reach "an understanding" over a temporary route through the Strait of Hormuz to allow commercial shipping to resume. The statement came after US President Donald Trump said new talks on ending the war in Iran would begin on Monday - and that he had called off "massive" strikes on the country for this purpose. Trump did not specify who would take part in the talks. Earlier he had said the "perimeters" of a deal had been agreed - and would include reopening Hormuz, the vital waterway whose closure by Iran has sent oil prices soaring. In its response, Iran said it was not negotiating with the US - and had no plans to do so. Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei added that Tehran was negotiating with Oman to reach "an understanding over a path to ensure the security of shipping passage through the Strait of Hormuz". Tehran has repeatedly closed off the strait since the US and Israel started attacks on the country in February. Talks to end the conflict - mostly facilitated by mediators - collapsed last month, ending a ceasefire agreed in April. Trump has repeatedly vowed that a negotiated end to the war is near, only for tit-for-tat strikes to resume. Speaking on board Air Force One on Sunday, he said Iran "knew the extent" of the planned US strikes "because they saw it forming", adding: "We're talking to them in the form of a negotiation. It begins tomorrow afternoon." Trump declined to outline a deadline for a deal to be struck with Tehran, adding: "We'll just see how it is. We're ready to go anytime we want... I'm not looking to kill people." Trump added that Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman - as well as US partners such as the United Arab Emirates and Qatar - had urged him against conducting strikes over the weekend. "We were all set to go," Trump said. "The reason they asked is [that] they think there's a deal," he said. "There's a deal on Hormuz, and there will be a deal on the nuclear." Global oil prices fell on Monday morning in Asia trading after Trump's announcement. Brent Crude oil was down by 4.5% at $83.98 (Â£62.26), while US-traded oil was 4.6% lower at $80.74 (Â£59.85). Energy prices have fluctuated since the conflict started on 28 February as traders reacted to disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Around 20% of the world's crude oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) usually flows through the strait. Vessel-tracking data from trade intelligence company Kpler suggests commercial shipping through the strait has slowed. According to the data, 51 vessel crossings occurred through the strait between 30 July and 2 August. This is a drop of around 28% compared to the previous 4 days, in which 71 crossings were recorded through the strait. Iran's semi-official Mehr news agency denied that Tehran had asked the US to hold off on further military action, saying Trump's claims were "nothing but a new lie". During his remarks on Air Force One, Trump said that the planned strikes would have been "the biggest attack since World War Two", and could have derailed prospects of a negotiated end to the months-long war. Trump declined to answer if he had been planning to strike Iranian energy infrastructure, which international law experts have said could constitute a war crime . Back on 7 April, the US president warned that "a whole civilisation will die tonight" if Iran refused to engage in peace talks. That threat did result in historic face-to-face talks in Pakistan, led by Vice-President JD Vance. However, those negotiations did not result in a deal. The Trump administration has also been largely dismissive of data showing the war - and its economic impact - are broadly unpopular with Americans, including with many Republicans. Polls showing widespread dissatisfaction with the handling of the war have prompted alarm among some conservative strategists ahead of the coming November midterms. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce85.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The Sudanese army recently rallied its supporters as it continues to fight the Rapid Support Forces By Damian Zane Published 3 hours ago Thirty-five people were killed in a drone strike by the Sudanese army on a traditional court session in the north of the Darfur region, a local rights organisation has said. Dozens more were reported injured in Sunday afternoon's attack. The Emergency Lawyers Group, which monitors violence against civilians, said the attack occurred in Ghara al-Zawiya village that is controlled by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The army has not commented. The RSF holds most of Darfur, in the west of the country, as the two sides continue to fight in the three-year-long civil war that has devastated the country, killed tens of thousands of people and forced millions from their homes. Sunday's "court session was being held under a tree with the participation of local community leaders," a witness is quoted by the AFP news agency as saying. Four tribal leaders and two RSF commanders were among those killed in the attack, according to the witness. The privately owned Darfur 24 website quoted a local resident who said that two drones flew over the town "before launching more than four missiles". The Emergency Lawyers Group called for an investigation into the drone strike and condemned the targeting of the court saying that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a "grave violation of international humanitarian law". It also noted that drones are being increasingly used "to target civilian areas and gatherings, which exacerbates the risks faced by the population". The RSF has also been accused of war crimes including drone attacks on civilians over the past three years. The paramilitary group's siege and attack on el-Fasher, one of Darfur's main cities, last year bore the "hallmarks of genocide" according to a UN fact-finding mission. The RSF has denied the accusations. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdrv.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The remnants of the 2020-2022 civil war are still visible in parts of Tigray By Kaleb Moges Â and Â Yemane Nagish ,Â BBC Tigrinya Published 2 hours ago Hundreds of Ethiopians from the Tigray region have crossed into neighbouring Sudan following fighting between regional forces and the Ethiopian army over the weekend. In one of the most serious confrontations since the end of the civil war in the area four years ago, intense clashes broke out on Saturday morning in Shererina, near the border with Sudan. A member of the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) said the violence, which continued into Sunday, involved heavy artillery and drones. The two-year civil war in northern Ethiopian between the TPLF and the federal government, which led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, ended with an African Union-brokered peace deal in 2022. But there are fears there could be a return to full-scale conflict as the deal has not been fully implemented and the TPLF is back in control of Tigray after pushing out the interim administration that was created as part of the resolution of the conflict. There are also concerns that the fighting could become a proxy for the Sudanese civil war, with accusations that the warring parties there are backing opposing sides in Ethiopia. Both the TPLF and the federal authorities blamed each other for Saturday's clashes. The TPLF-led regional administration accused the federal government of launching an "open war" in the Shererina area. It said the offensive violated the peace agreement and was aimed at "subjugating and dividing" the people of Tigray. The federal government and the federal army have not issued an official statement but minister Abraham Belay confirmed that clashes had occurred. In a social media post, he accused the "TPLF clique" of starting the fighting and warned of "worse consequences" if the conflict continued. The minister also called for dialogue, saying disputes should be resolved through peaceful negotiations rather than war. "Today, it is better to reach out for peace before destruction," he wrote. The death toll from the weekend's fighting was not clear but Sudanese medical and local sources told the AFP news agency that civilians and wounded fighters fled across the border, while witnesses reported hearing explosions, heavy gunfire, and aircraft throughout Saturday. Shererina, a small locality in western Tigray, is strategically sensitive because western Tigray has been disputed between Tigray and Amhara, the regional state just to the south, since the civil war. https://www.adn.com/nation-world/2026/07.text: ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Nation/World For Subscribers The Tate brothers fight extradition to the UK where they are charged with rape and sex trafficking By David Fischer, Associated Press Published: July 20, 2026 Andrew Tate, left, watches his brother Tristan speak, outside a police station in Voluntari, Romania, May 21, 2025. (AP Photo/Vadim Ghirda, File) MIAMI — Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate will fight extradition to the United Kingdom where the brothers are accused of rape and sex trafficking, their lawyer said Monday, suggesting their arrest in Miami was politically motivated without explaining why. The Tates appeared in federal court Monday for the first time since their arrest on Saturday and are being held in federal detention. In the coming weeks, a U.S. district judge will consider whether they meet the conditions for extradition. U.S. Magistrate Lauren Louis set another hearing for Monday July 27. The brothers, through their social media empire promoting wealth, male dominance and misogyny, are among the world’s most polarizing internet personalities. Normally photographed in tailored suits and fitted shirts, they wore tan jail uniforms and handcuffs during the brief hearing. Neither brother said a word. Their attorney, Joseph McBride, insisted they should remain in the U.S. “We are of course objecting to extradition because Andrew and Tristan are innocent,” McBride said after the hearing. “They’ve never done nothing wrong. They shouldn’t be extradited for crimes they did not commit.” The brothers were surprised when they were arrested, McBride said, adding that the attempt to have them extradited was politically motivated. “There’s no question about it,” he told reporters. ADVERTISEMENT Attorney Joseph McBride arrives for a court hearing for his clients Andrew and Tristan Tate after they were arrested to face rape and sex trafficking charges against them in the United Kingdom, Monday, July 20, 2026, in Miami. (AP Photo/Marta Lavandier) He suggested the Tates’ case “had a lot to do with” former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s decision to step down, without providing any details, and said it was no coincidence that the brothers were arrested after meeting “friends in Washington, D.C.” “We went to see our Congress people in D.C. and now we’re getting arrested. This feels political,” McBride said. He didn’t specify who the pair met with or what was discussed. On Sunday, McBride said he was confident the extradition request would be denied. Prosecutors in Britain said the new charges relate to four new victims and were brought after authorities received evidence from Bedfordshire Police in southeastern England. The allegations, spanning 2010 to 2017, include rape, assault, trafficking and offenses relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.” ADVERTISEMENT McBride said none of the latest accusers have been identified, adding “we’d like to know who’s accused Andrew and Tristan of what.” The brothers are already charged with rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other alleged victims in the U.K. between 2012 and 2015. Their lawyer said in a statement Saturday that he believed the arrests were “greenlighted by a low-level functionary” at the Justice Department without input from leadership. The Justice Department told The Associated Press that the arrests were approved by leadership of its Criminal Division. The new allegations are the latest in a long-running international legal saga involving the Tates that has spanned the U.S., Britain and Romania. The brothers have repeatedly denied wrongdoing. The dual U.S. and British citizens moved to Romania in 2016. They were arrested there in 2022, accused of participating in schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations and the Romanian case hasn’t gone forward because of legal and procedural problems. ADVERTISEMENT Last year, they were allowed to leave Romania and flew to Florida. The former professional kickboxers have millions of followers on social media and are vocal supporters of President Donald Trump. Andrew Tate, 39, first became known a decade ago when he was a contestant on the U.K. reality television show “Big Brother.” He was booted from the show when a video appeared to show him assaulting a woman. He has amassed over 10 million followers on X but has been banned from other platforms for violating hate speech guidelines, including YouTube, TikTok and Instagram. He has made widely condemned comments, such as saying women who are sexually assaulted should bear some responsibility for the attacks and sharing graphic descriptions of how he might attack women. The Tate brothers have consistently denied allegations of abuse and human trafficking, claiming their violent and misogynistic statements have been taken out of context or were intended as jokes. ___ Associated Press reporters Alanna Durkin Richer in Washington, D.C., and John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed. The British-American Tates were arrested on Saturday and held in Miami after being charged by UK authorities with rape and sex-trafficking charges and an extradition request has been issued. Britain’s Crown Prosecution Service said the new charges relate to four further victims and were brought after authorities received evidence from Bedfordshire Police in southeastern England. The charges include rape, assault, trafficking and offenses relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.” The charges announced Saturday, which bring the total number of alleged victims in the U.K. to seven, are the latest in a long-running international legal saga involving the brothers that has spanned the U.S., Britain and Romania. The brothers have denied wrongdoing. The Tates had formerly been living in luxury in Romania when they were arrested on charges of rape and sex-trafficking. In Romania, the siblings were arrested in late 2022 along with two Romanian women. The four were accused of participating in criminal schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations and the Romanian case hasn’t gone forward because of legal and procedural problems. The case hasn’t been closed, and there is also a separate legal case against the brothers in Romania. … But in February 2025 they were allowed to leave Romania after authorities lifted travel restrictions, and they flew to Florida on a private jet. The Tates had boasted about their close connection to Trump and were delighted when he became president again in 2025, seeing him as their protector, especially because of his willingness to pardon criminals merely because they support him. And it seemed to have worked. Romania’s foreign minister said at the time that a U.S. official in the Trump administration had expressed interest in the brothers’ legal case in Romania. Trump said he knew “nothing about” the case when asked if his administration pressured the Romania government to release the Tates. But the new charges and extradition request put Trump in a bind. The brothers are expected to appear Monday before a magistrate judge in Miami, where they are currently being held in federal detention. Bail is rarely granted to those held for international extradition, and their lawyer said he expects they will remain jailed for the time being. In the coming weeks, a U.S. district judge will consider whether they meet the conditions for extradition. The ultimate decision about whether to order the extradition will fall to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. While the State Department has some discretion to deny extradition requests from the U.K., it has granted nearly every British request since ratifying a strengthened extradition treaty in 2007. In the June 15, 2026 issue of The New Yorker , Heidi Blake had a detailed expose of the sordid world of the Tates in a piece titled Andrew Tate’s Empire of Abuse where, among other things, the Tates spoke of their admiration for Trump and saw him as their guy (Trump’s son Barron seems to be particularly close to the Tates), and the MAGA world rushed to defend them. Blake writes that Trump’s people seemed to have secured the removal of Romania’s travel restrictions on the Tates and even boasted about it. Tate’s enormous reach made him a political force. He had always been an enthusiastic supporter of Donald Trump—“He’s grabbing bitches by the pussy. I like that guy,” he’d once said—and he became a singularly influential proponent of masculinism: a creed, devoted to countering feminism and restoring the patriarchy, that helped unite the disparate factions of the maga coalition. Tate called for women to be stripped of the vote, barred from the workplace, and forced to procreate. … When Tate was arrested on human-trafficking charges, his allies defended him. Donald Trump, Jr., called the case “absolute insanity,” and Musk suggested that the authorities were targeting the Tates while ignoring “actual sex trafficking.” Carlson, who had just released a documentary called “The End of Men,” devoted hours of airtime to proclaiming Tate’s innocence; so did the right-wing podcaster Candace Owens. The activist Charlie Kirk praised him onstage. “What he says is so powerful,” Kirk said. “Our society is configured towards collapsing the American man.” … As the 2024 U.S. election approached, the team saw an opportunity. Tate forged relationships with Barron Trump and Donald Trump, Jr. In the weeks before the vote, he pumped out pro-maga content, mobilizing young men in such large numbers that Kamala Harris later named him as a key factor in her defeat. When the result was in, Tate posted jubilantly on X: “the patriarchy is back.” After the Inauguration, he added, “The Tates will be free, Trump is the president.” Weeks later, under pressure from the U.S., Romania lifted the Tates’ travel ban. Since then, the brothers have travelled the world, while the case appears stalled and the evidence remains sealed. … The President’s counsellor Alina Habba appeared on a podcast with Tate, telling him that she was a “big fan” and declaring, “I’ve got your back.” But their triumphant return to the US was not without a hitch. A source who was present when the Tates learned that they were free to travel told me that the message was delivered by a senior Romanian politician—one who had recently been to Mar-a-Lago. The politician turned up at their compound at night in a black S.U.V. “The Americans are asking questions now,” he told them. “Here’s your passports back. Happy flying.” … In February 27, 2025, the Tates flew from Romania to Florida. Thousands of fans tracked their private jet as it crossed the Atlantic. When it landed in Fort Lauderdale, a crowd of journalists and onlookers was gathered outside the executive terminal to watch the brothers arrive. “They were expecting this grand tour—the martyr comes home, a free-speech hero,” Petrescu told me. There was a hitch, though: border officials seized the Tates’ phones. They were working on behalf of the Department of Homeland Security, which had quietly opened an investigation into the brothers under the Biden Administration. The fact that it was the Biden administration that had opened this investigation may be a factor if Trump decides to drop it, since reversing everything that Obama and Biden did seems to be Trump’s main passion. The sheer viciousness of the rhetoric of the Tates particularly and manosphere generally is appalling, as Blake writes. Even in this milieu, Tate’s violent rhetoric stands out. “I saw a woman crossing the road today but I just kept my foot down,” he posted after Trump’s reëlection. “Right of way? You no longer have rights.” His influence is being felt around the world. Last year, a seventeen-year-old boy in New Jersey allegedly drove his car into two teen-age girls, killing them both, after joking on a live stream about women getting raped by Tate. In Britain, a man who had recently watched about ten of Tate’s videos raped his ex-girlfriend and murdered her, her mother, and her sister using a crossbow. British police have warned that Tate’s teachings are radicalizing young men in a “terrifying” manner and declared that violence against women is a national emergency. Reports of rapes and sexual assaults in British schools—some involving victims as young as five—have soared in the past five years, and education leaders describe violent misogyny spreading on an “epidemic scale.” Similar concerns have been reported across North America and Asia. British law enforcement has already been harshly criticized for not taking action against the Tates much earlier, which is what may have triggered the new action. Yet Tate could have faced justice more than a decade ago, when Navarro, Walker, and Price accused him of assault, if British police had taken their allegations seriously. “They failed to protect the initial victims and created this problem,” the senior Romanian law-enforcement source told me. In my reporting, I discovered something that the British police had hidden for years: their officers bungled the investigation from the start, making it almost impossible to bring Tate to trial. When Price first came forward, officers neglected to take a statement and discouraged her from pressing charges, telling her that it would be a long and difficult process. They also failed to make a digital recording of Walker’s initial statement, instead jotting her words down on paper so sloppily that Tate was at one point referred to as “Michael.” This introduced discrepancies that undermined an account she later gave on video. Multiple items of evidence were also stored incorrectly—including Tate’s phone, which was left lying around the station while the case stalled. When the phone was eventually searched, it apparently contained important evidence—Tate later said that officers had found proof of twelve “bad things I did”—but the chain-of-custody lapse made it practically useless. Prosecutors, hoping to salvage the case, gave police a list of leads, but they failed to act on them. A longtime Hertfordshire detective blamed the malfeasance on “overworked, overstretched” officers who failed to take the women’s allegations seriously, partly because two of them were sex workers. “It was one of many cases that were completely cocked up because of poor policing,” he told me. This spring, after I reached out to current and former officers about the investigation, the Independent Office for Police Conduct suddenly announced that it had launched an inquiry into gross misconduct in the case. The next day, the Hertfordshire police declared that they were reopening their own investigation, more than a decade after the women first came forward. The new UK charges and the extradition request will be something that Trump and the new UK prime minister Andy Burnham will have to deal with. The Tates will clearly expect Trump to intervene on their behalf, since they see him as a kindred spirit, to get the extradition charges dropped, or at least have them released on bail at the hearing in Miami today, so that they have the chance to escape to some country that does not have extradition treaties with the UK. http://www.bgnes.com/politics/chess-lege.text: Chess legend Judit Polgár has rejected an offer to become Hungary’s president, saying she does not feel able to assume the historic responsibility of bringing a divided nation together. “I do not feel that I have the strength to take on the historic responsibility of uniting a divided nation, and therefore I cannot accept the invitation,” Polgár wrote on social media. She added that she would do everything in her power to support a new, independent and respected president of the republic in achieving those goals. Until a successor is elected, parliament speaker Ágnes Forsthoff is serving as interim head of state. Parliament is required to elect a new president within 30 days. Polgár announced her decision after the parliamentary group of the ruling Tisza Party publicly backed her candidacy in parliament. Critics, however, noted that unlike earlier pledges, her nomination was not preceded by broad public consultations. Prime Minister Péter Magyar responded to Polgár’s decision by saying: “Dear Judit, thank you for everything you have done for Hungary. I believe I can say on behalf of millions of Hungarians that, even in another capacity, we will continue to count on you in the future.” Magyar had backed Polgár late on Sunday as “a president all Hungarians can be proud of” following the removal of unpopular President Tamás Sulyok through a constitutional amendment last week. The amendment brought Sulyok’s mandate to an end on Monday. Leaders of the governing Tisza Party have repeatedly said they want the president to be elected directly by the people rather than by parliament. As a result, the newly elected president may only hold office temporarily until a new constitution is adopted. | BGNES

https://www.irishdentist.ie/energy-drink.text: Politics July 20, 2026 Energy drinks banned for under 16s: why England says stop and what can change in Italy They promise immediate energy, concentration, resistance to tiredness. They have brightly colored cans, aggressive names and a now constant presence in sports, video games, social networks and influencer content. For many teenagers, energy drinks have become an almost ordinary drink, to be consumed before a match, during a study session or simply to imitate adults. In England, however, they will soon no longer be able to be purchased freely by anyone under 16. The British government has confirmed that from April 2027 the sale of high-caffeine energy drinks to minors will be banned. The measure has yet to complete parliamentary passage, but the political decision has been made and the executive intends to introduce it through secondary legislation under the Food Safety Act. This is not a ban on any energy drink or, more generally, on all caffeinated drinks. The established threshold is 150 milligrams of caffeine per liter : above this level, the product cannot be sold to under 16s. Tea, coffee and soft drinks with lower concentrations will be excluded. The ban will also affect vending machines and online sales The restriction will be extended to all main commercial channels: supermarkets, small shops, bars, restaurants, cafes, websites and vending machines. Traders will have to verify the age of buyers, while checks will be entrusted to local authorities. Fines could reach up to £2,500. It is an important step because several British chains had already spontaneously adopted limits on sales, but the system left large areas uncovered. A boy could have the can rejected at the supermarket and buy it a few meters later in an independent shop, online or from a vending machine. According to government estimates, approx 100 thousand English children and teenagers consume energy drinks with a high concentration of caffeine every day . Consumption would also be more widespread in families and economically disadvantaged areas, transforming the issue into a problem of health and education inequality. The choice comes after a public consultation held between September and November 2025. 1,095 responses were collected and 90 percent of participants declared themselves in favor of introducing an age limit. Support came mainly from parents, teachers, doctors, local administrations and organizations involved in the protection of minors. More critical, however, is a part of the beverage industry, which considers the measure disproportionate compared to the available scientific evidence. How much caffeine does a can contain A standard 250 milliliter can generally contains approx 80 milligrams of caffeine a quantity similar to that of an espresso. The concentration, however, is around 320 milligrams per liter, more than double the threshold identified by the English government to trigger the ban. Larger formats or particularly concentrated products can provide significantly higher quantities in one go. The problem is not only the absolute value, but the relationship with body weight. The European Food Safety Authority, EFSA, indicates a caffeine level for children and adolescents that does not cause concern at approximately 3 milligrams per kilogram of body weight per day considering all food sources. For a 40-kilo boy that means about 120 milligrams daily. A single standard can already provides 80; to this can be added cola, tea, coffee, chocolate and other products containing caffeine. Furthermore, the EFSA reference does not represent a threshold beyond which intoxication automatically occurs, but a prudential level referring to the healthy population. It is precisely this difference that makes the often used comparison between a can and a cup of coffee misleading. Caffeine may be similar, but the audience, consumption patterns and context change: energy drinks are often drunk quickly, in large formats, sometimes in multiple consecutive units and in combination with other sources of stimulants. The effects of energy drinks on sleep, anxiety and the heart Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system and temporarily reduces the perception of tiredness. In more sensitive subjects or when quantities increase it can cause agitation, tremors, headaches, nausea, palpitations, increased blood pressure and difficulty falling asleep. In adolescents, energy drink consumption has been associated with poorer quality sleep, anxiety, gastrointestinal disorders, difficulty concentrating and some acute cardiovascular effects, such as increased heart rate and blood pressure. However, a distinction is necessary on this point. The English government itself recognizes that much of the available research is observational: that is, it shows a relationship between consumption and health problems or academic performance, but does not always allow it to be demonstrated that it was exclusively the drink that caused them. Those who sleep little, lead an irregular lifestyle or exhibit other risky behaviors could, for example, also be more inclined to consume energy drinks. The evidence, therefore, is not definitive. However, they are coherent enough to have pushed London to apply a precautionary principle, especially considering that the product already contains the indication on the label not to recommend it to children. The sugar problem Next to caffeine there is sugar. According to the briefing from the European Parliamentary Research Service, a typical 250 milliliter can can contain approximately 27 grams equivalent to five or six teaspoons. In a single product it is therefore possible to reach or exceed the daily quantity of free sugars indicated as a prudential objective by the World Health Organization. Sugar-free versions eliminate this specific problem, but not the caffeine one. For this reason the English measure is based on the concentration of the stimulant and not on the calories of the drink. Another particularly risky habit is pairing it with alcohol. Caffeine may make a person feel more alert, but it does not reduce blood alcohol levels or restore normal coordination, judgment, or reaction times. The Italian guidelines for healthy eating remind us that the exciting effect of energy drinks can mask, but not cancel, the neurological effects of alcohol. In Europe, six countries have already introduced limits England is not the first European territory to intervene. Lithuania and Latvia introduced bans on sales to minors in 2014 and 2016 respectively. Poland and Romania followed in 2024, while Hungary and Bulgaria adopted restrictions in 2025. The Spanish region of Galicia also banned sales and consumption by minors, partly equating these drinks with alcohol. However, the rules are not uniform: the minimum age, the definition of energy drink, the concentrations considered and the places where sale is prohibited change. At community level there is currently no specific law that prevents teenagers from purchasing them. The European Food Information Regulation requires drinks with more than 150 milligrams of caffeine per liter to clearly display the warning “high caffeine content” and the indication that the product is not recommended for children and pregnant or breastfeeding women. Brussels still considers the scientific advice published by EFSA in 2015 to be sufficient and has not announced a joint ban. However, Member States remain free to introduce more stringent national rules, provided they are justified. Energy drinks banned in Italy? Not for now In Italy Today there is no national age limit for purchasing energy drinks . A teenager can buy them at the supermarket, at the bar, online or through a vending machine, while the only mandatory protection is represented by the information on the packaging. The English decision will not automatically produce consequences in our country. However, it could reopen the debate on the effectiveness of a simple warning printed in characters that are often not very obvious, especially when the product is promoted through extreme sports, gaming, music, creators and campaigns capable of speaking directly to young people. A possible Italian intervention could follow the English model, limiting only drinks with over 150 milligrams of caffeine per liter, or focus on schools, vending machines, advertising and sponsorships aimed at minors. However, a ban alone would not solve every problem. A study cited by the European Parliament found that in Poland, after the restrictions were introduced, only a minority of children attempting to purchase were subjected to regular age checks. The issue is therefore not to establish that a single can is necessarily dangerous for every teenager. The point is to decide whether a product already declared not recommended for children should continue to be available without any limit, even in large formats and at any time. England chose to answer no. From 2027 the can will remain on the shelves, but to buy it you will need to be at least 16 years old. Now the debate is destined to move to other European countries too, including Italy. https://www.local10.com/news/local/2026/.text: MIAMI — Influencer brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate appeared before a federal magistrate in Miami on Monday for the first time since they were arrested to face rape and sex trafficking charges in the United Kingdom. The Tates have been held in federal detention following their arrest on Saturday. In the coming weeks, a U.S. district judge will consider whether they meet the conditions for extradition. An attorney for the brothers, Joseph McBride, has blasted the charges as “filth and slander,” as well as “salacious and defamatory.” Prosecutors in Britain said the new charges relate to four new victims and were brought after authorities received evidence from Bedfordshire Police in southeastern England. The allegations, spanning 2010 to 2017, include rape, assault, trafficking and offenses relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.” The brothers are already charged with rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other alleged victims in the U.K. between 2012 and 2015. Their lawyer said in a statement Saturday that he believed the arrests were “greenlighted by a low-level functionary” at the Justice Department without input from leadership. But the Justice Department told The Associated Press that the arrests were approved by leadership of its Criminal Division. McBride, outside of the Miami federal courthouse, said he plans to fight extradition on the Tates’ behalf. “We are going to fight them at every turn, and at every corner, because they are American citizens,” McBride said. McBride claims the new allegations are politically-motivated. “I’ve never seen evidence that indicates these guys are guilty of anything,” he said. “They are being punished and attacked for what they say and not for what they have done. You can love them, you can hate them, but nobody should go to jail for free speech.” Taking a swipe at the U.K., McBride said, “We will make sure that we exhaust all remedies before they are sent over to the communist regime previously known as the free place of the United Kingdom.” McBride, explaining his ties representing people in Jan. 6 cases, implied that he believes President Donald Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio would be sympathetic to the case. “I believe that Marco Rubio and the rest of the trump administration are not fans of communism, for prosecuting people for free speech, this is one of the reasons why they were elected,” he said, noting that after the Jan. 6 prosecutions, “I would just think as a matter of principle, based on the reasons why they were elected, that they would not want to see two free citizens go to a country where they are going to be thrown in jail for political reasons.” According to the U.S. Department of Justice, “If the court finds the fugitive to be extraditable, it certifies the extradition and sends the record to the Secretary of State, who decides whether to surrender the fugitive.” Former federal prosecutor David Weinstein said even though the charges the Tates face are not considered “political offenses” by definition, under the extradition treaty, “the executive branch of the U.S., including the president, can block the extradition request if they determine that the request was politically motivated.” “So yes, President Trump is able to help prevent an extradition to the U.K. if he wanted to,” Weinstein said. The new allegations are the latest in a long-running international legal saga involving the Tates that has spanned the U.S., Britain and Romania. The brothers have repeatedly denied wrongdoing. Their social media empire promoting wealth, male dominance and misogyny has made them among the world’s most polarizing internet personalities. The dual U.S. and British citizens moved to Romania in 2016. They were arrested there in 2022, accused of participating in schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations and the Romanian case hasn’t gone forward because of legal and procedural problems. Last year, they were allowed to leave Romania and flew to Florida.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c629.text: Figure caption, Watch: BBC reports from inside Tate brothers court appearance By Brandon Drenon Â and Â Tom Bateman ,Â in Miami Published 20 July 2026 Controversial influencer Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan have appeared in a federal courtroom in Miami, marking the beginning of extradition proceedings to the UK over a slate of new charges that includes rape and sex trafficking. Speaking outside the court after the hearing, a lawyer for the brothers said they would fight extradition. The Tates have been held in a Florida jail since their arrest on Saturday, after the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), which prosecutes criminal cases in England and Wales, announced 38 new charges against them. The Tate brothers, who arrived in Florida in 2025 after departing Romania where they face similar charges, have repeatedly denied any wrongdoing. In court on Monday, the pair wore light brown prison uniforms and were handcuffed and shackled at the waist and ankles. They spoke only when asked if they understood their rights to which they replied together "yes your honour". Image source, Pool/Getty Images Image caption, Tristan and Andrew Tate are both facing extradition to the UK The brothers' attorney, Joe McBride, told reporters after the brief hearing that his clients are innocent. "They've never done nothing wrong. They shouldn't be extradited for crimes they didn't commit," McBride said. "It's garbage. It's a stitch up job," he added. He compared the charges against the men to the legal proceedings against US President Donald Trump - which he called a "witch hunt" - and referred to the attempted extradition as "political kidnapping". When asked how long the extradition proceedings would take, McBride estimated ahead of the hearing that it would be "around 60 days". The judge set the brothers' next court hearing for 27 July, according to AP News. Any final decision on extradition would ultimately have to be made by the Trump administration. The latest allegations against the men were said to have occurred between July 2010 and August 2017. Will the Tate brothers be extradited from the US to the UK? Published 21 July Image source, PA Image caption, Joseph McBride and Thomas Maniotis represent Andrew and Tristan Tate Malcolm McHaffie, Head of the Special Crime Division at the CPS, said the charges "followed receipt of a further file of evidence from Bedfordshire Police" that brings the total number of alleged victims in this case to seven. The brothers now face a total of 59 charges, police said. They were arrested on Saturday nearby a venue where Andrew Tate was due to co-host a bare-knuckle fighting event. They also face charges in Romania, accused of human trafficking and forming an organised group to sexually exploit women. Andrew Tate has also been accused of rape in that case. They deny those allegations. The pair, dual British-US citizens, have been in the US since 2025, after Romanian prosecutors lifted a travel ban against them. The two are still required to check in with Romanian authorities as the case winds through procedural hurdles. In the US they also face a civil case from a woman who alleges the brothers coerced her into sex work, and then defamed her after she gave evidence to Romanian authorities. Andrew Tate is a self-proclaimed "misogynist" who reached viral acclaim on social media platforms for his portrayals of extreme wealth and hyper-masculinity. He was banned from social media after making controversial remarks about women needing to "bear responsibility" for being sexually assaulted but was later reinstated. https://themunicheye.com/breaking-news/t.text: Mon 20th Jul, 2026 Andrew and Tristan Tate, dual citizens of the United States and United Kingdom with significant social media influence, were detained in Miami after British prosecutors issued additional charges of rape and sex trafficking against them. The Crown Prosecution Service in the UK stated that the latest indictments involve four alleged victims, increasing the total number of claimants in the UK to seven. The new allegations stem from evidence provided by the Bedfordshire Police in England, covering incidents said to have occurred between 2010 and 2017. Background on the Tate Brothers Andrew Tate, aged 39, and his brother Tristan, 38, are known for their presence on social media platforms where they promote themes related to wealth, masculinity, and dominance. Andrew Tate, a former professional kickboxer, has accumulated a substantial following, particularly among young men, but has been banned from platforms such as YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram for violating rules related to hate speech. Both brothers are also known to be supporters of former US President Donald Trump and have operated online businesses targeting young male audiences. Summary of Charges The Crown Prosecution Service disclosed that Andrew Tate faces seven new counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating sex trafficking, three counts of assault, and nineteen counts relating to offences involving indecent images of a child and extreme pornography. Tristan Tate is charged with one count of sexual assault, two counts of rape, and three counts of arranging or facilitating sex trafficking. These charges are in addition to previous allegations dating back to 2012 through 2015, which include rape, bodily harm, human trafficking, and controlling prostitution for gain in relation to three other alleged victims in the UK. In a statement, the Crown Prosecution Service confirmed they have formally requested the extradition of the Tate brothers from the United States, and both are being held in federal custody while the extradition process is underway. The brothers' legal representative has criticized the charges and expressed confidence that the extradition request will be denied. Previous Legal Proceedings The Tate brothers have been the subject of ongoing legal action in both the UK and Romania. In Romania, they were arrested in late 2022 alongside two Romanian women, facing accusations of participating in criminal activities to lure women for sexual exploitation. The Romanian case has not advanced due to procedural and legal complications, but it remains open. Additionally, a separate legal process against the brothers continues in Romania. Both Andrew and Tristan Tate have denied all allegations and have claimed that the proceedings are part of a political effort to silence them. In June, the UK High Court dismissed a request from the Tates to access the identities of their accusers in the British cases. The complexity of the legal proceedings, spanning multiple jurisdictions, has prolonged the resolution of the charges against them. Extradition Process The next phase involves the Tate brothers appearing before a magistrate judge in Miami. Typically, individuals facing international extradition are not granted bail, and their legal counsel anticipates that they will remain in custody during the process. A US district judge will evaluate whether the legal requirements for extradition are satisfied, but the ultimate decision lies with the US Secretary of State, currently Marco Rubio. Historically, the United States has approved nearly all British extradition requests since a bilateral treaty was strengthened in 2007, with rare exceptions. Residence and International Movement The Tate brothers moved to Romania in 2016 and have been subject to legal restrictions and investigations in that country. In early 2025, Romanian authorities lifted travel bans, permitting the brothers to leave the country, after which they traveled to Florida. The Romanian Foreign Ministry noted that US officials had previously shown interest in their legal case. Despite speculation regarding political intervention, there has been no official confirmation that the US government influenced Romanian decisions related to the Tate brothers' travel or legal status. https://www.finanznachrichten.de/nachric.text: OTP BANK NYRT Nachrichten Analysen Kurse Chart Dividende OTP Bank to acquire Luminor OTP Bank to acquire 100% of the shares of Luminor Holding, the parent company of Luminor Bank, from a consortium of private equity funds managed by Blackstone, and DNB Bank, subject to regulatory approvals. THIS ANNOUNCEMENT RELATES TO THE DISCLOSURE OF INFORMATION THAT QUALIFIED AS INSIDE INFORMATION WITHIN THE MEANING OF ARTICLE 7(1) OF THE MARKET ABUSE REGULATION (REGULATION (EU) 596/2014). Today, Luminor announces that its shareholders, a consortium of private equity funds managed by Blackstone, and DNB Bank, have agreed to sell their shares in Luminor Holding to OTP Bank. The transaction marks an important milestone in Luminor's development as a leading pan-Baltic bank and provides a strong platform for its next phase of growth. The acquisition of Luminor by OTP Bank will support Luminor's strategy to strengthen further its position as a top three, universal, pan-Baltic bank, with a digital-first operating model, demonstrated track record, and a modern and scalable IT platform. Over recent years, Luminor has strengthened materially its business model, grown its customer franchise, and advanced the digitalisation of its operating model. Wojciech Sass, Chief Executive Officer of Luminor, said: 'This transaction is an important step in our development. Both Luminor and OTP Bank share a clear commitment to customers, long-term value creation and financing the real economy of our home markets. As part of OTP Group, Luminor will have the backing of an experienced international banking group with a strong presence across Central and Eastern Europe. I want to thank Luminor employees for their contribution to Luminor's development and their continued dedication to supporting our customers and the Baltic economies.' Péter Csányi, Chief Executive Officer of OTP Bank, added: 'As one of the leading banking groups in Central and Eastern Europe, OTP Group has demonstrated over the past decades its ability to create value in new markets. We invest capital, liquidity and technological expertise into acquired banks and apply a long-term ownership approach. Building on Luminor's strong market position, our goal is to further strengthen the bank's role in the Baltic states and contribute to the development of the region's financial system, lending activity and financial innovation.' Completion of the transaction is subject to obtaining the necessary regulatory approvals. This announcement is released by Luminor Holding AS and Luminor Bank AS and contains information in relation to its listed securities that qualified as inside information for the purposes of Article 7(1) of Regulation (EU) 596/2014 (the 'Market Abuse Regulation'). For the purposes of the Market Abuse Regulation and Article 2 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2016/1055, this announcement is made by Wojciech Sass, Chief Executive Officer of Luminor Bank AS and Mari Mõis, Chief Executive Officer of Luminor Holding AS. -ends- Notes to editors About Luminor Luminor is a leading independent bank in the Baltics and the third-largest provider of financial services in our region. We serve the financial needs of individuals, families, and companies. We are here to improve the financial health of our customers and our home markets, and to support their growth. The Trump administration is continuing its push to strip American citizenship from a record number of people , announcing 10 more cases against people accused of crimes or immigration fraud. Under President Donald Trump, the federal government has been seeking to drastically increase the number of so-called denaturalizations in recent months. Unlike revoking visas, the law has far stricter requirements for ending U.S. citizenship and yearly cases are generally low, but there has been a concerted effort to file a record number of cases, mainly against those the government believes fraudulently obtained citizenship. In a list released Monday, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Department of Justice (DOJ) said the group was accused or convicted of a range of crimes before they applied for citizenship in the United States. Newsweek sought attorney details for all ten defendants, but of the active cases listed in public court records, attorneys were not listed at the time of publishing. Read More on U.S. "We refuse to give a free pass to criminals who cheated their way into American citizenship," Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate, of the Justice Department’s Civil Division, said in a press release. "Under this administration, if you defrauded the naturalization process, you will face the full force of the Justice Department. We’ve only scratched the surface—many more complaints are coming." List of U.S. Citizens Facing Denaturalization The group listed by the DOJ and DHS included six people originally from Mexico, with one each from Cuba, Pakistan, Peru, and Poland. The DOJ said several of the cases involved alleged child sexual abuse, as well as using false documents or statements when seeking citizenship. The administration argues those citizenship grants should never have occurred because key information was concealed or misrepresented during the naturalization process. Several of the cases involve allegations that serious crimes were committed before or during the period in which the individuals were seeking U.S. citizenship. Former priest Urbano Vazquez Ortega, a native of Mexico who became a citizen in 2017, was convicted of multiple counts of child sexual abuse involving minors between 2015 and 2017 and was sentenced to 15 years in prison in 2019. Another Mexican national, Franscisco Montano, was convicted of aggravated sexual assault and indecency with a child after prosecutors said the abuse occurred during the five-year period before he naturalized in 1997. Jimmy Aguero, originally from Peru, was convicted on eight counts related to the sexual abuse of his minor stepdaughter and sentenced to a decade in prison, while Martin Garcia Cardiel, a Mexican immigrant who became a citizen in 2011, was later convicted on 19 counts of aggravated sexual abuse of a child stemming from conduct prosecutors said occurred in 2007, before his naturalization. Other cases center on fraud or identity-related allegations. Yoskmaikel Rodriguez Perez, a Cuban national naturalized in 2018, is accused of concealing a Medicare fraud operation that allegedly submitted more than $886,000 in false claims before he obtained citizenship; he later pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit health care and wire fraud. Murtaza Ali, originally from Pakistan, allegedly used multiple aliases to secure immigration benefits and later citizenship, ultimately pleading guilty in 2014 to making false statements to a federal agency. The DOJ also alleges that Antonio Alcantara-Ruiz, a Mexican national, obtained citizenship after using identity documents purchased from another person, while Ceflo Luviano-Mojica, also from Mexico, falsely denied previous arrests and jail time during the naturalization process. The remaining cases involve allegations tied to drug trafficking and financial crimes. Omar Cantu-Montalvo, a Mexican immigrant who became a citizen in 2005, later pleaded guilty to participating in a cocaine trafficking conspiracy that prosecutors say began months before he filed for naturalization. Marcin Stanislaw Garbacz, a native of Poland and former Catholic priest who became a citizen in 2014, was later convicted of wire fraud, tax-related offenses, and illicit sexual conduct involving a minor abroad. The Justice Department alleges Garbacz concealed that conduct while seeking citizenship. ... What Denaturalization Means In each case, the U.S. government has to argue that the individual either illegally procured naturalization or obtained citizenship through willful misrepresentation or concealment of material facts, often during the period when they were required to demonstrate "good moral character." Through civil denaturalization complaints filed in federal court, officials are seeking to revoke their citizenship, potentially returning them to noncitizen status and exposing them to further immigration consequences, including deportation. “When you commit fraud during the naturalization process, you forfeit the right to keep your U.S. citizenship,” DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in Monday's announcement. “These criminal aliens, comprised of drug traffickers, pedophiles, and fraudsters, lost that right and exploited our immigration system—harming real U.S. citizens. DHS is committed to ensuring we denaturalize and remove these fraudsters with every tool at our disposal.” Despite current political rhetoric, denaturalization remains extremely rare. From 1990 to 2017, an average of about 11 cases per year were initiated, according to the Brennan Center for Justice. During the first Trump administration, that number rose to roughly 25 cases annually, still a small fraction of the more than 24 million naturalized U.S. citizens.
