https://www.formula1.com/en/latest/artic.text: Max Verstappen McLaren 2026 Who is Dries van Langendonck, the McLaren junior driver signed by Max Verstappen? Max Verstappen has given his support and backing to Dries van Langendonck, but who is the 15-year-old Belgian? Jul 21, 2026 9:08am UTC Ahead of the Belgian Grand Prix last weekend, news surfaced that Max Verstappen had taken his first steps into driver development by giving backing to Dries van Langendonck. But who is the 15-year-old that has caught the attention of a four-time World Champion? Who is Dries van Langendonck? Van Langendonck is currently a McLaren junior driver, having joined the team's driver development programme in 2024 at the age of just 13 after winning the 2023 World Junior Karting title. A move into single-seaters beckoned last season, where the Belgian teenager became the youngest winner of a British Formula 4 race by winning on his debut at Donington Park. The 15-year-old also won the Iberia-based Formula Winter Series at the end of the year before returning for a full season of British F4 in 2026, where he currently leads the standings after winning four races. Verstappen answered questions about backing Van Langendonck before the Belgian GP Why has Verstappen supported him? Verstappen is no stranger to taking an interest in motorsport outside the realms of F1, having set up his own GT and sim racing teams. But this decision marks the first time that the Verstappen Racing squad will actively support a young driver in the lower ranks of single-seater racing. Speaking ahead of the Belgian Grand Prix, Verstappen gave his reasons for wanting to support Van Langendonck in his quest to reach F1. "Dries has been a big talent for a long time already in karting and I think you can spot quite quickly when someone is a little bit more special than someone else," said Verstappen. "I think that has carried on with what he is doing in F4 and that's why I think it's very exciting to try and help him, guide him, of course hand-in-hand from McLaren's side as well, to make the right decisions for his future. "He wants to get to F1 and I'm just trying to make sure that will happen in the future. It's an exciting project to be part of." Van Langendonck was in attendance at the Belgian GP with McLaren What does Van Langendonck think about Verstappen's support? Van Langendonck was present during the Belgian Grand Prix weekend with McLaren, where he will remain as part of the team's development programme as well as receiving support and guidance from Verstappen. "Max Verstappen has always been an idol for me. Growing up in Belgium, there was a natural connection to him, but beyond that he's an incredible driver and someone I've always admired," said Van Langendonck. "Verstappen Racing provides another layer of support and backing alongside McLaren, which will be important for my career. "It gives me access to additional resources and opportunities to continue developing as a driver, including extra simulator time at Max’s simulator facility. "Having support from both McLaren and Verstappen Racing means I can focus on improving every aspect of my performance and becoming the best driver possible." Van Langendonck hopes to reach F1 with the support of McLaren and Verstappen Van Langendonck's ultimate goal? Like every driver in the junior ranks, Van Langendonck hopes to reach F1 and believes that the support of McLaren and Verstappen together will allow him to get the most out of his potential. "Ultimately, my goal is to race in Formula 1 and obviously become a Formula 1 World Champion," he explained. "There's still a long way to go and a lot of hard work ahead, but I believe that's possible with McLaren and their support. "If I continue to develop, work hard and make the most of every opportunity, hopefully all the pieces will come together." Photograph: Pest Free Purerua View image in fullscreen Nine Lives, the feral cat that devastated a rare duck population in New Zealand for years, pictured in February 2024. Photograph: Pest Free Purerua New Zealand Nine Lives, the feral cat that terrorised New Zealand’s rare ducks, is caught after three years Large tabby cat that wiped out dozens of rare pāteke, or brown teal, has been killed after eluding trappers with its ‘very erratic’ behaviour Eva Corlett in Wellington Tue 4 Aug 2026 01.45 EDT Last modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 02.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A notorious feral cat given the name “Nine Lives” because it eluded trappers for three years has been caught and killed in New Zealand , ending its devastating rampage against one of the country’s rare duck populations. The cat, a large grey tabby, is estimated to have killed dozens of New Zealand’s rarest mainland duck – or 1% of its population – plus a host of kiwi chicks, native geckos and other native wildlife during the three years it was known to be roaming the Purerua peninsula, near the top of the North Island. “We don’t take for granted that we’ve had this success because it had us baffled for so long,” said Andy Mentor, the project manager for Pest Free Purerua, a conservation project. ‘Coming home’: kiwi enter parliament for first time as New Zealand marks conservation win Read more New Zealand has one of the highest rates of cat ownership in the world, and the impact of feral and domestic cats on biodiversity ignites fierce debate. Some on social media were horrified Nine Lives had been shot, believing it deserved to live, while others said its capture was “a fantastic result”. Nine Lives will form part of that debate long after its death, with its body set to be taxidermied for use as a tool to educate the community about the devastating impact of feral cats on native species. Nine Lives was first spotted on the Purerua peninsula in Northland in 2023. What ensued was a frustrating and twisted game of cat and mouse. View image in fullscreen Nine Lives ate dozens of pāteke, or brown teal, that were being introduced back into the wild. Photograph: Pest Free Purerua Pest Free Purerua had just introduced 20 pāteke, or brown teal – the country’s rarest mainland duck – to the peninsula, believing it had control over the feral cat population. “But within a week we had our first death. We put up some cameras and we identified a particular cat with specific markings,” Mentor said. Another 15 pāteke were killed, with the same cat turning up. “It was a really stressful time. So we brought in more traps, gear, night cameras to try and get to the root cause of the problem.” The project managed to catch other feral cats over the next year, but Nine Lives remained elusive. They decided to release more pāteke in 2024 but the same cat appeared, killing another 15 of the 20 birds. “This particular cat would be very erratic. It would show up in a particular place and then not show up for another two or three months. It would show up in the dusk, midnight, early morning, through the day, so it was never a predictable pattern, which made it very, very difficult to track,” Mentor said. The team came close to catching it on a number of occasions, but each time it slipped their grasp, earning it the name Nine Lives. At the end of July, Mentor and his team noticed the cat had turned up to a quarry three nights in a row, which was “quite unusual”. They laid out salmon, fried chicken and rabbit to attract the animal, and deployed cages and traps. On 30 July, a notification on a cellphone camera showed a cat in one of the cages. “We dispatched our trappers to check it out and there it was. So it was humanely shot,” Mentor said. The animal will have its stomach contents examined to see what it was feeding on before being taxidermied. Mentor said it has likely also fed on kiwi chicks, native geckos and other native wildlife. More than 2.5m feral cats roam New Zealand’s bush and on offshore islands, where they can grow up to a metre long, including their tail. They have destroyed native wildlife and hunted some bird species to the brink of extinction. In November, the government announced feral cats would be added to the country’s world-leading Predator-Free 2050 strategy. Mentor said moving from the suppression of cats to an elimination strategy will be a “real step up” for the peninsula and the team may restart introducing pāteke once more. But for now, conservationists will celebrate the capture of Nine Lives, as well as honour their most evasive adversary. “Nine Lives needs to be given a certain amount of dignity and respect,” said Mentor. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Daphne Caruana Galizia was killed in a car bombing in October 2017. Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/Reuters View image in fullscreen Daphne Caruana Galizia was killed in a car bombing in October 2017. Photograph: Darrin Zammit Lupi/Reuters Malta Daphne Caruana Galizia was investigating suspected corruption when killed, jury told Journalist’s son says his mother was examining leak from Electrogas, part owned by Yorgen Fenech who is on trial Juliette Garside Tue 4 Aug 2026 03.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Daphne Caruana Galizia was investigating suspected corruption by the businessman Yorgen Fenech and members of Malta’s government when she was killed, a jury has heard. The heir to one of Malta’s biggest fortunes, Fenech is on trial for murder, accused of commissioning and paying for Caruana Galizia’s killing in a car bombing in October 2017. The journalist’s son Matthew Caruana Galizia, a software engineer who was part of the reporting team that won a Pulitzer prize for the Panama Papers investigation into offshore companies, took the stand on Monday. He described being drawn in to helping his mother with her work, saying that as more facts came to light, it seemed to him a “portal” had opened and he could “see into hell”. View image in fullscreen Matthew Caruana Galizia Photograph: Matthew Mirabelli/AFP/Getty Images In 2015, Matthew said, he was working on the Panama Papers leak, uploading millions of files into a database that reporters were using to investigate tax havens. While processing the files, he said, he found information directly relevant to Malta. “I had to share what I was seeing with my mother. I believed it was too important.” Over time, material from the leak and Daphne’s own sources produced evidence that Malta’s then energy minister, Konrad Mizzi, and the prime minister’s chief of staff, Keith Schembri, had set up offshore companies soon after entering office. A firm of accountants was helping them to open bank accounts in the name of those companies, Matthew said. The jury was shown a comment left by Daphne in early 2017 under a newspaper article about the minister and the chief of staff. She wrote: “How unbelievably corrupt they are – and worse still, they were not tempted into corruption when they were already jaded in power, but actually got into power with the express purpose of being corrupt. It was their roadmap.” View image in fullscreen The Maltese businessman Yorgen Fenech. Photograph: Yara Nardi/Reuters At the time of her death in 2017, Matthew said, he had been helping his mother process another leak, consisting of thousands of emails stored in the servers of a company called Electrogas, partly owned by Fenech. One of the Muscat government’s flagship projects after winning the 2013 general election had been to privatise a key part of Malta’s electricity infrastructure. The contract had been won by Electrogas. “I was receiving this info, I couldn’t believe it, it was like a portal opened up and I could see into hell,” Matthew said. The defence objected, saying the witness was offering an opinion. Asked if Daphne had discussed the tendering process with him, Matthew said she had. “Factually, what did your mother tell you about the tendering process?” the prosecutor asked. Matthew replied: “That it was corrupt.” The judge interjected to remind the witness that this was an opinion, not a fact. Asked what he had seen in the emails, Matthew said: “When I started receiving the data and put it in a system to make it searchable, I could see that Yorgen Fenech was at the centre of everything. He was featured in countless emails.” Matthew said the Electrogas leak was ongoing the day his mother was killed. He said she had wanted to gather a group of journalists together to examine the data, in a collaboration similar to the one that had produced the Panama Papers. He had contacted the Guardian to begin work on the project, but his mother was killed a few months later. “We never got to do it, and in fact when I see these emails my heart beats fast because I’m taken back to that time when I was with my mother planning on what to do,” he told the court. After the murder, Matthew set up the Daphne Project, working with a wider group of publications, including the Guardian and Reuters, to continue investigating Electrogas and try to uncover who was behind his mother’s killing. The reporting uncovered evidence that suggested Fenech had intended to pay bribes in order to secure the power station concession, provoking international condemnation and a European parliament investigation. Fenech, Mizzi and Schembri reject any suggestion of corruption. The allegations were not repeated on Monday, after the judge ordered the testimony to focus only on what could be supported by documents shown in court. The prosecution’s questioning ended with a description by Matthew of the day his mother died. They were working together at home and she had prepared a mozzarella and tomato salad. She then left in her car to go to the bank. “I was working on some software and I heard an explosion. I opened the door, I felt the blood drain away … I started walking faster and faster towards the tower of smoke,” he said. “First I saw fire on the road – the road was on fire. I saw pieces of metal and flesh. My eyes followed the smoke and I saw a huge ball of fire. I ran towards it. The horn was going off, it wouldn’t stop. I saw a shadow in the car and I remember saying ‘that’s my mum’.” He told the court he had set aside everything to ensure those responsible were held to account, leaving his job, ending his career and returning to Malta. “We had to make it our mission, which we did. It came at enormous personal cost.” Fenech, who is on trial for complicity in the voluntary homicide of Caruana Galizia, denies the charges. The trial continues. Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPA Prisons and probation About 1,000 fewer prisoners to get early release as Burnham tightens rules Justice secretary says ministers would have liked to block more but doing so would cause prison system to ‘break’ UK politics live – latest updates Rachel Hall Tue 4 Aug 2026 04.16 EDT Last modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 04.21 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google About 1,000 fewer prisoners will be released early after Andy Burnham’s intervention to exclude those convicted of rape, serious child sexual offences and grooming from the scheme. The justice secretary, Alex Norris , said 5,000 prisoners would be released over 10 months from October in England and Wales, down from the government’s original plan for 6,000 from September. The prime minister announced on Monday that prisoners convicted of rape, serious child sexual offences and grooming would be excluded from the scheme to ease overcrowding, after pressure from MPs, victims, campaigners and frontline prison officers. Norris told Sky News that he would like to have gone further in blocking early release of some prisoners, but doing so would have caused the prison system to “break down”. He added that the government would not need further emergency release schemes as sentencing changes would provide “long-term security” for prison capacity. He said: “We’re out of where the previous government got to, which is this doom loop of getting to the end, having to do emergency release schemes where individuals were let out with none of the controls that we’re talking about.” But he acknowledged that the proposals had “created harm” for grieving families such as the wife of PC Andrew Harper, Lissie, and added that he was sorry. “I would express how angry I am too at being in a situation where we’re having to make significant changes that do have real impacts on people’s lives, so that we are able to have a functioning prison system,” he said. Harper’s mother, Debbie Adlam, said her family was “paying the price” after learning her son’s killers remained eligible for early release under the government’s plans to ease prison overcrowding. Some prisoners serving time for some sexual or violent offences will still be eligible for release at the halfway point of their sentence if they have not committed serious breaches of prison rules. This applies to Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, two of Harper’s killers, who were jailed for 13 years in 2020 for manslaughter. Henry Long, the main perpetrator, will not be subject to early release. View image in fullscreen Jessie Cole (left) and Albert Bowers, two of PC Andrew Harper’s killers, will be eligible for release. Photograph: Thames Valley police/PA Harper, a 28-year-old police officer, sustained fatal injuries while responding to a quad bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire, in August 2019. Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Adlam said: “It feels like we’re letting Andrew down again. We’ve been through the justice system, we thought we’d done as best as we could. Now we’re standing up to fight again with this evening’s announcement.” Harper died after he was caught in a strap attached to the back of a car and dragged down a country road as three teenage suspects fled the scene of the burglary. Long, the driver of the vehicle, received a 16-year sentence. Cole and Bowers were passengers in the car. While she accepted that Norris was sorry, she felt the decision was made “very quickly”, adding: “There surely has to be other answers.” Adlam told BBC Breakfast that “Andrew deserves better than this and so do we”, and that it was important that the Prison Service kept the family informed of when and whether they would be released. Burnham wrote in the Telegraph on Monday evening that the scheme had roots in previous governments’ “failure to add sufficient new places between 2010 and 2024”, when just 500 places were added and 23 prisons closed. He said he understood the “anger and anxiety” felt by victims’ families, which had informed his “significant changes”. “I know I can look people in the eye and say to them there is nothing more I could have asked for without risking the prison system collapsing within months. Such an outcome would expose the public to enormous risk: police would be unable to make arrests; courts would be unable to send new offenders to prison; and our justice system would grind to a halt,” he wrote. The prime minister has assured the public that offenders will face tighter community supervision, including new GPS monitoring for rapists to restrict their movements. He also promised a new package of support for victims, backed by £10m in new funding to provide trauma-informed contacts for victims, alongside a national helpline. He added that as well as building 14,000 new prison places by 2013, he had asked the justice secretary to review the indefinite sentences handed out between 2005 and 2012, to consider more early release for women’s prisoners given the lower risk they pose, and to look into faster returns of foreign national offenders to their country of origin. But the Conservatives have said victims “deserve better” than “learning their fate from press releases”. The Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, said her party would build more prison places, rent cells abroad and deport foreign offenders to ease overcrowding. She said: “This is only a partial climbdown. Killers, violent offenders, men who have terrorised their partners and more will all still walk out of prison in October.” Explore more on these topics Prisons and probation Andy Burnham UK criminal justice Alex Norris news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story PM to tighten early release rules but men jailed over PC Harper’s death can be freed More prisoners in England and Wales are recalled than released for first time Burnham stirs up political row with review of release plans for violent criminals Lack of safeguards over prisoners’ early release puts abuse victims at risk, Lammy warned Prison officers given more training to avoid being manipulated into illicit relationships with inmates Tens of thousands of prisoners in England and Wales at risk of cell fires ‘Missed opportunities’ to prevent woman’s death in prison cell fire, inquest finds ‘Supermax-style units’ for most dangerous criminals to be introduced in England and Wales Pepper spray use at young offender institutions in England ruled legal Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/AP BP BP profits more than double as Iran war sends oil prices soaring Energy company’s $5.73bn quarterly profits come after Shell posted second highest quarterly earnings on record Business live – latest updates Jillian Ambrose Tue 4 Aug 2026 02.54 EDT Last modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 03.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google BP has reported its highest quarterly profits since the first year of Russia’s war on Ukraine because of rising oil and gas prices caused by the Middle East crisis. The oil company’s quarterly profits more than doubled to $5.73bn (£4.27bn) in the three months to the end of June, up $2.5bn from the quarter before, as the ongoing conflict in the Middle East continued to disrupt energy exports from the Gulf. Despite the company’s better than expected profits, its new chief executive, Meg O’Neill, said there was “more to do” because BP was “not making the most” of its potential. BP puts North Sea oil and gas business up for sale Read more O’Neill is expected to undertake an overhaul of the 117-year-old company, including an exit from the North Sea after six decades of production from the UK’s oil and gas basin. O’Neill told CNBC on Tuesday morning that she had held a conversation with Andy Burnham, and that the new PM had “reinforced his desire to work closely with business” and be pragmatic”. “The UK is still using a huge amount of oil and natural gas every single day, and we ought to be using our domestic resources first instead of buying those resources from a third party,” O’Neill added. “You know, I think the new prime minister has come in with a focus on being pragmatic, and with a focus on understanding how communities around the nation can benefit from developing local economic outcomes.” Burnham was warned last week he could face the first revolt of his premiership over his apparent support for renewed drilling for oil and gas. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Preview latest after newsletter promotion Burnham risks first revolt as PM over apparent support for North Sea drilling Read more BP revealed its climbing profits days after Shell posted its second-highest quarterly earnings on record after months of market volatility caused by the Middle East crisis. Europe’s largest oil company doubled its net profit to almost $10bn in the three months to June, the highest since its record earnings in the months after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The Middle East crisis has also helped the Saudi ⁠oil company Aramco to a ⁠44% rise in ​net profits to $32.69bn in ​the three ​months ​ending on ​30 June, despite disruptions in ‌the strait of Hormuz, owing to higher ​sales revenue for refined and chemical products and crude oil. The windfall profits for the world’s biggest oil and gas companies have faced criticism. Households and businesses are struggling with rising energy bills, and millions have been affected by severe heatwaves across Europe, which are made more likely and more severe by the fossil-fuel-driven climate crisis. Donald Trump has said Chevron and ExxonMobil, which also reported sharp profit increases this week, are “making too much money” and should return some of their profits back to the public. Rosie Downes, head of campaigns at Friends of the Earth, said: “Clearly not everyone is feeling the pain of the energy crisis. Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPA View image in fullscreen A protester stands outside Delaney Hall detention facility during a vigil for Edwin Lopez Cornejo, in Newark, New Jersey. Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPA ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) Immigrant being held at Delaney Hall dies, marking 22nd death in ICE custody Edwin Lopez-Cornejo, 41, was arrested in New Jersey in June, and died after a ‘medical emergency’, agency said Abené Clayton Mon 3 Aug 2026 22.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An immigrant being held at a New Jersey ICE detention center died on 1 August, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced on Monday . Edwin Lopez-Cornejo, 41, is the 22nd person to die in ICE custody this year, according to agency data . Lopez-Cornejo, who is originally from El Salvador and first came to the US in 2006, was arrested by ICE agents in Plainfield, New Jersey , on 18 June and sent to Delaney Hall detention facility to await deportation. Less than two months later he suffered an unspecified “medical emergency”, and was later pronounced dead by University Hospital in Newark, New Jersey, ICE said. Lopez-Cornejo’s mother, Maria Cornejo told the New Jersey Monitor newspaper that her son had held a job since 2022 and tried to show the arresting officers his work permit, but he was detained anyway. Though she says she spoke to her son daily, she was unable to visit him because she is not a US citizen. “I never got to see him. He didn’t get to see his daughter for six weeks,” she told the Monitor. “When we told her what happened, she let out a big scream and hasn’t been the same since. She can’t sleep or eat. Neither can I. “I never imagined he would die in that place. I’m just destroyed. I have so much hurt in my heart,” Cornejo continued. In recent months Delaney Hall has been under the national microscope and the site of protests following allegations of issues such as physical abuse by guards and spoiled food. In late May these concerns prompted at least 300 detainees to organize a hunger and labor strike. Weeks after its start, women living in a separate unit of the same facility launched their own hunger strike . In addition to improvements to the facility, their demands include calls for ICE to release women under 21, those with medical conditions and mothers. In a statement that followed ICE’s announcement of Lopez-Cornejo’s death, Ras J Baraka, the Newark mayor, called for the closure of the facility and said this most recent loss of life reflects the lack of accountability and oversight that local residents, officials and those detained in Delaney Hall have been calling for. “GEO group and ICE have repeatedly demonstrated a disregard for transparency, public oversight and the laws designed to protect the health, safety and dignity of those in their custody. When accountability is absent, tragedies become all too common,” Baraka said in a statement released on Monday. “We cannot allow these disturbing failures to continue unchecked. We must speak out against these injustices, demand answers and continue to call for the closure of Delaney Hall,” he continued. Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters Opinion Migration Ceuta was a carnival of anti-migrant content for hateful opportunists on the right – and a lesson for the left Jonathan Liew It was framed as a perfect storm because nativists dearly wanted it to be. Looking on, progressives failed to meet the moment too Tue 4 Aug 2026 04.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 04.07 EDT Share T he live streams are still running, training their cameras on the beach at Ceuta, where nothing is happening. The self-styled citizen journalists are still pounding the streets, capturing their shaky smartphone footage. Zia Yusuf of Reform UK was out there at the weekend, wearing a crisp white shirt and smart tailored trousers, lest anyone confuse him with the other brown people there. The bad brown people. Why was the migrant incursion at Ceuta, on the Spanish-Moroccan border, such a big story across the world? How did it manage to pique the interest of Donald Trump and Elon Musk , to feature on NBC’s Nightly News, not – shall we say – a programme massively predisposed to spotlighting news stories from continental Africa? What about it so exercised Europe’s heads of government? What made it an irresistible front-page story in the Daily Mail, the Daily Express and the Daily Telegraph? Certainly not any kind of urgent or imminent threat to our own borders, much less the borders of the United States. The Spanish enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla operate under special exemptions from the Schengen area, rendering it almost impossible for an undocumented migrant to reach mainland Spain , about 12 miles away across the Mediterranean. Once many of the migrants realised this, they duly left. Nor any kind of humanitarian concern for those who drowned or were killed in the crowd crush. “About 48,000 of the up to 60,000 people who came into Ceuta from Morocco returned within a day. Still, the sudden influx created a crisis for Spain’s pro-immigration government. Nearly three dozen died.” So read a New York Times subheading on Friday. And once you fight your way past the tortured syntax, did you notice anything unusual there? First the integrity of the border, then the political ramifications, then the people who died: the hierarchy of rightwing immigration discourse expressed in three perfect sentences. The death toll has since risen to either 72 or 88 – authorities disagree on the number – and nobody seems over-fussed either way. Rather, Ceuta functions as a kind of border porn for the global far right: a locus upon which to project their most vivid and apocalyptic fantasies. If the historian Mike Davis once described the US-Mexico border wall as “a political stage set” , then in the age of the deepfake and the troll-farm, Ceuta has proved a similarly fertile source of content: the border interface reimagined as digital theatre, mass migration as primetime television. View image in fullscreen Migrants who entered the Spanish enclave by swimming or on foot from Morocco sit on a street in Ceuta, 3 August 2026. Photograph: Reduan/EPA The rich irony here is that from a securitisation standpoint, Ceuta functions almost exactly as it was intended. A six metre-high barbed-wire fence, reinforced by watchtowers and a network of video cameras, separates it from Morocco . From Ceuta, an internal checkpoint guards the only ferry route to mainland Spain. The European Union has spent years, and hundreds of millions of euros, on developing partnerships with Morocco on border management. None of which seemed to matter in the slightest as European leaders queued up to give the Pedro Sánchez government a ritual horse-whipping. Italy reintroduced air and sea border controls with Spain. Emmanuel Macron deployed mobile units to the Spanish border to strengthen controls. Giorgia Meloni – backed by Finland, Denmark and Czechia – has argued that Spain’s membership of the Schengen area should be suspended . And of course these are primarily domestic politicians catering to a domestic market, ahead of an electoral cycle in which incumbents in France, Italy and Poland are being outflanked by nativist insurgents to their right. Sánchez himself faces the ballot box in 2027, an election in which his government can boast strong economic growth and which his rightwing opponents will therefore be desperate to turn into a referendum on immigration. So that’s the political angle. But really the spectacle of Ceuta represents a more primal and guttural need, particularly in the English-speaking world, for the inflammatory anti-immigration crusade to be seen as well as spoken. The photos and footage coming out of the enclave in recent days, all shot from distance and almost never in closeup, are all geared towards a single end: to encourage the viewer to see these brown bodies as a single mass, each indistinguishable from the other, the accountants and surgeons from the bomb-makers and rapists, the living from the dead. And so, by small degrees, the line between nationalism and pure-blood white supremacy blurs a little more. Indeed, the very idea that a single border crossing 1,000 miles and two seas away from us is somehow our urgent problem, only really makes sense in a worldview whose real distinction is not between “Britain” and “abroad” but between an imagined white Christian Europe and a savage brown other. For all this, the right does not act alone. The palpable relief on many parts of the left as most of the original 60,000 migrants returned to Morocco spoke of a worrying acquiescence: a tacit acceptance of the dangerous trope of migration as a prima facie problem. Here’s a radical thought: what if migration is only a problem to those who want it to be? What if we started seeing the mass movement of people less as an existential threat and more as a simple inevitability of human existence? Nine years ago the great Gary Younge set out in the Guardian a utopian vision of open borders and no immigration controls. What happened to that sense of vision and idealism? When did border discourse, the conversation on why and how we move, become something to be feared and not embraced? skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Matters of Opinion Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more Preview latest after newsletter promotion Stronger EU borders needed after Ceuta crisis, von der Leyen says Read more Whether Ceuta was an accidental security lapse or a deliberately engineered event is actually beside the point. The point is that as the global right grows in confidence, as the migration industrial complex thirsts for new content, new border porn, there will be more Ceutas in the future. People will keep migrating and die trying, and because this is good telly it will keep happening. “Today more than ever,” writes the sociologist Mimi Sheller in her book Mobility Justice , “these borderlands are soaked in the blood of white nationalism, ethnic profiling, and enforced death in the no man’s land.” The endgame here is massacres, vigilante violence, not “stop the boats” but shoot the boats, the border reimagined as a computer-game war zone. The endgame is what the likes of Musk and his far-right meat puppets are already depicting: a world where zombie armies of “military-age males” invade our virgin turf, and the problem is not the forces that drove them from their homes, but your “suicidal empathy” , because these are not equal humans deserving equal treatment. These are the stakes. And frankly, when the next Ceuta happens, the left needs to think of a better response than simply being thankful they went home again. Photograph: Alexandra Beier/Getty Images Opinion Nato With Russia at the door and the US backing away, Europe has to build its own ‘way of war’ Nathalie Tocci Even in a Europe-focused Nato 3.0, Washington would still want to call the shots. We need an insurance policy Tue 4 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 00.01 EDT Share How can Europe defend itself against Russia without the US, or with much less of it? This question sums up the existential challenge now facing the continent. Russia’s imperial ambitions start with Ukraine, but they don’t end there. Moscow’s hybrid attacks , its political interference in support of Russia-friendly parties and its military sabre-rattling – including a warship’s live-fire exercise 45 miles off the UK coast – all point in the same direction. A kinetic war to defend ourselves against Russia in the coming months or years cannot be ruled out. This is why European defence budgets are rising across Europe, especially in countries closer to the frontline. Defence spending has accelerated since Donald Trump returned to office. This is less because of Trump’s jibes and insults – now extending even to far-right European leaders like Giorgia Meloni – and more that Europeans are waking up to the reality that in the event of a war against Russia, the US may not be there for them. While the US nuclear umbrella could hold – although France has launched an initiative to Europeanise its nuclear deterrent in case it does not – European governments and institutions are reckoning with the possibility that they might need to fight Russia without US conventional forces’ support or with much less of it. This explains the emergence of something that is unofficially being called Nato 3.0. At the Ankara Nato summit a few weeks ago, the initiative was pompously talked up – in part to placate Trump, in part to signal to Vladimir Putin that even if the US takes a back seat, a Europeanised Nato remains credible. The slogan that its supporters use, “A stronger Europe in a stronger Nato”, is misleading. Yes, Europeans will become militarily stronger, but as the US partly disengages, Nato overall will weaken. Working towards a Europeanised Nato is still sensible: even if the alliance weakens in absolute terms, it may still be strong enough to stand up to an encroaching Russia. But here’s why we need to be cautious and work on alternatives at the same time. Take a worst-case scenario in which Russia attacked a European Nato country in the coming months or years. That country’s European Nato allies would probably come to the rescue. Eastern and northern European countries would stand by each other, of course. Even Germany has arguably made the cultural and psychological leap of acknowledging that its troops may have to fight the Russians again. Its plans to permanently station a 5,000-strong brigade in Lithuania is a signal. If Germany were to respond, France and the UK would very likely come in too. And if these core countries stepped in, Italy and Spain would follow suit. The good news is that Europeans would probably remain united. But the bad news is that the US might not answer the call to defend Europe – and this in turn would instantly break Nato. The core pledge of the alliance’s founding treaty, article 5 , says that an attack on one Nato state is an attack on all. The nature of the rupture would be the same whether it came from an explicit triggering of article 5 to which the US did not respond, or from article 5 never being triggered in anticipation of that very outcome. A second, less catastrophic scenario is one in which there is no Russian provocation, Nato 3.0 moves forward in earnest, and in a few years’ time the alliance looks radically different to how it looks today, with the Europeans – along with Turkey and Canada – shouldering the lion’s share of the burden. But if non-US allies shoulder the bulk of the responsibilities, they will want the bulk of the rights. Europe’s defence markets would become less open to US companies, and Nato’s priorities would start reflecting European interests. Europeans would certainly not be happy to let the US call the shots indefinitely while they merely carry out orders. But it is hard to imagine any US administration, let alone one with Trump at the helm, happily giving up these rights and benefits. Since its inception in 1949, Nato has been organised around US capabilities, technologies and strategic culture. Europeans have been integrated into a US command structure and have adopted the US way of war. They lack the capabilities, manpower and command structures available to the US. If they had to deal with armed aggression in the near term they could not replicate Nato’s model. One way or another they would develop alternatives – but with the US still formally in Nato, albeit less committed to it, this could not happen within the alliance itself. None of the alternatives is ideal. The EU does important work on defence industry cooperation and even has a mutual assistance clause enshrined in its treaties, but due to a range of constitutional and political constraints, I don’t believe it constitutes a feasible path forward to defence. This leaves so-called coalitions of the willing – an idea with a problematic history that is now being resurrected. The US has led previous coalitions of the willing when it wanted to bypass formal multilateral structures like the UN. The most infamous example is the US-led coalition that invaded Iraq in 2003, without UN security council authorisation and in blatant violation of international law. Today, coalitions of the willing have formed around critical security flashpoints – including Ukraine, Greenland and the strait of Hormuz. As in the past, their establishment is driven by the fact that existing organisations – the UN, Nato and the EU – have proven unable to deal effectively with these challenges on their own. Interestingly, this time, rather than being US-led and aimed at bypassing international law, they are European-led, bypass Washington, and are aimed precisely at affirming collective European action on key security issues in compliance with international law. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Preview latest after newsletter promotion Coalitions of the willing, however, are ad hoc and ephemeral, lacking both a system for political strategic decision-making and an operational chain of command. While participating states’ militaries are now meeting regularly to develop joint plans, these coalitions still lack the permanence needed to structurally build a European way of war, ensure its consistent adherence to international law, and to convey a real sense of confidence in the public. Institutionalising such coalitions at political level will be critical. One option would be through a European security council, an idea that was born in the wake of Brexit to keep the UK involved in European security decisions. It is being resurrected now precisely to devise ways for Europeans to address the continent’s security. None of this should de-prioritise the Europeanising of Nato – but coalitions of the willing could be a critical insurance policy, should Nato 3.0 falter and fall. https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.text: Illustration: Nataliia Shulga/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Illustration: Nataliia Shulga/The Guardian The long read Ukraine ‘The war leaked into every lesson’: learning Ukrainian in a country under siege Soon after my first visit to Ukraine four years ago, I began language lessons. It taught me more than I ever expected Charlotte Higgins Tue 4 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Share Almost as soon as I returned from my first reporting trip to Ukraine , in October 2022, I decided to start Ukrainian lessons. Not as an act of solidarity, exactly, but as a marker that I was committed to returning. I wanted to know some Ukrainian in order to feel less helpless, to edge towards a better understanding of what I was reporting, and to be more courteous to those whom I encountered. And I hoped, in time, to be able to pull myself through a piece of poetry in the original. I began meeting Olha, my teacher, by weekly video call later that autumn. She was in Ivano-Frankivsk, her home town in the far west of Ukraine, I was in London. With endless patience and humour, she led me by the hand through the unfamiliar letters of her language, those elegant, sensuous shapes of the Cyrillic alphabet. I have not yet fully internalised them, as I have the Roman alphabet, whose shapes are so much part of me that I don’t see them any more. The unfamiliarity of Cyrillic characters, by contrast, allows me to enjoy the exhilarating ski-slope swoop of the Л (l), the generous expanses of the Ю (yu), and the majestic architecture of the Ж (zh), which spreads out its arms and legs like candelabra. (Enjoy, please, the extravagant double Ж in Запоріжжя – Zaporizhzhia – which has a particularly graceful etymology: it means “beyond the rapids”.) And, though I shrink from trying either to write or decode the curlicued Ukrainian cursive, just forming these letters is a joy for the hand: the twin sweep of a З (z) and the harsh angles of a Д (d), which I like to write as a triangle with a pair of sharp, inward-facing tails dangling from it. Then there is the special category of Cyrillic letters reserved only for the Ukrainian language. You may see, for example, on a Ukrainian necklace or bracelet, or on a T-shirt, the letter Ї – like our letter I, surmounted by a diaeresis. The character, which expresses the sound “yi” – as in Kyiv (Київ) – is absent from the Russian variant of the alphabet, and thus operates as a subtle signifier of allegiance. In occupied Mariupol, in 2022, the letter Ї was seen scrawled in chalk on the ­streets – a single letter as an act of defiance. I enjoy the fact that in the transliteration of my surname, Гіґґінс, there is another Ukrainian-only letter, Ґ, which, from its jaunty upturned serif, one can tell is the rare hard g, most commonly employed for loan words; it was removed from the alphabet in Stalin-era reforms, and formally given back a place in the Ukrainian alphabet after the fall of the Soviet Union and Ukrainian independence in 1991. There is a text artwork that I love, by the sculptor Nathan Coley, installed in a library in Edinburgh, which consists of the sentence: The Basic Material is Not the Word but the Letter. I often think of it when navigating a forest of Cyrillic signs. Thick accumulations of Ukrainian consonants conspire against my tongue and my memory: airless crushes of them, like the compressed folds of a concertina. I cannot tell you how many repetitions it took to memorise незважаючи на ( nezvazhayuchy na ) – “despite” in Ukrainian. It seemed important to master this phrase. How else could I say, “despite the war”? Emblematic of the many sound collisions in Ukrainian is the magnificent single letter Щ, expressed in English as “shch” – as in “fresh cheese” , as one of my grammar books puts it. After much deliberation, I have only come up with one word in English (with the exception of those we have borrowed, such as borshch) that contains this fricative-affricative alliance: “pushchair”. Four whole letters in English for a single pair of glorious, fat loops in Ukrainian. I had studied classics at university, and recklessly, perhaps arrogantly, felt that I needn’t be defeated by a tricky language. I knew, at least, what I was getting into with Ukrainian nouns, which, like those in Latin and Greek, come in three genders – masculine, feminine and neuter – and are inflected, meaning their endings change depending on what role they perform in a sentence. Even so, I feel that seven case endings, which is one more than Latin, and two more than Greek, is a lot. Their usage is almost baroque in its excess: I have a kind of stunned respect for a language in which some numbers – but by no means all, and for no perceptible reason – demand to be followed by the genitive case. One says п’ятдесят доларів ( pyatdesyat dolariv ), meaning $50, the genitive case; but п’ятдесят два долари ( pyatdesyat dva dolary ), $52, using the ordinary nominative. On the other hand, $51 has yet another ending, because the crucial extra dollar bill you have added to your 50 means that it is, according to the Ukrainian language, a singular, however hard you may protest that you are, in fact, clutching a fistful of dollars. View image in fullscreen A billboard shows a stamp issued in Ukraine on the invasion’s first anniversary. It reads ‘FCK PTN!’, set against a Banksy mural on a ruined house in Borodyanka. Photograph: Dominika Zarzycka/NurPhoto/Rex/Shutterstock I had heard rumours of the perils of Ukrainian “verbs of motion”, which turned out to be more than well founded. Speakers of Slavonic languages describe movement at a level of subtlety that, to an anglophone, seems absolutely bewildering. Ukrainian has two basic verbs where we have one to express the idea of “to go” – the first used for travelling on foot and the second for travelling by some form of transport. Both of those, in turn, come in different forms depending on whether you are moving in one direction only, or going there and back again. That is true for other verbs of motion, right down to, say, the verb to crawl. Is your baby moving across the floor in one direction? Or is she planning on taking an indirect route, or perhaps undertaking this journey regularly? Answer these questions before selecting your verb form! Learning Ukrainian, it turned out, was more than a side-interest, an extracurricular activity. It forced me to look at myself in entirely new ways. In my 50s – treading the pleasant plateau of knowing broadly how to do my job after all these years – it was confronting to be back at the bottom rung of knowledge, out of my depth. There would be moments – when Olha was speaking to me, or when I was trying to keep up with what Ukrainian friends were saying, or even during a seemingly predictable encounter in a cafe – when I would feel an unfamiliar, blind panic rising to engulf me. It would start out well, I would be clinging on to comprehension, and then there would be a block, a word or phrase I would snag on, or an unexpected conversational current – and I would lose my grip. I recognised the feeling from only one other area of my life: playing chamber music. When you lose your place in a Beethoven quartet, say, and everyone else is moving onwards at speed, you can feel stranded, as if you are watching the vessel of the music slip into the distance without you. The redeeming fact is that attempting to speak even terrible Ukrainian in Ukraine is met, in my experience, with a response on a scale set between courteous acceptance and ecstatic (and undeserved) gratitude. But my new language was also the language of war. From the very first, the experience was quite unlike that of studying Italian, the only other modern language in which I can claim any kind of proficiency – a language, for the learner, full of the pleasures of ordering cappuccino and gelato, for asking directions to the duomo, and exclaiming over the splendour of il paese più bello del mondo – the most beautiful country in the world. The very first sentences in Ukrainian that I read – when Olha introduced herself – were coloured by her wistfulness for a life that war had forced her to leave behind: До війни я жила в Києві. Я дуже люблю це місто і хочу знову там жити. “Before the war I lived in Kyiv. I love this city very much and want to live there again.” It would be wrong to suggest that every lesson was filled with darkness. We laughed a lot. Olha often steered us towards a world of red wine and ice-cream, of opera and music and reading. The Ukrainian delight in the consumption of delicious food (a constant pleasure, thanks to the excellence of produce grown in the чорнозем, or chornozem , the fertile black earth) was present in our lessons. Soon I learned the words смачний ( smachnyi ), tasty, and смачного! ( smachnoho !), bon appetit! – lip-smackingly onomatopoeic vocabulary, full of the joy of the Ukrainian table. But the war leaked into every lesson. Indefinite pronouns were explained to me via the example Ніхто не любить Путіна – “No one likes Putin”. The impersonal expressions communicating necessity, треба and потрібно ( treba and potribno ), were illustrated via a speech made on the eve of war by Valerii Zaluzhnyi, then commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian armed forces, about the urgent need to be equipped for battle. Треба готуватися до війни – “We must prepare for war.” Нам треба мати ресурси, потрібно 300 танків – “We need to have resources, we need 300 tanks.” View image in fullscreen People shelter inside a subway station during an air-raid alert in Kyiv, May 2023. Photograph: Alina Smutko/Reuters My vocabulary grew to include the words for drone and rocket, explosion, bomb shelter and air-raid alarm. There is a Telegram channel that is commonly consulted when an air-raid alert goes off in Ukraine, as it provides details on whether there are drones on the way, or ballistic missiles, and their direction of travel. For ease I switched this channel to English, using an automatic translate function. With every new siren, it leapt into life, asking, “Why the anxiety?” It took me a while to figure out that the word used for air-raid alarm, тривога ( tryvoha ) also means “anxiety” in Ukrainian. (The English word “alarm” behaves similarly, being both the mechanism that produces the sound, and the feeling it engenders.) But still, every time I checked it I imagined it was asking me, yet again, a sarcastic question about my state of mind. As Christmas 2022 arrived, Olha and I read a speech of Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s that contained a nice example of the compound future tense formed by an auxiliary verb and the infinitive: Ми будемо співати колядки – голосніше ніж генератор. “We are going to sing carols – louder than a generator.” The noisy chugging of generators side by side on a pavement, servicing a row of shops during a blackout, would become a familiar music to me. In the same speech, the president also provided an introduction to impersonal adverbial constructions suggesting a state or condition. Нам може бути темно, холодно і складно. Але нам більше не страшно. “It may be dark, cold and difficult for us, but we are no longer afraid.” That winter truly was dark. Even in far-western Ivano-­Frankivsk, Olya was affected by Russian attacks on power infrastructure designed to freeze Ukraine into submission. Blackouts meant the cancellation of several lessons. In time a kind of intimacy sprang up between us: there is something vulnerable-making about learning a language, when your normal ease of expression crumbles and you have to start again like a child acquiring speech for the first time, but oh, so much more slowly. You open yourself up to being and sounding foolish as you reach for ways to say what you mean. You build fragile little linguistic structures, and they collapse time and time again. You want to cry like a child with frustration. Olha – younger than me by a good 15 years – reassured me like an encouraging parent. Soon I was speaking excitedly of plans for another reporting trip. Olha’s notes recorded our dialogue. У які міста ти будеш їхати? Я буду їхати у Київ, у Ізюм, у Харків і теж яхочу їхати у Херсон. “What cities are you going to go to?” “I am going to go to Kyiv, Izium and Kharkiv, and I want to go to Kherson, too.” Olha must have asked what my partner thought of all this – an extremely good question. I offered the truthful although carelessly incomplete reply, Мій чоловік розуміє, як це важливо для мене. “My partner understands how important this is to me.” When I returned from that trip – it had been my first time to eastern Ukraine and to territories recently clawed back from Russian occupation – Olha asked for my impressions. I described seeing зруйновані вулиці, мости, будинки – “destroyed streets, bridges, buildings”. Це було дуже стресово для тебе? “Was it very stressful for you?” she asked. Another good question. Було стресово бачити міста зруйновані. “It was stressful to see destroyed towns,” I replied, evasively, perhaps enjoying wrapping my tongue around the word зруйновані – zruynovani , ruined. At that moment I lacked either sufficient insight into my own emotions, or the linguistic skill to explain precisely how stressful this trip had in fact been. It was a world away from any kind of journalism I had done before: the mass grave site; the hours with the grieving parents of a killed son; the sorrow of it all. In Lviv, a couple of months ago, I attended an intensive language programme. I put great hope into this course, as if it were not a series of lessons but rather a magical linguistic wand that would offer me the gift of tongues. When we arrived – the 20-odd students, an eclectic group of mainly Americans, some with Ukrainian roots, some at university, some volunteering for the Ukrainian cause in one way or another – we were given a written test and an interview. On the basis of this, I was placed in what became understood as the “top class”. I spent two weeks in this class, with three excellent female classmates, taught by a gentle and learned teacher, having my sense of myself as a competent person systematically undone. No English was uttered in these classes, as we discussed such subjects as the wartime rifts in Ukrainian society and were tasked with preparing presentations to the assembled staff and student body – something I would shudder to do even in English. View image in fullscreen A customer browsing the shelves in Sens bookshop in Pechersk, Kyiv. Photograph: Emre Çaylak/The Guardian Every evening, I went home to my flat fighting the urge to weep, convinced that there had been an error and I was simultaneously “holding everyone up” and “letting the side down”. One of the Americans – a level-headed economist who, when she finished her course, was told she held the record for speed of learning – gently pointed out that we had been placed in our classes based on our scores in a test. Perhaps, she offered, my response was gendered? Would many men be flailing around in quite this level of self-doubt? I despairingly messaged a colleague and friend who’d learned Russian as a teenager, who briskly informed me that he had cheated an aptitude test in his youth precisely to be in a confounding top class; that he had observed at work that I was a very competitive person; and that I should sit back and enjoy the sensation of not being the best at something. I had not expected to be recalibrating my relationship with myself, or to be confronting the gap between my own and others’ perceptions of myself, in this way. There were other moments of inner tumult, too – the day we discussed Victoria Amelina in class: a Ukrainian novelist who had become a friend, and who died of her injuries after a Russian cruise missile targeted a pizza restaurant she had just sat down in. Or the morning we were asked to read out our favourite Ukrainian poem. I chose a very recent work: My Day, by poet and film-maker Iryna Tsilyk. It anatomises the peculiar state of bei

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/04/soldi.text: Four people, including three civilians, were killed by an unidentified soldier in the Black Sea city of Sevastopol in Russian-annexed Crimea, the city's Moscow-installed governor said on Tuesday."A tragedy in Sevastopol...According to initial information, a soldier opened fire on his fellow servicemen, killing one person, before attacking civilians and killing three of them," Mikhail Razvozhayev wrote in a post on Telegram.He added the assailant, whose nationality was not specified and whose motives were not immediately clear, was arrested."Emergency services, investigators and forensic experts are currently working at the scene. All the circumstances and causes of what happened are being established," the Russian head of the city administration added.He also called on everyone to remain calm, trust only official information and not to spread unverified rumours.The civilian victims were two men aged 71 and 59, and a 64-year-old woman, Razvozhayev added.Crimea, a peninsula illegally annexed by Russia from Ukraine in 2014, has for weeks been the target of Ukrainian retaliatory attacks aimed at disrupting the logistics of Russian forces deployed in southern Ukraine.Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and has regularly struck its neighbour, including from the Crimean peninsula.

The fires mark a second straight week of major wildfires in Greece. Hundreds of firefighters remain deployed as strong winds and dry conditions make containment difficult. At least five people have died during the past two weeks, underlining the human cost as emergency crews work to protect communities and prevent further losses. http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/04/iran-.text: Iran announced that it would target any US warship that may try to impose a different route than the one that Tehran has allowed for ships crossing the Strait of Hormuz, Mohsen Rezaei, a senior advisor to Iran's supreme leader, said Monday."(We won't allow) the second corridor to open. Even if they (US) deploy warships, we will target them," Rezaei said in an interview with Iran's state media.Rezaei also warned of targeting US ships and bases if the country continued the naval blockade on Iran."There will certainly be serious dangers to the US ships and bases. We will not sit and watch the US continue the naval blockade," he added.While President Donald Trump said on Monday he expected negotiations to begin within the next day or two after threathening that newly planned talks with Tehran are the “last chance” for Iran to forge a deal before devastating strikes on the country, Iran immediatly denied holding new negotiations saying the Islamic Republic was only working out an agreement with Oman at the moment over a temporary route for shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.Foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei insisted the strait, the critical waterway where about a fifth of all traded oil and natural gas flowed before the start of the war, will "remain closed until US violations end".Cargo vessel hit by 'unknown projectile'Meanwhile, a cargo vessel in the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Oman was struck by an "unknown projectile", a British maritime agency said on Tuesday, without giving specifics on damage or injuries.Authorities started an investigation into the vessel, which has not been named, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said, adding the incident occurred 37 kilometres northeast of Al Khasab, Oman.

https://www.politico.eu/article/greece-k.text: Kyriakos Mitsotakis is the prime minister of Greece. Europe’s security environment has fundamentally changed. Alongside conventional military threats and cyberattacks, the EU is increasingly confronted with a more insidious form of hybrid pressure: the deliberate instrumentalization of migration by state and nonstate actors seeking to test Europe’s resilience, undermine its cohesion and extract political concessions. Advertisement Advertisement Recent events at Europe’s borders, most notably in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, are the latest reminder that migration is no longer just a humanitarian issue or management challenge. In some cases, it has become a tool of geopolitical coercion. The EU has made important progress on this issue with its Pact on Migration and Asylum . It has introduced mechanisms to manage migratory pressure, including flexibility in its procedures and solidarity among member countries. But these tools are designed for situations that remain, at their core, manageable. They do not adequately address scenarios in which migration is weaponized, or where flows are engineered, amplified or facilitated in a way that creates a de facto hybrid challenge. To be sure, we don’t yet know what caused the situation that unfolded in Ceuta last week. But scenarios like these are not unprecedented. Greece faced a similar situation at its land border with Turkey in Evros in 2020, as did Lithuania, Poland and Latvia at their borders with Belarus in 2021. What we are witnessing in these cases is not a gradual increase in arrivals but the sudden, massive and often coordinated movements of people — sometimes in the tens of thousands within just a few days — that overwhelm national capacities and test the EU’s resilience as a whole. In such extreme circumstances, the immediate and full application of standard asylum and reception systems for all arrivals is not simply difficult — it is often impossible. Systems risk paralysis, public trust erodes and the very functioning of Schengen is put under strain. Europe needs to acknowledge this gap and act decisively. Advertisement Advertisement What is required is a dedicated European framework for situations of mass and instrumentalized migratory pressure, with clear and objective criteria for its activation. These criteria should combine quantitative elements — such as the scale and speed of arrivals relative to a country’s capacity — with qualitative indicators, including any evidence of coordination, facilitation or involvement by third countries or organized criminal networks. Once triggered under a specifically defined EU emergency regime, a mechanism like this could allow for temporary, proportionate and strictly controlled adjustments to standard procedures. Accelerated asylum processes must also continue to be part of the toolbox, particularly for individuals coming from countries with low recognition rates for international protection. EU flags fly in front of the European Commission’s Berlaymont building in Brussels on Feb. 17, 2025. | Thierry Monasse/Getty Images But this is not sufficient. Europe has to be honest about the limits of its fast-track asylum procedures. In clearly defined exceptional situations of extreme and disproportionate pressure — whether at land borders or following mass arrivals by sea — member countries should be given the option, under a dedicated EU emergency regime, to temporarily suspend asylum applications for newly arrived persons while proceeding with the swift return of those not entitled to remain, in full compliance with the EU’s legal obligations. This is not a departure from Europe’s values but a necessary adaptation to new realities. Moreover, any such measures must be strictly time-bound, proportionate and subject to robust safeguards. Full respect for EU law, the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU and the principle of non-refoulement remains non-negotiable. At the same time, safeguarding international obligations must go hand in hand with the EU’s ability to protect its borders and preserve its internal stability. Advertisement Advertisement Crucially, this balance cannot be sustained without genuine European solidarity. No member country facing this kind of pressure should stand alone. Operational support from EU agencies, coordinated return efforts and financial and technical assistance must be automatically mobilized whenever a mechanism to this effect is activated. Without such a framework, the risks are clear. Frontline countries remain exposed, incentives grow for hostile actors to exploit migration for geopolitical purposes and internal divisions within the bloc deepen. Most importantly, citizens’ confidence in Europe’s ability to effectively, fairly and collectively manage its borders will continue to erode. Europe has always adapted its policies to changing realities. Migration is no exception. And recognizing that it can be weaponized is not alarmism — it is realism. The EU must now equip itself with the legal and operational tools needed to defend its external borders, deter those who seek to exploit its openness and respond to this new reality firmly, lawfully and collectively. POLITICO occasionally publishes opinion pieces from guest authors to offer our readers a range of perspectives on the intersection of power and politics. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not reflect the views of POLITICO.

https://www.politico.eu/article/europe-w.text: BRUSSELS — When French and German security chiefs announced plans last month to develop a “European sovereign digital backbone,” tech and defense industry insiders on both sides of the Atlantic knew what they really meant: Adieu Palantir. Across Europe, the hunt is on for alternatives to the U.S.-based data analytics company that a growing number of government officials believe is too deeply lodged in some of the most sensitive areas of government, from local policing and global intelligence to national defense and health systems. Yet it is precisely Palantir’s crucial functions in daily workflows, and its largely unmatched data expertise, that will make it extremely hard for Europe to cut it off in pursuit of greater digital sovereignty. Advertisement Advertisement “Let's be honest, Palantir’s product is very good and addictive, it's pretty much like the sugar in Coca-Cola,” said French digital sovereignty advocate, Philippe Latombe. “Palantir can treat massive amounts of data with great precision and with their experience, they had time to improve their algorithms with many clients and adapt them to many use cases.” Still, the drive to break free from Palantir is sweeping across the continent, from Madrid, where the government of Pedro Sánchez has instructed state-backed companies to block Palantir from future public procurement contracts, to France’s domestic intelligence services (DGSI) selecting French company ChapsVision over Palantir. In Britain, the next test may come in February 2027, when the new Labour government of Andy Burnham will face a choice of whether to cut off Palantir’s £330 million National Health Service Federated Data Platform contract. Last month’s decision by the French and German intelligence agencies to choose ChapsVision was a double-blow for Palantir’s leadership. CEO Alex Karp showed little patience for the sudden turn away from his company’s wares, declaring that he wasn’t worried about European competitors. “We have a model of what doesn’t work," he quipped last week on Fox Business. "It’s called Europe.” Palantir CEO Alex Karp visits "The Claman Countdown" at Fox Business Network Studios. | John Lamparski/Getty Images Olivier Dellenbach, ChapsVision’s chief executive, told POLITICO that his company has benefited from what he calls a “visceral rejection of Palantir” in Europe. But he also cautioned that he did not want ChapsVision reduced to an anti-Palantir way out. Digital sovereignty, he argues, will remain an empty phrase unless governments turn it into industrial policy. “We need more public procurement,” Dellenbach said. Belgium, Germany, Luxembourg, Romania, the Netherlands and Canada have already shown interest in the French Army’s Artemis AI, according to Patrick Moreau, one of the architects of the solution built by French aerospace and defense company Thales. Advertisement Advertisement “They all want to be able to choose a sovereign solution that is compatible with NATO standards,” he said. “Unlike Palantir’s black box.” But for now, even officials who want sovereign alternatives acknowledge that Europe’s replacement market remains fragmented and European companies are yet to match Palantir’s scale and track record. Admiral Pierre Vandier, NATO’s supreme allied commander transformation, recently told POLITICO the alliance has no viable alternative to Palantir’s battlefield AI technology. Another NATO official, granted anonymity to speak frankly, said that Palantir’s system has an unmatched capacity to sift through mountains of satellite imagery to help identify a target, advise on the weapon to strike it, inform how much ammunition is required — and automatically put in an order to replenish the stock. “As far as I know, today there is no real competitor for Palantir,” Vandier said in May. Freedom or democracy? Co-founded by Karp and billionaire investor Peter Thiel, Palantir built its reputation inside the U.S. national security apparatus. Today, the company has a market capitalization of $330 billion. Advertisement Advertisement Thiel has been one of Silicon Valley’s most prominent supporters of U.S. President Donald Trump, while the company’s work with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Israeli military has come in for criticism from Amnesty International and others for alleged human rights violations. Adding to unease about Palantir's ideology-driven business were recent revelations of Thiel’s secretive Dialog society , an invitation-only ideas club for the global elite, and Karp’s manifesto arguing that Palantir is the democratic West's best hope to stay ahead of authoritarian rivals. “Peter Thiel explains that the defense of freedom does not necessarily require democracy,” French member of Parliament Aurélien Saintoul, who wrote a report on foreign military dependencies, told POLITICO. “He is clearly putting technical means to serve his political project, and we are talking about technofascists here.” A Palantir spokesperson who declined to be named dismissed such accusations as "ludicrous," noting that similar characterizations about the company have been made recently by the Russian foreign ministry. Peter Thiel and his husband Matt Danzeisen attend the Allen & Company Sun Valley Conference at the Sun Valley Lodge on July 9, 2026. | Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images "We know what side we're on, and who we're standing with," the spokesman said, citing ongoing work to support the Ukrainian military. "Since our inception, protecting privacy and civil liberties has served as the foundation for how we conduct our work across both public and private sector institutions. Western politicians should think hard about who the real enemy is and not allow themselves to be ventriloquized by the Kremlin." Many of the company's European critics maintain that the Palantir question is much more about tech sovereignty than political ideology. Extracting the company from some of the most delicate corners of European security structures would offer a blueprint for claiming more technological independence. Instead, if governments in Europe cannot wean themselves off a company that provides software solutions, it would reveal how unrealistic hopes are to reduce dependence on U.S. technology giants that provide cloud infrastructure and hardware. Advertisement Advertisement There is also the uncomfortable reality that at the same time that political leaders are calling for a break from Palantir, Europe’s biggest banks and asset managers have dramatically increased their investments in the U.S. company over the past year as it positions itself to profit from the AI gold rush, reports investigative outlet Follow the Money . From crisis tool to critical infrastructure Palantir’s European foothold was built long before the current boom in AI. A hallmark of its growth was that it never wasted a crisis to demonstrate its value for governments in need. In France, for instance, Palantir arrived in the aftermath of the November 2015 Paris terrorist attacks as security services scrambled to respond to a fervent public backlash on how they could have allowed such a tragedy to happen. The domestic intelligence agency signed a contract with the data analytics giant in 2016. A similar pattern played out in Germany, where Palantir’s first major deployment came in Frankfurt, in the central state of Hesse, where police purchased Palantir’s Gotham in 2017 and deployed it under the name hessenDATA. It proved to be a crucial tool for officers to turn sprawling information into leads to help solve crimes. Germany remains deeply divided over whether to use Palantir’s software. At the national level, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has pushed to expand the use of Palantir and introduced legislation that could pave the way for broader federal use. But the move has run into opposition from coalition partners the Social Democrats, as well as senior security officials. The same crisis-to-contract pattern appeared in the U.K. during the Covid-19 pandemic. Palantir’s relationship with the National Health Service (NHS) began when it was paid a nominal £1 fee to help aggregate data during the crisis, according to Palantir’s U.K. lead Louis Mosley. Advertisement Advertisement Europol, the EU’s police agency, used Palantir’s Gotham platform from 2016 to 2021 before ultimately dropping it. For one Europol official who was granted anonymity to discuss the matter freely, the problem with Palantir is less ideological than practical. Yes, the platform is expensive, raises sovereignty concerns and leaves clients dependent on Palantir for updates, the official said. But the more basic question is whether every agency needs the full Palantir machine. “[Palantir] is really good when you have massive amounts of data and want to connect everything,” they said. “But that is not the case for us. In many cases, the alternatives are close enough. If we used it, I’m not sure our efficiency would increase dramatically.” Part of Palantir’s approach in Europe is to hire former officials from the institutions it wants as customers. OpenDemocracy reported that Palantir hired four former officials from the U.K.’s Ministry of Defence before winning a £240 million MoD contract. The influence drive Moreover, Palantir is now seeking new business on the continent in defense. On Jul. 1, Palantir’s Maven Smart System — which was first used by the Pentagon — became fully operational at NATO, meaning it's been given security clearance to operate on the classified network. According to a NATO statement , the platform links command-and-control systems across the Alliance. “I think this is a very important milestone for European defense,” said Palantir’s U.K. chief Louis Mosley. Advertisement But Palantir’s grip on Europe does not stop at the doors of government or army barracks. It also runs through some of the continent’s industrial crown jewels. Airbus signed with Palantir in 2015, making Palantir's Foundry the backbone of its aviation data platform. Automaker BMW, energy company British Petroleum and media publisher Axel Springer — POLITICO’s parent company — all use Foundry to improve their business productivity as well. Looking for alternatives Even if Europe manages to loosen Palantir’s grip, the company’s model built on top of the latest AI large-language systems appears to only be getting stronger. On Jun. 30, Amazon Web Services said it would invest $1 billion in a new “Forward Deployed Engineering” organization, embedding teams of engineers inside customer headquarters to build AI systems alongside them. Days later, Microsoft announced a $2.5 billion push to send 6,000 engineers and industry specialists into client organizations. Both initiatives echo Palantir’s pioneering model to not simply sell software but put engineers inside a buyer’s operation. Both the strength of its products and the sensitive areas where they’re applied, make Palantir Europe's sovereign test case par excellence. If governments and companies can replace a software layer that helps turn data into decisions, they may have a blueprint for clawing back some digital sovereignty. If they cannot, the next generation of AI tools from U.S. tech giants may prove even harder to quit. “Europe’s public institutions cannot become dependent on software built by a small circle of U.S. tech billionaires with an obscure political worldview,” said German Green MEP Hannah Neumann, who sits on Parliament’s defense committee. “It would be like outsourcing part of the democratic state to a private intelligence service that answers neither to voters nor to parliament.” David Pargamin contributed reporting from Paris.
