https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c151.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Ukraine has developed drones, picture here in July 2026, capable of striking deep inside Russia By Ben Hatton Published 4 August 2026, 08:20 BST Updated 47 minutes ago At least five people were killed and 10 more injured in a Ukrainian drone strike on a warehouse close to Moscow overnight on Tuesday, the region's governor has said. The official did not specify what had been targeted but Ukraine has been carrying out strikes on facilities operated by Wildberries in recent weeks, often dubbed the "Russian Amazon". Kyiv says the depots are used to supply the Russian military, which Moscow denies. Local officials also said Wildberries warehouses were targeted in the St Petersburg and Tver regions overnight. Russia also launched strikes against parts of Ukraine, killing at least four and injuring several people. Russia's defence ministry said it had intercepted and destroyed 320 drones overnight. Moscow region governor Andrei Vorobyov said an industrial site in Novoselki, Chekhov - about 69km (43 miles) south of the Kremlin - was attacked, triggering a fire at a warehouse. He wrote on Telegram that seven of the 10 people injured were in a moderate condition, with one in a serious condition. Ukrainian media reported that the site of the Moscow strike was linked to Wildberries. The company has not commented publicly but confirmed its facility in St Petersburg was hit. Meanwhile, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said an 89-year-old woman was killed and two girls, aged two and 12, were among seven injured in a Russian strike on the southern port city of Mykolaiv overnight. A woman and two girls, aged five and 10, were killed in a strike on a residential area in Sumy, and another four people were injured, it said. Russian strikes also injured two people in the city of Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi, while a food warehouse was set on fire in Dnipro, according to the State Emergency Service. Beállítom „Nagyon jól ismerem a NATO-t. Körülbelül tizenkét éven át személyesen is azon dolgoztam, hogy bevezessük a NATO-szabványokat, és évről évre azt a mesét hallgattam, hogy lassan tényleg csatlakozhatunk. Sajnos soha nem fogunk csatlakozni!” – mondta az ukrán nagykövetek kijevi találkozóján Valerij Zaluzsnij volt ukrán főparancsnok , jelenlegi londoni nagykövet, írja az Ukrainska Pravda . Zaluzsnij azzal érvelt, Ukrajna NATO-csatlakozásának egyik akadálya az, hogy „az ukrán fegyveres erők jelenlegi képességei mellett lehetetlen csatlakozni egy olyan szervezethez, amelyet a második világháborús doktrínák irányítanak”, és még legalább tizenkét évet fog azzal tölteni a szövetség, „hogy elérje az Orosz Föderáció szintjének akár csak a felét is”. Ezért szerinte Ukrajnának a NATO-n kívüli katonai szövetségekhez lenne érdemesebb közel kerülni. A nagykövet példaként hozta fel az „európai katonai biztonsági blokkot”, amely szerinte a közeljövőben létrejöhet, és a Nagy-Britannia által vezetett, észak-európai államokat összefogó Közös Expedíciós Haderőt (JEF). A volt főparancsnok azt elismerte, hogy Ukrajnának jelenleg szüksége van „azokra a technológiákra, amelyekkel jelenleg a NATO-országok rendelkeznek”, többek között a ballisztikus rakétavédelem és az űrtechnika területén. Ukrajna korábban az alkotmányában is rögzítette a NATO-ba és az Európai Unióba való csatlakozás stratégiai célját, írja a Reuters . Tillai Ernő 1927. március 3-án született Pécsett. Eredetileg festőművésznek készült, végül a Műegyetem Építészmérnöki karán szerzett diplomát 1950-ben. 1956-ban, mindössze 29 évesen, a Pécsi Tervező Vállalat igazgatója lett, 1961-ben már megkapta első Ybl-díját, 1974-ben pedig a másodikat. Három templom, negyven középület és 125 ezer lakás épült meg tervei alapján. Az építész kéznyoma Pécs számos épületén felfedezhető, a hetvenes években számos panelház épült a tervei alapján a pécsi Uránvárosban és Kertvárosban. Tillai tervezte a híres pécsi „TV-házként” és „Pizsama-házként” ismert paneleket, a Domus, Szliven és Konzum áruházakat, az egykori MATÁV Székházat és a város korábbi, ma kihasználatlanul álló, Vásárcsarnokát is. „Az uniformizált tömbházak karakterének módosításával a személyesség, egyfajta humanizálási szándék megjelenését érhetjük tetten tervezői jellemrajzában” – írta építészeti stílusáról az Építészfórum . Tillai Ernő tervei alapján épült az ikonikus siófoki Hotel Ezüstpart is. Az építész fotóművészként is aktív volt, első magyarként érdemelte ki a „Fotóművészet Nemzetközi Szövetségének” Mesterfényképészi címét. A Mecseki Fotóklubba 1958-ban lépett be, majd tagja lett a Magyar Fotóművészek Szövetségének. Életműdíjat kapott a Fotóművészek Szövetségétől, a MAOE-től és a MAFOSZ-tól is. Öt könyve jelent meg. „Emlékét, szellemi örökségét megőrizzük” – írta a Mecseki Fotóklub. 2009-ben Tüke-díjat kapott, 2017-ben Pécs díszpolgára lett. Péterffy Attila, Pécs polgármestere a Facebookon emlékezett meg róla, azt írta, Tillai Ernő „több évtizedes munkássága komoly nyomot hagyott városunkon”. Egy 2018-as interjúban az építész úgy fogalmazott, megdobban a szíve, amikor végigsétál az uránvárosi és kertvárosi panelházak között. „Egyébként most is Kertvárosban élek, mert meg vagyok azzal elégedve, ami ott született”, még úgyis, hogy „persze vannak hibái a panellakásoknak” – mondta akkor. Az Építészfórumnak adott 2022-es interjúban ezt azzal magyarázta, a „panelházak alaprajzi kiosztását egészen a ’80-as évek végéig a minisztériumi túlszabályozottság határozta meg”. Mire el lehetett térni ezektől, „jött a rendszerváltás, és meghalt az egész paneles téma. Pedig akkor lehetett volna igazán jó panelépítészetet csinálni. Tehát ez mutatja, hogy a panel önmagában, mint eszköz, nagyon alkalmas lenne bárminek a megépítésére, csak bízni kell az építészben” – mondta. Az persze nagyon látványos, hogy a kormány kommunikációjának mennyire hangsúlyos, szinte kizárólagos csatornája lett a Facebook, alig adnak interjúkat, keveset nyilatkoznak, viszont szinte minden fontos bejelentés Facebook-élőben, posztban, sőt, akár kommentben érkezik tőlük. (Amúgy ezt konkrétan a Fidesz kezdte el a Covid alatt, de ez most mindegy is.) Ez egészen logikus, sőt, szinte az egyetlen választásuk, ha olyan kommunikációs terepet akarnak, amit ők kontrollálnak és nagy az elérése. Közmédia még nincs, fideszes stílusú médiabirodalom nem is lesz, a szabad sajtónál meg mindig ott a veszély, hogy kényelmetlen kérdéseket kapnak, vagy legalábbis nem azt kérdezik meg tőlük, amiről éppen nagyon szeretnének beszélni. Marad a közösségi média, saját csatornákkal. Ami persze összességében nem éppen tökéletes a tájékoztatás szempontjából, de még mindig fényévekre van az „Orbán kinyilatkoztatást tesz a Kossuth rádióban” időkhöz képest. A számok szépen visszaigazolják, amit Róna Dániel mondott a Telex műsorában pár hete: Vitézy Dávid kinőtte magát a Tisza második legerősebb emberévé. Forsthoffer Ágnes és Kapitány István népszerűsége stabil még, a többiek mind elég erősen hullámzó számokat és helyezéseket hoznak. Még egy kicsit visszatérve a „mit tesz, ha az ember elkap pár jó pillanatot a több százezres nézettségű parlamenti közvetítésekben” témához: az új, ideiglenes házelnök Hallerné Nagy Anikó egy szál emlékezetes produkcióval olyan népszerű lett, hogy egyből a 400 ezer lájkos magasságig, és a 22. helyig vitte. Ez nagyjából Karácsony Gergely, Orbán Anita, vagy Dúró Dóra szintje – úgy, hogy egy hónapja elég kevesen ismerték még a nevét is. Eközben a Fidesz Bár a toplista azt sugallja, hogy a Fidesz összeszedte magát a KO-vereség után, ha megnézzük a tartalmaikat, azt látjuk, hogy még mindig kármentésben vannak, és csak a saját táboruk felé kommunikálnak, azt próbálják egyben tartani. Lassan négy hónapja mondták azt nekik a magyar választók, hogy kösz, ebből nem kérünk, és ehhez képest még mindig abban vannak, hogy ők mindent jól csináltak, nincs szükség önreflexióra, változásra, sőt, a vereség okait se kell keresni, az egy megmagyarázhatatlan, ezoterikus misztikum volt. Ugyanazok az ellenségképek, ugyanazok a mantrák, ugyanúgy harcolni és ellenállni kell, csak egyre kevésbé látni, hogy pontosan miért és hogyan. Mintha kifogyott volna a Fideszből az ötlet, a mondanivaló, a kreativitás, az üzenet. Mintha kifogyott volna a Fidesz, úgy, ahogy van. KDNP meg nem is volt, hogy még jobban rímeljünk a Bud Spencer-klasszikusra . Jelenleg ott tart a fideszes kommunikáció, hogy a Tisza első számú választási ígérete, amire megkapták a kétharmadot (a fideszes mélyállam szétverése és a lopott szajré visszaszerzése), az maga az önkényuralom, plusz a demokrácia és a jogállam halála. Pont ugyanilyeneket mondott az óellenzék is vagy tizenöt éven át, a fideszesek kiröhögték őket, a választókat meg nem érdekelte. A mesterterv most az, hogy a vesztes meccs után ne csináljunk semmit, csak reménykedjünk, hogy az ellenfél majd rúg egy csomó öngólt. Persze a dologban van azért némi ráció. Nagyjából ezzel a stratégiával tért vissza a hatalomba Amerikában 2024-ben Donald Trump is – igaz, ott a demokraták tényleg rúgtak egy csomó öngólt (például azt, hogy ők kampányoltak azzal, hogy jaj, a demokrácia meg a jogállam ). És persze az sem egy utolsó szempont, hogy az önkényezéssel valamennyire talán sikerül megágyazniuk a közvéleménynek arra az időre, amikor majd igazán beindul a vagyonvisszaszerzés, és elkezdenek potyogni a csontvázak meg a vádalkuk a szekrényekből. Két hónapja búcsúztunk a Lájkbajnokság mezőnyének egyik nagyon régi törzsjátékosától, Hadházy Ákostól, most pedig újabb visszavonulónk van, Szijjártó Péter. However, the Polish studio officially announced Songs of the Past in May after numerous rumors about it surfaced online. CD Projekt Red originally considered releasing The Witcher 3: Songs of the Past in 2026 but moved it to 2027 to achieve “the best possible result” for players. It will launch on PS5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC. The studio has also described the expansion as an indirect, nonliteral “prologue” to the Ciri-led The Witcher 4 . https://thebulletin.org/2026/07/forward-.text: About Magazine Events Contact Store My Account Login Donate Give Now Ways To Give What Your Gift Supports Annual Event Einstein Circle Legacy Society Donor-Advised Fund Meet the Bulletin 's new editor-in-chief, Sharon Weinberger Forward deterrence: What’s (not) in it for France’s partners By Oliver Meier | Analysis | July 21, 2026 The 'parapluie' is not for free: As European allies sign on to France’s "forward deterrence" concept, many are realizing that a French nuclear umbrella comes at a distinct price—namely, adapting to Paris's terms without gaining a vote on command or policy. (Illustration by Thomas Gaulkin; Photo (modified) by Dominique Jacovides / Abaca / Alamy) Copy link Linked copied Email Facebook Bluesky Twitter LinkedIn WhatsApp Reddit Spread Listen to this article: When French President Emmanuel Macron introduced the concept of forward deterrence during his March 2 speech on France’s nuclear policy at the Île Longue nuclear submarine base, many European governments enthusiastically endorsed it. Since Russia’s February 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Europeans have been increasingly concerned about deterring Russian aggression. At the same time, the Trump administration’s unpredictability and disengagement from European security undermine the value of NATO’s nuclear sharing arrangements. Against this backdrop, Macron’s proposal for a strengthened European nuclear deterrent seemed to square several circles for non-nuclear-weapon NATO members: It aims to bring French nuclear weapons closer into the European security equation, without angering Washington. And Macron emphasized that his initiative complements—rather than competes with—NATO’s nuclear-sharing arrangements, which many Europeans want to leave intact as long as possible. Four months on, things increasingly turn out not to be so simple. Implementation of the initiative is uneven, its level of ambition remains unclear, and questions remain around compatibility with the US nuclear extended deterrent. To address these problems, France’s non-nuclear partners should increase coordination among themselves on nuclear issues, rather than engage Paris on a one-to-one basis only. Earlier and better harmonization of their own positions would make it easier for them to pursue their own interests vis-à-vis Paris effectively. Increased coordination would also facilitate better alignment of the French concept of forward deterrence with NATO’s nuclear sharing arrangements. An uneven playing field. Nine partners have now expressed varying degrees of interest in participating in the French initiative on forward deterrence, which can involve participating in French nuclear exercises to practice support for nuclear-strike missions and, potentially, the temporary deployment of French nuclear-capable aircraft to bases on the territory of other participating countries. During crises or conflicts, dispersing French nuclear capabilities could help to improve their survivability and, therefore, strengthen deterrence. Different from NATO nuclear sharing , there would be no formal security guarantee, no permanent deployment of nuclear assets to third countries, and no joint decision-making on nuclear policies. During his address, President Macron mentioned Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Greece, Poland, the Netherlands, and Sweden as non-nuclear partners. Since then, Norway and France signed the Narvik agreement on bilateral defense relations , which includes Oslo joining the French initiative on European nuclear deterrence, bringing the number of non-nuclear partners to eight. The other European nuclear-weapon state, the United Kingdom, has a long-standing cooperation with France on nuclear deterrence. In addition, Finland has expressed an interest in joining the initiative and, on June 17, changed a law to make it legal to deploy nuclear weapons on its territory during a crisis or conflict. And in April, Czech President Andrej ‌Babis also expressed interest in discussing involvement in forward deterrence, but it remains unclear whether additional steps have been taken since. To avoid the perception of competing with NATO’s Nuclear Planning Group, which brings together all 32 NATO states except France, Paris will engage its nuclear partners bilaterally. Coordination of these dialogues is likely to impose a large burden on the French bureaucracy. But it also conveniently situates Paris at the center of a web of deterrence dialogues, making it easier to tailor the terms and conditions of partnerships to its liking. From the perspective of France’s partners, this arrangement of separate dialogues is less advantageous. Each partner will bring specific interests to the table, influenced by geography, domestic politics, strategic culture, and history. Two things unite them: the hope that participation in forward deterrence will improve their security, and a desire to shape French nuclear policies in ways that meet their specific interests. These core interests have always been two drivers behind the non-nuclear Allies’ involvement in NATO’s nuclear sharing arrangements. They hope that, in nuclear consultation, “ the gap between the interests of the nuclear power as security provider and nonnuclear protégés as security beneficiaries ” could be bridged. As a result, non-nuclear allies want their nuclear-armed allies to inform and consult them on nuclear policies, including on the existential question of when, where, and how nuclear weapons will be used. Such nuclear consultations have often been difficult and occasionally controversial in NATO, and France’s new nuclear partners will not just want to be consumers of what Paris has to offer but will bring their own demands to the table. Better alignment of their policies would make it easier to ensure that dialogue is a true two-way street. Such coordination would be easier if France’s partners were to approach Paris from a level playing field. However, at least for now, there appear to be different categories of nuclear partners. In his speech, Macron singled out the United Kingdom as “a major partner” and Germany as “crucial partners [sic].” London and Berlin will converse with Paris through newly established nuclear steering groups, which have already met at senior political levels. On the same day of announcing the French initiative, President Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz published a joint declaration , which is “based on the shared understanding that the nuclear dimension of deterrence remains a cornerstone of European security.” Nuclear cooperation between the two NATO nuclear weapon states—France and the United Kingdom—is long-standing, and both have recently intensified it with agreement on the Northwood Declaration . Sweden is the third country that has engaged Paris through a nuclear steering group . Two months after Macron’s speech, Paris and Stockholm signed a multi-billion-euro defense deal. President Macron placed the agreement squarely in the context of the closer strategic partnership that led to Sweden’s participation in the French initiative on forward deterrence. On July 10, France and Poland held their first Nuclear Steering Group meeting in Paris “to discuss European security issues.” Senior officials from defense and foreign ministries agreed on a “joint roadmap.” Paris may want to establish Nuclear Steering Groups with all nine current nuclear partners. But given the depth and range of cooperation under the forward deterrence initiative, it is likely to vary from country to country. A one-way street on nuclear policy? Non-nuclear allies participate in extended deterrence arrangements for two main reasons: They hope that positive security guarantees from the nuclear-armed ally will avert attacks against them. And they use consultations under these arrangements to influence the nuclear policies and force postures of the nuclear ally. This has been true under NATO’s nuclear consultative mechanisms and will also drive involvement of France’s partners in nuclear deterrence arrangements. But Paris has historically been opposed to the concept of joint nuclear discussions and decision-making. Preserving national autonomy was, after all, the main reason why Paris decided not to join NATO’s Nuclear Planning Group when it was set up in 1966. During his Île Longue speech, Macron repeated the “four noes” that are at the core of French nuclear autonomy: No joint decision on nuclear use, no joint planning, no sharing of the definition of French vital interests, no nuclear guarantee “in the strict sense of the term.” These limits suggest that Paris expects its partners to adapt to French traditional nuclear thinking with little room for give-and-take. It therefore remains unclear whether and to what extent France’s partners will be able to influence Paris to take their national security interests into account. A brochure published by the French Ministry of Defense after Macron’s speech repeats that “France’s nuclear deterrent is not subject to any form of sharing” and that the President “is the sole decision-maker concerning the deployment of nuclear forces and, more broadly, the doctrine and sizing of national capabilities.” The document emphasizes that this decision-making autonomy cannot be called into question, “including when implementing the European dimension of France’s deterrence strategy. While the interests of allies may be taken into account in the President’s decision-making process, that decision remains sovereign and is always based on an assessment of the Nation’s vital interests.” [Translation by the author.] However, the expectations of some partners may go beyond such loose assurances of being heard. For instance, Merz said on July 17 during a press conference after a meeting of the Franco-German Defense and Security Council that France and Germany are embarking now on a “new, common way” on deterrence. He described the work on a “joint doctrine” to involve discussions in the Nuclear Steering Group on the appropriate “mix of nuclear and conventional capabilities” to improve deterrence. [Translation by the author.] Still, differences between French nuclear priorities and those of its partners exist. Take nuclear arms control. NATO has historically paired initiatives to strengthen deterrence and defense with offers of engagement to Moscow. But Macron put out little hope for pursuing a similar dual-track approach, saying that “the field of rules has turned into a field of ruins.” He argued that because “the prevailing animosity does not inspire the confidence required to rebuild the norms of collective security,” France is “right to harden [its] position.” Unsurprisingly then, bilateral statements issued by Paris and its nuclear partners do not refer to arms control and only mention nuclear nonproliferation as a shared goal. Berlin and Paris merely state that they “will continue to comply with their obligations under international law including the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons” (NPT). France and the United Kingdom, in the Northwood declaration, reaffirm their “full support” for the NPT and for their obligations under the treaty. They promise to “coordinate ever more closely to uphold and reinforce the international non-proliferation architecture.” Even under the NPT, some of France’s non-nuclear partners have a level of ambition that goes beyond such generic support and is at odds with French nuclear policy. Germany, the Netherlands, and Poland, for example, are participants of the Non-proliferation and Disarmament Initiative, which has called on nuclear weapon states to improve the transparency of information related to their nuclear weapons. But in his speech, not only did Macron announce a nuclear weapons build-up, but he also reduced French nuclear transparency: “To put an end to any speculation, we will no longer release figures on our nuclear arsenal, as we have done in the past.” Will France’s non-nuclear partners be successful in urging Paris to reduce such discrepancies with their own policies? To be sure, they might be more successful if addressing such differences collectively, rather than in asymmetrical one-to-one dialogues. Alignment with NATO nuclear deterrence. In his nuclear speech, Macron was at pains to avoid any impression that his initiative could be seen as a competition to NATO’s nuclear sharing arrangements. Forward deterrence, he said, “is a distinct effort which has its own value and is perfectly complementary to NATO’s at both strategic and technical level.” Such separation may seem feasible and desirable from a French perspective. Paris, after all, is not ready to involve its non-nuclear partners in joint nuclear planning and restricts their participation to practical arrangements such as joint exercises or conventional support for nuclear strike missions. But things look different for non-nuclear partners. They would, for example, want to insist that France and NATO deconflict their nuclear targeting by making sure that the set of nuclear targets in respective operational plans does sit well together. Allies would also want to avoid a situation in which Paris is requesting support for one nuclear mission, while a separate request may come in from NATO, via the Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR). This concern is not abstract. On July 16, German fighter aircraft participated for the first time in a joint air activity in the context of the French concept of forward deterrence. The nuclear exercise involved two nuclear-capable French Rafale aircraft and two German Eurofighters from Nörvenich Air Force Base, as well as a French multirole tanker and transport Phenix aircraft for air-to-air refueling. The exercise took place ahead of the July 17 meetings of the Franco-German Defense and Security Council and the French-German Nuclear Steering Group. But non-nuclear NATO members only have a specific set of capabilities to provide such conventional support for nuclear missions, and they may not be able to put them on the table for NATO as well as possible French missions. The Northwood declaration adds another level of complexity because the United Kingdom has assigned all its nuclear weapons to NATO, meaning that SACEUR can request the employment of UK (but not of French) nuclear weapons. More difficulties for non-nuclear weapon states in aligning NATO nuclear sharing and forward deterrence may lie ahead. The United States is drawing down its conventional forces in Europe at the same time it is trying to compensate for the resulting commitment deficit by increasing reliance on NATO nuclear sharing. To that aim, Washington reportedly has been in talks with Poland and maybe other French partners to sell them additional dual-capable F-35 aircraft, which could be certified to carry US B61 nuclear gravity bombs. This shift away from conventional deterrence implies more emphasis on US nuclear weapons in Europe as warfighting tools. But this remains anathema to French nuclear thinking: Macron repeated in his March 2 speech the French nuclear mantra that “rejects the idea of flexible nuclear response.” In the Franco-German context, both countries have emphasized that forward deterrence will involve joint discussions “to manage escalation beneath the nuclear threshold and to develop the necessary conventional capabilities,” such as the “articulation of conventional, Deep Precision Strike and missile defence capabilities with nuclear deterrence.” For non-nuclear weapon states, this relationship between conventional and nuclear deterrence was always the crux of discussions within NATO. They feared either abandonment by their nuclear allies or, vice versa, entanglement in nuclear warfighting plans. It is therefore hard to imagine how debates on forward deterrence with France can be limited to conventional aspects of deterrence, without also involving discussions on nuclear doctrine. https://www.romania-insider.com/voluntar.text: Environment Romania opens first large voluntary waste collection center in Cluj-Napoca 21 July 2026 Irina Marica Like this article? Share it with your friends! Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn Romania inaugurated its first large voluntary waste collection center in Cluj-Napoca, marking the start of a national network of 13 such facilities financed through the Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR). The new center is designed to help residents dispose of bulky and special waste that cannot be collected through regular household waste collection services. The Environment Ministry said the project received more than RON 32.6 million in non-repayable European funding through the PNRR. Covering 1.4 hectares, the facility includes dedicated collection platforms and containers, a chemical analysis laboratory, administrative buildings, a refrigerated storage room for animal carcasses, and a heavy-duty weighbridge to monitor waste flows. The center accepts a wide range of waste, including bulky household items such as furniture and mattresses, construction and demolition waste, used tires, waste electrical and electronic equipment, textiles, wood waste, recyclable materials, biodegradable waste, and other waste streams that cannot be collected through the standard door-to-door system. “This center addresses exactly the problems that have frustrated citizens for years. Where do we dispose of an old mattress, used tires, construction debris, furniture or a broken refrigerator? From today, the people of Cluj have a clear, modern and civilized solution," interim environment minister Diana Buzoianu said. She added that hundreds of smaller voluntary collection centers are expected to be completed across Romania in the coming months through the PNRR, saying the country is taking "a major step toward the European circular economy model, where waste becomes a resource.” According to the ministry, the Cluj-Napoca facility is the first of 13 large voluntary collection centers planned nationwide. Similar projects are scheduled for cities including Craiova, Buzău, Brașov, Constanța, Iași, Bucharest, and Sibiu. irina.marica@romania-insider.com (Photo source: Facebook/ Ministerul Mediului - România ) Tags Positive Romania Read next 02 July 2026 Environment Clean Recycle analysis: Romania's waste imports increased nearly 19-fold in 2008-2024 Normal Environment Romania opens first large voluntary waste collection center in Cluj-Napoca 21 July 2026 Irina Marica Like this article? https://www.romania-insider.com/presiden.text: Politics President greenlights law establishing 2026 as Year of US in Romania 21 July 2026 Radu Dumitrescu Like this article? Share it with your friends! Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn President Nicușor Dan promulgated the law establishing 2026 as the Year of the United States of America in Romania on Monday, July 20. The bill was initiated by several lawmakers from the far-right, Eurosceptic but pro-Trump Alliance for the Union of Romanians party, or AUR. According to the law set to be implemented, 2026 is the Year of the United States of America in Romania. As such, events may be organized to strengthen the Romanian-American strategic relationship and reaffirm Romania's commitment to the values of the free world, freedom of expression, and genuine democracy, according to the law cited by Digi24 . To mark the celebration, central and local public administration authorities may organize or provide material or logistical support, within the limits of the approved budget allocations, for the organization and holding of conferences and public debates; cultural, academic and educational events dedicated to American history and values; Romanian-American public diplomacy and communication activities; any other activities promoting Romanian-American cooperation and democratic values. In addition, the Romanian Public Radio Broadcasting Company and the Romanian Public Television Company may broadcast thematic materials produced on the occasion of the Year of the United States of America in Romania. The AUR bill was passed by the plenary of the Chamber of Deputies on June 30, with 283 votes in favor, 8 against and 4 abstentions. radu@romania-insider.com (Photo source: Ruletkka|Dreamstime.com ) Read next 06 July 2026 People Romania declares 2026 the 'Year of Traian Vuia' to mark 120 years since historic flight Normal Politics President greenlights law establishing 2026 as Year of US in Romania 21 July 2026 Radu Dumitrescu Like this article? https://www.defensenews.com/global/europ.text: Europe Russia may use captured Ukrainian drones against Poland and Baltics, Warsaw warns By Linus Höller Tuesday, Jul 21, 2026 A Police officer looks towards damage to an oil tank after drones crashed at a storage facility in Rezekne, Latvia, May 7, 2026. (REUTERS/Janis Laizans) VIENNA — Russia has captured a large number of Ukrainian drones and may be planning to use them against NATO or to stage a false flag attack, Polish defense minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said, adding to earlier warnings of a potential escalation. The senior official’s statement comes after more than a month of unusual public warnings by several Eastern European countries that Russia was planning some form of a provocation or hybrid attack, with government officials citing numerous pieces of intelligence that pointed them to this conclusion. Poland, Lithuania and Latvia have been among the countries raising the alarm, some citing U.S. intelligence that had been shared with them. The latest information, first shared by Poland’s defense minister on Monday, outlines a concrete threat vector for what was previously a more general warning of Russian malicious intent. The threat appears to be taken seriously by the Eastern European capitals, and the Polish government prioritized the topic for discussion in Tuesday’s security committee meeting. Following the meeting, Kosiniak-Kamysz reiterated the specific warning. In addition to drone incursions, he also said GPS jamming and various acts of sabotage may be on the table. The countries surrounding the Baltic Sea have been affected by Russian GPS interference since the early days of the war, sometimes leading to airport closures and navigation problems. Sabotage, too, has featured, including the disabling of a rail line in eastern Poland last year. Government officials also noted cyber warfare as a possible avenue for Russian actions against NATO countries. In late June, Latvian intelligence first told Fox News they had detected Russian preparations for a hybrid attack that would fall short of the threshold for open war. The attack might include “missiles, drones or other actions designed to send a signal: stop supporting Ukraine, or you will have your own problems,” Fox News Digital quoted Latvian intelligence as saying. A week later, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he had been receiving warnings about a Russian test of NATO resolve and possible attack on Polish soil from allied intelligence agencies for weeks, adding in a press conference that “the coming months may truly be critical.” Polish publication Onet had previously reported from a source close to Polish president Karol Nawrocki that the U.S. had shared concrete warnings of hostile Russian actions with the government in Warsaw. Last week, Latvian and Lithuanian leaders warned specifically of “limited kinetic operations” targeting critical infrastructure. The Kremlin’s press spokesperson Dmitry Peskov dismissed this as “scare stories” that same week. Some officials have warned that Russia may also be inclined to stage a false flag attack on its own territory to give it a pretense to escalate the war in Ukraine or expand it to include strikes on NATO countries. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warned of such a scenario in late June, saying at the time that “I expect a false flag attack on Russian territory, to which Putin ‘will respond.’” “The Russians are planning something again; we have credible information,” Sikorski told the press several weeks later, on July 9. Similar public messaging − including the selective sharing of high-level intelligence by Western capitals − preceded the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine. At the time, the Biden administration took the unprecedented step of declassifying and sharing with the public a large number of previously secret intelligence signals that pointed toward Russia preparing for a wholesale invasion of its western neighbor. Some officials and analysts have suggested the open sharing of information delayed the start of the invasion by several weeks. Sikorski, the Polish foreign minister, said on July 9 that he hoped the current sharing of public warnings would similarly deter Russia from following through on its plans. However, no primary intelligence beyond the verbal statements made by high-level figures has been publicly shared so far by the Western countries now raising the alarm. Russia has previously found ways to redirect Ukrainian drones that were launched by Kyiv to fall on NATO territory rather than reaching their intended targets of Russian military facilities, industry and oil storage facilities. The Baltic States and Finland have had several instances of misguided Ukrainian-launched drones striking their territories, including an oil storage facility in Latvia − an incident that led to two high-level resignations there, including of the prime minister. Those cases have been publicly attributed to Russian electronic warfare and defensive signal jamming redirecting drones already in flight. Russia launching captured drones at the West would be a marked escalation from that precedent. About Linus Höller Linus Höller is Defense News' Europe correspondent and OSINT investigator. He reports on the arms deals, sanctions, and geopolitics shaping Europe and the world. He holds master’s degrees in WMD nonproliferation, terrorism studies, and international relations, and works in four languages: English, German, Russian, and Spanish. https://breakingdefense.com/2026/07/embr.text: Embraer and Anduril are pursuing putting the latters Barracuda cruise missile onto the C-390. (Embraer) FARNBOROUGH — Brazilian giant Embraer has signed an agreement with US firm Anduril to pursue a palletized weapons program on its C-390 Millenium aircraft, the company announced today. Under the Memorandum of Understanding, the firms will pursue integrating Anduril’s palletized Baracuda-500M cruise missile onto the Millenium, the first time an offensive capability would be put on the C-390 design. “We are receiving this demand from several countries around the globe,” Embraer defense boss Bosco da Costa Jr. said during a company presentation at the Farnborough Airshow. While he declined to identify those countries, Costa said the interest was from customers in “Europe, in Asia as well.” He also declined to give a timeline for when a test might happen of the technology, but said Anduril’s “very efficient, very flexible” methods mean Embraer believes it can be done “very fast.” “Integrating the pallet-launched Barracuda-500M with Embraer’s C-390 Millennium gives allied militaries a new way to generate massed, stand-off effects from a proven airlift platform,” Greg Kausner, senior vice president for global defense at Anduril, said in a statement. “Anduril’s Barracuda family of systems delivers rapidly producible, operationally relevant capabilities to meet the growing demand for affordable, scalable munitions.” The C-390 is currently operational with Brazil, Portugal, Hungary and the Czech Republic. The Republic of Korea, the Netherlands, Austria, Uzbekistan, Sweden, the United Arab Emirates, Slovakia, and Lithuania have all ordered the plane as well. Costa said today that Embraer expects to deliver the first two C-390s for the United Arab Emirates by 2028, roughly two years after signing. During the first day of the show, Embraer also announced two deals for C-390 training systems for Sweden and Austria. Embraer is also expanding its production of the Saab Gripen at its Brazilian facility, moving from 16 in planned production to 36. All those additional jets are for “international customers,” not Brazil, according to Costa. He also announced planned improvements to the A-29, with “fifth-generation avionics,” new datalinks and a focus on the cUAS mission that was first rolled out in the fall. Finally, Costa declined to give a timeline for when a test of a Northrop-designed boom for the KC-390 might be tested. The two companies teamed in February of this year , targeting the US Air Force. Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn Romania’s interim foreign minister, Oana Țoiu, announced on Monday, July 20, that the Visa Waiver program remains a priority in Romania's relationship with the United States, but the timing of its acceptance depends on political discussions, reducing the visa refusal rate, and the Trump administration. "Visa Waiver is a priority in the bilateral relationship. As you know, in the relationship between the United States and Romania, we had already managed to reach the threshold of under 3% for visa refusals, a threshold necessary for us to enter the Visa Waiver program," Oana Țoiu said on Monday evening on TVR Info . Romania was formally designated the 43rd country to join the US Visa Waiver Program (VWP) in 2025 by the Biden administration. However, just days before the official entry date, the US announced that it had temporarily suspended the implementation of the Electronic System for Travel Authorization for Romanian citizens. Weeks later, in early May, it officially rescinded Romania's Visa Waiver Program (VWP) designation . In October 2025, Romanian president Nicușor Dan stressed that the move should be seen as a domestic policy signal in the United States, where migration remains a contentious issue. Romania’s Visa Waiver application is currently handled by the Ministry of Internal Affairs. "When it moves forward depends on the political discussion, certainly, on reducing the refusal rate again to that threshold, but also on president Trump's administration in terms of the paradigm it has regarding travel and the opening of the border,” according to the acting foreign minister. She mentioned that the first criterion for resolving the situation is the percentage of visa application refusals. "When we received approval to enter the Visa Waiver program, we met this 3% criterion. Now, because, of course, many people obtained visas during that period and did not renew them because it was not necessary, the number of refusals is higher,” Țoiu said. radu@romania-insider.com (Photo source: Megaflopp|Dreamstime.com ) Read next 01 October 2025 Politics President Dan says Visa Waiver setback driven more by US migration politics than Romania's political situation Normal Politics Romania’s acceptance into Visa Waiver program depends on Trump admin, interim foreign minister says 21 July 2026 Radu Dumitrescu Like this article? Share it with your friends! Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn Sadhguru, one of the world’s most renowned yoga masters and a New York Times bestselling author, will take the main stage of the Untold festival on August 6 to deliver a message about the importance of inner balance, well-being, and building a more conscious world before tens of thousands of people. The famous yogi is known by hundreds of millions of people around the world for his programs dedicated to transformation and personal development through yoga and meditation, as well as for his global initiatives dedicated to the environment and society. Sadhguru’s participation in the festival comes after a collaboration between Untold festival organizers and Conscious Music Circle (CMC), a collaboration between artists and music industry professionals whose lives have been deeply influenced by Sadhguru’s practices and teachings. The organization’s mission is to contribute to raising awareness through music, providing artists, industry professionals and communities with access to yoga and meditation tools developed by Sadhguru and promoting well-being in the music industry. The partnership aims to promote mental health and awareness through scientifically validated yoga and meditation practices, integrated into festival and music culture, the organizers said. Through this collaboration, Untold becomes the first major festival in the world to offer free access to the Miracle of Mind meditation app to all festival participants, artists and team members. The app will be integrated into the festival experience through special activations and dedicated sessions held throughout the four days of the festival. “You cannot change the past. You can live the present. But you can build the future if you choose to do so. For the first time in history, we can be connected with all of humanity. If we want to transform the world, if we want to transform humanity, now is the time. Let’s do this together,” Sadhguru said in the press release. The Untold festival will take place from August 6-9 in Cluj-Napoca, and this year’s edition brings more than 200 artists to the festival stages, including STING, Lewis Capaldi, Zara Larsson, Flo Rida, The Chainsmokers, Kygo, James Hype, Solomun, Carl Cox, Sara Landry, Holy Priest and many others. radu@romania-insider.com (Photo source: press release) Tags Positive Romania Read next 16 July 2026 Events Bucharest's Armenian Street Festival celebrates 10th edition with free concerts, cultural events Normal Events World-famous yogi Sadhguru to take the stage at Romania’s Untold festival 21 July 2026 Radu Dumitrescu Like this article? Photo: Reuters Bucharest, July 21 (SANA) Romanian President Nicușor Dan announced on Tuesday that a Liberian-flagged vessel was subjected to an attack near Romanian territorial waters, leaving three crew members injured. Dan stated in a post on the X platform that the LPG tanker LPG Gas Lisbon was hit approximately 20 nautical miles (40 kilometers) off the Romanian coast while en route from Egypt to Ukraine . The president noted that rescue teams evacuated the ship’s crew, including the three injured members, while a tugboat was dispatched to ensure the vessel does not drift or pose a hazard to maritime navigation. Dan suggested that the strike was likely part of the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war and the recent escalation witnessed in the Black Sea over recent weeks, stressing that Romanian state institutions remain on high alert to clarify the circumstances surrounding the attack. European Union officials had previously stated that Russian and Ukrainian drones repeatedly violated Romania’s airspace and territorial waters this year as part of the military escalation between the two sides. The Russia-Ukraine war escalated further at the beginning of July, with both sides shifting toward targeting economic facilities and critical infrastructure to increase mutual pressure. https://jerseyeveningpost.com/news/2026/.text: A MAN on a mission to visit every parliament he can has declared Jersey’s States Assembly the best he has experienced so far… after touring 32 legislatures across Europe and beyond in around just 18 months. UK-based university learning technology technologist and TV quizzer Nicholas Elliott has turned an unlikely passion into an international pursuit, travelling to more than 50 countries and contacting parliaments one by one in the hope they will open their doors to him. Jersey became his 32nd parliament last month – and, he says, left the biggest impression to date. “I’m going to say this: they’re the best, the best I’ve ever been to,” he said in a Bailiwick Podcasts interview. Mr Elliott’s fascination with parliaments began around just two years ago, following what he initially assumed would be a fairly mundane tour of Westminster with his visiting Polish mother-in-law and daughter. “I thought to myself, ‘This is not going to be very interesting’,” he admitted, but explained that it was not long before he found himself captivated by the history and traditions of the Palace of Westminster. “I started learning things about a country which I’ve lived in all my life… I was so amazed by the rich history the UK has. That’s how it basically started. I got the bug from that moment onwards.” Since then, Mr Elliott has written to legislatures across Europe and further afield asking whether they would host him, comparing himself to a “mystery shopper” for democracy. “I’m just a normal person. I’m not a politician, I’m not an academic, I’m not a journalist,” he said, “But when I arrive, sometimes [parliamentary staff] think I’m a celebrity… They’re always asking, ‘Why do you want to visit our parliament?'” The answer, he says, is all about truly knowing how the people and institutions that shape citizens’ way of life operate, and being better able to hold them to account. Comparing elected politicians to tenants looking after a rented property on behalf of voters, Mr Elliott explained: “People vote for politicians and then go, ‘My work here is done. Carry on for five years.’ “I think, wouldn’t you want to meet the person? Wouldn’t you want to know what they’re doing? When the ‘contract’ comes to an end, I want to decide whether I want to keep you as my tenant or whether I want somebody better.” He believes ordinary people should take a greater interest in how their legislatures operate and says some of his visits have even prompted parliaments to rethink how accessible they are. “Some of them have actually set up tours afterwards. They’ve listened to my advice and made them available for schoolchildren or the general public. That’s transparency. Civic engagement is what I’m all about.” The Parliament of Hungary Not every parliament has been so welcoming, however. “There are countries which are, bluntly, not democratic,” he said. “Those are the countries who basically say, ‘No one can visit our parliament’ – even people who live there.” As for Jersey, Mr Elliott said the visit also transformed his understanding and appreciation of the Island. Like many people in Britain, he had assumed Jersey was simply part of the UK before discovering its unique constitutional relationship with the Crown, its own parliament, immigration rules and legal system – a revelation he likened to discovering that “a dolphin isn’t actually a fish”. He said he particularly enjoyed learning about William the Conqueror’s connection, King John’s loss of Normandy, the German Occupation and the role of the Bailiff during the Second World War. Inside the States Building, he was fascinated by the architecture, how the courtroom directly adjoins the Assembly chamber, and the Bailiff’s ceremonial mace. Mr Elliott in the Parliament of Canada Mr Elliott – who has been a contestant on numerous gameshows – also praised the member of the States Greffe who guided his visit, saying she answered every question he could throw at her. “I was trying to catch her out because I know my stuff,” he laughed. “Every question I asked, she knew the answer.” But more so, he was impressed by how “direct” Jersey’s political system felt. While Islanders may have their own gripes with representation, Mr Elliott said the proximity to local decision-makers was an asset he felt more people should appreciate, particularly given how challenging it can be to contact and exchange views with MPs in the UK. As a result, Mr Elliott said Jersey should be on every politics student’s itinerary. Mr Elliott in the Slovenian parliament “If you really want to see another [country’s parliament], go to Jersey,” he said. “You have a beautiful history that goes back more than 1,000 years, and you can see how a small Assembly can actually work. It shows you what pure democracy looks like.” His parliamentary world tour continued this month with Jamaica, where, he joked, he would have to swap shorts for a jacket despite the warm weather because of the chamber’s strict dress code. Ahead of that trip, however, he said that Jersey was proudly at the top of his parliamentary league table, even joking that, if someone could “put in a good word” to help him move to the Island, he might one day stand for election himself. https://visegradinsight.eu/citizens-are-.text: Commentary Democratic Security Think Tank Citizens Are First in Line Against Russia’s Sabotage in CEE No time to let one's guard down in Central and Eastern Europe 21 July 2026 Resilient Futures Fellow Clear legal obligations and public awareness campaigns will embolden citizens to report suspicious activities. How to build an effective system of cooperation between authorities and citizens in reporting suspicious activities? The EU governments should: Raise awareness of the nature and scope of grey-zone activities Inspire civic engagement through targeted channels and messaging Actively utilise and proliferate technologies that power the reporting The urgency is now clear On 20 July 2026 Lithuania’s Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas publicly warned that Poland and the Baltic states may become Russia’s ‘nearest target’ for escalation due to Moscow’s failure over Ukraine. The minister’s words supported an intelligence assessment earlier cited by President Gitanas Nausėda. In recent weeks, multiple news outlets have warned that Russia may seek to test NATO’s resolve through limited kinetic actions against NATO’s eastern flank, while remaining below the threshold that would trigger a collective response under Article 5 of the Treaty. The warnings have included scenarios, like drone and missile-related provocations , false flag operations , as well as border incursions . Since 2014, Poland and the Baltic states have invested heavily in preparing for potential Russian grey zone aggression. Yet the scale and diversity of such activities observed across Europe in recent years illustrate that public security and military services alone can no longer effectively monitor and identify every suspicious act that may undermine democratic resilience and threaten national security. As a result, the wider civilian society needs to play a more active role. Grey zone attacks in Europe Until 2022 Russia relied heavily on intelligence operatives working under diplomatic cover – officially posted in embassies, consulates, and trade missions – to conduct espionage, sabotage, and other forms of malign grey zone activity across Europe. Following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, many European countries have ousted such ‘diplomats’. According to the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine, by October 2025 up to 700 Russian operatives had been expelled , including 58 from Poland alone. Deprived of this traditional infrastructure, Moscow has since adapted its operational playbook and has turned to recruiting local actors to carry out grey-zone activities across the continent. At least 151 grey zone incidents linked to Russia have been confirmed between February 2022 and February 2026, with 31 of them occurring in Poland. In November 2025, Railway explosions southeast of Warsaw placed the lives of nearly 500 people at risk. A year earlier, a parcel bomb plot which was carried out by a locally recruited proxy who dispatched four incendiary packages came close to triggering a major aviation disaster. Clearly, the threat is not abstract. Critical infrastructure facilities are particularly vulnerable to kinetic activities that fall short of direct aggression. This demands a whole-of-society approach built on civil-military cooperation. Given the scale of grey zone incidents in CEE, it is worth assessing how civilian populations are able to recognise and report such activities, as well as the extent to which citizens feel responsible for contributing to public security. Awareness and willingness to report grey zone activities According to a survey conducted by the University of Latvia, a substantial portion of respondents across the Baltic capitals believe they already personally contribute to national security. Agreement with the statement that individuals are doing enough to keep their country safe reached 53 per cent in Vilnius, 65 per cent in Riga, and 72 per cent in Tallinn. Awareness levels also appear relatively high, with roughly two-thirds of the residents in the Baltic capitals reporting that they understand what constitutes critical infrastructure. Similarly, large majorities – 78 per cent of respondents in Riga, 80 per cent in Tallinn, and 92 per cent in Vilnius – would consider photographing, filming, or observing critical infrastructure or a military facility as suspicious activity. However, willingness to report such activities reveals notable demographic divides. In Riga, for instance, 76 per cent of Latvian respondents view drawing pro-Russia or anti-NATO graffiti as suspicious activity that should be reported, while only 35 per cent of Russian respondents share this assessment. Gender disparities are also evident: in Tallinn, 77 per cent of men report understanding what critical infrastructure facilities are, compared to just 55 per cent of women. These disparities across demographic groups highlight the need for targeted and evidence-based policy responses. Source: University of Latvia Legal obligation or public awareness? So, what is the most appropriate way to engage citizens in reporting suspicious activities? Should governments adopt a more coercive approach – similar to legal obligations requiring individuals to report witnessed crimes? This was the guiding question of the legal foresight prepared within the Resilient Futures Fellowship programme 2026. The brief emphasises the importance of fostering a strong sense of moral responsibility, combined with significantly improved public awareness of activities that may carry serious implications for national security. In this approach, citizens are not treated merely as passive observers bound by legal duty, but as active participants in safeguarding democratic resilience. Download the full brief An effective framework would therefore combine clear reporting channels with practical, behaviour-based guidance. It would strengthen internal reporting obligations for providers of critical services, invest in employee training, and ensure the availability of confidential reporting options. Crucially, authorities must also close the feedback loop – demonstrating that reports are taken seriously, handled professionally and genuinely contribute to security outcomes. This translates into several concrete steps: The governments must raise public awareness about the evolving and complex nature of the threat landscape. Citizens cannot report what they do not recognise, and grey-zone activities are becoming ever more sophisticated. Authorities should actively encourage civic engagement through targeted information campaigns, drawing on models such as ‘see something, say something’ . User-friendly and trustworthy technological solutions should be developed to enable both open and anonymous reporting, incorporate safeguards against abuse, including malicious or false submissions, and ensure that reporters receive timely and meaningful feedback. Featured illustration uses content elements by Wikimedia Commons / Kusurija , bne IntelliNews , Aleksander Kaasik . Resilient Futures Fellow Roberts Kits is a Resilient Futures Fellow 2026 at Visegrad Insight. He is a researcher at the Latvian Strategy and Economic Research Institute (LaSER Think Tank) and a doctoral researcher at the University of Latvia, focusing on defence innovation, regional security, and societal resilience. His recent publications explore defence cooperation in the Baltic region and the evolving architecture of civil defence. https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text: Plastic bottles and containers are seen in a domestic recycling bin in Manchester. Photograph: Phil Noble/Reuters View image in fullscreen Plastic bottles and containers are seen in a domestic recycling bin in Manchester. Photograph: Phil Noble/Reuters Seascape: the state of our oceans Plastics UK plastic ‘waste colonialism’ found to be polluting Turkey’s farming heartland A Guardian investigation finds irrigation canals polluted with microplastics in Turkey, a major destination for UK waste ‘Nobody cares’: Turkish farmers bear the burden of UK’s plastic waste problem Seascape: the state of our oceans is supported by About this content Karen McVeigh and Ayça Aldatmaz in Adana Tue 4 Aug 2026 05.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 05.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google High levels of microplastics and other plastic contamination have been discovered in a waterway close to a major recycling hub in Turkey supplied with plastic waste by British companies. The polluted waterway, which floods into agricultural fields after heavy rain, feeds into a larger canal used for irrigating crops on the Çukurova plain, in the city of Adana, in the south of the country. It is one of the largest and most fertile agricultural basins in Turkey. The findings from a Guardian investigation reignite concerns over Britain’s continuing role in “waste colonialism” – a term used to describe the export of plastic waste by rich nations to poorer countries with less regulated waste management. The UK government pledged to reduce plastic pollution and eliminate harmful plastics during talks to reach a global plastics treaty , which collapsed last year, but it has not committed to a ban on exports. Treaty negotiations are expected to resume in 2027. Britain, one of the world’s largest exporters of plastic waste, exported 675,000 tonnes in 2025, its largest amount in eight years, of which 139,000 tonnes was shipped to Turkey . The EU’s plastic waste exports to Turkey that year rose 19% on the year before to more than 500,000 tonnes . Environmental campaigners in the UK and Turkey say that British and EU plastic waste exports are driving the operations responsible for the pollution, leaving the city’s poorer residents to pay the price. About 13% of UK plastic waste to Turkey was shipped to eight facilities within the recycling zone in Adana between May 2021 and July 2024, according to an analysis of import and export data carried out for the Guardian by an international NGO, the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA). Thirteen British companies sent 545 shipments, totalling 52,000 tonnes, of plastic waste to the hub during the three-year period. There is no suggestion that the companies exporting plastic waste are acting illegally. British exporters of plastic waste do, however, have a duty under various regulations to ensure that the plastic they export is recycled in an environmentally sound manner. View image in fullscreen A plastic waste recycling plant near Adana. Samples taken from a canal downstream from the recycling zone were 10 times higher than upstream sites. Photograph: Ayça Aldatmaz Sedat Gündoğdu, a Turkish marine biologist at Sabancı University’s Istanbul Policy Center, who conducted the microplastic sampling, has called for a ban on all plastic imports to Turkey. “The discharge of microplastic-laden wastewater into irrigation canals raises critical concerns about agricultural contamination and food safety,” he said. Plastic pollution from recycling centres that contaminates canals ultimately ends up in the Mediterranean Sea, he added, which “exacerbates marine plastic accumulation” and undermines efforts to protect the sea from contamination. Samples taken from the canal downstream from the recycling zone were 10 times higher than upstream sites, according to Gündoğdu’s research, published in Environment Monitoring and Assessment . He also found pellets, films and fragments “highly characteristic of [waste] recycling processing”, he said. He has called for mandatory installation of microplastic filtration at all facilities and independent monitoring of all wastewater discharges in agricultural zones. Amy Youngman, a legal specialist at the EIA, said that, by its continued reliance on exporting rather than investing in reduction or domestic recycling, the UK had failed to “keep pace with the EU” and had created a “structural imbalance”. “This results in pollution occurring overseas in ways that would not be tolerated within the UK itself and passes the devastating human health, economic and environmental harm to communities in Turkey,” she said. The findings added to an “expanding body of irrefutable evidence exposing waste colonialism in the UK’s waste-export system”, she said. We need to talk about plastic: five everyday items choking the planet Read more A Greenpeace investigation in 2021 found plastic waste from British supermarkets waste dumped and burned in Adana . The same year, the Turkish government announced a ban on certain waste, including polyethylene , which is used in 94% of UK plastic waste exports including yoghurt pots, salad bags and plastic film, but revoked the ban after pressure from the recycling industry . The EU has recently imposed strict controls on plastic waste exports . From November, exports other than to mostly rich OECD countries will be banned. Environmentalists fear this could lead to more exports to Turkey, an OECD country and already the main importer of EU waste. A spokesperson for the UK’s Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs said: “There are already strict controls in place on the export of waste set out in UK legislation. Businesses involved in the export of waste from the UK are required to ensure that the waste they ship is managed in an environmentally sound manner, and we have already taken action to further reduce our need to export plastic waste.” The Turkish government was approached for comment but did not respond. Photograph: Linda Nylind/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Peter Gill in 2014, the year he directed his play Versailles at the Donmar in London. Photograph: Linda Nylind/The Guardian Peter Gill Peter Gill, playwright who turned ordinary lives into extraordinary drama, dies aged 86 Beginning his career as an actor, Gill went on to write plays including The York Realist as well as directing for the Royal Court and National Theatre Mark Fisher Tue 4 Aug 2026 09.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Tributes have been paid to the director and playwright Peter Gill who died on Monday at the age of 86. His agent Mel Kenyon said Gill’s work had a “rare emotional delicacy” and was “beautifully observed and finely tuned” while the director Michael Grandage said Gill’s “contribution to the British theatre will come to be regarded as quietly seismic”. Gill began his career as an actor at London’s Royal Court in 1958 when still in his teens. Over the next six years, he played Silvius opposite Vanessa Redgrave as Rosalind in Michael Elliott’s lauded RSC production of As You Like It, as well as several roles in the British premiere of Brecht’s The Caucasian Chalk Circle. Uncertain of his strengths as an actor, however, he moved into directing. He was encouraged by the Royal Court’s artistic director George Devine who took him on as an assistant director. He would go on to stage as many as 100 productions. The first, in 1965, was A Collier’s Friday Night by DH Lawrence, a writer whom he championed in the following years. He revived the play in 1968 as part of a trilogy of Laurence’s neglected mining plays, adding The Daughter-in-Law and The Widowing of Mrs Holroyd. He also staged The Merry-Go-Round in 1973. In 1976, he became the first artistic director of Riverside Studios in Hammersmith in London, where he staged The Cherry Orchard, with Eleanor Bron, Julie Covington and Michael Elphick, and The Changeling, with Brian Cox and Robert Lindsay. He also established an eye-catching programme of international work. Central to his operation was the Riverside theatre studio, a series of actors’ workshops designed to foster a company spirit. View image in fullscreen Stephen Hagan and Matthew Burton in The York Realist at Riverside Studios in 2009. Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian In 1980, he became associate director at the National Theatre , where, in 1984, he set up the National Theatre Studio to give playwrights and directors space to develop ideas. He remained with the National until 1997. His many productions for the company included Christopher Hampton’s Tales from Hollywood, with Michael Gambon, Billie Whitelaw and Ian McDiarmid; Thomas Otway’s Venice Preserv’d, with Ian McKellen, Michael Pennington and Jane Lapotaire; and Harley Granville-Barker’s The Voysey Inheritance, with Dominic West and Julian Glover. Elsewhere, he staged plays by Chekhov, Pinter, Orton, Shaw, Mamet and Hare. His work as a playwright was no less impressive. His first play, The Sleepers Den, about a family falling apart in a claustrophobic Cardiff slum, was produced in 1965 and starred Eileen Atkins. He returned repeatedly to the working-class Catholic Wales of his childhood, drawing out the extraordinary in ordinary lives and frequently focusing on male relationships, gay or otherwise. Subsequent work included Over Gardens Out, about two teenage tearaways, and Small Change, a coming-of-age tale about two Cardiff boys, which he staged three times over his career. In the Blue, an expressionist play about two gay men, was written in such a way as to make it impossible to know what was real and what was fantasy. In Sheffield in 2002, Grandage devoted a month-long season to Gill’s plays. It included the premiere of Original Sin, about an upwardly mobile Victorian street boy, and a revival of Small Change. Also revived were Kick for Touch, about two brothers, one of whom has had an affair with the other’s wife, Mean Tears, a romantic drama set in the greed-is-good 1980s, and Friendly Fire, aimed at teenagers. The York Realist, staged by English Touring theatre in 2002 before a run in the West End, considered the class system through the lens of an affair between a Yorkshire farmer and a London theatre director. Guardian critic Michael Billington rated it among the best plays of the 21st century. His other later plays included Versailles, As Good a Time as Any and Something in the Air. Gill was appointed OBE in 1980 and reflected on a life of theatre-making in his book Apprenticeship in 2008. Kenyon said that Gill “loved actors and acting” and added: “Whenever we talked, I walked away a wiser person … He was a singular man, a kind, generous and curious man. I will miss him greatly.” Tamara Harvey, co-artistic director of the Royal Shakespeare Company, said that Gill’s “unerring ability to capture the complexity of human existence will live on in his writing but he will, nevertheless, be deeply missed”. Gill is survived by his nieces and nephews. He was predeceased by his brothers Bernard and Paul, and his sister Mary. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Gatwick airport will slightly reposition its emergency runway and use it routinely for short-haul passenger aircraft Photograph: PA/Alamy View image in fullscreen Gatwick airport will slightly reposition its emergency runway and use it routinely for short-haul passenger aircraft Photograph: PA/Alamy Gatwick airport Gatwick airport to open second runway after legal challenge fails £2.2bn project will allow about 100,000 more flights a year to use Britain’s second busiest airport Business live – latest updates Gwyn Topham Transport correspondent Tue 4 Aug 2026 08.09 EDT Last modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 08.27 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Gatwick airport is to start development of its second runway after campaigners lost a legal challenge to the plans. The court of appeal on Tuesday dismissed a bid by local campaign groups to challenge an earlier high court ruling that the scheme could proceed. The £2.2bn project, approved by the transport secretary , Heidi Alexander, in September, will allow about 100,000 more flights a year to use Britain’s second busiest airport. Heathrow passengers face higher fares as airport can recover early expansion plan costs Read more Pierre-Hugues Schmit, the Gatwick chief executive, said the airport was “very pleased that this ruling brings to an end an eight-year planning and legal process which has carefully tested and scrutinised every aspect of our expansion plans on multiple occasions”. The plans will involve the West Sussex airport slightly repositioning its emergency runway and using it routinely for short-haul passenger aircraft. It is now among the busiest single-runway airports in the world, and hopes to have the second runway in operation as early as 2030. The government declared the court ruling a “major milestone for Gatwick and for local communities”. Alexander said: “Around 13 million more passengers and 100,000 more flights will give holidaymakers greater choice and strengthen global links to help make the UK one of the most attractive places in the world to invest. “We’ll back expansion that supports growth and our climate goals. To drive forward sustainable change, we’re also investing more than £219m for green fuel production to cut emissions from flying and secure the future of aviation.” Campaigners had sought a judicial review of the Department for Transport’s decision to approve the plans, arguing that the government had not properly assessed the scheme’s climate impact. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Preview latest after newsletter promotion One of the applicants, Peter Barclay, the chair of Gatwick Area Conservation Campaign, said he was disappointed with the ruling. He said: “It is time for governments to wake up and realise that saying yes to the expansion of any and every airport will not kickstart the economy … It will further lock in aviation’s climate, noise and air pollution impacts, increase congestion on roads and public transport and blight local communities.” Meanwhile, Luton Rising, the council-owned company behind Luton airport, announced that all legal challenges to its expansion plans had now been cleared. The supreme court has dismissed any final possibility of appealing against a high court ruling last November upholding Alexander’s signoff on plans to increase the airport’s annual capacity from 19 million to 32 million passengers by the mid-2040s. The airport owner said it would create up to 11,000 new jobs and generate up to an additional £1.5bn in annual economic activity, and pledged strict controls on noise and carbon emissions, air quality and surface access to the airport. Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen People disembark from a French rescue ship after their boat caught fire during an attempt to cross the Channel from France. Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty Images UK news Dinghy carrying 157 people capsizes in Channel after engine catches fire All passengers thought to have been taken to Boulogne after major air and sea rescue operation by France and UK Diane Taylor Tue 4 Aug 2026 07.33 EDT First published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 06.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A dinghy carrying 157 people has capsized after its engine caught fire as it attempted to cross the Channel from France . The people onboard were rescued from the water after a major air and sea operation was launched using UK border security and French vessels along with an RNLI boat. According to French authorities there were initially 162 people onboard but five were rescued overnight in an earlier incident and taken back to Boulogne. The rest of the passengers said they wanted to continue their journey. The dingy was carrying the second highest number of people so far this year. A boat that arrived on 23 Julywas carrying 165 passengers. A coastguard spokesperson said: “A vessel caught fire earlier this morning whilst in the French search and rescue region. UK vessels and a lifeboat are assisting.” An RNLI spokesperson said Eastbourne’s all-weather lifeboat launched at 6am on Tuesday. On Monday, Reform UK proposed using the Royal Navy to return people to France or Belgium under a plan they called “operation fortress”. The party has described the scheme as a humanitarian response. Responding to Tuesday’s incident, Nigel Farage wrote on X: “We must put a stop to this. Our plan will save lives.” The party’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, said: “Just like Reform policy: rescue and return. It’s the humanitarian thing to do. We must stop people dying.” Last week, four people died on overcrowded boats trying to cross the Channel. Smugglers are using increasingly dangerous techniques in response to successive UK government clampdowns to stop crossings. They are also launching boats from parts of the French coast that are farther away from the UK in the hope of evading French police interceptions. The boat on Tuesday reportedly left from Dieppe, about 70 miles (112km) from the UK compared with the Calais to Dover route of 27 miles. The new prime minister, Andy Burnham, has promised to continue working to stop the crossings, although more than 2,000 people have crossed the Channel since he became prime minister. The government has put a number of deterrents in place to stop crossings, but desperate people continue to get into increasingly dangerous dinghies. According to a statement issued by French authorities on Tuesday, the people in the boat initially refused an offer of assistance. “Given the structural fragility of the overcrowded boats, the decision was made not to force the migrants to board state rescue vessels, to avoid endangering their lives in the event of a shipwreck,” the statement read. All 157 people are thought to have been returned to Boulogne.
