Reuters reported Nawrocki rejected two measures that would have allowed same-sex couples who live together to enter into “cohabitation contracts.” Reuters noted the bills would have allowed same-sex couples to make decisions on issues that include access to medical information, property rights, and burial. The country’s coalition government backed the bills that MPs approved. Nawrocki, a socially conservative Catholic, in a statement said they “create a new, formalized institution of family law, ​equipped with a broad catalogue of rights similar to those of marriage.” “As the guardian of the Constitution, I cannot accept a solution that would lead to the loss of the ‌special ⁠status of marriage, defined in Article 18 of the Constitution as a union of a man and a woman under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland,” said Nawrocki, as Reuters noted. Prime Minister Donald Tusk sharply criticized Nawrocki. Miko Czerwiński of the Campaign Against Homophobia, a Polish LGBTQ advocacy group, in a statement noted nearly 80 percent of Poles “believe that the status of same-sex couples should be protected.” “Once again, the voice of society has proven irrelevant to those in power,” said Czerwiński. “We are not willing to accept this. We will continue working towards full marriage equality.” The EU Court of Justice in Luxembourg last November ruled in favor of a same-sex couple who challenged Poland’s refusal to recognize their German marriage. Poland’s Supreme Administrative Court in March reaffirmed the decision. The couple, who lives in Poland, brought their case to Polish courts in 2019. The Supreme Administrative Court referred it to the EU Court of Justice. The Polish government in May announced it will recognize same-sex marriages legally performed in other EU countries. The Supreme Administrative Court referred it to the EU Court of Justice. Prime Minister Donald Tusk on Tuesday apologized to same-sex couples for the “years of rejection and humiliation” they suffered because Poland did not recognize their relationships. “I hope that after the ruling of the (European Union) court and the Supreme Administrative Court, we will also find swift and necessary legislative solutions in parliament,” said Tusk, according to TVP, Poland’s public broadcaster. Warsaw Mayor Rafał Trzaskowski, a member of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition party, who supports LGBTQ rights, said his city will begin to recognize same-sex marriages legally performed in other EU countries before the national government does. Tusk, for his part, said this recognition is “no way a path to the possibility of adoption.” Any marriage recognition bill that MPs pass will go to President Karol Nawrocki, who is a socially conservative Catholic, for his signature. “We welcome these decisions and announcements with hope,” said the Campaign Against Homophobia, a Polish LGBTQ advocacy group. “The true confirmation of these words, however, will be the signing of the aforementioned regulation and the actual certificates held in the hands of those Polish couples who were forced to fight for their dignity and justice before Polish courts.” Karolina Gierdal, a lawyer with Lambda Warszawa, another Polish LGBTQ rights organization, criticized Tusk’s adoption comments. “It is sad that the LGBT community is once again presented as a threat, as if society needs reassurance that adoption rights ‘won’t happen.’” she told TVP. “The reality is that children are already being raised in same-sex families in Poland, and maintaining the current legal situation means reducing the level of legal protection available to those children.” Continue Reading Poland Polish court rules country must recognize same-sex marriages from EU states Poland ‘must comply with European Union law’ Published 4 months ago on March 23, 2026 By Michael K. https://www.forbes.com/sites/lidiakurasi.text: Leadership Leadership Strategies Poland Seeks To Curb Dependence On Big Tech With "Sovereignty Test" By Lidia Kurasinska , Contributor. Forbes contributors publish independent expert analyses and insights. Lidia Kurasińska covers Eastern European politics and business. Follow Author Jul 21, 2026, 02:16pm EDT Summary Poland is preparing to introduce a mandatory "technological sovereignty test" for major public-sector technology purchases as it looks to reduce dependence on foreign tech providers and strengthen control over critical digital infrastructure. The proposal reflects a broader shift across Europe, where governments are increasingly treating technology as a matter of national security rather than just public procurement. Show More Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk speaks during a news conference following the European Council summit in Brussels on June 19, 2026. (Photo by Daniel Gnap/NurPhoto via Getty Images) NurPhoto via Getty Images Poland is preparing to implement a "technological sovereignty test" for major public-sector technology purchases, becoming one of the latest European governments seeking to reduce strategic dependence on U.S. technology providers as governments increasingly treat digital infrastructure as a matter of national security. The proposed mechanism would apply to large public IT projects and assess whether public institutions retain control over critical systems and data while reducing reliance on foreign vendors. The initiative reflects growing concerns that dependence on a small number of foreign technology providers could expose essential public services to political or legal decisions made outside Poland. Rather than eliminating foreign technologies altogether, the government says the goal is to strengthen resilience, maintain operational continuity and give the state greater control over critical digital infrastructure. How the sovereignty test would work Announced by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, the assessment would apply to government technology procurements worth more than 5 million zloty ($1.3 million) and infrastructure projects valued at more than 15 million zloty ($3.9 million). Among other criteria, it would assess the state’s control over a system’s architecture, ownership or access rights to AI model weights, and freedom from vendor lock-in. The greatest threat is "jurisdictional, not technical," says Albert Szczepaniak, director of Security and Quality at Polcom, a Polish data center and cloud services provider. He argues that relying on providers governed by foreign legislation exposes critical infrastructure to external legal regimes, specifically pointing to U.S. laws such as FISA 702 and the CLOUD Act. MORE FOR YOU Under the CLOUD Act, U.S. authorities may request access to data held by American companies even if it is stored on servers located in Europe. Why Poland wants greater technological sovereignty The proposal comes as Poland's dependence on imported digital technologies continues to grow despite being one of the European Union's leaders in the digitalization of public administration. Poland's digital imports increased from 9 billion zloty ($2.3 billion) in 2016 to nearly 48 billion zloty ($12.5 billion) in 2024, growing by an average of 25% annually. Over the same period, digital exports remained largely unchanged at around 3 billion zloty ($780 million), leaving the country with a digital trade deficit of roughly 45 billion zloty ($11.7 billion). Analysts estimate that by the end of the decade, digital imports could exceed the total value of Poland's imports of oil, gas and coal. The cloud computing market illustrates this dependence. Microsoft, Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google together account for more than 70% of Poland's cloud market, limiting competition and increasing reliance on a handful of global providers. Reducing dependence without abandoning U.S. technology Government officials stress that technological sovereignty does not mean cutting Poland off from foreign technology providers. According to recommendations by the Ministry of Digital Affairs and the Future Council, an advisory body appointed by Tusk, completely replacing U.S. technology providers would be neither technically feasible nor economically desirable. Instead, the government aims to build domestic alternatives in strategic segments representing roughly 20% to 30% of the market, including government cloud services, databases and simpler enterprise systems. Officials argue that developing alternatives in these areas would give the state greater negotiating power, improve resilience and keep a larger share of digital spending within Poland. Marcin Wysocki, deputy director of the Cybersecurity Department at the Ministry of Digital Affairs, said technological sovereignty should not be understood as isolation from foreign suppliers, but rather as the state's ability to make informed choices, maintain control over its data, ensure operational continuity and manage technological dependencies. Szczepaniak believes reaching that target is ambitious but achievable within five years. He points to European estimates suggesting that retaining just 15% of current spending on cloud services and software within Europe by 2035 could generate €37 billion ($42 billion) in added value and create more than 460,000 jobs. Public procurement has strengthened Big Tech's grip According to the Warsaw-based Instrat Foundation, Poland’s current procurement model has reinforced dependence on foreign technology providers. In its recent report , 99% of 72 public tenders analyzed directly or indirectly excluded alternatives to Microsoft products, despite procurement rules prohibiting specifications that unnecessarily restrict competition. As a result, domestic and European companies are often limited to acting as resellers of Microsoft licenses rather than competing with their own software. "Lower security, lower resilience, and lower investment in technologies developed in Poland and Europe are the consequences of relying to such an extent on a single supplier from outside the EU," said the report's author, Jarosław Kopeć. He warned that dependence on one provider leaves public administration vulnerable to price increases, service disruptions and the withdrawal of services. Szczepaniak argues a Polish institution buying a “domestic cloud” that simply resells infrastructure from U.S. hyperscalers does not improve technological sovereignty. “The entire supply chain, not the logo on the invoice, should be assessed," he says. A separate report by the Polish Network of Economics argues that digital sovereignty should be treated as a national security issue, with cloud services, government IT systems and public data regarded as critical infrastructure on par with energy and transport networks. Wiesław Wilk, president of the Polish Cloud Association, said continued reliance on technologies outside Poland's control to deliver public services could create long-term strategic vulnerabilities. "In an extreme scenario, losing access to such services could have consequences for the functioning of the state comparable to a disruption in supplies of critical raw materials or energy," he said. A broader European push for technological sovereignty Poland's initiative reflects a broader trend taking shape across Europe, where governments are seeking to reduce strategic dependence on non-European technology providers while avoiding complete technological decoupling. As the relationship with the U.S. has become more uncertain, concerns over the concentration of cloud services among a handful of American companies have grown, alongside efforts to strengthen Europe's technological resilience. In June, the European Commission unveiled its most comprehensive initiative yet to strengthen the bloc’s technological sovereignty. The package aims to reduce Europe's dependence on non-European providers in strategic sectors including semiconductors, cloud computing, artificial intelligence and open-source software. Sources inside the federal detention center report a dawning clarity on the face of the self-described misogynist, who fled rape and human trafficking charges in Romania with the help of the U.S. Trump Administration. “He seemed to think he was getting some kind of exclusive police escort,” explains U.S. Marshal Inspector William Berckett, “but that was actually just us coming to arrest him. It’s probably why he kept asking me to light his cigar.” Behind the prison walls, where the Tates wait to be arraigned before extradition, various prisoners report the famous brothers’ inability to understand that they are facing justice as opposed to ascending to a higher circle of the online “manosphere”. “Man, I been in prison for 10 years on assault charges, but I still got creeped out when this Tate guy kept explaining to me how women shouldn’t be able to vote and marital rape doesn’t exist,” explains Tate cellmate Vernon “Mad Dog” Jascowicz. Some assume the Tates manosphere misunderstanding stems from being surrounded by hundreds of angry, physically-imposing career criminals, with nary a woman in sight, though others insist it’s actually just the brother’s legendary lack of self awareness. Inmates report the Tate brothers demanding to be seated in the VIP area of the prison commissary, using their one phone call to record a podcast about cryptocurrency, and mistaking an initiation beating for “a new alpha male workout routine”. Warden Calvin Anderson attempts to explain the Tate brothers confusion. “The real online manosphere is an enclosed, tightly-enforced space full of bitter volatile men venting their anger and refusing to take accountability for their actions, so I kind of see how Tate confused that for actual prison. America 250 Objects The Bagel A poppy seed bagel on a plate photographed in Phoenix, Ariz., Monday, July 20, 2026. (AP Photo/Dario Lopez-Mills) AP Photo/Dario Lopez-Mills America 250 Objects The Bagel A plain bagel with cream cheese is photographed in Phoenix, Ariz., Monday, July 20, 2026. (AP Photo/Dario Lopez-Mills) AP Photo/Dario Lopez-Mills America 250 Objects The Bagel A breakfast egg and cheese on an "everything" bagel photographed in Phoenix, Ariz., Tuesday, July 21, 2026. (AP Photo/Dario Lopez-Mills) AP Photo/Dario Lopez-Mills America 250 Objects The Bagel Salt flecks and poppy seeds can be seen near the center of a poppy seed bagel in Phoenix, Ariz., April 5, 2026. (AP Photo/Dario Lopez-Mills) AP Photo/Dario Lopez-Mills ( 1 /4) Share This Gallery: Share This: share on facebook share on X share on threads share on linkedin share on email print NEW YORK (AP) — The bagel in America is an immigrant story with a hole in the middle. It came to America with Eastern European Jews escaping poverty and antisemitism. It landed in New York street carts and neighborhood bakeries. Later, it made its way to supermarket freezer aisles and into the breakfast order of so many every day. And like every food story, it starts with the first bite. As a layer of crunch prepares your brain for a crusty piece of bread, it’s immediately met by the soft yet dense chew of the inside. Eating the two textures together brings a feeling of joy, along with whatever toppings you’ve added. A schmear of cream cheese to keep it simple. A flavored spread to add a bit of zest. Or a bagel topped taller than the human mouth can handle with fish, tomato, cucumber and red onions. And we haven’t even talked about the flavor choices. A simple plain or egg bagel works for some (no judgment). Others insist on seeds — poppy, sesame — or shards of onion or salt. Others say it’s not a bagel unless it’s an everything, each bite snapping back at you with a different cascade of flavors. Purists will tell you to keep it simple. But with a bagel, like so much in American life, you can have it any way you’d like. The bagel started in Jewish communities in Poland and was brought here by Eastern European Jews escaping growing antisemitism in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. After arriving from Poland, Harry Lender worked at a New Jersey bakery to earn enough to bring his family to America. His sons grew the family’s work from their New Haven, Connecticut, bakery to supermarkets around the country with frozen bagels. The bagel, then, is another story of the success of immigrants in America. The shops that now sell them are run by families of those original immigrants and new groups who’ve come for a better life. But no matter how far the bagel spreads, it maintains a special place for American Jews. Many moments in the circle of life for Jews in America include boiled rings of dough stacked high to celebrate or eat away the grief. Ritual circumcision for a baby boy? Snip snip, then bagels for all. Bar mitzvah day 13 years later? Months of practice for an hour of work. Then: bagels. Shiva house mourning a loved one? “Sorry for your loss.” “Thank you. Bagels are in the other room.” In these situations, the bagel brings comfort — just as it has for generations of American Jews, immigrants, and anyone else looking for their place at the table. ___ Part of a recurring series, “American Objects,” marking the 250th anniversary of the United States. https://www.bursa.ro/a-letter-lost-in-a-.text: Our country is in a critical situation, and Sorin Grindeanu, the president of the Chamber of Deputies and, by a happy political coincidence, the president of the Social Democratic Party, yesterday took up the pen to officially announce, through a letter addressed to the leaders of the parliamentary political parties, what Romanians had already found out firsthand: the state has blocked, hospitals no longer have enough people, fuel is getting more expensive, IT systems are crashing, real estate transactions are getting bogged down, and the billions from the PNRR are waiting patiently on the border between promise and impossibility. The situation is serious, but not desperate, because, when institutions no longer function, Romanian politics always has the ultimate solution at hand: the establishment of a committee. Or a committee, as my uncle Iancu would have said. A committee whose head or president would be none other than the "honorable", "esteemed" Sorin Grindeanu. "Romania is going through a period in which the government gridlock is affecting the state's capacity to respond to the country's urgent problems," writes Sorin Grindeanu at the beginning of the letter. An accurate, clear and almost courageous observation, if it did not come from the very center of the political system that produced the gridlock. But let's not be grumbling. The important thing is that the diagnosis has been made. The patient is not responding, the administration's pulse is barely felt, European funding is in the waiting room, but political doctors are still discussing who will occupy the main office and who has the right to hold the stethoscope. The PSD president informs us that "there are essential areas in which the lack of decisions already produces serious effects." In other words, the lack of decisions produces effects, an administrative discovery worthy of being recorded in the Official Gazette. Until now, it was probably believed that indecision is a superior form of prudence, that postponement is a public policy and that a gridlocked government can lead the country through its simple decorative existence. Reality, this eternal opponent of government programs, however, had the impudence to intervene. In support of the above statement, Sorin Grindeanu gives the example of children's hospitals, where the hiring freeze has begun to threaten the functioning of critical departments. "If we do not urgently supplement, through legislative measures, the staffing scheme in Health, the staff shortage in critical areas, the latest example being the ICU Department at Marie Curie Hospital, will lead to the irremediable degradation of hospital services," warns the PSD leader. "Irremediable" is a difficult word, even for a political letter. It means that we are no longer talking about a small budgetary inconvenience, about two signatures lost in a ministerial corridor or about an organizational chart that must be walked from one office to another, but about vital medical services that risk being compromised. Sick children, however, do not know the subtleties of budget balance, they do not know that hiring is blocked in the name of great fiscal principles and they cannot wait for the installation of a Government with full powers. They have this deeply unadministrative impatience to need doctors and nurses right now. The real estate market is not feeling any better either. The platforms of the National Agency for Cadastre and Real Estate Advertising have been affected by cyber attacks, and activity in the field has been blocked. The digitalization of the Romanian state has thus shown its full efficiency: where, in the past, the citizen was stopped by a file with a rail, now he can be stopped instantly by an unavailable computer system. This is progress, without a doubt. The queue at the counter has been replaced by the server error, and the clerk who said "come back tomorrow" has been modernized into an automatic message that no longer specifies when to come back. On top of this technological achievement comes the deadline of July 31. "If we do not adopt a transitional legislative measure by July 31, all real estate transactions will have a 21% VAT rate applied. Which will deepen the crisis in the construction sector," warns Sorin Grindeanu. The deadline was, of course, known, but Romanian politics has a special relationship with the calendar: they ignore it while there are months left, they contest it when there are weeks left, and they declare it a national emergency when there are a few days left. Only then do responsibility, mobilization, and a call to unity appear. If the deadline had been dealt with in advance, the drama would have been lost, and the extraordinary session would have risked becoming a banal one, which, it must be admitted, does not serve anyone from a rhetorical point of view. And fuels are stubbornly increasing in price without waiting for the political crisis to be resolved. "If we do not put the fuel price compensation mechanism back into operation, we will have a new explosion of prices for Romanians," writes the president of the Chamber of Deputies. The explosion is for Romanians, the compensation is for the budget, the explanations are for the press, and the responsibility, being a very sensitive political commodity, is kept in a cool place and away from light. The citizen will pay at the pump the cost of the time lost by those who represent him, but he will be able to have the satisfaction that his price increase was foreseen in an official letter. Faced with these dangers, Sorin Grindeanu proposes "the establishment of a crisis committee at the level of Parliament, formed by representatives of all parliamentary groups". Here, finally, is the solution! When the Government cannot govern, the Parliament will form a committee that will discuss how the Government could be helped to govern without, for the time being, a Government with full powers. It is an institutional architecture of such finesse that only Romanian political practice could conceive it. However, let no one think that it is a committee in the rigid, regulatory and boring sense of the word. Grindeanu clarifies the matter carefully: "I emphasize that this is strictly an informal working group and not a classic parliamentary procedure.” In other words, there is an official crisis, official problems, official deadlines, official billions and official effects on citizens, but the group that will seek solutions will be informal. A happy reconciliation between solemnity and lack of responsibility. If things go well, the committee will be proof of political maturity. If things go badly, it was not even a committee, but only an informal working group, a responsible conversation between concerned people. This group would be "to identify and prepare, on an emergency basis, the amendments and legislative solutions necessary to unblock these situations.” It is comforting to learn that solutions exist and can be identified. All that remains is the small mystery of why they were not identified before the situations needed to be "unblocked.” The fruit of the discussions will form the basis of the "extraordinary session of Parliament that I intend to convene next week," writes Sorin Grindeanu, who, by the way, announced yesterday, in a press conference, that we will have this session on July 27, during which the elected representatives will have to adopt the urgent measures and legislative projects assumed through the PNRR, which, according to the letter, "will bring Romania over 3 billion euros." Three billion euros is, without a doubt, a convincing argument. Not so convincing that the projects would have been adopted on time, but convincing enough to be invoked now, when the need for urgency can be presented as proof of responsibility. From the letter of the President of the Chamber of Deputies, we also note that the said informal committee or group would function "exclusively until the installation of a Government with full powers." Until then, the state will be kept alive by amendments prepared informally and adopted extraordinarily. After the installation of the Government, the committee will be dissolved, the crisis will be declared over, and the parties will resume their usual activity of preventing the next crisis by ignoring its early signs. We have a letter since yesterday. We will have a committee. Then, an extraordinary session. Therefore, the crisis can rest easy: it has entered the parliamentary circuit and, with a little luck, will soon receive a registration number. Articol despre Sorin Grindeanu, lost letter, crisis committee, PNRR.

https://www.dailyrecord.co.uk/news/uk-wo.text: The Trump administration is reportedly allowing the extradition of Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan to Britain. The US president apparently has no plans to step in to intervene after the pair were arrested in Miami on Saturday by US police at the request of British detectives, reports The Telegraph . The pair now face being brought back to the UK where they face a litany of alleged sexual offences including rape and human trafficking. When the Tate's were first arrested in Florida last year following a period of house arrest in Romania, Andrew suggested in leaked texts that the Trump administration had helped him and his brother to flee the country. Trump said he knew "nothing about it" when he was asked about this at the time, reports The Mirror. Their latest arrest was met with calls from some leading Republican figures and administration individuals for Trump to step in. The brother's lawyer, Joe McBride has claimed they are victims of a "politically motivated witch hunt". The Telegraph has now said a US official told the paper that the White House will not get involved in the case. The official reportedly said: "The White House has no involvement and no feelings on the issue." The pair have "unequivocally" denied wrongdoing, with Andrew Tate describing himself and his brother as "very innocent men". A total of 38 new charges were authorised against Andrew Tate, 39, and Tristan Tate, 38, by the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS). Andrew Tate was charged with seven further counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, three counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and 19 additional charges for offences relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography. Tristan Tate was charged with one count of sexual assault, two counts of rape and three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation. Charges were previously authorised by the CPS following a file of evidence submitted by officers from Bedfordshire Police into allegations dating back to 2012. Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Hertfordshire Major Crime Unit have been continuing to investigate a number of other alleged offences reported to both Bedfordshire Police and Hertfordshire Constabulary. The total number of charges against the brothers now totals 59. Of these, 42 charges have been authorised against Andrew Tate, and 17 against Tristan Tate. The CPS confirmed it had requested the extradition of Andrew and Tristan Tate from the US. Malcolm McHaffie, head of the CPS's Special Crime Division, previously said: "We have decided to prosecute Andrew and Tristan Tate for further offences including rape, arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation and offences relating to indecent images of a child. "These charging decisions followed receipt of a further file of evidence from Bedfordshire Police and bring the total number of alleged victims in this case to seven." The offending is alleged to have taken place between July 2010 and August 2017, according to the CPS.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: The Fuego volcano in Guatemala erupts, with rivers of lava running down the slopes. Photograph: Johan Ordóñez/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The Fuego volcano in Guatemala erupts, with rivers of lava running down the slopes. Photograph: Johan Ordóñez/AFP/Getty Images Guatemala Guatemala volcano eruption prompts evacuation of hundreds of people Eruption of the Fuego volcano sends lava and ash nearly four miles into the sky as country declares second-highest alert Agence France-Presse in San Juan Alotenango Tue 4 Aug 2026 13.31 EDT Last modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 13.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Hundreds of people living on the slopes of Guatemala ’s Fuego volcano have evacuated their homes after a huge eruption spewed lava and plumes of ash. Central America’s most active volcano erupted on Monday morning, with conditions intensifying by nightfall and prompting authorities to issue the country’s second-most severe alert warning. By Tuesday, rivers of lava were streaming down the 3,763-metre (12,346-foot) volcano, which is located less than 100 kilometres (62 miles) from Guatemala City. Ash rose six kilometres (3.73 miles) into the red sky. “Since early morning it was active. That night, the alarm was raised that we needed to evacuate,” a local resident, Alejandro Garcia, 68, told AFP. Villagers left of their own accord out of fear, Garcia said, describing terrifying scenes of lava tumbling down the mountainside. Firefighters said they transported at least 350 residents of the El Porvenir and Las Lajitas villages to the eastward San Juan Alotenango municipality. Evacuees are staying in a community hall, where makeshift beds have been set up, while the number of people taken to other nearby towns remains unknown. “If there were any chance of moving to a different house, it would be better, because you’re always afraid since the volcano doesn’t give any warning,” Lidia Ortiz, 40, said at the shelter. Escuintla, to the south, was sheltering dozens more families, including children, local authorities reported. “If an evacuation is ordered or conditions pose a risk to your life, follow the principle of self-evacuation,” Conred spokesperson Valeria Urizar said in a video posted on social media. The country’s Institute of Volcanology warned of hot volcanic debris flows down Fuego’s slopes, with communities on the western and southern flanks at the greatest risk. Fuego had been erupting for 23 hours straight by Tuesday morning, it said, although the intensity was easing. “We’ve already gotten used to having the volcano constantly active, but this time it was really too much,” 50-year-old resident Sonia Vasquez said. Guatemalan authorities urged “precautions with air traffic”, but there has so far been no impact on the capital’s international airport. The education ministry ordered the suspension of face-to-face classes in communities within two municipalities near the volcano. Guatemala volcano: rescuers battle boiling ash to recover Fuego’s dead Read more Traffic police also closed a road encircling the mountain range that connects the south coast with the colonial city of Antigua, the country’s main tourist destination and a Unesco World Heritage site. Guatemala lies on the Pacific ‘ring of fire’ and experiences frequent seismic and volcanic activity. There have been several such mass evacuations in recent years because Fuego erupted. Authorities evacuated more than 500 people last year after Fuego spurted gas and ash, with residents moved to shelters from communities near the crater. Another eruption in 2023 pushed around 1,200 people to evacuate. In 2018, 215 people were killed and a similar number left missing when rivers of lava poured down Fuego’s slopes and destroyed a village. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: School Naplan results have been released by the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority for 2026. Photograph: Lincoln Beddoe/Getty Images View image in fullscreen School Naplan results have been released by the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority for 2026. Photograph: Lincoln Beddoe/Getty Images Australian education Reading and writing worsens in Australian schools as one in three students fail to meet Naplan benchmarks Education minister Jason Clare says the results showed ‘real challenges’ but numeracy scores were heartening Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Caitlin Cassidy Tue 4 Aug 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Reading and writing scores are going backwards for almost every age group in Australia’s national standardised school tests, with one in three students still failing to meet Naplan benchmarks. This year’s tests were taken in March by 1.2 million students across years 3, 5, 7 and 9 to measure literacy and numeracy proficiency, with results released on Wednesday by the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority (Acara). Participation was down compared with last year due to industrial action in Tasmania and flooding in the Northern Territory, which has led Acara to not report Tasmanian state-level results as it lagged “far below” the body’s data standards for accurate reporting. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The tests were also marred by disruption over a technical issue on the first day for students completing writing papers in years 5, 7 and 9. Acara said national average scores in writing remained similar to last year but it has included a caveat for results, instead of implementing marking adjustments. One in three students weren’t meeting benchmarks across reading, numeracy and writing, which had not budged since 2025 , and one in 10 needed “additional support”, meaning they would need further help to progress and were not working towards expectations. Average reading scores in years 5, 7 and 9 went backwards compared with 2025, and more students were needing additional support in both reading and writing. Average reading scores were stable for year 3 students. The average proportion of students “exceeding” and “strong” at reading was 66.3%, down from 68.2% last year There were some improvements in national numeracy levels since the tests were reset in 2023 for students in years 5, 7 and 9, with the highest national average score of 67% meeting benchmarks and 29,000 more students “exceeding”. A chart showing the proportion of students meeting reading benchmarks The gains were also evident among Indigenous students, with more “exceeding” in years 7 and 9 compared with 2023 and average scores among year 5 and 7 students at the highest level since the tests were reset. But for year 3 students, the average national numeracy score was the lowest it had been since 2023. The education minister, Jason Clare, said the results showed “real challenges” as well as “how to fix them”, pointing to an ongoing numeracy review across primary school levels, spearheaded by Acara as a result of previous Naplan data. “There is good news here in numeracy,” Clare said. “It’s going up and up in years 5 and in high school. “Year 3 maths is a different story. That’s why we are fixing the maths curriculum for the first three years of school. “The reading results show we still have real challenges. They also show us how to fix them … This year’s results show that in schools using explicit teaching methods , including phonics, and small-group tutoring to give kids who are struggling extra intensive help, results are going up and up.” The federal government’s additional $20bn injection to the public system , to be rolled out over a decade, includes requirements that states and territories implement year 1 phonics and numeracy checks and back “evidence-based” teaching practices, including explicit teaching. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion Victoria had the highest average scores across year levels and domains, followed by the ACT and New South Wales, governments which have backed explicit teaching methods. The ACT is also the only jurisdiction to have reached full funding of public schools. The remaining states and territories fell below the Australian average in the majority of year levels and study areas. Montessori learning is being shut down at Leah’s school – is a push towards ‘explicit instruction’ to blame? Read more The chief executive of Acara, Stephen Gniel, said it was “encouraging” to see continued improvement in national numeracy, especially among the stronger students, but the drop in results among year 3 students was “clearly concerning”. “Education ministers are addressing this through a range of measures including the rollout of the national year 1 numeracy check,” he said. “Acara is also playing its part by reviewing the foundation to year 2 mathematics curriculum at the direction of education ministers.” Gniel said reading and writing needed “our collective attention”, as did continued disparities depending on geography and background. The average Naplan scores across year levels and domains were substantially higher for students from the highest socio-educational background, which is measured on parental education and occupation. Similarly, students tended to perform better in urban verses regional areas, with just 23% of students at very remote schools “exceeding” in reading and numeracy compared with 70% of students at major city schools. “It is … disheartening to see disparities persisting over the years in the attainment of students from our regional and remote areas, Indigenous students and those from a disadvantaged background,” Gniel said. “This needs to be a continuing focus for all in the coming years.” Gender differences also persisted, with female students outperforming males in literacy and males tending to perform better in numeracy . Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP View image in fullscreen Damien Tudehope (right) has not been named as a person of interest in Operation Rosny but has stood down as shadow attorney general. Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP Independent Commission Against Corruption Analysis ‘Did you send that report?’ The Icac bombshell that came late for Damien Tudehope Anne Davies The former Liberal finance minister was questioned by Icac counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer, on Tuesday Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Tue 4 Aug 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 11.02 EDT Share The bombshell came in the last five minutes of former finance minister and rightwing powerbroker Damien Tudehope’s examination before the Independent Commission Against Corruption . At 3.30pm on Tuesday, Tudehope was shown an email which he sent in February 2023, attaching a leaked draft parliamentary report into branch stacking in the Hills area by the Reformers, the shadowy group at the centre of Icac’s Operation Rosny. It has probably imperilled his parliamentary career. “Would you regard yourself … as being bound by keeping it confidential?” asked counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer, SC. Tudehope visibly tensed. “Did you send that report in draft to Mr Greenwood?” she asked, showing him the email. “It appears that I did,” Tudehope replied quietly. Jeremy Greenwood is one of the group of conservative Catholic men who set up the Reformers, recruiting like-minded conservatives to the Liberal party in order to take over branches from the moderate and centre-right factions. In 2023, during the parliamentary inquiry, the key Reformers and associates – Christian Ellis, the then premier’s brothers Jean-Claude Perrottet and Charles Perrottet, and Greenwood – had left NSW to avoid being called to the parliamentary inquiry. NSW Liberal admits to leaking confidential report to young conservative powerbrokers, inquiry hears Read more Tudehope told Icac he had had a conversation with the premier, Dom Perrottet, who said he knew his brother had gone to Fiji. Leaking a draft parliamentary report is a serious breach of parliamentary rules and contempt of parliament. It may even constitute corrupt conduct depending on the motivation of the leak. Tudehope has not been named as a person of interest in Operation Rosny but has stood down as shadow attorney general. Wednesday’s evidence, however, raised questions of just how tightly Tudehope was tied into the activities of the Reformers and the donations they are alleged to have taken to fund their branch takeover activities. The day started well enough. A politician for 20 years, Tudehope was happy to talk expansively about his alignment with the Reformers’ causes on conservative social issues. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email He’d been happy to be a speaker at events advocating for safe schools and opposing gender fluidity and marriage equality. But when it came to questions about whether funds flowing into the Reformers were political in nature, the lawyer in Tudehope emerged. “I don’t necessarily accept the premise that every event where someone signs up to a party as a result of attending the event is necessarily a contribution for the benefit of a party, and I think I identified to you that there are people who may sign up to a party to provide no benefit to a party,” Tudehope said. “So, to the extent that you identify for the benefit of a party, I think that’s a very moot point about the definition of a benefit to the Liberal party.” Dwyer wasn’t letting him off the hook so easily. In painstaking detail, she ran him through text messages and WhatsApp groups that she alleged showed knowledge of the secret money trail. Tudehope’s close friend and former law partner Michael O’Hara, who became a successful hotelier, became a major donor to the Reformers, giving $165,000 to a number of entities after introductions at a function at Tudehope’s home where the News Corp columnist Miranda Devine was the speaker. Tudehope agreed he might have introduced Ellis to O’Hara, but denied he had encouraged illegal donations. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion “If you think that I would expose a friend of mine to that level of scrutiny that he was exposed to, 83 years of age with stage three/four cancer, you think that I would have done that in circumstances where I knew that he would be a prohibited donor for the purposes of the Electoral Funding Act, not on your life!” he said. Under sustained questioning, Tudehope agreed that using invoices to public relations firms to channel payments was “concealment” as the commissioner, Fabian Gleeson, phrased it. The other major backer of the Reformers was Catholic Schools NSW and here Tudehope has several connections. He was friends with the CEO, Dallas McInerney, also a powerful key figure in the right, while his son James worked in communications at Catholic Schools NSW. Icac heard on Wednesday that at a Sunday lunch, James Tudehope told his father he was being pressured to pay an invoice from Ellis. He was “very agitated” because he didn’t think they were getting value for money, Damien Tudehope said. Tudehope said he recommended his son take it up with McInerney, his boss. In Dwyer’s opening address we learned that Ellis, who has moved to London and declined to appear, had used his public relations firm, Beckington, to take donations for Reformer work. Tudehope was also an employer of key Reformers in his ministerial office. In August 2019, the federal member for Berowra, Julian Leeser, who was unaligned to a faction, went public with his concerns about the branch stacking in the Hills in the Sydney Morning Herald. Icac heard that Ellis had said publicly at a Reformers event that “Leeser was a lefty and had to go”, drawing the ire of several in the party. Dwyer tabled an article by Tom Rabe written in 2019 about the factional war and the involvement of two of the Reformers, Ellis and Jean-Claude Perrottet, who were employed in Tudehope’s office. He suggested Liberals were concerned the pair spent most of their time on branch stacking. By October 2019, Tudehope’s office let Ellis go, concerned about the adverse publicity his activities were drawing. Tudehope said it was the chief of staff who made the call. By 2020, the heat on the Reformers was increasing. Tudehope was on Tuesday shown messages from 2020 between members of the Reformers in which they said MPs “were getting scared about ICAC,” and that “Scott and Damien are afraid”. Tudehope denied knowing what they were about. But by the end of the day, he could have little doubt he now had reasons to fear Icac. Fiona Simpson, the Queensland minister for women, says claims that she deems the word ‘gender’ to be ‘on the nose’ and ‘loaded’ are utterly false. Photograph: Darren England/AAP View image in fullscreen Fiona Simpson, the Queensland minister for women, says claims that she deems the word ‘gender’ to be ‘on the nose’ and ‘loaded’ are utterly false. Photograph: Darren England/AAP Queensland politics Mentions of ‘gender’ scrubbed from Queensland Office for Women website amid alleged effort to ‘dewokify’ Comparisons of live and archived pages show more than 20 mentions have been removed, including in reference to the gender pay gap Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Joe Hinchliffe Tue 4 Aug 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google References to “gender equality” have been removed from the Queensland Office for Women’s website amid claims by former staffers that the Liberal National party government wants to “dewokify” the public service. Guardian Australia has seen an email from a manager, sent in January, tasking staff with scanning the website for the word “gender” so that it could be “reframed”. Web archives from that month show six prominently displayed references to “gender equality” or “gender equal” were removed from the Office for Women’s “About” page , including from its mission statement that had said: “We’re working towards a gender equal Queensland.” A new Queensland bill aims to ‘streamline’ major projects. Matt and Caitlin fear it could hand their farm to developers Read more “A gender equal Queensland” previously appeared as the first tab on the page’s toolbar. The phrase also appeared in the first sentence of text and was used in the first dot point describing the office’s role. As of Tuesday, no mention of “gender” appears on that page. Across the website, comparisons of archived and live pages show more than 20 mentions of “gender” were removed, including in reference to the gender pay gap. Some mentions of “gender equality” remain, including on the homepage. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Former department staff said they had received internal requests to have the term “gender” scrubbed from much of the office’s online portal, claiming they were told that the minister for women, Fiona Simpson, deemed the word to be “on the nose” and “loaded”. In a statement to the Guardian, Simpson said this was “utterly false”. “The website was recently updated for the launch of Queensland’s first Women’s Economic Security Strategy – which was designed by Queensland women, for Queensland women,” Simpson said. “While some are worried about words on websites, the Crisafulli government is focused on backing Queensland women.” The former department staffers, who asked to remain anonymous, alleged their managers relayed to them that the word “gender” should be obscured as it “made the LNP think of the LGBTIQA+ community” and they needed to “dewokify”. One ex-employee said they pushed back against the requests. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion “I was like: ‘Sorry I can’t think of an alternative for gender,’” they said. “Because, I’m sorry, but black and white, on paper, in this instance, gender is men and women and the pay gap that women are experiencing and have been experienced. “Why are we making this a queer issue?” During parliamentary estimates last week, the shadow minister for women, Shannon Fentiman, asked the department of women’s director general, Natalie Wilde, why references to phrases like “gender equality” were removed from the website. Wilde replied that her portfolio “continues routinely to review and update its web presence to improve the user experience for all Queenslanders”. “Editorial changes to web copy are something that is very operational,” Wilde said. “It is approved and managed through my strategic communication unit and is done very much at a business level.” As well as removing many instances of the word “gender”, the recent revamp of the Office for Women’s website also included changing its banner colour from purple to blue and stamping it with the slogan “delivering for Queensland” – both of which are associated with the LNP brand. The Centre for Public Integrity director, Geoffrey Watson SC, has previously criticised such use of the logo across government departments and agencies as politicising the public service. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: 1:04 Mourners hold funeral for 112 people killed in 2023 by Israeli strike in Gaza – video Gaza Mass funeral held in Gaza for victims of 2023 Israeli strike Remains of 112 victims, including 40 children, recovered from rubble more than two years after residential block was destroyed William Christou Tue 4 Aug 2026 13.24 EDT Last modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 14.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Mourners gathered in central Gaza on Tuesday for a mass funeral for 112 people, including 40 children, who were killed in 2023 in one of the deadliest Israeli strikes of the Gaza war. Their bodies could not be recovered until now because of Israel’s continuing strikes, which have slowed, though not halted, since the ceasefire in October. Hundreds of people gathered around more than 100 coffins wrapped in Palestinian flags and arranged in rows on the ground in Deir al-Balah. Mourners prayed for the victims before carrying the bodies through rubble-lined streets and past destroyed buildings for burial in a nearby cemetery. The victims had been among more than 300 people killed on 22 November 2023, when Israeli warplanes demolished a residential block in Gaza City. The bodies of only about 40 people could be recovered by people at the scene, who dug through smouldering rubble with their bare hands and basic tools. Last weekend, Gaza’s civil defence dug through the levelled apartment block and recovered the remains of a further 112 victims, including women and children. It said 157 people were still missing after the attack. The ceasefire that was established in October – which has not stopped Israeli bombing of Gaza – has allowed first responders to dig through the rubble where thousands of remains are still buried across the territory. View image in fullscreen Palestinians carry the bodies through the rubble-lined streets of Deir al-Balah for burial in a nearby cemetery. Photograph: Mohammed Saber/EPA At least 7,400 people have been reported by relatives as still buried under the rubble, Zaher al-Waheidi, head of the Gaza health ministry’s records department, told the Associated Press. He added that the true number was probably thousands higher because some strikes had killed entire families, leaving no loved ones to report them missing. A UN commission, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have found that Israel committed genocide in Gaza. In June, a UN commission found that Israel was continuing to commit genocide in Gaza and that its security forces “deliberately targeted and killed” Palestinian children. At least 26 Palestinians were killed by Israeli strikes over the weekend, despite the announcement of a deal intended to solidify the second phase of the October ceasefire. The killings happened just a few days after the US president, Donald Trump, hailed the latest deal – intended to lead to Hamas disarming and Israeli troops withdrawing from Gaza – as a “historic agreement”. More than 73,000 people in Gaza have been killed by Israel since 7 October 2023, including more than 1,250 people since the October ceasefire. Israel launched the war in Gaza after a Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage. Five Israeli soldiers have been killed since the October ceasefire. Ceasefire talks intended to move the agreement into a second phase have largely stalled. Senior Hamas officials said that the group’s disarmament is conditional on Israel withdrawing from the strip. Israel said that it had “serious security concerns” about last week’s agreement. Most of the Gaza Strip remains in ruins, with the vast majority of its 2 million population displaced and living through a humanitarian crisis in unsanitary, overcrowded tent cities. The US, Europe and Saudi Arabia are reportedly putting pressure on Oman to accept an arrangement on reopening the strait of Hormuz with a temporary shipping route. Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters View image in fullscreen The US, Europe and Saudi Arabia are reportedly putting pressure on Oman to accept an arrangement on reopening the strait of Hormuz with a temporary shipping route. Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters Iran US and Qatar report progress on Iran ceasefire and reopening Hormuz strait Optimism echoes Trump’s claims on Monday that deal is close as mediators say they are exchanging proposals Middle East crisis live – latest updates Julian Borger and Patrick Wintour Tue 4 Aug 2026 13.19 EDT First published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 12.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google US and Qatari officials have said progress is being made in restoring a ceasefire in the US-Iran war and reopening the strait of Hormuz. The optimistic speculation on Tuesday brought oil prices down 2%, but the strait remained closed to shipping and a cargo vessel was reportedly struck by an unidentified projectile off Oman’s coast close to the strait. Britain’s maritime security agency, UKMTO, reported the strike on Monday night but did not name the vessel. The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said the US and Iran were negotiating and told CNBC television: “I think there is a chance we may have a deal today ​or tomorrow to open the strait and move towards a more normalised ​position in this conflict.” His remarks echo similarly upbeat comments on Monday from Donald Trump , who claimed that a breakthrough was imminent, though Tehran quickly denied it was involved in any direct talks with the US. Qatari and Pakistani mediators said they were talking to both sides in an effort to close gaps, restore the ceasefire deal from the memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed in mid-June and reopen the Hormuz strait, which was the portal for a fifth of the world’s oil and liquified natural gas. Qatar’s ‌foreign ministry spokesperson, Majed al-Ansari, said Qatar, Pakistan and Oman were mediating in close coordination and exchanging draft proposals between Washington and Tehran. He said the diplomatic contacts had reached “very progressive stages”. A senior Pakistani security official told Reuters news agency: “A lot is happening in the ‌background … We are talking to both sides. Our sole goal at this moment is to make both parties at least agree to start talking.” However, neither Qatar nor Pakistan are directly involved in the focus of negotiations in recent days, which has been between Iran and Oman on a temporary transit scheme that would allow ships to enter and leave the Gulf. The MoU broke down in July when vessels tried to cross the strait along the Omani coast without seeking Iranian approval, and Iran attacked them. Regional diplomats involved in the talks said Oman was under concerted US, European and Saudi pressure to accept a temporary scheme that would allow shipping to enter the Gulf via a route through the strait close to Iran, and then leave on a southern route along the Omani coast, which would be jointly controlled with Iran. The contentious issue of Iran’s demand to charge transiting vessels tolls or other fees would be left to be decided during a 60-day negotiating period, during which time Iran’s nuclear programme would also be addressed. The Omani government has been resisting the Hormuz proposal out of fear it could become permanent and give Tehran an enduring say over sea routes in Omani waters, the regional diplomats said. The Iranian state-run broadcaster IRIB reported on Tuesday evening: “These negotiations, taking place between the two coastal countries of the strait of Hormuz, are focused on determining safe routes for ships to transit. The talks have so far been assessed as positive at both the technical and political levels, and Iran is working with Oman to develop the necessary mechanisms for future arrangements to manage shipping traffic in this strategic waterway.” The talks are complicated by splits in Tehran, according to the diplomats, with the foreign ministry keen to do a deal and fearing Iranian control of the Hormuz strait could prove to be a wasting asset over time as sea traffic finds alternative routes. Regime hardliners, on the other hand, oppose the deal on the grounds that the US administration cannot be trusted to deliver the financial benefits promised in return for opening the strait. “I think the regime understands the magnitude of the hold Iran has over the strait, and they smell the desperation coming from the US in terms of [trying to] strike a deal,” a diplomat from the region said. Another diplomat said Riyadh was putting particularly heavy pressure on Oman because the Saudis thought “we may be on the brink of a regional war because there is a big faction in Iran that does not want a deal under any circumstances”. Photograph: Mark Richardson/Alamy View image in fullscreen The number of people in England and Wales being electronically monitored has doubled in five years. Photograph: Mark Richardson/Alamy Prisons and probation Electronic tagging system failing to alert authorities of probation breaches, watchdog warns Probation inspector for England and Wales says ‘clunky’ system needs huge increase in staff Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor Tue 4 Aug 2026 13.45 EDT First published on Tue 4 Aug 2026 10.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The electronic tagging system that will be relied upon to monitor thousands of offenders released early from prison is failing to alert the authorities of potential breaches of conditions, a watchdog has warned. Martin Jones, HM inspector of probation in England and Wales, said the system relied on hard-pressed police and probation officers looking up individual cases and then deciding whether potential breaches needed to be investigated further. He said it needed to be updated to send alerts to the authorities if a former inmate breached an exclusion zone from which they were banned. His demand comes after the government announced that up to 5,000 prisoners would be released from 1 October to ease the prison overcrowding crisis. At present, there are 86,500 people behind bars with 2,400 spare places. Andy Burnham paused the scheme last month and on Tuesday he announced plans to exclude prisoners guilty of rape, serious child sexual abuse offences and grooming, reducing the number of releases by 1,000. Killers and domestic abusers will still be eligible for early release, the Ministry of Justice has confirmed. Line graph showing projected prison population in 2030 The prime minister has assured the public that offenders will face tighter community supervision, including new GPS monitoring. Jones, in an interview with the Guardian, said he had recently launched an inspection of offender tagging, and had seen that the system was coming under strain and needed to be upgraded to “minimise the risk to the public”. “Some of the systems are pretty clunky and it’s far too reliant on people looking for the information rather than the information being fed or pushed to practitioners as a matter of course,” he said. “Tagging has potential to improve public perception of victims’ safety. But only if it used properly and if there is a wider system and enough staff to support that. If not, there is a risk that you give false assurances to the public.” The number of people in England and Wales being electronically monitored has doubled to 28,700 in five years, and the number of newly tagged each year is expected to rise to 22,000 from 2027. Jones said this expansion needed a huge increase in staff to monitor offenders. The prison population has fallen under Labour An early review of Jones’s inspection, across six regions in England, found: Probation officers wrongly assuming they would be notified about breaches of exclusion zones, when they were required to conduct a specific search. Data was not being actively monitored or analysed to reduce risk to the public. “Significant complexity” was involved in managing the monitoring process, leaving probation officers “overwhelmed and disengaged” by the volume of correspondence. Jones said: “My concern is this: have the processes and the system kept apace with the number of people being tagged? Because ultimately all tagging gives you is information about where somebody is at a particular point in time. You are relying on having sufficient police officers and probation officers to look at that information and make a decision about how it informs your picture on the activities of that individual.” Last month the National Audit Office found that the rapid expansion of electronic tagging to reduce pressure on prisons would put public safety at risk unless there were robust improvements. ‘We fought for a tougher sentence’: victims’ families’ fury over early release scheme Read more Jones also called for the government to ensure that there were enough staff in approved premises , which are hostels set up to monitor 2,000 of the most serious offenders when they are first released from prison. “Our research shows that approved premises work. [They] are extremely effective at managing people after their initial release from custody. What a missed opportunity if those premises cannot remain open because of our insufficient staff,” he said. After a review of the plans, rapists and serious child sexual offenders, including grooming gang perpetrators, will no longer be eligible for the early release scheme. But those given custodial sentences for domestic abuse, and criminals guilty of manslaughter, will still be eligible to be freed halfway through their sentence. Alex Norris, the justice secretary, has apologised to families affected, saying they were “carrying the can from previous failures”. He acknowledged the proposals had “created harm” for those grieving, such as the wife of PC Andrew Harper, Lissie. “I would express how angry I am, too, at being in a situation where we’re having to make significant changes that do have real impacts on people’s lives, so that we are able to have a functioning prison system,” he said. Harper’s mother, Debbie Adlam, said her family was “paying the price” after learning her son’s killers remained eligible for early release under the plans. Sarah Champion, the Labour MP for Rotherham, has written to Burnham, telling him that victims would “remain in a state of fear and limbo” unless domestic abusers were no longer included in the early release scheme. She told the prime minister: “I fully support the government’s ambitious goal to reduce violence against women and girls and tackle serious sexual offences. However, without reinstating the exemption to the early release scheme, I fail to see how that is possible.” Explore more on these topics Prisons and probation UK criminal justice England Wales news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Prisoner early release scheme gives Burnham his first taste of unpopularity About 1,000 fewer prisoners to get early release as Burnham tightens rules PM to tighten early release rules but men jailed over PC Harper’s death can be freed More prisoners in England and Wales are recalled than released for first time Burnham stirs up political row with review of release plans for violent criminals Lack of safeguards over prisoners’ early release puts abuse victims at risk, Lammy warned Prison officers given more training to avoid being manipulated into illicit relationships with inmates Tens of thousands of prisoners in England and Wales at risk of cell fires ‘Missed opportunities’ to prevent woman’s death in prison cell fire, inquest finds Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

Photograph: Ethan Swope/AP Los Angeles Devastating LA wildfire sparked by utility company tower, long-awaited report finds Investigators pin blame for Eaton fire, which killed 19 people and ruined thousands of homes, on ‘electrical arcing events’ at out-of-service tower Associated Press Tue 4 Aug 2026 15.13 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The deadly 2025 Eaton fire in the Los Angeles area was caused by equipment belonging to the utility company Southern California Edison, fire officials said in a report released on Tuesday. Los Angeles county fire officials found that the cause of the fire that killed 19 people and destroyed or damaged more than 9,000 homes and businesses was a tower that was not in service, according to the report. “After 18 months of thorough review of all evidence, alongside retained electrical and metallurgical experts, the investigation concluded that the cause of the wildfire conflagration was due to the electrical arcing events that took place on the out-of-service Southern California Edison (SCE) tower,” the agency said in a statement. It took firefighters nearly a month to extinguish the blaze, which scorched 22 sq miles (57 sq km). View image in fullscreen The Eaton fire in Altadena in January 2025. Photograph: Josh Edelson/AFP/Getty Images Kathleen Dunleavy, a spokesperson for Southern California Edison, said the utility has received the report and is reviewing it. “We have taken our potential role in the start of this fire seriously from the very beginning,” Dunleavy said. She said SCE previously acknowledged “it was likely our equipment was associated with the ignition of the Eaton fire”. She said the utility continues to support the community as it recovers . SoCal Edison has claimed in lawsuits earlier this year that Los Angeles county agencies failed to send timely evacuation warnings to residents in east and west Altadena. Eighteen of the 19 people who died in the fire lived in west Altadena. The utility also has claimed water agencies, including Pasadena Water and Power, did not provide enough water as the fire spread, leaving firefighters with limited resources. Los Angeles county declined to comment about the latest court filings. The Los Angeles county arson fire investigation unit jointly conducted the investigation with California department of forestry and fire protection. It found electrical arcing on the utility’s out-of-service tower sparked the dry brush below and that the utility was responsible for maintaining and operating its electrical lines and equipment “in a manner that would minimize the risk of catastrophic wildfire posed by them.” Their homes burned in the LA wildfires. A year later, thousands still can’t return Read more The blaze was sparked during extreme weather conditions that included high temperatures, low humidity and powerful winds. Two “electrical arcing events” occurred in quick succession, causing an unknown burning material to fall from the tower to the ground below, according to the report. Within 12 seconds, dry grass and brush was ignited and the fire swiftly developed “into a conflagration engulfing the areas of the San Gabriel Mountains, Altadena, Pasadena, Sierra Madre and La Cañada Flintridge”, the report said. It took more than two weeks to fully contain the wildfire. The report cites an interview with a Pasadena resident who called 911 on 7 January after spotting flames across the canyon from his home’s rear window. The caller described it “as a 10in x 10in fire at the base of a high-voltage electrical tower”, the report said. The Eaton fire burned at the same time as the Palisades fire, the most destructive blaze in Los Angeles to date and among the five worst in California’s history. The blaze killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 homes and buildings in Pacific Palisades. The fire ripped through hillside neighborhoods, destroying mansions with spectacular ocean views. The man accused of sparking the Palisades fire will be tried again this fall after his first federal arson case ended in a mistrial in June. Prosecutors said Jonathan Rinderknecht used a barbecue lighter on 1 January 2025 to spark a blaze that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up 7 January. Photograph: Baltimore Sun/TNS Texas University of Maryland ‘teacher of the year’ detained by ICE in Texas DHS said pharmacy instructor Berhanu Kibret overstayed visa and arrested him at Dallas-Fort Worth airport Maya Yang Tue 4 Aug 2026 15.11 EDT Last modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 15.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An instructor at the University of Maryland, Baltimore who only just received a “teacher of the year” award has been arrested by federal immigration agents under the command of the Trump administration . Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) officials detained Berhanu Kibret, an instructor at the university’s pharmacy school, at the Dallas-Fort Worth airport in Texas, according to multiple news reports. The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, confirmed Kibret’s arrest, citing an expired visa – but it stopped short of providing a location. In a statement, the University of Maryland said Kibret was arrested while returning from a meeting of the American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy, where he received a “teacher of the year” award. Immigrant being held at Delaney Hall dies, marking 22nd death in ICE custody Read more “Dr Kibret has a valid work authorization, so it is our hope that any issues surrounding his status will be quickly resolved and that he will be permitted to continue his work at the University of Maryland School of Pharmacy,” the institution added, according to CBS. Kibret’s research focuses on how the brain’s cannabinoid system influences mental health, brain disease and the effects of addictive drugs, the university’s website says. He obtained bachelor’s and master’s degrees in science as well as a PhD in Ethiopia – and he completed his postdoctoral fellowship at William Paterson University in Wayne, New Jersey. Calling Kibret a “highly valued member of the University of Maryland, Baltimore community”, the school said it was “greatly troubled” by his arrest. The university added: “He is an effective and beloved teacher, and a highly regarded colleague. His detention has generated not only great sympathy for his plight, but also a heightened sense of apprehension here on campus.” In a statement to the Guardian, the DHS said ICE arrested Kibret after he entered the US on 21 June 2021 on a visa set to expire on 31 May 2024. “Against our nation’s laws, he overstayed his visa and failed to depart,” the DHS statement said. “He will remain in ICE custody pending his immigration proceedings.” The Guardian has reached out to the University of Maryland, Baltimore for additional comment. Arrests such as that of Kibret have drawn criticism, particularly in light of the Trump administration’s repeated pledge to focus on targeting the “worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens” for arrest and deportation. A Guardian analysis published in February found that 77% of people placed into deportation proceedings for the first time after Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025 had no criminal convictions. Kibret’s arrest came after ICE in July detained and later released a Johns Hopkins researcher at the Baltimore/Washington international airport. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion Federal authorities detained Fatima Ameaka, a Cameroonian citizen with a doctorate in pharmacy who works at Johns Hopkins University’s Bloomberg School of Public Health. Speaking to several outlets during Ameaka’s detention, a Johns Hopkins spokesperson described her as a “respected member of our community”. “The university understands the fear and concern this instills in members of our community,” the spokesperson added. “Dr Ameaka was traveling in a personal capacity, and though we cannot comment on the specifics of her situation, we want to assure our community that the university is actively working to provide support for Dr Ameaka, including ensuring she has access to legal representation.” Documents reviewed by ABC indicated that Ameaka held a work authorization valid through 2029 and had a pending asylum case. Nonetheless, as ABC reported , the DHS had initially said of Ameaka: “In violation of our nation’s laws, she overstayed her visa. She will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.” Ameaka’s attorney on Sunday confirmed that she had been released from ICE detention. Photograph: Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images Trump administration Ex-Olympian weighing ‘all options’ after reflecting pool charges dropped David Hearn has ‘number of potential remedies’ after being prosecuted in connection with pool damage, attorney says Edward Helmore Tue 4 Aug 2026 15.07 EDT Last modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 15.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An attorney for the former Olympic canoeist who was charged with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool has said that “all options are on table” for legal recourse after prosecutors recently abandoned the case abruptly. David Hearn “has a number of potential remedies” after being prosecuted in connection with pool damage now attributed to faulty work by a contractor, attorney Steven Levin said in a statement. Levin added that those could include “civil suits, bar referrals for the prosecutors involved, request for sanctions and reimbursement of attorneys’ fees and expenses”, and requests for investigations by various government entities, including Congress. Hearn, 67, was arrested on 19 June and faced one felony count of property destruction – a charge that could have resulted in a 10-year prison sentence and a $1,000 fine – which he denied. The charge came after Donald Trump’s administration spent $14m to change the reflecting pool’s color. A new pool liner almost immediately began to peel off, and the president blamed vandals. Four people were arrested, but only Hearn was charged with a felony. On Friday, Trump’s justice department moved to dismiss the charge against Hearn, saying in a filing that the damage to the pool liner was “the result of flawed installation by the contractor” who worked on it. In a 20-page court filing in Washington DC superior court on Friday, prosecutors said they had received information about a “rush to complete the project” prior to events associated with the celebration of the US’s semiquincentennial on Fourth of July. Washington DC’s US attorney, Jeanine Pirro, said that her office – which handles cases in the city’s superior court – had received key documents from the federal department of the interior after the indictment was filed. Those documents “indicated a rushed and flawed installation process, with repeated failures of the lining during the installation process, and extensive peeling of the lining throughout the reflecting pool,” Pirro wrote in Friday’s court filing. Trump accuses Jeanine Pirro of ‘folding’ by dropping reflecting pool charges Read more The resulting decision to drop the charge against Hearn set off a dispute within Trump’s administration. The president said Pirro had “choked” and “folded like an umbrella” leading to speculation that she might be fired from her post. Trump has continued to blame vandalism for problems with the pool makeover. On Monday, the president ducked questions about Pirro’s charge dismissal but maintained his criticism of her, saying “I disagree 100% with [her]”. Pirro was spotted at the White House hours after Trump’s comments on Monday. Attorneys for Hearn have previously said the government “owes Mr Hearn an apology”. “The Trump administration’s case against Davey Hearn should have never been brought,” his attorneys, including Levin, said on social media . “Its dismissal … does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American who did nothing wrong.” Hearn told the Associated Press that he had been detained by the national guard and US park police for five hours after stopping by the reflecting pool during a bike ride. He acknowledged that he briefly touched a part on the liner attached to the side and told NBC News the pool’s condition “was the same after I stepped away from the water as it was before I got there”. Lawyers for Hearn have also called on prosecutors to disclose the legal instructions they gave to grand jurors about the elements of the criminal charge handed up against him. “The grand jury transcripts disclosed to the defense thus far contain other irregularities that reflect a misleading presentation to the grand jury and a need for review of the entire grand jury record in this matter,” Hearn’s attorneys wrote. Hearn’s opportunities for legal recourse against the federal government may come only after his attorneys petition the court to dismiss the case “with prejudice”, meaning that it could not be refiled. The justice department dropped the charge “without prejudice”, meaning that it can be refiled. “We are responding with our own motion to dismiss with prejudice so that he is not longer at risk of being harassed by the government further,” Levin said on Tuesday. “Once that is resolved Mr Hearn will focus on what comes next. “He’s considering all options.” In a statement to the Wall Street Journal, Hearn’s attorney Norm Eisen said the team plan to go on the offensive against the government: “All legal remedies are on the table going forward to respond to the miscarriage of justice,” Eisen said.
