https://www.record-bee.com/2026/07/22/un.text: By Submitted PUBLISHED: July 22, 2026 at 6:27 AM PDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... By Jared O. Bell When word came down that USAID was being dismantled in Nicaragua, I was sorting through old documents amid the chaos of the mission close-out. On the desk next to mine sat a book abandoned by a colleague: The Dictator’s Handbook, by political scientists Bruce Bueno de Mesquita and Alastair Smith, which lays out, in plain and clinical language, how dictators actually operate. It felt fitting: Nicaragua had been seized and was being run as a family enterprise by Daniel Ortega and Rosario Murillo, according to Human Rights Watch. I snatched the book, sensing it would be relevant. What Trump did last week in his primetime address was not a policy speech. It was a page out of that handbook. On July 16, Trump used a national address to revive claims the 2020 election was tainted, alleging China had covertly obtained 220 million voter files and citing a Department of Homeland Security review claiming roughly 278,000 noncitizens were registered to vote. He closed with a line that sounded protective but read like a threat: “We can never watch a stolen election again.” None of it held up. NPR reported voter files are largely public records, and a declassified 2021 intelligence report already concluded “we have no indications that any foreign actor attempted to alter any technical aspect of the voting process.” This was not new information his administration lacked. Trump’s own attorney general, William Barr, told the Associated Press weeks after the 2020 election, “To date, we have not seen fraud on a scale that could have affected a different outcome,” and his own Department of Homeland Security called that election “the most secure in American history.” CBS News found neither Trump nor Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin explained how the administration reached the noncitizen number, and that its method is prone to false positives. David Becker of the Center for Election Innovation and Research said bluntly, “that data includes a ton of people, maybe even a majority of people, who are absolutely eligible voters.” Governor Gavin Newsom rejected the claim outright, saying “they have provided NO evidence,” and Senator Alex Padilla called it “a political stunt built on sham numbers.” This is the part where the book on my shelf stopped being an abstraction and started reading like a roadmap. Bueno de Mesquita explains why authoritarian election theater exists: “Rigged elections are not about picking leaders. They are not about gaining legitimacy. How can an election be legitimate when its outcome is known before the vote even occurs?” The book describes the mirror image of what Trump did nationally: a regime rigs a vote while making it look clean, so “observers will easily conclude that elections were free and fair” when “we can all recognize that they were neither really free nor fair” (The Dictator’s Handbook, p. 124). Trump ran that trick in reverse, inheriting a legitimate system and trying to make it look rigged, a cheaper manipulation since manufacturing doubt requires only a microphone and a willingness to lie. The objective is identical either way: make the public stop trusting the count. Casting doubt on elections is not a side effect of authoritarian rule; it is a core tactic. Protect Democracy’s research on the authoritarian playbook identifies “corrupting elections” as one of seven defining moves would-be autocrats use, flagging Trump’s effort to block certification of the 2020 results as a textbook example. This is not new. We have the private version on tape: on January 2, 2021, Trump called Georgia’s secretary of state, Brad Raffensperger, asking him to “find 11,780 votes, which is one more than we have, because we won the state.” Raffensperger refused: “What I knew is that we didn’t have any votes to find.” It is also a documented pattern abroad: Kenneth Roth, former director of Human Rights Watch, noted that after Peru’s 2021 election borrowed the same fraud claims, Trump’s example “creates a bad example that other leaders and countries can follow.” Researchers have connected these dots. The V-Dem Institute dropped the United States from the 20th most democratic country in the world to 51st, between Slovakia and Greece, and its director Staffan Lindberg did not hedge: “What we are seeing now is the greatest democratic backsliding the country has ever seen.” The rollback that took Orbán four years in Hungary, and a decade for Erdoğan and Modi in Turkey and India, took Trump about one. Manufacturing doubt about elections is part of what makes that speed possible: a public convinced its elections are already compromised is far less likely to mobilize in defense of the ones still ahead. I did not expect to find a warning this precise on a shelf while an American foreign aid mission burned down around me in Managua. Bueno de Mesquita and Smith were not writing about the United States; they were describing a general theory of political survival that applies with equal force to any country willing to follow its rules. The president stood in the East Room last Thursday and, without evidence his own intelligence agencies say does not exist, told the country it can no longer trust its own democracy. If Nicaragua, Venezuela, Turkey, and Hungary have taught me anything, the goal was never to fix an election. It was to make sure that when the next one does not go his way, enough people already believe it could not have been legitimate. Jared O. Bell, PhD, syndicated with PeaceVoice, is a former U.S. diplomat and scholar of human rights and transitional justice, dedicated to advancing global equity and systemic reform. https://www.newsday.com/entertainment/tv.text: Peter Lassally, pictured here in 2007, left an indelible mark on late-night TV. Credit: Getty Images for AFI/Mark Mainz By Verne Gay verne.gay@newsday.com @vernejgay Updated July 23, 2026 4:40 pm Share Peter Lassally, who produced Johnny Carson's "Tonight Show" for nearly a quarter century and masterminded David Letterman's move from NBC to CBS, certainly led a remarkable life. There were, however, no guarantees that Lassally — who died earlier this week at the age of 93 — would actually survive to live out the one he did. Around the age of 10, in 1943, he was sent to Theresienstadt in Czechoslovakia, along with his mother and sister. "A strange place," he once elliptically recalled, while the Holocaust Encyclopedia elaborated: In preparation for a 1944 visit by the Red Cross, "German authorities ordered the beautification" of the death camp, but to make it "appear less crowded" also sent 7,500 inmates to Auschwitz. "You never knew if the next time you were called out, it might be to board another transport," he said in an interview with Dennis Carlyle Darling, author of a 2023 history, "Borrowed Time: Survivors of Nazi Terezín Remember" ("Terezin" was the camp's Czech name.) Theresienstadt was liberated in 1945. By 1947, Lassally was living in New York. By 1951, he was an usher, along with lifelong friend Regis Philbin, at Radio City Music Hall, then at 30 Rock. By around 1958, he was president of Arthur Godfrey's production company. By 1972, he was producer of "Tonight." By 1993, he had launched a late night show on CBS. Only in America, as the saying goes. Lassally was one of a small group of people who effectively created the golden years of late night TV. Some are natural-born showmen who knew how to shape talent (Lorne Michaels). Some knew how to coddle that talent (NBC's Dave Tebet). Some were enforcers (Jay Leno's longtime producer Helen Kushnick.) Sign up for Newsday's Entertainment newsletter Get the latest on celebs, TV and more. By clicking Sign up, you agree to our privacy policy . What (or who) then was Lassally? Among the many hosts he mentored over the years, Garry Shandling once explained that "one of Peter's real strengths is getting the host to understand how to listen, how to ask the questions that an audience might want to hear, and to listen to the answer and to not be thinking ahead with the joke." Shandling's alter ego on "The Larry Sanders Show" (1986-90) of course pointedly ignored all of this. What Lasally had in abundance was advice, counsel and wisdom, to be dismissed at one's own peril. Few ever did. Lassally was centered in an uncentered TV world, where ego, narcissism and insecurity ruled, while talent scrambled for a footing, or for survival. Could Carson have thrived all those years without Lassally by his side, or could Letterman? We'll never know although (in fact) we probably do. Admirers called him the "host whisperer," as if he were some sort of oracle with a mystical hold as opposed to a producer who needed to get the show on every night. HIs speaking style was sotto voce: Quiet, unadorned, direct. You leaned in to listen, the words freighted with significance, and a sense that the man speaking them understood life-and-death stakes — and that show business was hardly life-and-death. He had some stumbles. When Shandling exited as "Tonight Show" guest host, he was left with the other guest host, his friend Joan Rivers. She later claimed, falsely, that Lassally had agreed to produce her late-night Fox show. That led to a breach with Rivers, and nearly with Carson. After the triumph with Letterman, he had hoped to groom his successor — Craig Ferguson, who hosted the 12:30 show — and when CBS chose Stephen Colbert instead, he finally retired, his disappointment palpable. By then, this Carson confidant, this Letterman anchor, the death camp survivor who had witnessed the worst of humanity, had changed late night TV forever and for the better anyway. He hardly ever talked about the deep past because "I learned to block out all the ugly things," he told Darling. "I want to move forward, not return to the past." In a statement, his family said, "Peter built a life defined not by the horrors he endured as a child but by resilience, generosity, curiosity and optimism." Indeed, the host whisperer's ultimate triumph. By Verne Gay verne.gay@newsday.com @vernejgay Verne Gay is Newsday's TV writer and critic. He has covered the media business for more than 30 years. https://enrsi.stvr.sk/articles/news/4539.text: During its presidency of the Three Seas Initiative, Slovakia wants to closely cooperate with Poland on further developing regional cooperation and advancing priority infrastructure projects, said Foreign Affairs Ministry's State Secretary Rastislav Chovanec, who received a Polish delegation led by deputy director of the Polish Foreign Affairs Ministry's Economic Section Sebastian Barkowski on Tuesday (21 July). "Poland, as the largest and founding member of the Three Seas Initiative, is striving to raise awareness of its importance, while it is essential for Slovakia to take into account the interests of individual participating countries. During our current presidency, which will culminate with the presidential summit and business forum in Bratislava in April 2027, we are keen to work closely and exchange experience with our Polish partners," said the state secretary. At the same time, both sides agreed that cooperation within the Three Seas Initiative must be based on sound economic principles and the principle of return on investment, while it must create opportunities to increase investment in the participating countries and help reduce regional disparities between them. The talks also followed up on the conclusions of the Three Seas Initiative presidential summit held in April in Dubrovnik, Croatia. The partners discussed the priorities of Slovakia's leadership, focusing in particular on the further development of infrastructure projects in the areas of transport, energy and digitalisation, as well as on fostering innovation. The State Secretary also highlighted Slovakia's strengths in advanced industries and confirmed the country's interest in developing bilateral cooperation in innovative sectors. "Slovakia has a high-quality talent pool in emerging digital technologies and artificial intelligence. We would like to deepen our dialogue with Poland in these areas," said Chovanec. The Three Seas Initiative was established in 2016 and brings together 13 EU countries. Its aim is to strengthen cooperation and support the development of macro-regional projects in the area of energy, transport and digital connectivity along the north–south corridor between the Baltic, Adriatic and Black Sea. Source: TASR

https://www.satellitetoday.com/governmen.text: : European Commission Defence and Space Commissioner Andrius Kubilius and Polish Minister of Interior and Administration Marcin Kierwiński sign Poland's commitment to IRIS² on July 21. Photo: European Commission Poland has committed 656 million euro ($748 million) to Europe’s IRIS² constellation, which will fund nearly 10% of the constellation. Under the agreement signed Tuesday in Warsaw, Poland will fund six satellites in Medium-Earth Orbit (MEO) and six satellites in Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) to function as a Polish constellation, within IRIS². In addition, a satellite gateway will be built in Warsaw to connect the satellites to the government’s GovNet fiber-optic network. The Polish government also announced signing MoUs with both SES and Eutelsat, which are leading the IRIS² constellation, but did not specify what the MoUs cover. The Polish government said in a release that strategic communication investment has had “years of neglect” and “technological fragmentation.” This investment is aimed at reversing this neglect to create “an integrated satellite dome” above Poland. “Poland is joining a major European program to build secure satellite communications. This is a fully independent system, based on European satellites, that will ensure our security and strategic independence,” Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said in a statement. Kierwiński said the system is set to provide police, state fire service, and border guard with communications capabilities. Poland is allocating funds from the National Recovery Plan to IRIS². The nation received nearly 60 billion euro from the EU in a mix of grants and loans for post-Covid recovery. IRIS² is planned to be Europe’s third flagship space program after Galileo and Copernicus, with more than 290 satellites in total between both MEO and LEO to provide secure connectivity services to the EU and its member states, along with broadband connectivity. It’s funded through a public-private partnership between EU budget, member states, the European Space Agency (ESA), and private sector contributions. Service is targeted to begin in 2030. “By integrating the Polish system with IRIS², Poland chooses to go European instead of going alone,” European Commission Defence and Space Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said Tuesday, according to prepared remarks. “Poland’s investment today will make the entire Eastern Flank stronger. Will make Poland a connectivity hub for the entire Eastern Flank.” Poland has made a number of recent investments into sovereign space capabilities — the Polish Armed Forces purchased a four-satellite synthetic aperture radar (SAR) constellation from Iceye which entered service in May ; and the Polish MoD recently ordered a GEO satellite for defense communications. Poland’s Ministry of Development and Technology has also ordered a three-satellite Earth Observation (EO) constellation called CAMILA for land analysis . “With this project, we are also demonstrating that Poland aims to be a leader in the European space industry and remain at the center of European Union security efforts,” Kierwiński said of the IRIS² deal. LNP file photo Facebook Twitter Email Print Copy article link A plan to redevelop a former Lititz area pizza restaurant into a commercial building featuring a tower evoking a 15th-century Bohemian castle is getting a $3 million boost from a state-sponsored capital grant program. DTL Partners LLC, a company led by Dan Cicala of Lititz-based construction management firm Fidevia, plans to tear down the 4,300-square-foot La Piazza Italian Restaurant & Bar at 800 Lititz Pike. In its place, the firm will build an 8,500-square-foot building with room for several tenants. The planned brick-and-stone building will include a tower modeled after Castle Litice, a fortress in the modern-day Czech Republic that inspired the Moravian founders of Lititz when naming the town. The redevelopment along Lititz Pike in Warwick Township is one of 16 redevelopment projects in Lancaster County set to receive a combined $40 million through the Redevelopment Assistance Capital Program. Gov. Josh Shapiro announced funding for the projects last week. Three of the projects, totaling $18.25 million, were announced by Shapiro in March. State legislators recommend projects for RACP grants, which are awarded at the governor’s discretion. The projects are authorized in the Redevelopment Assistance section of a Capital Budget Itemization Act and are intended to have a regional or multijurisdictional impact while generating substantial increases or maintaining current levels of employment, tax revenue or other economic activity. RACP projects are state-funded projects that cannot obtain primary funding under other state programs. A state timeline for the program notes that grant funds are typically released 19 to 24 months after applicants accept the award—a process that includes a state consultant assigned to each project. https://if.com.au/kuba-dorabialskis-agat.text: ADVERTISEMENT Kuba Dorabialski’s ‘Agata the Writer’ selected for Venice’s Giornate degli Autori Mia Wasikowska in 'Agata the Writer'. Agata the Writer , the debut feature from Polish-born Australian visual artist and filmmaker Kuba Dorabialski, will have its world premiere in Venice Film Festival sidebar Giornate degli Autori. It marks the first Australian title selected for the independent parallel section, also known in English as Venice Days, since Ben Young’s Hounds of Love in 2016. Mia Wasikowska leads the film as a Polish-Australian satirical novelist who travels from Sydney to Sarajevo to write a war novel. While in Bosnia she finds herself within a startling mystery, forcing her to question her role as a storyteller. The film is one of 10 in competition, with the all-female jury headed by Spanish director Carla Simón. Dorabialski, based in Sydney, is known for an art practice that bridges gallery-based video installation and cinema. In addition to writing and directing, he also served as Agata the Writer ‘s cinematographer, editor and composer. Alex White, whose film Babyteeth premiered in official competition at the Venice Film Festival in 2019 , is the producer. “It is an honour and absolute thrill to be having the world premiere of Agata the Writer in Giornate degli Autori at the Venice Film Festival, a forum known for its belief in cinema in its most daring and surprising form,” Dorabialski and White said in a joint statement. A Whitefalk Films and Produktion Productions project, the film was executive produced by Erik Black, Wasikowska and Australian fashion brand Alémais. Screen Australia provided principal production funding, with further financial support via Creative Australia and the Adelaide Film Festival Investment Fund. Bonsai Films will handle local distribution. Agata the Writer is the second Australian project bound for Italy so far this year, with Jessica di Costa’s Mothmama selected for the main festival’s Orizzonti short films international competition. Established in 2004, Giornate degli Autori is modelled on Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight and supported by the Italian film directors’ and authors’ associations ANAC and 100autori. Its focus is on cinema with “special care for innovation, research, originality and independence”. Dorabialski presented a 30-minute distillation of Agata the Writer, titled Field Report , at the Biennale of Sydney earlier this year. Venice Film Festival runs September 2-12. https://www.baltictimes.com/metrosert_in.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Metrosert Invests EUR 2 million in a Synthetic Biology Pilot Plant in Estonia 2026-07-22 Estonia’s Applied Research Centre and national metrology institute Metrosert has signed a contract worth nearly EUR 2 million with construction company Savekate OÜ to establish a unique synthetic biology pilot plant in Estonia. The new facility will provide biotechnology companies with a long-awaited opportunity to test and develop new production processes before making substantial investments in industrial-scale production. The pilot plant will serve both Estonian as well as international companies developing new products and ingredients from biological and renewable feedstocks. It will enable the production of proteins, enzymes, yeasts, plant-based fats and other bio-based substances used in food, materials, chemicals and pharmaceuticals to be developed and tested at a larger scale. Such technologies can help replace fossil-based raw materials while making production more resource-efficient and environmentally sustainable. According to Kaupo Reede, Head of Biorefining Unit at Metrosert’s Applied Research Centre, the pilot plant will provide Estonian biotechnology companies with a previously unavailable opportunity to progress from laboratory trials to production-ready solutions. “Synthetic biology is no longer a technology of the distant future, but a practical tool for building a new-generation economy. Estonia has a considerable number of entrepreneurs and researchers with strong ideas and promising initial laboratory results. To advance to the next stage, however, they need an environment in which technologies can be tested at a larger scale,” Reede said. According to Kaupo Reede, the absence of such a pilot facility has been a major bottleneck across the whole the region, preventing many biotechnology companies from successfully bringing their products into production. “Biotechnology is a capital-intensive and highly regulated field. Before industrial-scale production can begin, the process must be proven to work, its reliability must be assessed, and initial batches must be produced for prospective customers and partners to test. In most cases, it is neither feasible nor sensible for a company to build its own intermediate-scale facility for this purpose. The shared pilot infrastructure provided by Metrosert will help reduce development risks and bring solutions into actual production more quickly,” Reede explained. “The contract signed with Savekate OÜ is an important step towards ensuring that the ideas of Estonian entrepreneurs and researchers do not remain within laboratory walls but can reach production readiness in an environment that complies with international requirements. The pilot plant will serve as a bridge between science and commercial application,” he added. At the new pilot plant, companies will be able to develop their production processes, gradually scale up production volumes and manufacture their first larger product batches. Metrosert will also support companies in planning their development pathways, establishing international collaborative projects, and engaging partners and prospective customers. As the facility will also be used to develop and test solutions intended for the food industry and novel foods, it will be built to comply with stringent international food safety requirements. This will enable companies to develop processes and produce prototypes in an environment that supports their further progression towards industrial-scale production and international markets. Construction of Metrosert’s synthetic biology pilot plant will begin shortly, and the facility is expected to be completed by the end of 2026. About Metrosert AS Metrosert is Estonia’s national applied research centre and national metrology institute. The state-owned company employs approximately 140 specialists and supports sustainable economic growth through applied research, measurement and quality systems, as well as cooperation between industry and research institutions. The Applied Research Centre focuses on five areas: drone technologies, autonomous vehicles, hydrogen technologies, biorefining and health data. https://www.baltictimes.com/baltic_minis.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Baltic ministers sign energy reserve deal, discuss grid security 2026-07-22 BNS/TBT Staff VILNIUS - Baltic energy ministers agreed in Riga on Wednesday to jointly strengthen energy system reserve capacities and discussed sharing emergency power grid equipment. Energy Minister Lukas Savickas and his Latvian and Estonian counterparts signed a declaration under which the countries will jointly assess the need for transformers, transmission towers, generators and other emergency equipment required in the event of threats or failures. "Joint reserves and an agreement to coordinate actions during emergencies will help ensure a more reliable energy supply for the public, while joint decisions will allow for more efficient and cost-effective strengthening of energy infrastructure security," Savickas said. The countries' transmission system operators are expected, after assessing their needs, to jointly apply for European Union funding for the purchase and maintenance of reserve capacities. The ministers also discussed the protection of strategic energy facilities. According to the ministry, the ministers emphasised that drones have "become a new security reality" and that protection against them is an "integral part of critical infrastructure protection at the regional level". The agreement comes amid growing concerns over potential threats to critical infrastructure. Leaders of NATO's eastern flank countries have warned of possible Russian provocations, while President Gitanas Nauseda has said that critical transport and energy infrastructure in Lithuania could become targets. Since June, the Lithuanian military has been assisting in the protection of key energy sites, including the liquefied natural gas terminal in Klaipeda, the LitPol Link electricity interconnection switchyard in Alytus, a transformer substation and the Kruonis pumped storage hydroelectric plant. https://www.baltictimes.com/seimas_speak.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Seimas speaker says Zemaitaitis impeachment should await final ruling 2026-07-22 BNS/TBT Staff VILNIUS - Lithuania's parliament speaker Juozas Olekas said on Wednesday that impeachment proceedings against opposition Nemunas Dawn leader Remigijus Zemaitaitis should wait until the deadline for an appeal expires or the Supreme Court issues a final ruling. "Impeachment is initiated once a final decision is in force, either from the Supreme Court or if the Court of Appeal ruling is not contested through cassation," the speaker told reporters. "We must wait for either the appeal period to pass or for the Supreme Court's decision." However, Olekas did not rule out the possibility of lawmakers gathering the necessary signatures to propose starting the impeachment process sooner. Zemaitaitis' fate will likely be decided in the autumn, the speaker said. On Wednesday, the Lithuanian Court of Appeal found Zemaitaitis guilty of inciting hatred against Jews and grossly trivialising the Holocaust, increasing his fine from 5,000 to 10,000 euros. The court ruled that the politician's public statements about Jews crossed the boundaries of lawful freedom of expression, systematically mocking, disparaging and promoting hatred against people of Jewish nationality. The ruling took effect immediately but can be appealed. Zemaitaitis has pledged to challenge the verdict. The criminal case stems from Facebook posts and public remarks made in May and June 2023. In the posts, he referred to Israelis as "animals" and claimed that Jews contributed to the destruction of the Lithuanian nation. Impeachment proceedings were previously initiated against the politician over the posts. In April 2024, the Constitutional Court ruled that he had broken his oath and committed a gross violation of the Constitution. Following that ruling, Zemaitaitis resigned his seat in the Seimas but was re-elected to parliament in the autumn of 2024. The speaker suggested that consideration should be given to preventing situations in which a politician can avoid the consequences of impeachment by resigning and then running for office again. He said proposals for such procedural changes could be prepared by the autumn session of the Seimas. Olekas also emphasised that the Lithuanian state's position on anti-Semitism and hatred was clear, and that statements by individual members of parliament did not reflect official state policy. Home Paid news feed Foto Agerpres Press Monitoring Bucharest Phone: +4 021.2076.110 Pasca challenges CoE Human Rights Commissioner over alleged use of unverified information in Dumbrava case Category: English Date: 2026-07-22 17:29:46 Foto: Grigore POPESCU / AGERPRES Photo Viorel Pasca, founder of the care facilities in Dumbrava, Bihor County - currently under DIICOT investigation - has published an open letter addressed to the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, Michael O'Flaherty, in which he challenges the statements made in the Commissioner's letter to the Romanian Prime Minister regarding the Dumbrava case and argues that the European official relied on unverified information. In the open letter posted on Facebook, Pasca writes that he read with interest Michael O'Flaherty's message to Romania's Prime Minister and appreciates the Commissioner's concern for vulnerable persons; however, he criticises the references made to the activities carried out at the Dumbrava locations, maintaining that the Council of Europe official should have verified the information before including it in the letter. 'I don't know where you received your information from, but I believe that, regardless of the source, you should first have verified whether it is true and whether those who provided it are credible sources and have evidence to support it. Do not forget that the presumption of innocence should also apply in Romania,' Pasca wrote. Responding to the letter's mention of 'illegal homes', Pasca rejects the characterisation, noting: 'I can tell you that Dumbrava has never operated as a centre or care home. All locations were, in fact, residential houses in which Romanian citizens lived and had their domicile. None of them lived there illegally, none were detained, abused or tortured as has been alleged in mass media. Those who wished to leave did so whenever they wanted, and they returned of their own free will whenever they wished.' Pasca further disapproves of the manner in which, in his view, information about the activities in Dumbrava was collected and disseminated, asserting that some publicly cited sources presented false information. He also expresses disagreement with the Commissioner's assessment of the intervention carried out by the Directorate for Investigating Organised Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT) in the Dumbrava case. 'If you consider such an intervention to be 'normal', necessary and justified - legally, logistically, morally or from any other point of view - then I am firmly convinced that what you have been told has no connection with reality, and that you have 'fallen into the trap' of those who supplied you with this information,' he wrote. In conclusion, Pasca asks the Commissioner for Human Rights to carefully verify information before making public statements and argues that, in his view, it would have been appropriate to await the court's decision in the Dumbrava case. The letter is signed, 'With highest consideration, Viorel Pasca'. The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, Michael O'Flaherty, published on Tuesday a letter addressed to Romanian Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan, following his visit to Romania between May 26 - 29 this year, in which he formulates a series of recommendations concerning the long-term care system for older persons, the Strasbourg-based organisation said. The Commissioner welcomes progress in the reform of social services and the dedication of staff working in care centres for older persons. At the same time, he expresses concern regarding several challenges, including the insufficient recognition of residents as full rights-holders, the shortage of services, and the difficulties faced by vulnerable persons in accessing care. He also draws attention to care centres operating without licences and calls for a thorough and independent investigation into the Dumbrava case. According to the letter dated July 10, the matter concerns the unlicensed care centre in the village of Dumbrava, Bihor County, which is alleged to have housed thousands of vulnerable persons in abusive conditions and where more than one thousand deaths were reportedly recorded. https://www.baltictimes.com/entrepreneur.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Entrepreneurs for Peace opens civil-military cooperation Hub in Riga 2026-07-22 On 21 July, the Entrepreneurs for Peace Foundation opened a new Civil-Military Cooperation Hub in Riga. The hub will serve as a meeting place for entrepreneurs, public institutions, non-governmental organisations and members of the public to work together to strengthen Latvia's resilience and continue supporting Ukraine. The hub will foster cooperation with developers of military products and services, support new initiatives aimed at strengthening Latvia's security, and bring together the foundation's partners to develop joint solutions. It will also host events and educational activities designed to increase public awareness of national defence, societal resilience and preparedness to respond to crises. During the opening event, the foundation highlighted three key messages: the importance of cooperation, the need to remain vigilant, and the achievements made to date, demonstrating that civic initiatives can make a significant contribution to strengthening Latvia's security while continuing to support Ukraine. "Over the past four and a half years, we have shown that the greatest results can be achieved by working together with Latvian businesses, strategic partners, non-governmental organisations and active members of society. The foundation will continue supporting Ukraine while placing increasing emphasis on strengthening Latvia's resilience and implementing new initiatives that will enhance the country's ability to respond to hybrid threats," said Laura Skrodele, Director of the Entrepreneurs for Peace Foundation. She added that the new hub is intended to become a place where cooperation is transformed into practical action and thanked the foundation's partners, without whose support its work would not have been possible. Speaking about the security situation, representatives of the foundation stressed that Russia's war against Ukraine continues and that security challenges in Europe have not diminished. Ukrainian civilians continue to suffer daily attacks, while Latvia must further strengthen its resilience and preparedness for a wide range of security threats. Since 2022, Entrepreneurs for Peace has delivered more than €23 million worth of assistance to Ukraine, including 1,000 drones, 300 generators, 1,300 vehicles, and 1,200 units of medical and technical equipment. The organization has also supported Latvian volunteers serving in Ukraine, implemented social infrastructure reconstruction projects in Ukraine's Chernihiv region, and organized humanitarian aid convoys in cooperation with the Latvian State Police, the National Armed Forces and numerous Latvian companies. The importance of civil-military cooperation was also highlighted by Colonel Volodymyr Rusinov , Commander of the 26th Artillery Brigade, who emphasized that close cooperation between the armed forces, businesses and society is essential for strengthening national security. "Modern security depends not only on the capabilities of the armed forces but also on the willingness of society as a whole to participate and cooperate. Civil-military cooperation is one of the cornerstones of national resilience, and initiatives such as this strengthen our collective ability to respond to security challenges. I would like to thank the Entrepreneurs for Peace Foundation for its selfless and consistently timely support to Ukraine and its soldiers," said Colonel Rusinov. Latvian volunteer fighter Aleksandrs Sverčkovs , who had recently returned from Ukraine, shared his experiences from the front line and emphasized the importance of public support for those defending Ukraine every day. "On the front line, what you feel most is that every soldier is backed by people who genuinely care. Every donation, every shipment of aid and every word of encouragement give us the strength to keep fighting," said A. Sverčkovs. Ieva Vārna, who had also recently returned from the Donbas region, spoke about the situation in Ukraine and stressed that international support remains critically important. "After what I witnessed in Donbas, one thing is clear: the war is far from over, and Ukraine still needs our support every single day. Everyone who gets involved truly helps save lives," said I. Vārna. The event concluded with remarks by the foundation's chaplain, Elmārs Pļaviņš , Senior Expert on International Military Religious Affairs at the Ministry of Defence, who thanked the organisation's partners for their trust and long-standing cooperation. "Every step we take together proves that we are not alone. Thank you to every partner whose work and support help strengthen both Latvia and Ukraine," said E. Pļaviņš. Viesturs Silenieks also introduced guests to the activities of Drone House and the opportunities offered by the new hub, inviting participants on a guided tour of the centre's main areas of operation. About Entrepreneurs for Peace Since 2022, the Entrepreneurs for Peace Foundation has brought together entrepreneurs and partners to provide practical support to Ukraine while strengthening Latvia's security and societal resilience. The organisation coordinates humanitarian and military assistance deliveries, works closely with public authorities, and implements projects that advance civil-military cooperation. https://www.baltictimes.com/estonia_supp.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Estonia supports Latvia in fight against illegal migration - Taro 2026-07-22 LETA/BNS/TBT Staff TALLINN - Minister of the Interior Igor Taro, during a two-day visit to Latvia, received an overview of the country's crisis preparedness, refugee policy, and the situation at its external border, pledging Estonia's support in the fight against illegal migration. The meetings also focused on cooperation between Estonia and Latvia in combating organized crime and cross-border drug trafficking. Estonia also plays a significant role in curbing illegal immigration: in total, Estonian border guards have helped apprehend 133 illegal migrants on Latvia's border with Russia and Belarus. According to Taro, Latvia is one of Estonia's most important partners in the security field. "Latvia is not only Estonia's closest neighbor but also one of our most reliable allies. The cooperation between our law enforcement agencies is practical and effective, based on mutual trust and common goals," the interior minister said. On Tuesday, the delegation reviewed border security on the Latvia-Belarus border. According to Taro, the situation for Latvia is considerably more tense compared to Estonia, and the struggle to prevent illegal border crossings has unfortunately become routine. "The Latvians' experience in dealing with malicious attacks is invaluable, and our police colleagues benefit from it occasionally when we send our personnel to assist them during major malicious incidents. This cooperation will continue," Taro said. As an important part of the visit, Minister Taro visited the disaster management center in Salacgriva, which is one of the first centers to be completed in a nationwide network being established in Latvia. The purpose of these centers is to consolidate rescue, police, border guard, ambulance, and other critical services under one roof to improve preparedness for natural disasters, technological accidents, climate risks, and security crises. The meetings included an overview of the implementation of the joint Estonian-Latvian action plan for combating cross-border drug trafficking and organized crime. According to Taro, the action plan is being successfully implemented, and cooperation covers both strategic and operational levels. "Unfortunately, we face common challenges here, but we are certainly ready to continue our close cooperation." In addition, the Estonian Minister of the Interior familiarized himself with the operations of an asylum center in Latvia and the services provided to applicants for international protection. https://www.baltictimes.com/a_european_b.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive A European bank's operations in Russia are cynical and criminal - Paet 2026-07-22 LETA/BNS/TBT Staff TALLINN - According to Urmas Paet, Vice-Chair of the European Parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee, it is cynical and criminal for any European bank to be operating in Russia now, when Russia's war against Ukraine has been ongoing for years. "It is strange and painful to read the comments from the former head of the Estonian Financial Supervision Authority, Kilvar Kessler, suggesting there is nothing special about the continued operations in Russia of Hungary's OTP Bank, which is seeking to acquire Luminor, simply because other major European banks also operate there," Paet noted. "For a European bank to operate in Russia now, when the Russian war against Ukraine has been ongoing for years, claiming many lives, and while Russia's hybrid war against Estonia and all of Europe continues, is exceptionally cynical and criminal. Yes, there are still a few banks in Europe that are completely indifferent to Russia's slaughter of the Ukrainian people. But the majority of European banks left the Russian market long ago," he said. "Hungary's OTP Bank, which is acquiring Luminor, is one of those few European banks that continues its cynical business in Russia, just as the Hungarian government led by Orban has done for years. OTP Bank was also on the sanctions list imposed by Ukraine as a business entity supporting Russia's war against Ukraine. If this deal goes through and OTP does buy Luminor, then I can't imagine which Estonian customers would want to do any business with a bank that is indifferent to Russia's war against Ukraine," Paet remarked. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Russia is likely to blame Ukraine for the bombing, which comes just days after an explosion outside a restaurant in central Moscow. Photograph: Pavel Bednyakov/AP View image in fullscreen Russia is likely to blame Ukraine for the bombing, which comes just days after an explosion outside a restaurant in central Moscow. Photograph: Pavel Bednyakov/AP Russia Head of drone manufacturer critically injured in car bomb in Russia Assassination attempt demonstrates Ukraine’s ability to continue clandestine operations deep inside Russian territory Europe live – latest updates Pjotr Sauer Wed 5 Aug 2026 08.10 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 09.26 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The head of a leading Russian drone manufacturer has been critically injured in a car bomb near Ekaterinburg, in what appears to be the latest in a series of assassination attempts targeting figures linked to the country’s war in Ukraine. Vladimir Tkachuk, the founder of the private drone manufacturer Uraldronzavod, was rushed to intensive care on Wednesday after a bomb planted beneath his Mercedes exploded, according to Russian state media, citing emergency services. His bodyguard was killed in the explosion. The Russian news agency Tass reported that Tkachuk was in a critical condition and doctors were “fighting [to save] his life”. Images circulating on social media showed the charred wreckage of a Mercedes, with blood stains visible on the pavement nearby. Uraldronzavod is one of several private drone manufacturers that sprang up in Russia after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine . The company is best known for producing the Upyr (Ghoul), a low-cost first-person-view (FPV) kamikaze drone manufactured using 3D-printing technology at its facility in Ekaterinburg and widely used by Russian forces in Ukraine. In 2024, Vladimir Putin visited the factory, where he was given a tour by Tkachuk. Uraldronzavod and Tkachuk have been hit with sanctions by western governments for their role in supporting Russia’s war. Tkachuk is also the founder of the popular pro-war Telegram channel Obsessed with War, which has more than 500,000 followers and has been used to raise funds and procure military equipment for Russian soldiers fighting on the frontline. Russia is likely to blame Ukraine for the bombing, which comes just days after an explosion outside an upmarket restaurant in central Moscow that killed five people. Russian authorities have not identified the intended target of that attack, but pro-Kremlin bloggers and independent Russian media suggested it was aimed at Col Gen Aleksandr Chayko, the commander of Russia’s aerospace forces, who was reportedly celebrating his birthday at the restaurant. Among those killed was Chayko’s son-in-law Daniil Peredrya, the independent outlet Agentstvo reported on Wednesday, citing government records. Since the start of the full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s intelligence agencies have targeted dozens of senior Russian military officers and Russia-installed officials, accusing them of involvement in war crimes. Ukrainian intelligence services have previously employed a range of tactics in operations inside Russia, including planting explosive devices beneath vehicles that can be detonated remotely. The latest assassination attempt demonstrates Ukraine’s ability to continue its clandestine operations deep inside Russian territory, and is likely to intensify scrutiny of Russia’s internal security apparatus and its inability to protect senior officials and pro-war figures. A forensic technician works alongside a bomb-disposal robot at Leipzig airport on Wednesday. Photograph: Hendrik Schmidt/DPA/AP View image in fullscreen A forensic technician works alongside a bomb-disposal robot at Leipzig airport on Wednesday. Photograph: Hendrik Schmidt/DPA/AP Germany Bomb disposal robot deployed after drone carrying explosives found at German airport Counter-terror team investigating after DHL plane also collided mid-air with unknown object at Leipzig airport Europe live – latest updates Deborah Cole Wed 5 Aug 2026 09.47 EDT First published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 07.37 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google German police deployed a bomb disposal robot after a drone carrying explosives was found at Leipzig airport overnight, causing alarm and the diversion of several flights. A DHL cargo plane that had been forced to abort its landing at the airport then collided with an unknown object. It later landed safely elsewhere. The counter-terrorism team at the Dresden prosecutor’s office and the Saxony state police have taken over the investigation, which security experts said could amount to a serious escalation in tensions with Russia if it is determined the Kremlin played a role. Investigators said that overnight on Wednesday “a drone carrying an unknown explosive device was spotted by an airport employee in the security area of the cargo operations zone near the south runway” of Leipzig airport, a facility classified as “critical infrastructure”. View image in fullscreen Footage by News5 from 5 August shows the nose of an Ukrainian ‘Antonov’ plane at Leipzig-Halle airport. Photograph: News5/AFP/Getty Images “A suspected second unidentified flying object collided with a cargo aircraft after it had taken off again following the previous closure of the runway. Minor damage was detected on the aircraft after it landed in Hanover.” The airport in eastern Germany serves as a hub in the transport of military goods, including by the German armed forces and Nato allies, and also serves as a base for Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines. The drone, a quadcopter with four rotors that was fitted with an explosive device, was found near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane, according to media reports. Some of the Ukrainian aircraft have patriotic slogans including “Be Brave Like Kherson” and “Be Brave Like Bucha”, the site of a civilian massacre early in the full-scale Russian invasion. A Nato official said: “We are aware of the incident, which the German authorities continue to investigate.” The newspaper Die Zeit said investigators were examining several possible scenarios including an attempt by Russia to launch an attack on Ukrainian equipment in Germany . Konstantin von Notz, the opposition Green party’s spokesperson on intelligence oversight, called for an investigation to be conducted with the utmost urgency and hinted at possible Russian involvement. “Should it transpire that a state is behind this action, this would not merely constitute terrorism, but state terrorism directed against the federal republic of Germany and its citizens,” he told Der Spiegel. Several aircraft, including a passenger plane from Mallorca, were diverted due to the incident. Operations in the northern part of the airport resumed two hours later. The southern runway, where the drone was found, remained closed. Police deployed a bomb disposal robot to examine the object. View image in fullscreen German media reported that investigators were examining several possibilities, including that the incident was an attempt by Russia to attack Ukrainian equipment in Germany. Photograph: News5/AFP/Getty Images “There is no danger to the lives or safety of passengers or airport staff,” police and prosecutors said. “Passenger air traffic is unaffected.” Germany and other European countries have had a series of suspicious unauthorised drone overflights at airports, military facilities, ports and logistics companies. They have accused Russian agents of being behind some of the flights, which Moscow has denied. European security agencies have investigated incendiary devices concealed in parcels that caught fire in 2024 , raising concerns about sabotage of air cargo operators. Some of the devices were ⁠found at a DHL warehouse in Leipzig and in freight shipments in ​transit across Europe. Tobias Meyer, the chief executive of DHL, said in a quarterly results call:: “We’ve ‌got plans for cases ​like this, and ​we’ll try to make sure that the influence on our customers will be as low as possible.” Germany is the biggest single national supplier of military aid to Ukraine and has accused Russia of orchestrating a campaign of sabotage, espionage and disinformation against it, which the Kremlin has denied. Last year a Chinese national was convicted for passing on information about flight schedules and cargo movements at Leipzig-Halle airport to a man spying for Beijing. Separately, Die Zeit reported that Russian secret services were plotting an attack against Stefan Thumann, the head of German drone manufacturer Donaustahl. The report said German investigators were tipped off by a foreign intelligence service at the end of last year and arrested a Ukrainian man and a Romanian woman this spring. Thumann is said to be under police protection. In 2024, US intelligence services reportedly foiled a Russian plot to assassinate the chief executive of Germany’s leading arms manufacturer, in an apparent attempt at retaliation over the company’s role in providing a large amount of armaments for Ukraine. The plan to murder Armin Papperger, the chief executive of Rheinmetall, was reportedly one of several Russian government schemes to kill defence industry executives in several countries in Europe that have been supporting Ukraine’s war effort. The plot against Papperberger was believed to be the most advanced. Photograph: Dado Ruvić/Reuters AI (artificial intelligence) AI models shock UK testers by using stolen identities to trick developers AI Security Institute says models by OpenAI and Anthropic went rogue during a cybersecurity test and showed a new type of risk Dan Milmo Global technology editor Wed 5 Aug 2026 08.04 EDT First published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 04.40 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Advanced AI models developed by OpenAI and Anthropic went rogue during a cybersecurity test and showed a new type of risk posed by the technology, according to the UK’s AI Security Institute. AISI described the actions carried out by the agents – the term for AI systems that can perform tasks without human help – as a “serious incident”. In one example, an agent powered by Anthropic’s Mythos model sent targeted emails to people. AISI said the rogue behaviour was carried out by agents powered by two models – Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol. AISI said it detected unusual activity during a routine cybersecurity test for AI models on 28 July. It found that some of the agents had engaged in “sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations”. It took an hour to contain the incident. In the most serious case, an agent powered by Mythos tried to insert malicious code into an open-source software project on GitHub, a platform used by software developers. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent then created fake online identities based on real people and used them to press the project’s overseer into accepting the code. These attempts were blocked by a human developer. Democracy is at stake when foolish humans bet on machines being intelligent | Rafael Behr Read more AISI said the agent used techniques commonly associated with real-world hackers. It sent emails to specifically chosen individuals – a technique known as “spear-phishing” – that attempted to manipulate the recipient. Some of the messages contained harmful software. AISI said no harm was caused but the agents’ actions were unprecedented. “This is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real world,” said AISI in a blogpost . The incident followed recent similar episodes at OpenAI and Anthropic. In July, OpenAI said an agent powered by its models had hacked an AI startup during a test, and days later Anthropic said its Claude model had hacked three organisations during an evaluation. AISI said the incident, taken alongside similar occurrences at OpenAI and Anthropic, represented a “shift in the risk landscape”. This was not an example of deliberate misuse of publicly available models, AISI said, but showed models in a research environment taking unintended action “beyond their authorised scope”. AISI said 17 of the 19 cases of rogue behaviour that occurred during the evaluation were carried out by Mythos and two by Sol. AISI said this was not a case of a model escaping its “sandbox”, or secure testing environment. The institute said it had intentionally permitted internet access and disabled filters within the models that blocked dangerous behaviour. The models are not publicly available in those operating conditions and there is no sign of such behaviour happening outside tests, AISI said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Preview latest after newsletter promotion The incident should be interpreted with “caution and nuance”, AISI said, but the signs of deceptive behaviour were “to an extent and severity we did not anticipate”. It was a small number of events that occurred under specific conditions, AISI added, but it had not happened before. “What we can say is that the behaviour was possible, sustained and new. That alone warrants attention,” AISI said. AISI admitted it was not actively monitoring the agents’ behaviour during the evaluation. It said it was putting tighter controls on internet access in tests as a result of the incident, introducing constant monitoring of tests and reassessing its design of tests. It said evaluations should assume a model would attempt to act beyond its remit. The UK’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, said it was “absolutely vital” that the UK had a world-leading AI safety organisation. “Identifying new behaviour like this and sharing our findings, so we can tackle it, is exactly what AISI was set up to do,” he said. OpenAI said the testing occurred during “conditions that do not reflect ordinary use”. An OpenAI spokesperson said: “We’ll continue working with evaluators and other stakeholders across the industry to strengthen shared practices for conducting evaluations safely as models become more capable.” Anthropic said the incident “underscores the need for a broader conversation about how to safely evaluate increasingly capable AI agents” and it would continue to work with AISI on evaluating what happened. Photograph: Supplied UK news Former Pakistani minister arrested over alleged child rape in 1990s Manchester Exclusive: Rukhsar Ahmed was re-elected as an MP in Pakistan last week despite being on police bail in the UK Shah Meer Baloch , Josh Halliday , Raphael Boyd and Rajeev Syal Wed 5 Aug 2026 07.30 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 08.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A former Pakistani state minister has been arrested on suspicion of raping vulnerable young girls in Manchester in the 1990s, the Guardian can reveal. Rukhsar Ahmed, who was re-elected as an MP in Pakistan last week after five years out of office, is on police bail in the UK after his arrest in July 2024 on suspicion of rape and trafficking children in care as part of a grooming gang. It is understood that Ahmed, 62, was expected to answer bail at a police station in Manchester last month, but failed to attend because he was “too unwell to fly”. At the same time, he was pictured on social media campaigning at various election gatherings in Mirpur in northern Pakistan. He was elected last week as an MP in the Azad Jammu and Kashmir legislative assembly for the party of Pakistan’s prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif. Ahmed, who represents the centre-right Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N), was a minister in various state governments from 2006 until he lost his seat in 2021. The Guardian understands that Greater Manchester police (GMP) had wanted to restrict Ahmed’s ability to travel abroad as part of his bail conditions, but a judge rejected tougher measures in July 2024. Ahmed was arrested at Manchester airport on 18 July 2024 in relation to past child sexual abuse allegations linked to the Rusholme area of the city, where he lived for many years. View image in fullscreen Rukhsar Ahmed. Photograph: Supplied Ahmed, who has more than 17,000 followers on Facebook, was pictured with friends in Rusholme as recently as May, with associates saying he has visited regularly. He is the owner of a former restaurant, the Gujjar Palace, near Manchester’s curry mile. One friend said people travelled for hundreds of miles to see the businessman, given his role in Pakistani politics. Detectives questioned Ahmed in July 2024 about allegations from at least two women who claimed that Ahmed was involved in raping and trafficking them when they were young girls. It is understood that detectives learned about Ahmed’s involvement in Pakistani politics when he was in custody for questioning. The ongoing investigation relates to allegations from several women about sexual abuse of children at care homes in the early 1990s, when Ahmed was in his late 20s. He is understood to be expected to answer police bail in the next six weeks. If he does not attend, GMP may issue a warrant for his arrest or take steps to extradite him – potentially causing a diplomatic row. A senior leader of PML-N in Pakistan-administered Kashmir said he had known Ahmed for at least two decades. but did not know about the rape allegations against him. He said: “We just heard that he was part of some groups in Manchester in 1990s. But I personally didn’t know about such severe allegations existed against Ahmed.” Ahmed did not respond to requests for comment. The revelation comes weeks after Pakistan refused the UK government’s attempts to deport a freed ringleader of a Rochdale grooming gang. Shabir Ahmed, 73, was released from jail in July after serving 14 years of a 22-year sentence for 30 child rape offences. Friends of Rukhsar Ahmed described him as “incredibly influential” in Manchester’s Pakistani community given his political role. One associate in Rusholme said he was a “man of the people” and “one of the least corrupt people”, adding that he had visited the area recently. He is known to have visited a popular Pakistani restaurant on Stockport Road in Rusholme on numerous occasions. Photos from one visit, which he posted to his Facebook account, show him and several others standing outside the restaurant. Those on Stockport Road speak highly of Ahmed. One man described him as “a man of conviction who helps people who need it”. He is particularly respected by people from Azad Kashmir, the self governing region near northern Pakistan where his LA-4 Mirpur-IV seat is based. His influence in the community is such that people come from across the UK to meet him when he visits Manchester, which he is believed to do every few months. The Gujjar Palace was boarded up and derelict when the Guardian visited on Tuesday. One local business owner said it had been closed since at least 2009. Ahmed is the only director of the company that owns the restaurant, but it was almost struck off earlier this year after failing to file its accounts. Photograph: Ronen Tivony/NurPhoto via Getty Images Maryland Two US men charged for allegedly using snakes, a lemur and a monkey for exotic photoshoots Men allegedly used exotic animals for photoshoots featuring a ring of fire in a parking garage in Maryland Edward Helmore Wed 5 Aug 2026 09.33 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two Baltimore , Maryland, men are facing charges for allegedly using exotic animals – including snakes, a lemur and a spider monkey – in photoshoots featuring three semi-clothed models and a ring of fire in a garage beneath a luxury shopping complex. Photographer Vernon Crowfey III, the 32-year-old owner of the company Photogeniks, was arrested in Towson, Maryland , on 16 July after an undercover officer arranged a shoot with the animals. A second man, Jayden Evans, 25, a collaborator who owns Tarzan Exoticz, which sells personalized photoshoots with exotic animals, was also arrested with Crowfey. The pair allegedly staged a photoshoot in a parking garage beneath Towson Town Center where Crowfey photographed three women posing with the exotic animals. Video footage and photos circulating online show the garage floor lit on fire. Charging documents state Crowfey and Evans obtained the animals from North Carolina without a permit. Evans’s website , Instagram and Facebook pages show photos of him and others with various animals, including “nonhuman primates”. “Vernon Crowfey was observed in a multitude of joint posts with Jayden Evans where he is the photographer for the animal shoots, and Jayden Evans is the animal handler during the photoshoots,” the documents said. The arrests came in a sting operation after a Baltimore police detective confirmed with the US Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service that neither of the men had a valid Class C exhibitor or dealer license as required under the Animal Welfare Act. An undercover officer later arranged a photoshoot with Evans involving the lemur and spider monkey. A search warrant was executed at Evan’s home, where both men were arrested. Police also found snakes, lizards, rabbits, a tarantula and several other animals at the home. “Based off of what the USDA specialist and Animal Control Officers observed at the scene, neither the lemur or spider monkey were in proper living conditions, which led to their overall neglect,” charging documents said. Both men are each facing 23 misdemeanor and felony charges, including animal cruelty and arson-related offenses, for allegedly setting fire to the mall parking garage. Crowfey claimed to CBS News Baltimore that he was given permission by mall security to use the parking garage as the backdrop for his photoshoot. “We spoke with the security at the mall as well. We explained to him that we was gonna have the fire flame photoshoot. He told us basically just be out before the mall closed,” Crowfey told the network. He also said he wanted to use the space because “we talkin’ about an empty parking lot, with no civilians, full of concrete and I don’t think I’ve ever seen a parking lot be set on fire with lighter fluid.” The lemur and spider monkey were transported to the Maryland Zoo. “Primates are not domesticated. They are wild animals. They have not been in captivity and bred long enough to get that wildlife feature out of them,” Jacob Thompson, owner of Global Pets, told WBAL. “All it takes is for these animals to hit a maturity point or something triggers them to react in a way that’s wild-like.” The arrests come as a new documentary on the exotic wildlife trade, Monsters of God, is released by HBO on Thursday. Film-maker Eric Goode, whose previous hits include pandemic streamer Tiger King, told Vanity Fair last week that pop culture drives demand for exotic and endangered species. “Jurassic Park had this crazy paradoxical effect on pet sales in the US. Finding Nemo made everyone want to buy a clown fish,” Goode said. “When I used to travel in Asia 10 to 15 years ago, I would see owls in the marketplaces, and people would say: ‘Oh, those are Harry Potter birds.’” Explore more on these topics Maryland Baltimore Animals Wildlife US crime news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution Green light

Photograph: Eric Lee/Reuters Donald Trump FAA investigates air ‘safety incident’ involving Trump’s Marine One Controllers allegedly failed to halt flights, leading to a ‘loss of separation’ with a departing passenger jet Richard Luscombe and agencies Wed 5 Aug 2026 08.58 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 08.59 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An air “safety incident” in which Donald Trump ’s Marine One helicopter came closer than permitted to another aircraft over Washington DC is under investigation by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). Air traffic controllers are believed to have mistakenly failed to halt commercial flights at Ronald Reagan national airport in northern Virginia on Tuesday afternoon when the military helicopter lifted off from the White House with the president on board. A “loss of separation” incident occurred in which the helicopter and a recently departed passenger jet bound for Florida came closer to each other than regulations allow, a source told Reuters. The aircraft are not believed to have been on a collision course. The FAA said in a statement that it was “investigating a safety incident involving Marine One but it didn’t appear to be a dangerous close call and the aircraft weren’t apparently converging”. The episode followed a tightening of proximity rules in the wake of a January 2025 collision between a commercial airliner and an army Black Hawk helicopter over the nation’s capital that killed 67 people. The government eventually admitted negligence in what was the deadliest crash on US soil in more than two decades. The aircraft involved in Tuesday’s incident was an Embraer E170 jet operated by Envoy ​Air, a wholly owned subsidiary of American Airlines, as flight 3742 to Pensacola. Tracking website Flightaware showed it left its gate at Reagan national at 2.18pm on Tuesday, 34 minutes later than scheduled, and was in the air 16 minutes later at 2.34pm. Marine One took off from the Ellipse near the White House at 2.33pm to take Trump to Joint Base Andrews and a flight to Los Angeles, according to a pool report. FAA rules implemented after last year’s tragedy require aircraft to remain separated by at least ​1.5 miles horizontally and 500ft vertically around airports, and the sources told Reuters that it appeared Marine One and the plane did ​not maintain separation. One said it appears they were not converging during the incident. Marine One and the Envoy jet continued their journeys without incident, with the Embraer landing in Pensacola at 3.33pm CT after a flight of 2hr 16min. The Guardian has contacted the White House and American Airlines for comment. Reuters ‌learned from its sources, who were speaking under the condition of anonymity, that the FAA planned to convene a safety review team to investigate the incident. A third aircraft, regional flight Republic 4700 from North Carolina’s Raleigh-Durham international airport to Washington DC, was three miles (5 km) from Reagan national at the time of the incident and was ordered to fly around before landing at 2.52pm, one of the sources said, confirmed by Flightaware tracking . The FAA ⁠imposed permanent restrictions on helicopter operations around Reagan national following last year’s mid-air collision. The US government conceded in December in a response to a lawsuit filed by one of the victims’ families that failures of the FAA and army played a role in the crash. “The United States admits that it owed a duty of care to plaintiffs, which it breached, thereby proximately causing the tragic accident,” it said. The ​National Transportation Safety Board said in January that a series of systemic failures by the FAA led ​to the collision, ⁠citing its decision to allow helicopters to travel close to the airport with no safeguards to separate them from airplanes. The FAA has since banned mixed helicopter and jet traffic around the airport, and commercial traffic is typically halted when Marine One is in flight around ⁠the airport. Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters US Congress Republican Chuck Edwards drops bid for re-election after report finding sexual harassment of staffers Congressional ethics panel had recommended Edwards face censure over its findings on ‘hostile work environment’ US politics live – latest updates Guardian staff Wed 5 Aug 2026 08.34 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 08.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Chuck Edwards announced he would not run for re-election after the US House of Representatives ethics committee determined the US congressman “fostered a hostile work environment and engaged in sexual harassment” by giving gifts and lavishing attention on two young female staffers. Edwards, a Republican for North Carolina , said he would complete his current term, which is due to end in January. In a statement posted on social media early on Wednesday morning, Edwards said: “After much prayer and reflection, I’ve decided to withdraw from my re-election campaign. I will complete my current term. Serving sestern North Carolina has been the honor of my life. Thank you for your trust, prayers, and support” US House ethics panel recommends censure for Republican Chuck Edwards Read more The bipartisan congressional ethics panel recommended on Monday that Edwards face censure over its findings. Should the House agree, he will have to stand in the well of the chamber while the text of a resolution rebuking him is read aloud. The ethics committee launched an investigation into Edwards earlier this year, after receiving complaints about his conduct. In a report approved by Democratic and Republican committee members, it said there was “substantial reason to believe” that Edwards had broken House rules by singling out the two unidentified aides for special treatment that made them uncomfortable and harmed relations with other employees. While the investigation uncovered no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with the staffers or suggested it, his behavior likely violated provisions in the House code of conduct that prohibit sexual harassment and unwanted advances. The congressman “acknowledged at least some of the behavior at issue could be viewed as inappropriate”, but “has not acknowledged or taken responsibility for the harm he caused”, the committee wrote in its report. Edwards was already viewed as vulnerable to losing re-election to his western North Carolina district in the November midterm elections. Last week election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball announced it was rating his race a “toss-up”, in a sign of improving Democratic chances. Officials said the detonator has been removed from an as-yet unidentified explosive device. Authorities say they are not ruling out a political motive, noting that the Leipzig/Halle airport in eastern Germany forms part of the country's critical infrastructure. The drone carrying the explosive device was found late on Wednesday by an airport employee on the southern runway, according to investigators. Another flying object later apparently collided with a cargo aircraft which was taxing on the ground. Minor damage was discovered after the aircraft landed in Hanover. Flight operations were initially halted completely after the drone was found. The northern runway was eventually reopened following a large-scale security sweep overnight, while the southern runway was due to remain closed on Wednesday for maintenance. Investigators said there was no danger to passengers or airport staff and that passenger flights were not affected. https://p.dw.com/p/5IKej Skip next section Court rules owner can criticize restaurant online after her dog ate mouse poison there 08/05/2026 August 5, 2026 Court rules owner can criticize restaurant online after her dog ate mouse poison there A German court has ruled in favor of a woman who publicly criticized a restaurant after her dachshund ate mouse poison while she was dining there. The Frankfurt Higher Regional Court rejected the restaurant operator's attempt to stop her from describing the incident on Instagram and a review platform. The woman had visited the restaurant in the Rhine-Main region in spring 2026 with her dachshund, which was lying under a bench inside. The dog ate mouse bait from a pest-control bait station that had somehow been left accessible and later needed treatment at a veterinary clinic. That same day, the owner posted about the incident on her own Instagram account and on an account she ran for the dog. She described what happened as "shocking" and a "massive failure of safety and hygiene." The court found that readers would understand those remarks as referring to a single incident rather than suggesting the restaurant had permanent or structural hygiene problems. Judges said the woman was entitled to describe the fact that her dog had been able to reach poison as a "massive" failure, even if her wording was emotional and somewhat exaggerated. They also found that her inaccurate description of the harmful substance as "rat poison" was not so serious a mistake as to warrant restricting her comment. The statements were therefore protected expressions of opinion, it ruled. https://p.dw.com/p/5IKIn Skip next section German court jails members of far-right youth terror cell 08/05/2026 August 5, 2026 German court jails members of far-right youth terror cell A court in Hamburg has handed down prison sentences of up to five years to eight alleged members and supporters of the far-right group "Letzte Verteidigungswelle" (Last Line of Defense). The Higher Regional Court convicted the young defendants on charges including membership in a terrorist organization and attempted murder. Prosecutors said the group had planned bomb and arson attacks targeting refugees and left-wing activists and had already carried out several attacks. Seven defendants received juvenile prison sentences ranging from two years and four months to five years. Another was given an 18-month suspended sentence. Three defendants were also convicted of leading the group. The presiding judge said they had aimed to "create chaos." Authorities dismantled the group in May last year after investigations spanning several German states. Prosecutors said members carried out an overnight arson attack on an occupied cultural center in Altdöbern in October 2024 and a pyrotechnic attack on a refugee accommodation center in Schmölln, Thuringia, in January 2025. No one was injured, although investigators said that was partly down to chance. The group had also been planning another attack on a refugee center in Senftenberg, Brandenburg. Several suspects were arrested in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Brandenburg and Hesse. They were between 14 and 21 years old at the time. Because some defendants were minors, much of the trial was held behind closed doors.
