Read more about the story here . https://p.dw.com/p/5IJn7 Skip next section Low Rhine levels could push up German inflation 08/05/2026 August 5, 2026 Low Rhine levels could push up German inflation Low water means that barges cannot carry as much cargo as they usually would Image: Rüdiger Wölk/IMAGO Persistently low water levels on the Rhine could temporarily push Germany's inflation rate up by as much as half a percentage point, economists have warned. Low water levels are forcing ships to carry much lighter loads, driving up the cost of transporting chemicals, energy supplies and other industrial goods. Traders said tanker and barge transport costs from Rotterdam to Karlsruhe have climbed to around €150-160 per ton, compared with about €45 at the end of June. "The German inflation rate could temporarily rise by up to half a percentage point as a result," Berenberg economist Felix Schmidt told the Reuters news agency. ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski also said shortages and disrupted deliveries could make a wide range of goods more expensive. "If ships can only be loaded to one-third of capacity or less, correspondingly more ships have to be used, or more expensive alternatives such as trucks or rail," Hamburg Commercial Bank chief economist Cyrus de la Rubia said. Economists also warned that the disruption could last for months. In previous years, Rhine water levels have often not recovered significantly until November. https://p.dw.com/p/5IJ4l Skip next section German employers warn against U-turn on early retirement 08/05/2026 August 5, 2026 German employers warn against U-turn on early retirement A German employer group has sharply criticized calls to preserve the country's early retirement scheme as debate grows over a proposed overhaul of the pension system . A government-appointed pension commission presented 33 proposals in June, including abolishing the option of retiring without deductions for people who have paid into the system for particularly long periods. Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) leadership initially said they wanted to implement the package as closely as possible to the commission's recommendations. However, several state premiers from both Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union and the SPD have since pushed back against parts of the plan, with particularly strong criticism coming from eastern Germany. Steffen Kampeter, head of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations, told the Bild newspaper that Germany would not be able to protect jobs and remain competitive without reforming the welfare state. "I am stunned that central elements of the pension package are already being called into question before they have even been implemented," Steffen Kampeter, head of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations, told the Bild newspaper. "Anyone who at the same time sticks to retirement from 63 is ignoring the shortage of skilled workers, demographic change and the economic situation," he said. He warned that watering down the reforms could squander "perhaps the last chance" to make the pension system sustainable as Germany's population ages. "A future-proof pension system needs more employment, more contributors and solid financing - not ever more promises at the expense of the younger generation," Kampeter said. Police said the affected roads are the only direct links between the western and eastern parts of Harburg and can no longer be crossed by car. Residents now face detours of several kilometers, while road crews were working on Wednesday morning to set up alternative routes. It was unclear when the damage would be repaired. Police said the disruption could continue into the morning rush hour. A Deutsche Bahn technician has been notified, but repairs may take time because of numerous other weather-related faults. Until then, the barriers will remain closed. Police also warned drivers not to use unofficial shortcuts or attempt to drive around the lowered barriers. https://p.dw.com/p/5IIJ7 Skip next section Welcome to our coverage 08/05/2026 August 5, 2026 Welcome to our coverage Richard Connor | Roshni Majumdar Editor The Rhine is unusually low, which has hit river traffic badly and could help fuel inflation Image: Marc John/Bonn.digital/picture alliance Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn. https://www.dw.com/en/hungary-s-lake-vel.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IHL4 Lake Velence's water levels have dropped to a record low Image: Tobias Zuttmann/DW Advertisement A dead fish lies half-decayed on the shore. Its eyes have been picked out by the birds. Hungary's Lake Velence will likely experience a massive fish kill. That's because oxygen levels in the body of water are too low, according to environmental experts. This means more and more fish will suffocate. Hungary has seen temperatures soar to 40 degrees Celsius, with barely any rain. This heat is having a major impact on the country's third-largest natural lake. Its water has never been particularly deep, but the current situation is dire. Water levels have been recorded in Agard, on the southern shore, since 1933. It dropped to a historic low in September 2022, measuring just 53 centimeters. Yet as of today, August 4, the water level has dropped to a mere 29 centimeters (11 inches). As long as it doesn't rain and temperatures remain hot, the water level will continue to drop every day, by half a centimeter per day on average. The water is currently evaporating at such a fast pace that there may soon be no continuous body of water left, only isolated pools. This could mark a critical tipping point for the lake. The impact of Hungary's ongoing drought is already clearly visible. The lake has receded by dozens of meters. Ground once covered in water is now so dry that the soil is cracking. The reed belt surrounding the lake, which serves as a habitat for numerous bird species, is now largely rooted in dry soil. But not all living creatures are suffering under the current conditions: that's evident from a constant hum in the air near the water's edge. As fish and aquatic plants find their habitats shrinking, flies, bacteria, and other decomposers take over, breaking down what the drought leaves behind. No swimming The water shortage isn't just changing the lake — it's changing the entire region. Lake Velence is a popular tourist destination, located just 50 kilometers from Hungary's capital, Budapest. It is considered less crowded than nearby Lake Balaton. Swimming is not an option this summer at Lake Velence Image: Tobias Zuttmann/DW But these days, there are barely any visitors. The remaining water has turned a brownish-green and taken on a slightly musty odor. A "No Swimming" sign has been put up, with yellow tape blocking access to the water. Five swimming spots have been closed to the public since July 23. The Velence municipal government says the beach will only reopen once the lake's water quality improves, though it is unclear when that might happen. The persistent heat and low water levels mean the lake's water is getting warmer and warmer, leading to a growth in bacteria and blue-green algae. Tourist industry under pressure The people living around the lake, who make their living in the region's tourist sector, are hard hit by the lake's falling water levels. Today, only one family is visiting the northern beach — not for swimming but sunbathing. There is a water slide, slowly rusting away, with the end of the chute not even reaching the water anymore. Only one kiosk is open today. A woman is selling langos, Hungary's well-known fried bread, as well as ice cream and lemonade. "The slide hasn't been used for years," the saleswoman tells DW. "It really needs fixing, but who will pay for it when fewer and fewer tourists come here?" Campsites and holiday homes around the lake seem deserted, with many stores closed. Peggy Barath works in an ice cream shop on Velence Promenade, telling DW, "We've always had a lot of tourists here." She says many visitors were from East Germany , the Czech Republic and the Netherlands. But in recent years, their numbers have been dwindling "because of the lake's low water levels." Peggy Barath hopes the situation will improve and tourists will return Image: Tobias Zuttmann/DW Peggy says that the ice cream shop now focuses on cyclists rather than tourists looking to swim, as cyclists are undeterred by low water levels. No long-term solution in sight Major interventions in the region's water cycle have made the lake more vulnerable to droughts over the years. "The lakeshore has been subject to significant construction activity over the past 15 years," Zoltan Kun, president of the Hungarian Great Lakes and Wetlands Association, tells DW. "The water management authority has focused on quickly draining excess water from the region rather than storing it using nature-based solutions. And the agricultural industry destroyed our soils, which means they are less able to absorb water." This isn't the first time Lake Velence has dried up. When this happened in the early 1990s, the lake was replenished with water from various other sources, a solution that proved effective but also expensive and time-consuming. That's why experts are calling for a more sustainable solution today, especially since climate change means more drought periods are expected. The Zamolyi and Patkai reservoirs could, for instance, be renovated so that water could be stored there during periods of heavy rainfall. During dry spells, this water could then be diverted into Lake Valance. The dry, cracked bed of Hungary's third-largest lake Image: Tobias Zuttmann/DW Yet little has happened so far. In 2021, the government at the time, led by Prime Minister Viktor Orban , rejected a broad investment program for the lake on the grounds that it was too costly. Other projects, however, went ahead. A new canoe center Although it has long been clear that water levels drop to a critical level in summer and fall, authorities built a brand-new canoeing center on the north shore between 2021 and 2024, suitable for international competitions. The project cost about 140 million euros in government funds. Lanes are marked off in the lake with buoys in front of the newly built spectator tower. It's very quiet, like elsewhere along the body of water. Floating docks sit low in the greenish-brown water. The World University Canoe Championships were supposed to be held here in August, the first major event to be staged at the newly built center. Yet due to persistently low water levels, the event was moved to Szeged, southern Hungary, instead. This means that for the time being, the Lake Velence facility remains nothing more than an expensive training center. A sandbank has formed in front of Budapest's Margaret Island Image: Tobias Zuttmann/DW Nuclear power plant on brink of shutdown Hungary's ongoing heat wave is being felt all over the country. Water levels of the Danube River have dropped significantly, exposing stretches of dry riverbed around Budapest's Margaret Island. Tourists and locals alike are taking in the unusual sight, snapping photos on a sandbar that has emerged off the island. The low water level has also attracted scrap-metal collectors, who use magnets to pull rusty metal objects from parts of the river that are normally submerged. The low water level has dramatic consequences. With the exception of a few sightseeing steamboats, boat traffic has almost ceased on the Danube River. Not only that. Paks nuclear power plant, located about 100 kilometers downstream from Budapest, can no longer be cooled with Danube water. The site's electricity output, which covers about half of Hungary's power consumption, has been gradually reduced over the past few days, and it is set to be shut down later this week for the first time ever. Hungary's power options after drought shuts nuclear plant To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "We are facing a crisis that is beyond our control and putting us to the test," Prime Minister Peter Magyar said at a joint press conference with Interim President Agnes Forsthoffer on Monday. He added that the next five days would be the most critical of the summer of 2026. Magyar has asked the Hungarian public to conserve electricity. Many companies have agreed to voluntarily reduce their power consumption. Some public buildings and bridges are no longer illuminated at night, and rail freight traffic is suspended between 5:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m. Hungary faces a very challenging time, with temperatures over 40 degrees Celsius expected over the next days. https://www.dw.com/en/tiktok-influencer-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IIBn The killing comes amid persistent violence in Culiacan [July 2026] Image: Jesus Verdugo/AFP Advertisement Mexican social media influencer Cesar Gastelum was shot and killed on Tuesday while livestreaming with friends outside a fast food restaurant in Culiacan, in the northwestern state of Sinaloa, local authorities said. Gastelum, who had close to 600,000 followers on TikTok , was known for comedy content. He was broadcasting live outside the restaurant with two friends, all reportedly dressed as delivery drivers as part of a challenge for the video. What do we know? During the stream, a motorcycle carrying two people pulled up beside them. Footage from the livestream appeared to show the motorcycle driver shooting at Gastelum's head directly. The broadcast cut out at that moment. While the video was later taken down by the platform, portions of it continuted to circulate online. A security official in Sinaloa confirmed Gastelum's death and said a major security operation was under way. Local television footage showed soldiers and police at the scene, a busy commercial plaza near the state prosecutor's office in Culiacan, while forensic investigators collected evidence. Initial police reports described the victim as a delivery worker. He was later identified as Gastelum, who local media reported was around 25 years old, after the video and witness accounts helped confirm his identity. We met a cartel killer — who really runs Mexico? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Culiacan at the center of a conflict between rival crime factions Culiacan, the capital of Sinaloa, has been gripped by violence for the past two years amid an internal power struggle within the region's dominant drug cartel. Local press have reported that several influencers, some allegedly linked to criminal groups, have been killed in Sinaloa in recent years. The killing echoes the May 2025 death of beauty influencer Valeria Marquez , 23, who was shot while livestreaming on TikTok at the salon where she worked in Zapopan, in Mexico’s western state of Jalisco. Her death was investigated as possible femicide. Local authorities arrested Ramon Angel Alvarez Ayala, also known as "El R-1," in Jalisco in July. Security Minister Omar Garcia Harfuch described him as the head of a criminal cell tied to the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG). Investigators say Alvarez Ayala played a role in Marquez's death and that he financed and directed the November 2025 assassination of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo. https://www.dw.com/en/south-korea-police.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5II8M The controversial promotion led to protest and boycotts, particularly in Seoul [File: May 21, 2026] Image: Yonhap/REUTERS Advertisement Police raided Starbucks' nation headquarters in South Korea on Wednesday, the company confirmed, after a controversial promotional event led to large protests and boycotts of the coffee chain across the country. "The Seoul police raided the headquarters of Starbucks Korea this morning as part of the ongoing investigation," said a spokesman for the Shinsegae Group, which operates Starbucks Korea. What was the controversial promotion? This past May, Starbucks advertised large to-go cups they called "tank tumblers" and seemed to refer to the Gwangju Uprising as "tank day." On May 18, 1980, the ruling military junta violently put down a pro-democracy protest in the city of Gwangju. At least 165 civilians were killed when the army rolled tanks out into the streets to quell the demonstation. The Starbucks promotional event also appeared to allude to statements made by the government at the time to deny that they had tortured a student protest leader to death. The backlash was swift, and led to protest and boycotts against the coffee giant in what is the company's third-largest market after the United States and China . President Lee Jae Myung also expressed his outrage, and Shinsegae Group chairman Chung Yong-jin and Starbucks Korea CEO Son Jung-hyun resigned following a public apology. What are police investigating? Starbucks Korea said it conducted its own internal investigation into the matter and found no evidence of wrongdoing. However, the firm admitted that the inquiry had been hampered by, amongst other things, not being able to compel the people involved in planning the promotion to hand over their phones. Police told the Yonhap news agency they were looking for evidence that executives knowingly trivialized the 1980 massacre. Edited by: Roshni Majumdar Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.politico.eu/article/european.text: Former European Parliament President Klaus Hänsch has died, current Parliament President Roberta Metsola confirmed on Wednesday. “His Parliament mourns the loss of a champion of Europe, who took office at a time of profound change for our continent, and who never stopped believing in the potential of this project,” wrote Metsola in a social media post . “At our last meeting just a few weeks ago, his unwavering optimism shone through as he described his ongoing efforts to promote civic engagement and nurture young European leaders. Europe will miss him. May he rest in peace,” she added. Hänsch, a German Social Democrat, served as Parliament president from 1994 to 1997, and was an MEP from 1979 to 2009. He was 87 years old. https://www.politico.eu/article/russia-c.text: The European Union has collected €1.4 billion in revenue from immobilized Russian central bank assets and will channel the proceeds to Ukraine, the European Commission announced Wednesday. In a press release , the Commission said the payment, received Monday, was the “fifth transfer of its kind.” Since the assets have been immobilized, they have generated a total of €8 billion in windfall profits. Brussels said 95 percent of the latest tranche would go through the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism, helping Kyiv repay EU and G7 loans, while the remaining 5 percent would flow through the European Peace Facility to meet Ukraine’s “pressing military and defence needs.” Advertisement Advertisement “Once again we wake up to the news of horrible atrocities by Russia through its aerial attacks on Ukraine,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X. “Russia must pay for the destruction it has caused. And we are using the proceeds from the immobilised Russian assets to make sure it does.” Von der Leyen said the EU was making “a further €1.4 billion” available to support Ukraine’s “continued resistance against Russia’s illegal war.” Her comments came after one of the deadliest Russian attacks on Kyiv this year. Ballistic missiles and drones killed at least 17 people and wounded 44 overnight, striking residential buildings, warehouses and a railway station. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated Wednesday that additional missile interceptors “could have saved lives” and blamed delays in Western air-defense deliveries for the mounting casualties. Over €210 billion in Russian central bank reserves were frozen by the EU after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in 2022. Since 2024, financial institutions holding those assets have been required to ring-fence the extraordinary profits they generate, allowing Brussels to redirect the proceeds to Ukraine while leaving the underlying reserves untouched.

https://www.politico.eu/article/italy-sp.text: Italy will use extra leeway from the EU to spend billions of euros on energy and defense, Finance Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti told members of the country's parliament on Wednesday. Rome is set to boost its expenditure on green energy and defense over the coming three years, said Giorgetti following a relaxation of rules from Brussels, which allows the additional spending to be exempted from the EU’s strict spending targets and waived from Rome’s deficit figures. Italy is poised to issue a formal request to the European Commission — laying out the investments it intends to undertake with the extra flexibility — by a mid-August deadline. Advertisement Advertisement Giorgetti said Italy will request to spend an additional 0.6 percent of gross domestic product on green energy investments and 0.9 percent on defense — the full amount that is envisaged under the new fiscal guidelines. The additional defense spending will “include both new multi-year investment programs and proposals to reallocate resources already provided for under current legislation,” Giorgetti told MPs. Italy's parliament is expected to approve Giorgetti's request to the Commission on Wednesday. The extra flexibility is aimed at reducing dependence on fossil fuels and moving toward NATO’s target to spend 5 percent of GDP on defense. With 2 percent of GDP allocated to defense in 2025 , Italy is among the alliance’s spending laggards. However, the decision to raise military spending is set to inflame political tensions within the country ahead of a crucial election year that will see incumbent Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni seek a second mandate. The governing coalition is split on the issue, and the right-wing League party — from which Giorgetti himself hails — has repeatedly campaigned against spending more money to counter the Russian threat. In a further constraint, the government is under heavy pressure from the right-wing, Russia-friendly National Future party led by former Gen. Roberto Vannacci, which is eating into support for the other governing parties, according to the polls . Advertisement Advertisement More leeway In June, the Commission gave EU countries suffering from the ongoing energy crisis more fiscal breathing room by exempting some green investments from public spending rules. The goal was to allow heavily indebted governments to mobilize resources for green expenditure , including subsidies for electric vehicles, geothermal and solar energy to reduce dependence on fossil fuels. Italy lobbied the EU to offer this concession after the war in the Middle East fueled a surge in oil prices. However, Giorgetti failed to lay out which green investments will be included in Italy's request to the Commission. In another gaping omission, he did not reveal whether Italy will tap into the EU’s cheap loans for defense — another divisive issue within the government coalition. Rome had initially earmarked €15 billion under the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program , prompting defense companies to factor in those investments. Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani recently suggested that Rome will use the SAFE money, but said the exact amount will be decided later in the year. Jacopo Barigazzi contributed to this report . Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.politico.eu/article/uk-jeffr.text: LONDON — Britain’s justice ministry said it is not “actively” considering holding a public inquiry into the U.K. activities of sex offender Jeffrey Epstein after the prospect of a probe was raised by two government ministers. Victims Minister Alex Davies-Jones told the BBC on Tuesday evening that Britain’s new Prime Minister Andy Burnham was considering holding an inquiry following discussions with him and Cabinet Secretary Antonia Romeo when she was reappointed victims minister last month. Asked about a potential inquiry on Wednesday morning, Justice Minister Jake Richards told Sky News the prime minister “will look into it.” Advertisement Advertisement “He’ll take his time, no doubt, to think about the best route for victims, but also to crucially ensure lessons are learned, to make sure that these sorts of things never happen again,” Richards said. But in a statement to journalists issued later on Wednesday, a Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “The Prime Minister is committed to meeting with victims, but a public inquiry is not being actively considered.” The spokesperson said the department is “reviewing what is possible and will look at all options to support victims and survivors.” Davies-Jones, who accused the previous Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s government of failing to listen to Epstein’s survivors, told the BBC’s Newsnight program Wednesday that Burnham had already agreed to meet the late financier’s victims. “We are looking into this, we are reviewing what is possible,” Davies-Jones said. “I have been assured that the prime minister is taking this very seriously. He will meet with those victims and he is looking at what is possible, now he has access to all of the information as prime minister to see what action we can take.” A BBC investigation last year found around 90 flights linked to Epstein arrived and departed at U.K. airports, some with alleged British victims on board. This article has been updated to include a statement from the U.K. Ministry of Justice. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cyvl.text: Image source, Reuters By Bethany Bell BBC correspondent ,Â Reporting from Leipzig Published 5 August 2026, 13:48 BST Updated 17 minutes ago A drone carrying an explosive device has been found at a German airport, police say. A robot was deployed at Leipzig/Halle Airport after the device was spotted in the cargo operation area overnight, according to Saxony police. A second unidentified object collided with a cargo aircraft near the same airport. Minor damage was detected on the aircraft after it landed in Hanover. There have been a series of unauthorised drone flights in Germany in recent months over sensitive sites including military bases, airports, energy terminals, seaports and logistics companies. German airports are on high alert. Federal police have warned that the overflights could have been organised by Russian agents. A police spokesman told the BBC that the object discovered at Leipzig Airport overnight had been spotted close to parked Ukrainian Antonov transport planes. The object was examined with the assistance of the Federal Police and an explosive-detection robot. The Federal Police's Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) unit removed the detonator from the explosive device. Flights on the northern runway resumed at 01:55 (23:55 GMT on Tuesday). The southern runway, which is a major hub for the logistic group DHL, remains closed. Saxony's Interior Minister Armin Schuster has described it as a "very serious security incident". In July 2024 a parcel burst into flames on the ground at Leipzig airport before it could be loaded onto a DHL cargo plane, one of a series of parcel fires that targeted the UK and EU countries. There are suspicions it could have been sabotage linked to Moscow. The parcels had contained explosive devices that were set off by electronic timers hidden in vibrating massage pillows, according to authorities. Russia has denied any involvement in those incidents. Last year a Chinese woman was convicted for passing on information about flight schedules and cargo movements at Leipzig-Halle Airport to a man spying for Beijing. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62q.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, The last time it was confirmed that part of a rocket had collided with the Moon by accident was in 2022 By Pallab Ghosh Science Correspondent Published 2 hours ago A stray SpaceX rocket is believed to have crashed into the Moon, forming a crater near a famous lunar landmark and giving scientists a unique research opportunity that could help future missions. The empty upper stage of a Falcon 9 rocket was due to strike the Moon near the Einstein crater at a speed of about 5,400mph (8,700km/h) on Wednesday. The short, dramatic flash it created would have been hard to catch by amateur astronomers even with high-end telescopes, but larger observatories in the Americas are analysing the information. It could be days or even weeks before the full picture of what happened and what we can learn from it is known - but for planetary geologists, this accidental collision is a scientific gift. Figure caption, Watch: Science Museum's head of space on what scientists will look for after crash Space X's Falcon 9 rocket is a reusable model and has been sent into space on several missions. Its design allows part of the rocket to return to Earth, but other sections are shed in space. The rocket blasted off from Florida in January last year, carrying two lunar landers into space. Its job was to fire the upper stage hard enough to send both of the landers out of Earth's orbit and onto a path towards the Moon - mission accomplished. The spent stage - which is about the size of a five-storey building and weighs at least 4,000kg - was left drifting in a long, looping orbit that swung out towards the Moon and back again. Over the next 18 months, the gentle gravitational tug of the Earth, Moon and Sun, along with even light from the Sun, gave a faint push. Astronomers tracking the rocket part eventually worked out that those small nudges had put it on a course towards the Moon and was picking up speed every day. The impact at around 07:35 BST (06:35 GMT) on Wednesday happened in broad daylight for many parts of the world, but the tiny flash it produced would have been far too faint to see, even through a telescope. Amateur astronomers observing in darkness would also have had little realistic chance of seeing the flash, given that it would have lasted a fraction of a second. But they may have seen a plume of dust stretching as far as 100km (62 miles) that lasted for several minutes. Even spacecraft orbiting the Moon were not in the right place at the right time to watch the impact happen live. South Korea's Danuri orbiter had the best chance, having passed near the crash site shortly beforehand. Its team has told Korean media that any footage will only be released once researchers have completed their analysis. Over the next few days, Nasa's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter will be in position to photograph the site, allowing images before and after the crash to be compared. Image source, NASA Image caption, The Einstein crater is over 180km (112 miles) wide, and is large enough to contain a smaller crater inside The science and probably the first images will come from powerful telescopes in the Americas where the sky was still dark. Even then, turning the detection of a 14m object hitting the lunar surface 385,000km away won't be easy. Image processing to clean up the picture can take hours, days or even weeks, as scientists check and process the data. Because researchers already know the rocket's exact size, speed and point of impact, this collision turns from being a random accident into a rare, controlled experiment. It is a dream moment for planetary scientists because it lets them test their models of how impacts dig out craters, throw debris across the surface, and send tremors through the Moon's interior. That has real practical value. Understanding how much rock and dust an impact throws up will help engineers design safer landers and future Moon bases, working out how far flying debris can travel and how hard the ground might shake nearby. Material thrown up from beneath the surface offers fresh clues about the Moon's geology, adding to what scientists already know about how the Earth-Moon system formed some 4.5 billion years ago. This is not the first time a human-made object has struck the Moon. Since 1959, dozens of spacecraft have crashed into it, some by accident and many deliberately for science. The Soviet probe Luna 2 was the first, followed over the decades by Nasa's Ranger probes in the 1960s, several Apollo-era rocket stages, and more recently the LCROSS mission in 2009, which was deliberately crashed to search for water ice. The last confirmed accidental impact , in 2022, was thought to be the leftover booster from a Chinese lunar mission launched back in 2014 - a reminder that this sort of space debris has been quietly piling up above our heads for well over half a century. https://telex.hu/english/2026/08/05/duna.text: Menü Kereső Aerial footage shows just how low Danube levels have dropped in and around Budapest English The Danube river at Szentendre – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka Németh Sz. Péter Madzin Emília Andrea Horváth Kávai (translation) Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom The soutnern tip of Margit island with the Margit bridge – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The water level of the Danube river has never been as low in Budapest as it is now. Although the situation may improve minimally towards the end of the week and the prospects are more optimistic now than they were a few days ago, due to the extreme drought, the water level will likely continue to drop in the coming days. Because of the current heat wave, all sorts of interesting objects which had previously been submerged in the Danube have been emerging from the river that runs through the city: the remains of the former Franz Joseph Bridge are now visible beneath Szabadság Bridge; World War II explosive devices have been unearthed from the silt near Batthyány Square; and weapons have been recovered from the river near Margit Island. The aerial photos taken by photographer Ferenc Sztraka on July 30, along with his commentary provide an overview of what the Danube looks like these days between Budapest and Esztergom. All sorts of wild rumors have been circulating online about the causes behind the low water levels, but according to a statement from the National Water Authority, the primary cause of the extremely low water levels is typically the lack of precipitation in the watershed, which leads to low natural water yields. And while exploring the now-exposed Danube riverbed might be a tempting adventure, the Budapest Waterworks has strongly urged everyone not to venture into this area either for a sports activity or for other reasons, under any circumstances, as they are typically classified as water protection zones. “If, as a result of human activity (normally not present here), any pollution should occur in these currently accessible areas, the consequences could, in extreme cases, render that particular section of the water source unusable for years or even decades. In other words, that section could be excluded from the process of producing drinking water,” the Budapest Waterworks said. The northern tip of Margit island – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka “We flew north along Margit Island. I immediately noticed something interesting: when rivers are confined between levees, it is not easy to tell from the air whether the water level is high or low. Even when the river was flooding, the only clear indication was the strange angle at which the docks’ planks were tilted. “The situation was similar this time as well, except it was the other way around," wrote Sztraka. The southern tip of Óbudai Island and the entrance of the Újpest bay – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka In mid-July we reported on the Danube’s water flow being very low—just 835.6 cubic meters per second at the time—and, on top of that, the water’s temperature kept rising. Because of this, experts at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant returned to the continuous monitoring of the river's temperature along the affected section to ensure the safe operation of the plant and compliance with environmental regulations. By 2 August, Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced that the Danube’s water level is just one centimeter away from necessitating a complete shutdown of the power plant. As of Wednesday afternoon, this hasn’t happened yet; the last Paks turbine still in operation continues to generate power. The highest temperature previously recorded at the wter gauge on the Danube in Budapest was 27.2 degrees Celsius in August 2018; on the evening of June 30 this year, it already reached 28.2 degrees. This coincided with a heat wave peaking at 42 degrees, prompting Minister of Economy and Energy István Kapitány to authorize increasing the maximum temperature limit at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant from 30 to 31.5 degrees to ensure a secure power supply—a measure environmentalists said could only be maintained temporarily. A sandbar at the northern tip of Óbuda Island; the ongoing construction for the upcoming Sziget Festival is already visible – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka According to Sztraka, as they travelled further from the massive levee that characterizes the Budapest section of the river, the grim reality of the drought immediately became more pronounced. “At the northern tip of Óbuda Island, we were greeted by the sight of a sizable sandbar. It’s quite possible that those attending the Sziget Festival—the stages for which were under construction at the time—will immediately take possession of the sandy beach which will now come as a bonus with their ticket price. During the flight we noticed that a wide strip of sand now encircles each island all the way to Esztergom—and surely beyond as well. Népsziget and the almost dried out bay – Photo: Ference Sztraka The winter harbor in Újpest, also known as Népsziget Bay, is a 28.6-hectare bay in the capital. It is an important hub of Budapest’s water life and is a favorite destination for anglers and boaters alike. The Kossuth public beach on Római part – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The southern tip of Szentendrei Island and the Megyeri bridge – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka Apart from the two anchored tankers visible near the southern tip of Szentendrei Island, the photographer did not see any bigger sightseeing or cargo ships along the entire route. Due to the extremely low water level, boat traffic has also come to a standstill. The Rév street Dunayacht quay in Megyer, and the remains of a ship visible in the water – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka Even at the Dunayacht boating station on Rév Street in Megyer, the water is not deep enough to receive bigger vessels. More than a dozen hotel boats have been stranded along the Hungarian section of the Danube in recent days due to the low water levels, and most cargo ships have also been forced to stay put. The remains of what appears to be a ship have also emerged from the water near Megyer. The mouth of the Szilas Stream, located on the south side of the Megyeri Bridge – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The mouth of the Szilas Stream, located on the south side of the Megyeri Bridge has taken on a rather strange, tropical-like appearance, with what looks like several-previously not visible-tires scattered across the riverbed. Lupa island and the Megyeri bridge from the north – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka Sediment formation in the river is also clearly visible near Lupa Island. A ferry at Szürkő island, between Horány and Dunakeszi – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The ferry was still running between Horány and Dunakeszi by Szürkő Island, although some of the boats on the island were already stranded on dry land. Protruding sandbars at Szentendre – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The Danube near Szentendre, with the Tildy bridge in Tahitótfalu – Photo Ferenc Sztraka “The Tildy Bridge in Tahitótfalu comes into view suddenly when flying over the Szentendre section of the Danube. Near the bridge, on the side of the island, the exposed sandbar is wider, but at the next bend in the river, the alluvial deposits that have surfaced turn up on the opposite side,” wrote Sztraka. The public beach in Dunabogdány – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The public beach in Dunabogdány was bustling with activity when the photos were taken. This is the settlement whose residents refused to reduce their water consumption despite repeated warnings—until the ice eventually broke and they began to exercise restraint, which even earned them special praise from the waterworks. The curve above Szentpéteri Island – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The harbour at Kisoroszi – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka Things weren't looking too good at the Kisoroszi ferry crossing either. Kisoroszi, a village of nearly 1,000 residents located on Szentendre Island, is best known for becoming completely cut off from the outside world by floodwaters almost each time there is major flooding on the Danube. Two years ago, the water level was so high that the road connecting Kisoroszi and Tahitótfalu had to be closed. In recent days, however, 89 percent of the country has been experiencing a moderately severe or severe drought. Sólyom Island and riders on the sandbar – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka “Whenever I’m flying over the Danube Bend, I always look out for Sólyom Island, located at the northern tip of Szentendre Island. Even during a minor drop in water levels, a fairly large sandbar tends to form here quickly, but I’ve never seen this much exposed land in this spot before. There were beachgoers here too, and from high above, we spotted something moving quite fast. At first we got excited, thinking that there were zebras running around, but as we got closer, it turned out to be just two adult horses and a foal galloping below us.” The northern tip of Szentendre Island at Kisoroszi – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The Visegrád Citadel, with the tip of the Szentendre island at Kisoroszi in the background – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The view from the Visegrád Citadel is truly dramatic. From here, you can see all the way to the tip of Kisoroszi Island. No wonder the town is one of the most popular tourist destinations in the country. A strangely shaped formation under the water along the Upper Bay in Visegrád – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka Sandbars at the estuary of Ipoly – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The sandbar in front of Sas Hill – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka “The sandbar located in front of Sas Hill, halfway between Pilismarót and Esztergom, at the foot of the infamous Hideglelős Cross, becomes visible even during minor droughts, though not nearly as much as now. This part of the landscape is one of my personal favorites.” The Kis-Duna in Esztergom – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka There isn’t much water left in the Little Danube (Kis-Duna) in Esztergom either; the photos clearly show that due to the current water level, the motorboats are neatly parked one behind the other. The Prímás Island just above Esztergom – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka Once we reached the westernmost point of our journey at Prímás Island above Esztergom, we turned around to head home. A small trickle of fresh water could still be seen flowing towards the upper part of the island here. As a side note, I would like to mention that when I first saw the Danube from an airplane in February 1990, in very gray weather, it was anything but blue. But under the right weather conditions—against the backdrop of a blue sky on clear days—the Danube truly does appear blue, just like every other river and lake in Hungary that I’ve flown over”, Sztraka writes in conclusion. Körtvélyes Island between Esztergom and Tát – Photo: Ferenc Sztraka The situation isn’t only dramatic in Hungary. All of Europe is suffering from the heat. Power plants, factories, and industrial facilities are shutting down or reducing production one after another. Water levels have dropped to dangerously low in several rivers, leading to restrictions or even the suspension of navigation, which is causing billions of euros in damage to the continent’s economy. We still have some tough days ahead of us though. According to Időkép’s forecast, daytime highs will hover around 40 degrees Celsius in Hungary through Thursday, but midweek temperatures could reach as high as 42 degrees, which would set a new record for the second time this summer. Occasional thunderstorms may develop, and at night, temperatures will only drop to between 20–25 degrees Celsius.

Beállítom Megkezdődtek a magyar nyelv és irodalom érettségi vizsga korrekcióját előkészítő konzultációk – tudatta posztjában Lannert Judit. Az oktatási és gyermekügyi miniszter szerint az új Nemzeti alaptanterv előkészítésével párhuzamosan a közoktatás teljes tartalmi szabályozását is megújítják. A tárca tervei szerint az új, átmeneti szabályozás végleges formája ősszel kerülhet a nyilvánosság elé. „Miután az elmúlt években számos jogos szakmai kritika érte a jelenlegi magyar nyelv és irodalom érettségi vizsga szerkezetét és tartalmát – megkeserítve a középiskolás tanulók és tanáraik életét – ezért ennek a vizsgának az átalakítását már most megkezdtük. Első lépésként teljesen megújítottuk az érettségi tétel-előkészítő bizottságot. Az új szabályozásra vonatkozó javaslatot már az új bizottság készíti el” – írta. A cél egy sokkal átláthatóbb és igazságosabb magyar nyelv és irodalom érettségi, amely: csökkenti és egyértelművé teszi a középszintű követelményeket, pontosan megszabja az egyes feladattípusok sajátosságait, továbbá növeli a magyartanárok szakmai szabadságát . A tervek szerint nyár végén széles körű szakmai egyeztetés kezdődik a tervezetről, hogy a végleges szabályozás a pedagógusok és a szakmai szervezetek tapasztalataira is épüljön. „Ezzel végleg felszámoltuk azt a gyakorlatot, hogy egy politikai bizalmi tanácsadó egyszemélyben határozza meg egy ágazat jelenét és jövőjét, Takaró Mihály immár semmilyen befolyással nem bír az oktatás irányítására ” – közölte. Lannert Judit oktatási és gyermekügyi miniszter kinevezése után hamar belekezdett az oktatás átalakításának előkészítésébe. Szinte naponta ül le egyeztetni különböző szereplőkkel, jelent be változtatást, intézkedést a tanárok és a diákok életében, közben nyilatkozataiban a rendszerben lévő évtizedes problémákra mutat rá. Előre tudható volt, hogy az oktatáskutatóból lett miniszter egy olyan terület irányítását kapta meg, amiben kódolva vannak a konfliktusok. https://balkaninsight.com/2026/07/22/rom.text: Western city of Oradea again says no to Pride Parade for fourth consecutive year – adding to concerns about backsliding on LGBTQ+ rights in the EU-member country. Oradea’s unauthorised Pride March in 2025. Photo: Photo: Ovi D. Pop/Oradea Pride. Just over 250 kilometres separate Romania’s western city of Oradea from Budapest in Hungary, but until recently the two cities shared another distinction: both had refused to allow Pride marches. Hungary’s capital hosted a Pride event this year despite government opposition. Oradea is now the only major city in the European Union where local authorities continue to deny permission for a Pride march, after refusing to authorise the 2026 event on Wednesday. “The City Hall has decided not to approve the event. All 115 possible routes proposed by the organisers are concentrated in the city’s central area … These routes are unavailable because they overlap with other authorised events, or are affected by major public infrastructure works,” municipal spokesperson Octavian Haragoș said, as quoted by the local news outlet ebihoreanul.ro . The municipality did not explain why alternative routes outside the city centre could not be considered. The decision followed weeks of delays by the city council in ruling on the organisers’ request, where conservative councillors and religious groups dominated the debate. Human rights groups condemned the decision, arguing that it violates the constitutional right to peaceful assembly. “We consider this decision completely unacceptable because it effectively blocks people’s constitutional right to peaceful assembly,” Victor Ciobotaru, director of ACCEPT, Romania’s leading LGBTQ+ rights organisation, told BIRN. “Under Romanian law, local authorities cannot ban a public march. Their role is to identify practical solutions to ensure that such events can take place safely and under appropriate conditions, not to prevent them altogether,” Ciobotaru added. Citing the same legal argument, ARK Oradea, the organisation behind the city’s Pride Parade, said the march would go ahead on July 25 despite the municipality’s refusal to authorise it. “Our march will take place … As a sign of solidarity and concern for the situation in Oradea, representatives of nine diplomatic missions accredited to Romania, as well as representatives of the Ombudsman Institution, will be present in Oradea to monitor the unfolding of events,” ARK said, adding that the presence of diplomats reflects growing international concern over restrictions on freedom of assembly and LGBTQ+ rights in Romania. This marks the fourth consecutive year that Oradea’s authorities have refused to authorise the Pride Parade. Last year, however, an unauthorised march was still held through the city centre, attended by several hundred mostly young people. There were brief scuffles between some participants and the police but the situation did not escalate. Authorities later imposed fines totalling 19,800 lei (about 3,900 euros) on organisers and participants in the unauthorised march Romania has made progress on LGBTQ+ rights since joining the European Union in 2007 but continues to rank among the bloc’s weakest performers in terms of legal protections and social acceptance. Consensual same-sex relations have been legal since 2001, but same-sex marriage and civil partnerships are not recognised, despite a 2023 ruling by the European Court of Human Rights requiring Romania to provide legal recognition and protection for same-sex couples. Public attitudes toward LGBTQ+ people remain largely conservative, particularly outside major cities. Pride marches have been held annually in Bucharest for two decades, however, and in several other cities, generally under police protection and without major incidents. Human rights organisations have urged Romania to strengthen anti-discrimination protections and fully implement European human rights standards, arguing that it is lagging behind in terms of the country’s commitments as an EU member. https://www.jezebel.com/the-timeless-twi.text: The Timeless, Twisty Appeal of Snake Jewelry By Katy Kelleher | February 10, 2020 | 5:00pm In Depth Copy to clipboard × Copy Link Facebook Reddit Bluesky 0 Image: Benjamin Currie/G/O Media Neither the actress nor the character liked the outfit, but that didn’t matter. It was the early 1980s, and Carrie Fisher wasn’t quite a household name. She was famous, certainly, and she had been acting for years, but very few actresses got to choose what they wore on-screen, especially back then. When George Lucas showed her the outfit, she “thought he was kidding,” she later said . She called it “what supermodels will eventually wear in the seventh ring of hell.” Although already thin, Fisher was pressured to lose weight in order to wear the gold bikini with the gold metal snake armbands and the gold chains. (Lucas “ didn’t want any creases ” to show in her sides, because god forbid a leading lady have skin that moves like a human.) She wore the bikini for just three minutes of screen time, but the outfit became famous. It was so rigid, so confining, so fantastical, so beautiful. I do think it’s beautiful. I can’t help it. When I remember what it symbolizes—a tough woman held captive, both onscreen and off, by male expectations and an amorphous extraterrestrial sexpest, respectively—I love it less. But the look itself is timeless; it exists outside time. The outfit could have come from a futuristic runway show or an ancient Pompeian brothel. This is due, in part, to the ubiquity of snake jewelry and serpentine iconography across history. Humans have a thing about snakes. Maybe it’s because they’re so easy to draw. Or maybe it’s because their bodies are so fundamentally unlike ours, their movements so foreign. Either way, we’ve been dressing in snake armbands and necklaces, snake earrings and engagement rings, since practically the dawn of jewelry. I know this because I’ve spent the last two years searching for the perfect snake ring. Inspired by an increased presence of snakes in my backyard (her name is Esmeralda, and she may be many small green snakes, but I chose to believe she’s one queenly lady), I started looking for snakes. First, I started looking online for gold ones, and I wound up at Mejuri contemplating their small gold number and cruising Erica Weiner for their antique-inspired coils. Then, I started looking for dreamy serpent-bedecked dresses, like this vintage Halston number or this slinky Roberto Cavalli one-sleeve or this glamorous Gucci embroidered tulle gown . Eventually, I started seeing snakes everywhere. They were in ads targeted towards me, snake jewels and snake clothes. They were also out on the trails, slithering away in the sand between the pines, lying in wait on top of warm stones, copulating in old stonewalls. Like the Hot Priest in Fleabag followed by foxes, I began to suspect that I was being trailed by serpents. That led me down another rabbit hole (or snake hole?) and even as I doubted my own sudden snake-sight, I began to earnestly research the symbolism of the snake. Fittingly, snakes wiggle in and out of stories and cultures, in and out of associations and meanings. You can’t pin those fuckers down. Unlike the elephant, which is associated with memory and longevity and good luck, or the fox, known for its wiles and predation and speed, the snake can mean pretty much anything. Growing up Catholic, I’ve always been familiar with stories about the snake as the devil. Snakes, I learned rather passively, were creatures that could lie and slither and seduce—like women. In one of my favorite childhood books, The Silver Chair by C.S. Lewis, some kids go to Narnia and they find the land tormented by a shape-shifting woman in a green gown, an emerald witch who can turn herself into (what else?) a tiny green snake. I knew of Medusa, that man-killer with her head of snakes. I knew of Saint Patrick and his miracle cure of Ireland from the scourge of snakes. But I didn’t know Medusa was a rape victim, and I didn’t know Narnia was a deeply religious text that borrowed entire plotlines and characters from the Bible. I didn’t know that Ireland was snake-free for the same reason that Iceland is—it’s a cold island, too cold for most cold-blooded creatures. And I didn’t know that Queen Victoria, in 1839, at the age of 16, received a serpentine wedding ring from Prince Albert. I didn’t know that Victorians were all about that snake jewelry. I had no idea that, for many people around the globe, including many Christians, snakes symbolized more than just temptation. They were signs of eternal love, ever-renewing, ever binding. While some historians suggest that Prince Albert kicked off the snake jewel trend, that’s not exactly the whole story. Victoria already had several snake-shaped pieces in her jewel box, and the trend had been building for a few years before they became engaged. Albert knew her style, and it seems that he was very good at giving gifts. She cherished his presents long after his death. For the engagement, he picked out a gold serpent that wrapped around the finger once, overlapping head and tail, with a central emerald stone (Victoria’s birthstone) surrounded by small flush-set ruby eyes and diamond accents. While it would be out of place at most weddings today, it wasn’t strange at the time to have an engagement ring that featured birthstones more prominently than diamonds. The South African diamond mines had yet to be discovered and drained, the iconic De Beers “ A Diamond is Forever” ad campaign was still a century away, and it was pretty normal to get engaged with a slightly more subtle, personal ring. Serpent jewelry became fashionable in Europe in the 18th century, thanks in part to the nobility’s continued fascination with terra incognita and the people who lived there. In the non-white world, snakes weren’t viewed as devilish or disgusting. It was normal to fear them, certainly, but the fear came with respect and admiration, not necessarily repulsion. According to The Book of Symbols , the snake has long been linked to the “secret, subterranean, oracular mysteries of knowledge” and “always conveyed power of life and death, making it everywhere a form of the ancestral spirit.” According to Egyptian mythology, snakes were immortal and could shed their skins again and again, emerging fresh and young ad infinitum. What luck! People have always wanted to be able to shed their old skins, becoming new and better versions of themselves. How else can you explain the annoying proliferation of “New Year, New You” content that appears without fail come January 1st? I suspect that humans have always been a bit jealous of snakes, envious of their ability to leave the discarded husks of their outward-facing personas behind and slither gaily on the earth. Being linked to the process of birth also meant snakes were often linked to the mother goddesses. Despite their phallic shape, snakes are often seen as female in spirit, and some cultures even believed that snakes were able to regenerate only if given access to menstrual blood. Both men and women have worn snake jewelry, but in the modern era, these twisty emblems tend to be wrapped around female-identifying forms. And when the right woman dons a serpent, the effect is nothing short of iconic. I was a pre-teen when Britney Spears burst out of a wavy-barred cage on the stage at the MTV Music Awards and began dancing with a live snake. Although it wasn’t a piece of jewelry, Britney wore it like one, with the ease of a Minoan goddess (though without the breast-baring dress). Before Britney, there was Maria Félix. A Mexican movie star from the 1950s, she supposedly refused to learn English because she didn’t want to appear in Hollywood films, though she was perfectly willing to learn French to be a part of their cinematic tradition. Félix was known in the English-speaking world, in part, for her decadent jewelry. She wore bejeweled crocodiles and panthers, but her favorite emblem was the snake. After decades of appearing in public dressed in snake bracelets and earrings, in 1966 she walked into the Cartier flagship store in Paris and commissioned what was to become her most famous piece of jewelry: a life-sized snake necklace . The finished piece took two years to make and was covered from head to tail in 2,473 diamonds. It was fully flexible and unlike anything Cartier had made before or since. But before Britney and Maria and Aaliyah and Taylor Swift and Elizabeth Taylor and Carrie Fisher and the hundreds of other women who have appeared on screen with serpents highlighting their lines and curves, there was Sarah Bernhardt. Sarah Bernhardt is the reason I never found my perfect snake jewel, because it does exist but I cannot have it. Designed by Czech artist Alphonse Mucha and constructed by French jeweler Gorges Fouquet in 1889, the piece is an incredible example of art nouveau style, created for the actress to wear on stage to play the tragic, violent figure of Medea, who died of an adder bite after going scorched earth and killing her entire family and then some. The item in question is a green-scaled enamel bracelet with a gold underside that coils around the wrist before resting its winged head (covered in opals, rubies, and diamonds) on the back of the hand. This large snake is linked by small, delicate chains to a second snake that Bernhardt wore as a ring. Bernhardt’s talent inspired Mucha to create this, and many other works. She was a star. Also, like too many stars, Bernhardt burnt out and fell. She lost her fame, she lost her money, she lost her health and her looks. She sold her jewelry off, piece by piece, including those perfect slithering green snakes. Unexpectedly, the piece wound up in a museum in Japan dedicated to Mucha’s works. It now resides under glass. I imagine it will stay there for the time being, or until some star or another gives it new life on a red carpet, because jewelry is made to be worn, to be warm against skin. I can only hope. A recent trip to Poland by its founder and president is a prime example of what the relatively new Coalfields and Cobblestones is all about. Blake Moss founded the nonprofit organization in July 2025, shortly after returning from his first visit to Poland. After coming home from his second trip in May of this year, Moss had already put his words into action. "I'm trying to connect Appalachia with the rest of the world," Moss said in explaining the organization's purpose. "I believe that our comparative advantage, which is the thing that we're best at compared to the rest of the world, is developing relationships. I think our people have a lot of potential, and I think that potential can be unleashed by developing relationships with the world." Moss is a public administration specialist for the Big Sandy Area Development District, but he is quick to point out that the ADD and Coalfields and Cobblestones are separate entities that are not associated with each other. In 2025, Moss said he was "getting fed up with my life in Eastern Kentucky" and looking for other jobs outside the Big Sandy Region. To get away from his frustration and stress, Moss decided to take a trip to Poland. The excursion changed his life, he said. "It completely transformed me as a person, and it completely transformed how I see this place," Moss said. "I went there, and the people were just so friendly, and everyone was so interested in America and wanted to connect. I saw so many things that I wanted to bring back home." He founded Coalfields and Cobblestones a month after returning home. Moss demonstrated the purpose of the organization when he returned to Poland in May. "During my two weeks in Silesia, Poland, my first few days there, I met with a young lady who is a college graduate, and she studies cognitive science, which is essentially like an AI-related tech field," he said. "She's been looking for fellowships in New York City and Los Angeles, and has not received anything, has not heard anything back. I showed her Bit Source, a local tech company in Pikeville. She said she was interested. We were able to work out a fellowship, so in September she'll be coming to Pikeville for a fellowship with Bit Source. This is a microcosm of what Coalfields and Cobblestones can become. More than just fellowships, but bringing in engineers, artists, businesses by cutting out the middleman and making things person to person. Really, this is grassroots diplomacy. Diplomacy is connecting countries; I'm connecting people in countries." Moss said Silesia is known as the historic coal-mining capital of Europe. "A very interesting thing about their mines is each mine in Poland has a chamber of heritage that keeps track of the mine's history throughout the mine's operation," he said. "When that mine closes, they don't have to scramble to get everything together. It's already been keeping track, and they will usually take all that history and give it up to a central entity, who then digitizes it and stores it and displays it." Moss said he met with several institutions that had to do with cultural preservation and historical preservation. "I realized that we have a lot we can learn from them in that regard," he said. "And there's also a lot they can learn from us. The main thing I see there is, in 2049, all mining in the European Union has to stop. It's European Union mandate. Poland's in the European Union, and in the Silesian Region, they have 100,000 people that work in mining or mining adjacent industries, industries supported by mining. They're not all miners. As you know, for every one miner, you have two people to support that miner. Mining-connected industry is a huge economic driver, and right now the main thing they're doing is severance packages for people who retire and things like that. That doesn't give anybody a purpose. One thing we've done very well here is through things like eKAMI, the community colleges, we're extremely good at upscaling workers and at finding people a new purpose. Unfortunately, those purposes are not always here in the region. They sometimes have to go other places to get jobs, but nonetheless, we're very skilled at that." https://www.biometricupdate.com/202607/v.text: Vietnam has approved its National Digital Transformation Strategy for 2026–30, which sets out a long-term plan to build a data‑ and AI‑driven digital nation by 2045.The strategy, issued under Decision 1266/QD‑TTg, puts people and businesses at the center of digital transformation and positions digital technologies as a core engine of economic growth. Deputy Prime Minister Ho Quoc Dung approved the plan, reports Vietnam News.The government aims to fully digitalize administrative records by 2030, achieve 99 per cent satisfaction with online public services and ensure all ministries and provinces use shared national digital platforms.Key databases will be standardized and interconnected. Provincial smart operation centers will be upgraded with AI for forecasting, monitoring and decision support. Every public servant will receive digital skills training and an AI assistant account.The strategy targets a digital economy contributing at least 30 per cent of GDP by 2030. At least 500,000 SMEs will receive digital transformation support; e‑commerce will reach up to 17 per cent of retail sales, and cashless payments will expand to 30 times GDP. Secure national data exchanges will be established, and more than 40 per cent of SMEs are expected to adopt AI‑based services.To narrow the digital divide, fibre‑optic broadband will be extended to all households; 95 per cent of people aged 15 and above will hold bank or financial accounts, and electronic health records will cover the entire population. Ten million working‑age people will receive basic digital skills training.Data is defined as a strategic national resource. The government plans a unified data governance framework and an integrated national database incorporating AI to support policymaking and service delivery. Priority databases include population, land, business, finance, healthcare, education and social security.The strategy also emphasizes building a competitive “Make in Vietnam” digital technology ecosystem. Domestic tech firms will be supported through public procurement, regulatory sandboxes and investment. Funding is prioritized for R&D, cybersecurity, cloud, semiconductors and digital platforms. The government encourages collaboration across enterprises, universities and research institutes to strengthen national digital value chains.Broadens digital ID platform to support public services, secure transactionsVietnam is growing its national digital identity ambitions with a new government resolution that broadens its role in public services and digital transactions.The upgraded platform will give citizens access to their digital data and offer free digital signature certification for use in online administrative procedures. In addition, it will provide electronic identification and authentication.It will also support online public service delivery, enable electronic submission of documents, link payment accounts for public service and social security transactions, and serve as a secure communication channel between citizens, government and businesses.The Ministry of Public Security’s Department of Administrative Management of Social Order has been assigned to operate and further develop the national digital identity system. The Government has also designated October 15 as Vietnam Digital Citizen Day to promote awareness and adoption.The resolution takes effect from August 15 through February 28, 2027.Vietnam’s VNeID digital ID system has surpassed 102 million identity records and 71.5 million activated accounts. The country has looked to Estonian e-governance experts for digital identity and data unification experience in a bilateral exchange.

REUTERS Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save KISVARDA, Hungary/GDANSK, Poland (Reuters) — Facing a choice between upsetting businesses and a public opinion backlash, the Polish and Hungarian ruling centrists are opting ​for curbs on foreign labor — something economists warn may hurt the two countries' growth prospects. Both Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar, who won in a landslide ‌in April, and his Polish counterpart Donald Tusk, in power since 2023, have been painted by their nationalist rivals as soft on immigration. Now, both are taking action to prove them wrong. Tusk's government slashed work permits for non-EU citizens by 22% last year, while Hungary's new government in June stopped issuing worker visas to employees from the Philippines, Georgia and Armenia, calling it a first step towards regulating guest workers. Public opinion ​polls show broad support for such curbs. In Poland, around two-thirds of respondents in an IBRiS survey for Wirtualna Polska news website in January said Poland ​should accept fewer non-EU migrants. In Hungary, an analysis published by Republikon Institute earlier this month showed that almost half of Hungarians would ⁠not allow any migrants from poorer countries and another 40% only a smaller number. That contrasts with what economists and business groups say both countries badly need. "Fewer workers mean slower ​growth and less tax coming in, while an older population costs more in pensions and health," said Marcin Tomaszewski, lead economist for the EU region at the European Bank for Reconstruction ​and Development, who noted Poland and Hungary face steeper challenges than Western Europe. "Both are aging before they are rich, and both only recently became places people move to rather than leave," he said. The Polish Economic Institute forecast in 2024 that Poland, whose labor force already relies on over 1 million foreigners, around two-thirds of whom are Ukrainian, could have 2.1 million fewer workers by 2035, with declines in industry ​alone potentially knocking 6% to 8% off gross domestic product. A 2026 report by Deloitte, Ipsos and the Institute of Public Affairs, showed non-EU workers contributing up to 10.7% of Poland's ​economic output last year amid birth rates which are at their lowest since World War II. Warsaw says, however, that reconciling employers' needs and transitioning from being a source of migration to hosting non-European ‌migration is ⁠a fine balancing act. "If we changed our status from typical emigration country to migration one, we have to also adjust our whole system of functioning of the society," Polish Deputy Interior Minister Maciej Duszczyk told Reuters, adding that Poland did not want an economy based largely on “cheap labor.” In June, the ministry said it had issued eight times fewer work visas in the first quarter of 2026 compared to the same period in 2022, though that comparison was affected by a change in rules for Ukrainians. Political storm In Hungary, Magyar, whose pro-European course ​and promise to break with Viktor Orban's crony ​capitalism were welcomed by investors, found ⁠himself embroiled in a public spat with one Hungarian business, which said it might halt a factory expansion because of the new migration policies. Magyar accused the Master Good poultry producer, which had received state support, of trying to "threaten the government and the Hungarian people," and said ​it could hire locally if it paid more. Owner Laszlo Barany, however, argued his 580 Filipino staff was essential given an aging ​population. "People get old, they retire ⁠and there is no demographic supply, while those entering the workforce are not looking for this type of job," he said. In Poland, businesses complain about long processing times, with work permits taking over six months and residence permit applications taking nearly a year to process, said Nadia Winiarska, deputy director of the labor department at Polish business federation Lewiatan. While Duszczyk said the visa system ⁠was being ​updated, business owners warn skilled workers could be heading elsewhere. Rahul Jha, a 35-year-old restaurant owner, said he lost ​a chef at his South Indian restaurant who got tired after waiting for over a year for a temporary residence permit. "Denmark gave him a five-year visa ... like immediately, a skilled visa. So he just moved out from ​here." https://www.bucksfreepress.co.uk/news/26.text: People High Wycombe High Wycombe woman died after fall at home, inquest hears By James Richings News and Sports Reporter Share 0 Comments (Image: NQ) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A retired librarian who "loved books, animals and people" died after suffering a spinal injury following a fall at her High Wycombe home, an inquest heard. Beaconsfield Coroner's Court heard how Wanda Jadwiga Van-Der-Zyden, known to family and friends as Blue, was found dead at her home in Cumbrian Way on April 18 this year, at the age of 72. Assistant Coroner Gemma Brannigan, who conducted the inquest on July 22, recorded a conclusion of accidental death. The hearing was attended by Ms Van-Der-Zyden's sister Barbara, daughter Zara, and Zara’s partner, David. A pen portrait written by Zara was read out by the coroner, describing her mother as a caring and compassionate woman. Born in Lancaster, Lancashire, she was of Polish heritage and grew up with two siblings. The court heard how the 72-year-old had fond memories of family life and was particularly proud of returning to education as a mature student in her 40s. She later worked as a librarian at Buckinghamshire New University, where she enjoyed helping students and supporting them in their studies. However, several serious health conditions, including brain surgery, a stroke and breast cancer, meant she retired on ill-health grounds. Zara described her mother as a devoted animal lover who cared deeply about the natural world. A pescatarian, she supported charitable causes and adored her pets, including an energetic kitten which now lives with her daughter. "She loved books, animals, people, was always caring and had a good heart," Zara said. The inquest heard the family became concerned after messages sent to Ms Van-Der-Zyden went unanswered, with the last known contact taking place on April 16, two days before she was found. After emergency services were called, South Central Ambulance Service and Thames Valley Police attended the property and discovered the 72-year-old near the bottom of the staircase. Her death was formally confirmed at 9.39pm on April 18. Evidence heard during the inquest suggested she may have been heading upstairs when she fell, although the precise circumstances could not be determined. Consultant pathologist Dr Sukhvinder Ghataura, who gave evidence remotely, said Ms Van-Der-Zyden had suffered a fracture-dislocation at the top of her spine, close to the brain stem. He also found evidence of significant heart disease, including an enlarged heart and narrowed coronary arteries. Dr Ghataura said it was not possible to determine whether a cardiac event had caused the fall or whether the fall occurred first and led to fatal complications. It was concluded that both factors likely contributed to her death. Recording her conclusion, the coroner accepted the medical evidence and found that Ms Van-Der-Zyden died from traumatic spine fracture dislocation with heart disease. She said it was unclear exactly how the fall occurred and that she could not determine whether a cardiac event had preceded it, but was satisfied that Ms Van-Der-Zyden had suffered a fall at home. The inquest, which lasted roughly an hour, ended with the coroner offering her condolences to the family and reminding them to "remember the fond memories" they shared with Ms Van-Der-Zyden. By the Monitor's Editorial Board July 22, 2026, 3:33 p.m. ET The rule of law across Europe is on a “broadly positive trajectory,” according to the just-released 2026 European Commission Rule of Law Report. Reforms that bolster independent justice systems and align anti-corruption rules to continentwide principles are part of this arc. In a global context, where democratic norms appear to be on the back foot and several governments are flexing authoritarian muscles, this is good news. But in a note of caution, the same document also points to uneven progress – particularly among Eastern and Central European countries. The report found that 47% of its 2025 recommendations for improved rule of law had been acted on. Other data shows that citizens in 17 EU countries, and businesses in 18, perceived judicial independence as having improved or stayed stable from the previous year. And despite some evidence of hostility to journalists, the EU-Balkans zone remains in first place in regional rankings in the latest World Press Freedom Index. Alongside these findings, there is a renewed openness to new members joining the 27-country union. Last week, the EU held talks with Albania and Montenegro, which have already completed more than half the requirements to join, and with Moldova and Ukraine, which are only just beginning negotiations. “It’s really a super Tuesday for enlargement,” Le Monde reported EU Commissioner Marta Kos as saying on July 14, the day of the most recent membership discussions. “For more than two decades, we haven’t had four accession conferences in one day.” The last time a new member was added to the EU was 13 years ago – Croatia, in 2013. To overcome this expansion inertia, EU founding nations France and Germany have called for a new process of “structured gradual integration.” This would grant candidate countries some early trade and integration benefits, but would hold off on granting full voting and representation rights until all required structural and governance changes are in place. The prime minister of Albania had earlier indicated a willingness to waive voting and veto rights, to speed up inclusion. EU members are supportive of enlargement, Commissioner Kos noted, “but only if the candidate countries are delivering” on good governance. Her comment points to the stalled membership negotiations with countries including Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and North Macedonia, over failure to implement reforms. Even EU members such as Slovakia and Hungary have seen declines in rule-of-law indicators. But with April’s decisive popular vote against longtime autocrat Viktor Orbán, Hungary now signals hope for democratic renewal and recovery. “A new, active political generation is beginning to unfold before our eyes,” a Hungarian political analyst told The Associated Press. Its “strong sense of justice,” the analyst said, is incompatible with “the authoritarian exercise of power [and] the corruption.” Deepen your worldview with Monitor Highlights. Already a subscriber? Log in to hide ads . This trend is in evidence across the region, where voting constituencies have consistently protested corruption and called for democratic decision-making in recent years. The citizens of Central and Eastern Europe prize the rule of law as much as the rulemakers in the EU. Both forces, together pushing for transparent, honest governance, will likely be hard to resist in the long run. You've read of free articles. Subscribe to continue.
