https://aa.com.tr/en/europe/ai-generated.text: Europe AI-generated 'Polish soldiers' part of coordinated anti-Ukraine disinformation campaign, fact-checkers warn Concerns coincide with growing strains in Polish-Ukrainian relations about historical memory, with recent disputes surrounding Ukrainian Insurgent Army in WWII Jo Harper 22 July 2026 • Update : 22 July 2026 VARŞOVA A coordinated disinformation campaign using artificial intelligence has emerged on Polish social media, spreading fabricated videos of supposed Polish soldiers criticizing Ukraine in what Ukrainian and Polish experts said is an attempt to undermine support for Kyiv and sow divisions among Western allies. Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation (CCD) wrote Tuesday on US social media platform X that the operation had been identified in the Polish-language information space and highlighted findings by Polish fact-checking organizations Demagog and Konkret24, which concluded that the videos were AI-generated. A network of accounts on YouTube, TikTok, Facebook and Instagram present themselves as "the voice of Polish soldiers," publishing short interview-style videos in which uniformed figures accuse Ukrainians of ingratitude, repeat false claims about high crime rates among Ukrainian refugees and exploit sensitive historical issues, including the Volhynia massacres, according to the CCD. The massacres were anti-Polish ethnic cleansings and mass murders by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists during World War II. It said the campaign's objective was to weaken public support for Ukraine in Poland, damage trust between NATO allies and inflame existing political and historical tensions that Russia has repeatedly sought to exploit. The warning comes amid concern about Russian information operations targeting Poland. Earlier this month, analysts at Disinfo Digest said Kremlin-linked narratives had increasingly focused on Poland's military modernization, NATO cooperation and support for Ukraine ahead of the alliance's summit in Ankara. The campaign coincides with a period of growing strain in Polish-Ukrainian relations about historical memory, particularly following recent disputes surrounding the wartime UPA. news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription LATEST NEWS All Guatemala’s Fuego volcano intensifies, prompting US security alert Houthis claim they hit 2nd Saudi oil tanker in a day Israel's Netanyahu hints at unilateral military action against Iran amid regional de-escalation efforts Top US, UK diplomats discuss European security, Iran's nuclear ambitions NATO chief vows air defense support for Ukraine following Russian strikes PROFILE - Abdul El-Sayed to vie for midterm Senate seat amid wave of pro-Palestinian wins in Democrat primaries Multiple people killed in mass shooting in North Carolina, US See All Iraqi premier appoints new counterterrorism, federal police chiefs France records 12,500 wildfire outbreaks as probe opens into firefighters' deaths

Home Paid news feed Foto Agerpres Press Monitoring Bucharest Phone: +4 021.2076.110 Rise of ultra-identitarian and sovereignist currents is not attributed to manipulation, but to structural causes (presidential report) Category: English Date: 2026-07-22 21:22:23 Foto: presidency.ro The rise of ultra-identitarian and sovereignist currents cannot be explained exclusively by manipulation, but is based on structural causes - the crisis of democratic representation, inequalities, distrust in institutions and a European project that 'speaks the language of the administration' in an era of emotions, according to the Report of the Strategic Reflection Group 'Romania in the EU' - National Identity, European Identity and the Challenge of Populism, published by the Presidential Administration. According to the document, public opinion data show that Romanians' support for the European Union is majority, but pragmatic and conditional - a pro-Europeanism 'by calculation, not by conviction', easily eroded in the absence of clearly felt benefits. The report outlines a unitary thesis: national and European identity are not competing loyalties, but concentric, and the tension between them is not inevitable, but politically induced. The authors of the document believe that the answer to radicalism is neither minimization nor demonization, but good governance, the reduction of inequalities, civic and historical education, the recovery of patriotism by democratic forces, the protection of the information space and the assertive affirmation of Romania as an influential actor in the Union. Combating extremism is done on the ground of ideas, not through criminal instruments, and the defense of democracy requires firmness in the face of hostile operations, but openness towards citizens attracted by these ideas. Overall, the document proposes a vision in which the Romanian specifics and the European vocation mutually reinforce each other. Romania is European not in spite of its identity, but through the way it was built at the intersection of tradition and modernity, of diversity and unity. 'The ultimate stake is not the choice between the national and the European, but the quality of the democracy capable of harmonizing them - a democracy that demonstrates that solidarity, pluralism and cooperation are resources of strength, not weakness, in an increasingly fragmented world,' the report states. Among the authors of the contributions are Teodor Baconschi, Sergiu Miscoiu, Adrian Papahagi, Remus Stefureac and Sever Voinescu. The report also emphasizes that patriotism and membership of the European Union are compatible. 'Loving one's country and supporting the European project are objectives that can reinforce each other,' the report states. At the same time, the document highlights the importance of consolidating democracy by reducing inequalities, developing civic and historical education, combating disinformation and promoting democratic patriotism. The Strategic Reflection Group 'Romania in the EU' (RUE) brings together independent experts who analyze developments in the European Union and propose solutions for Romania to consolidate its position and make the most of the opportunities offered by EU membership. RUE was established at the level of the Presidential Administration and is coordinated by presidential advisor Valentin Naumescu. Photograph: Instagram/cesarselectivo/Reuters View image in fullscreen César Gastélum had nearly 600,000 followers on TikTok and was known for making comedy videos. Photograph: Instagram/cesarselectivo/Reuters Mexico Mexican influencer shot dead while streaming live on social media César Gastélum was filming outside a fast-food outlet in Sinaloa state when he was killed by a motorbike driver Oscar Lopez in Mexico City Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.31 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A popular Mexican influencer has been shot dead while doing a live stream on social media outside a restaurant in Sinaloa state, where lethal cartel violence has become widespread. César Gastélum, who had nearly 600,000 followers on TikTok and was known for making comedy videos, was filming with two friends outside a fast-food restaurant in the city of Culiacán. The three were dressed in the bright orange jackets and backpacks of food delivery drivers. A motorcycle with a driver and pillion rider suddenly pulled up beside them and the driver pulled out a gun and shot Gastélum at point-blank range. A security official in Sinaloa confirmed Gastélum’s death to Reuters and said a major security operation was under way. The killing is the latest example of bloodshed in Culiacán, which has become an epicentre of violence as factions of the Sinaloa cartel battle for control of the city. View image in fullscreen Onlookers stand behind a police cordon at the scene of César Gastélum’s killing Photograph: Jesús Bustamante/Reuters Mexico’s security cabinet wrote on X that it was investigating several of Gastélum’s posts, “some of which referred to a faction of a criminal group”. It also said video surveillance footage and other evidence were being analysed to identify and apprehend those responsible. Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, said on Wednesday that authorities were investigating the killing and working to identify the killer. In a war in Mexico between cartel factions, influencers become targets Read more “The actual perpetrators, and if applicable the mastermind, must be arrested, and the reason behind this tragic homicide must be uncovered,” she said in her morning press conference. At least 12 social media influencers have been murdered in Culiacán since two factions of the Sinaloa cartel began their battle in September 2024, according to local media . They have also been targeted in Jalisco state. Valeria Márquez, 23, was shot and killed at a beauty salon last year while live-streaming on TikTok, where she had thousands of followers. Authorities announced last week that they had arrested Ramón Ángel Álvarez Ayala, the leader of a criminal cell with links to the Jalisco New Generation cartel, in relation to the killing. They also accused him of ordering and financing the November 2025 assassination of Carlos Manzo , the mayor of Uruapan, the second largest city in Michoacán state, in a killing that shocked the country. Photograph: Sam Mooy/AAP View image in fullscreen Australia’s 5% deposit scheme for first home buyers ‘shouldn’t benefit the wealthy and property investors’, the Greens say. Photograph: Sam Mooy/AAP Housing Nearly 1,500 properties bought using first home buyers’ 5% deposit scheme converted into investments New data shows the federal government scheme has been used by high-income borrowers, including one couple earning an annual $674,000 Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Luca Ittimani Wed 5 Aug 2026 11.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The government’s 5% deposit scheme for first home buyers has enabled the purchase of nearly 1,500 properties that were turned into investments, new data shows. The scheme is also helping hundreds of Australians earning more than $300,000 a year, after Labor stopped excluding high-income borrowers. First-time buyers can borrow 95% of a property’s value and have the government guarantee the loan, waiving costly lenders’ mortgage insurance, under the scheme. Housing Australia, which runs the program, provided the data in response to a Senate estimates question on notice in June. House prices slide across Australia as Middle East conflict and tax changes begin to bite Read more From its launch in 2020 until May 2026, the scheme released 1,486 homes because they were converted into investment properties, the agency said. The conversions were a small proportion of the 208,000 total guarantees issued over that time. Barbara Pocock, the Greens’ housing spokesperson, said the scheme was supposed to help first home buyers on lower incomes to get a roof over their heads. “It shouldn’t benefit the wealthy and property investors,” Pocock said. Guardian Australia asked the housing minister, Clare O’Neil, whether investment purchases were undermining the scheme’s intention. A spokesperson said: “When a participant transitions out of the scheme, and the government is no longer guaranteeing their mortgage, the owner is entitled to decide what they do with their home.” If buyers stop living in the property, they are no longer covered by the guarantee and must negotiate with their bank but are not forced to sell or refinance. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Bob Tasevski, a Mortgage Choice broker, said buyers would typically try to avoid being forced off the guarantee as their bank would probably charge them the unpaid lender’s mortgage insurance. “Banks generally wouldn’t waive that unless there’s a special reason for it,” Tasevksi said. NAB’s executive for home ownership, Lin Lu, said the bank asked customers to advise if their circumstances changed. “When this occurs, we’ll work with them to understand their individual situation and discuss the options available to them,” Lu said. The government did not directly answer when asked if it could rule out the prospect of more 5% scheme buyers fraudulently renting out their purchases without notifying lenders or the government. A spokesperson said Housing Australia monitored rental listings, property datasets, participants’ transaction activity and changes to addresses to ensure properties remained owner-occupied. Booming popularity The Albanese government amended the scheme so it no longer excluded high-income earners in October 2025. Since then, it had enabled more than 5,600 home purchases each month on average, compared with just over 3,400 the year before. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion More than 5,000 homes a month bought with 5% deposit scheme graph Prices of homes eligible for the scheme have since risen faster – and fallen more slowly – than the rest of the market. Guardian Australia in July revealed one in three new participants was earning above the scheme’s previous annual income caps of $125,000 for singles and $200,000 for couples. The new data shows the scheme had been used by 155 singles earning more than $300,000 and 92 couples earning over $400,000. The highest-earning recipient was a couple on more than $674,000. The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, dismissed criticism of high-earners’ access on the ABC on Monday. “There are some markets around the country, where people, even on relatively good incomes, have found it difficult to get a toehold in the market,” Chalmers said. Australia has had housing crises before: what can we learn from them? | Anne O’Brien Read more Participants in the scheme are in strong financial positions, with 89% ahead on their repayments, according to Housing Australia’s data. They were less likely to fall behind on loans than the average homebuyer. Since the scheme began, 1,392 guarantees of the 207,000 had fallen more than 90 days behind on their loan and 436 of those were still in arrears by May. Of the 45,300 homes bought under the scheme from its expansion up to May, just two households were in arrears, a separate answer revealed. The government has only had to foot the bill on 13 defaults over the lifetime of the scheme, at a total cost of $604,537. Most of those claims emerged in the last 12 months. While rising interest rates and falling house prices have added to the risk of defaults, fewer than 1% of all home borrowers across the country are in negative equity. Do you know more? https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: The bomb attached to the drone did not detonate, due to a faulty detonator. Photograph: Axel Schmidt/Reuters View image in fullscreen The bomb attached to the drone did not detonate, due to a faulty detonator. Photograph: Axel Schmidt/Reuters Germany Analysis The Leipzig drone bomb marks a dangerous escalation for Europe Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor Initial evidence suggests aerial drone, found near Ukrainian cargo planes at German airport, came from Russia Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.32 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 14.53 EDT Share The armed drone found at Leipzig airport on Wednesday may not have exploded, but the fact that it got inside the perimeter, close to Ukrainian cargo planes , raises obvious concerns for the security of international aviation. Though the identity of the culprits is unknown, the initial evidence points firmly towards a Russian-orchestrated plot. It is the first time that a drone with explosives has been found in Europe far from the Ukrainian border. Photographs published by German newspapers show a quadcopter, a design familiar from the Ukraine war, with a package attached. It lies a few metres short of a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane, with its easily identifiable yellow and blue trim livery. Police from the German state of Saxony confirmed that the drone was “carrying an unknown explosive device” discovered by an employee in the “secure cargo flight operations area” near the airport’s southern runway. German media reported the attached bomb was made of PETN and semtex plastic explosive – the second of the two being the munition that exploded inside Pan Am 103 over Lockerbie. But the bomb attached to the drone did not explode, because the detonator was faulty. A local newspaper, Leipziger Volkszeitung, said police discovered as much as 800g of explosive. This would be “enough to do considerable damage” to a plane, according to Trevor Lawrence, an explosives expert with Cranfield University, not least because “aeroplane bodies are ridiculously thin, often only 3mm aluminium”. Whether the explosive was specifically semtex, invented in the Czech Republic, or from another country may not have been determined. But any type of plastic explosive has typically only been available to militaries or well-established terror groups, not to reckless amateur drone pilots messing around. A second unidentified flying object, which could well have been another drone, also collided with a DHL cargo plane in the aftermath of the first incident several hundred metres above the ground. The cargo plane only sustained minor damage. Leipzig airport is a sensitive site, the European base of Ukrainian Antonov jets, used for heavy cargo. The airport is also used by Nato and the German military for transport, as well as being a DHL hub, and the Ukrainian planes suggest it may also have been a node for supplies to Kyiv. Nato would only say it was aware of the incident on Wednesday, though it is eye-catching that the western alliance appears to have not been able to prevent drones from flying into and over a strategic airport. It is not the first time Leipzig airport has been involved in a dangerous incident. A firebomb, posted via DHL, exploded at the airport in July 2024 while a second travelled to the UK and caught fire at a warehouse in Birmingham . Two similar packages were also found in Poland. A subsequent pan-European investigation identified 22 suspects in Lithuania and Poland who are suspected of having been employed by Russian intelligence. The investigation found perpetrators were recruited and given instructions online, and frequently paid in cryptocurrency, their knowledge of the full plot apparently limited. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Preview latest after newsletter promotion Russia has also been behind a string of drone incursions into Europe over the past year, some more blatant than others. Around 20 unarmed Russian delta-wing Gerbera drones crossed into Poland last September , forcing a major alert, with people in two of the country’s eastern provinces told to shelter indoors. An analysis by the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) thinktank concluded last month that the Kremlin was behind a concerted drone surveillance campaign that targeted the US airbase at RAF Lakenheath and other key military sites in France, Belgium and the Netherlands. In the first case, Nato jets struggled to shoot down the incoming drones, most of which eventually crashed or lost power and glided to the ground. In the second, western militaries struggled to work out who were the culprits, failing to capture any of the drones or react to the surveillance efforts promptly. Russia, in sum, has so far been able to conduct other firebomb operations, as well as drone harassment and surveillance campaigns with relative impunity. Moscow is already subject to a wide range of sanctions following the invasion of Ukraine, and it is likely to believe that the west has little more it is willing to punish the country with. “A drone carrying a charge with a detonator that failed is a different proposition to what we have seen before,” said Charlie Edwards, a senior fellow with the IISS, adding ominously: “It is likely, though not yet certain, that this was intended to function rather than to be found.” Explore more on these topics Germany Ukraine Russia Europe analysis Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Baghaei added that any such agreement between Iran and Oman would not, by ⁠itself, guarantee security in the strategic waterway. The proposed deal between ​Iran and Oman would ‌give Tehran control ‌over ships entering the gulf through the strait of Hormuz, ‌a senior Iranian source and two regional officials told Reuters on Wednesday, in one of the biggest concessions yet to Iran . Baghaei described the negotiations between Tehran and Muscat as “professional” and “moving forward”, saying “the two sides had reached a mutual understanding ⁠on the geographical parameters of the route under discussion.” Baghaei ​added ​that, if some third ​parties do not obstruct the process, the joint ​statement between ‌the two ​countries, containing the ​main considerations and key points of understanding, was in the final stages of review and drafting. Photograph: Mohammed Zaatari/AP Israel Israel strikes southern Lebanon killing one and injuring 11 Hits on two towns among deadliest bombings since start of June ceasefire William Christou in Beirut Wed 5 Aug 2026 12.34 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.29 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An Israeli airstrike in south Lebanon killed one person and injured 11, the Lebanese ministry of health said, in one of Israel’s deadliest bombings since the start of the June ceasefire. Israel carried out an airstrike in the town of Tebnine, south Lebanon hitting a cemetery, the Lebanese health ministry said. It said the town of al-Mansouri, also in south Lebanon, was bombed too, forcing families to flee. The Israeli military issued a displacement order about 30 minutes before the strike, saying it was destroying Hezbollah’s infrastructure in the area in response to the group’s “violation of the ceasefire”. Two Israeli troops were killed and seven wounded in an explosion in south Lebanon on Wednesday, with the origin unknown. In recent weeks, Israeli troops have been wounded by booby-trapped vehicles and mines laid by Hezbollah in south Lebanon. View image in fullscreen Israeli tanks in south Lebanon on Wednesday. Photograph: EPA Wednesday was the first time Israel has issued a displacement order since the start of the June ceasefire. Such orders were a near daily occurrence during the most recent round of Hezbollah-Israel fighting, which started on 2 March and displaced more than 1 million people in Lebanon. Since the June ceasefire, Israel has occupied swathes of Lebanon as part of a so-called security zone. It has continued bombing parts of the area and killing people who have come near. It is a similar approach to in Gaza, where Israel occupies more than 60% of the strip under what it calls its “yellow line”, and continues to carry out bombings there. Earlier this year, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said he had ordered the army to seize control of 70% of the Gaza strip . Gaza 'yellow zone' More than 1,200 people have been killed in Gaza since the beginning of the October ceasefire. At least 26 Palestinians were killed by Israeli strikes in the strip over the past weekend. In Lebanon, Israel has continued mass demolitions in areas it occupies, including a blast last week that used 700 tons of explosives around Beaufort Castle, outside Nabatieh. Israel has said it is targeting Hezbollah infrastructure, but rights groups, including Human Rights Watch, say the indiscriminate nature of the explosives could comprise the war crime of wanton destruction. Talks between the Lebanese government and Israel for a more permanent peace are continuing, with the two sides meeting in Rome on Tuesday. The Lebanese government is seeking Israel’s withdrawal, while Israel wants the disarmament of Hezbollah. View image in fullscreen A woman and child stand next to Lebanese military vehicles in Zawtar al Gharbiya, southern Lebanon, one of the pilot zones. Photograph: EPA The meetings in Rome are the seventh between the two sides, with talks expected to focus on the Ali Taher area in south Lebanon, where Israeli troops have been conducting detonations. So far, negotiations have resulted three “pilot zones” in south Lebanon where the Lebanese army has assumed control. The two sides are using these as tests of whether the Lebanese army can prevent Hezbollah from entering and can continue to dismantle the group’s infrastructure there. Progress in the pilot zones is slow and the Lebanese government has asked for a quicker Israeli withdrawal, which Israel is unlikely to agree to. The fighting this year started after Hezbollah launched rockets at Israel on 2 March in retaliation for the killing of Iran’s late supreme leader, Ali Khamenei. Israel then began a bombing campaign and invaded south Lebanon. Israel has since killed 4,321 people in Lebanon, while at least 40 Israelis, 38 of them troops, were killed by Hezbollah. Photograph: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/Reuters Sheikh Hasina Exiled PM vows to return to Bangladesh despite execution threat Sheikh Hasina plans a December comeback two years after being ousted in a bloody uprising led by students Penelope MacRae in Delhi Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.45 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 14.46 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Bangladesh’s ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina has vowed to return home by the end of the year, even though she faces a death sentence. “They may put me in a cell. They may kill me. Anything may happen, but still I have to go,” said Hasina, two years after a student-led uprising toppled her government. Hasina, 78, who has lived under tight security in India since fleeing Dhaka, said on Wednesday she would return in December – Bangladesh’s “month of victory”, marking the defeat of Pakistani forces in the 1971 war of independence. “Whatever fate awaits me, I will return to my people,” the former Awami League leader told a news conference at the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia in Delhi, speaking via audio link. View image in fullscreen Sheikh Hasina, the then newly elected prime minister, speaking at a press conference in Dhaka in January 2024. Photograph: Mohammad Ponir Hossain/Reuters Her son, Sajeeb Wazed Joy, told the news conference she was being treated well in exile. “She is staying with the full services and security of a head of state,” he said. “Prime minister [Narendra] Modi’s government has shown her the utmost respect, and for that I am eternally grateful.” The exiled Awami league members plotting a political comeback in Bangladesh – from India Read more India officially distanced itself from the news conference, saying it had no role in organising it and did not endorse the political views expressed. India has been walking a diplomatic tightrope over Hasina, who was one of its closest regional allies. Bilateral ties have deteriorated sharply since her downfall and India has been seeking to mend relations with Bangladesh while resisting demands for her extradition. Hasina’s flight ended more than 15 years of increasingly authoritarian Awami League rule. The Bangladesh Nationalist party, led by Tarique Rahman, the son of the former prime minister Khaleda Zia, swept to power earlier this year in an election that barred the Awami League. The government has said Hasina would probably be arrested the moment she set foot in Bangladesh. View image in fullscreen Sajeeb Wazed Joy, the son of Sheikh Hasina, addressing the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia on Wednesday via video link. Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/Reuters Last November, Bangladesh’s international crimes tribunal sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over the violent suppression of the protests. The demonstrations began over government-job quotas and snowballed into a mass movement against Hasina’s government. The UN estimates up to 1,400 people may have died. Hasina’s supporters say the death toll was about 800. She has rejected the court’s verdict as politically motivated and said the execution threat would not change her plans. Hasina was imprisoned several times during her fierce rivalry with Zia, who died in 2025. The two women traded claims of using corruption cases and arrests against each other in a “Battle of the Begums”, an honorific title for a senior woman. View image in fullscreen Sheikh Hasina, right, and her former political foe, Khaleda Zia, at a wedding reception in Bangladesh in 1997. Photograph: Reuters Bangladesh has prohibited domestic media from broadcasting or publishing Hasina’s statements. She has demanded that the ban on the Awami League be lifted, political prisoners be released and “false cases” against party activists be dropped. Claiming Bangladesh is sinking into lawlessness and economic ruin, she accuses the new government of trying to erase the country’s secular character. The government has been grappling with high inflation and sluggish economic growth while blaming many of the country’s problems on alleged corruption and mismanagement during Hasina’s years in power. Photograph: Rahat Dar/EPA Rights and freedom Pakistan Pakistan precinct suspends all 78 officers and staff over alleged rape at police station Lahore police official says all personnel were responsible for preventing and reporting any wrongdoing at station Supported by About this content Haroon Janjua in Islamabad Wed 5 Aug 2026 11.23 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 12.05 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The alleged rape of a 20-year-old woman with learning disabilities in a police station in Lahore, Pakistan , has prompted authorities to suspend all 78 police officers and staff at the precinct, in one of the country’s biggest ever disciplinary actions against its police force. The woman alleges that an assistant sub-inspector apprehended her, took her to Ghaziabad police station and raped her in a room on the second floor. The woman’s family said she disappeared on the street, before returning home in tears and stating that she had been sexually assaulted at the station. The accused officer has been arrested and is now facing a criminal investigation for rape. All 78 police officials and staff members of Lahore’s Ghaziabad police station were suspended on Tuesday. Lahore’s deputy inspector general of police (operations), Faisal Kamran, told the Guardian that the officers were suspended because, under police rules, all personnel were responsible for preventing and reporting any wrongdoing within the station and they had failed to do so. “No officer questioned why the assistant sub-inspector had brought the woman to the station without any female police personnel present,” Kamran said. “I suspended all 78 police officials, and the gender crime wing is investigating the case, and we will dismiss the culprits, and we will ensure the safety of all police stations in the city,” he added. The case has sparked outrage in Pakistan, where rights groups have long claimed many women are reluctant to report sexual violence because of stigma and a lack of confidence in law enforcement. Allegations of misconduct by police officers have further eroded public trust, activists say. “This is an extremely disturbing incident and reflects the longstanding lack of accountability within the police,” said Farzana Bari, a women’s rights activist. “It is a stark example of the abuse of power. Allegations of police misconduct and custodial rape are not new, and we have seen such cases over the years. “We campaigned relentlessly in the 1990s for women’s police stations because survivors often did not feel safe reporting abuse to male officers. While the police’s record on protecting women remains poor, the fact that this case has been reported offers some hope that justice will be served.” Convictions for rape remain rare despite legal reforms in recent years. The Sustainable Social Development Organisation said the national conviction rate was about 0.5% in 2024, while official data showed the rate in Punjab, where the incident occurred, was 4% in 2025. Rights groups attribute the low rates to weak investigations, poor evidence collection, delays in prosecutions and the stigma surrounding sexual violence. According to police data , there were more than 20,000 crimes against women in Punjab province in the first half of 2026, up from the same period in 2025. “Unless state institutions are held accountable, such crimes will continue. What is needed is structural reform and stronger oversight to ensure justice for ordinary people,” Bari said. Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images Immigration and asylum More than 1,100 people convicted of illegal arrival in UK since 2022 Data shows victims of torture and trafficking among those prosecuted for crossing Channel by irregular means Diane Taylor Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.54 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 15.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More than 1,100 people, including survivors of torture and trafficking, have been convicted of illegally arriving in the UK since 2022, according to freedom of information data. The Home Office introduced the offence of illegal arrival in 2022 in a bid to deter those planning to come to the UK by small boat or by other irregular means such as lorries. The decision was widely condemned at the time because the refugee convention states that those seeking sanctuary should not be criminalised for the way they travel, as they often do not have the option to move legally from an unsafe country to a safe one. FoI data obtained from the Home Office by the criminologist Dr Victoria Taylor, a research fellow at the University of Manchester, reveals 1,109 people were prosecuted for illegal arrival between July 2022 and January 2026. The data shows 628 arrived on a small boat, 296 of whom were captured on surveillance drone footage steering a dinghy. Others had previous immigration history in the UK. Just 12 people have been convicted of the separate offence of facilitation, after steering the dinghies they arrived on. It is harder for the Home Office and Crown Prosecution Service to secure evidence that people on a dinghy were involved in organising a journey across the Channel than to prosecute them for illegal arrival. Dinghy carrying 173 people capsizes in Channel after engine catches fire Read more People have been identified as having their “hand on the tiller” for many reasons, including having boating experience, steering in return for discounted passage, taking it in turns, or being under duress. In one illegal arrival case, the Home Office settled a judicial review relating to a trafficking survivor from South Sudan who was forced at gunpoint to pilot a small boat. Officials have now agreed to ensure greater protection for trafficking victims in these cases. Emily Soothill, partner at Deighton Pierce Glynn, who represented the man, said: “Unfortunately it is clear from our client’s case that potential victims of trafficking are regularly being convicted for illegal arrival and imprisoned for many months. The concessions made in our client’s case underline the need for a robust and consistent application of the UK’s modern slavery framework to prevent survivors of trafficking from being wrongly treated as criminals.” Some of those convicted of the various offences were survivors of torture and trafficking, and there were at least 30 age disputed children among them, 19 of whom had spent time in adult prisons. The organisation Captain Support UK has worked with hundreds of people imprisoned in illegal arrival cases, all of whom sought asylum in the UK in the hours before they were arrested. A spokesperson said: “We see first-hand the negative impact these prosecutions have on people and their families. We urgently call on the government to stop imprisoning people on the move. No one should be put in prison for seeking safety and a better life.” Taylor said: “The process of who is selected for prosecution is arbitrary and cruel.” She added that the most of those imprisoned for illegal arrival since 2022 had claimed asylum in the hours before they were arrested. Many have been granted asylum since their release or have been recognised as victims of trafficking, or both. “There are serious questions about the compatibility of these prosecutions with the refugee convention, which was drafted to prevent states from penalising refugees for how they seek safety. There is no evidence to support the government’s claims that these prosecutions will ‘deter’ people from attempting to cross the Channel,” Taylor said. The Home Office has been approached for comment. A woman is arrested in Covent Garden after the stabbings. Photograph: SWNS View image in fullscreen A woman is arrested in Covent Garden after the stabbings. Photograph: SWNS UK news Woman arrested after four men stabbed in London’s Covent Garden Metropolitan police say 47-year-old woman arrested on suspicion of possession of offensive weapon and assault Covent Garden stabbings – latest updates Caroline Davies and Helena Horton Wed 5 Aug 2026 12.42 EDT First published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 09.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A woman has been arrested after four men were stabbed in Covent Garden, central London, police said. The Metropolitan police said the men, aged 34, 39, 42 and 52, were found with stab wounds. They were taken to a major trauma centre after the lunchtime incident on Endell Street. Two of the men were being treated for injuries that were not believed to be life-threatening or life-changing and the other two had been discharged. A 47-year-old woman remained in custody after being arrested on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon, believed to be a pair of scissors, and assault. Ch Supt Jason Stewart, who leads policing in the area, said: “Officers responded within minutes of this incident after receiving a number of reports. While still at an early stage of the investigation, we would like to reassure the community that we currently believe this to be an isolated, mental health-related incident. “A visible police presence will remain in the area while evidence is gathered at the scene and we thank the public for their understanding.” A London ambulance service spokesperson said: “We sent an ambulance crew, a paramedic in a fast-response car and an incident response officer. We also dispatched London’s air ambulance. We treated four patients at the scene and took them all to a major trauma centre as a priority by road.” map of Covent Garden One witness said the stabbing happened outside the Shaftesbury Theatre before the woman allegedly made her way down Endell Street, a popular location for eating and drinking in the area. The witness, who wanted to remain anonymous, said: “We noticed she stabbed three people with scissors by the theatre then she came down here and the police were here.” One of the victims ran into a barber shop and took his shirt off, revealing a large gash in his back, workers there said. Arjan Gjorga, who works at the Rock and Sole Plaice restaurant and witnessed the attack, said a woman involved in the incident was known to people who worked on the street. He said: “I see her all the time, she’s a homeless person. She walks up and down asking for help, she visits the church at the top of the street.” Gjorga, who did not have to close his restaurant, said: “We all saw a commotion, people were running away. It was totally random, just random people. She suddenly started stabbing them. The police reacted immediately, they arrested her right away.” View image in fullscreen Emergency services near the scene on Endell Street in Covent Garden. Photograph: James Manning/PA Matt Bishop, 42, who works at a consultancy firm next to the cordon in Covent Garden, said he had seen a woman having a “standoff” with three police officers and waving a weapon around. Andrea, the manager of Da Mario restaurant on the same street, said the attack happened in the middle of lunch service. Gesturing at a pair of men enjoying cocktails on the shaded terrace, he said: “They saw it all but they weren’t fazed. They had a police cordon right over their heads but they kept on enjoying their lunch. It’s just another day in London.” He also recognised the alleged perpetrator, saying: “She’s often on the street. We’ve seen her do things like this before, she’s recently got in an argument with a mate and thrown a bottle of vodka on the floor and it smashed outside the restaurant.” By 3.30pm, the area was calm with the cordon down. Photograph: Josh Edelson/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Chimneys are seen where houses once stood in a residential community during the Old Trails fire in Spokane, Washington, on Tuesday. Photograph: Josh Edelson/AFP/Getty Images Wildfires Suspect in Washington state wildfire was questioned about blazes last year Aaron Farinacci is accused of starting the Old Trails fire that has destroyed homes and forced thousands to flee Dani Anguiano Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.15 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Washington state man accused of starting a wildfire that has destroyed homes and forced thousands to flee around Spokane was previously questioned in connection with two fire investigations last year, according to court documents. Authorities allege that Aaron Farinacci, 37, of Spokane, started Old Trails fire, one of three major wildfires burning in Spokane county in north-eastern Washington. He was arrested on Monday and booked on suspicion of first-degree arson. Man charged in Washington state with starting largest wildfire in the area Read more The Old Trails fire is one of more than a dozen large blazes burning in Washington. The state has faced devastating fires in recent days amid what officials have described as an “extraordinary” fire season in the Pacific north-west due to extreme heat, drought and limited resources. Farinacci has denied that he set the Old Trails fire. The fires burning around Spokane have scorched more than 10,000 acres. Officials reported that cooler weather and higher relative humidity have aided firefighters in recent days, allowing them to establish containment lines along all three fires. Crews are now focused on strengthening containment, and preparing for the return of critical fire weather this week and over the weekend. John Nowels, the Spokane county sheriff, has said Farinacci was first questioned shortly after the Old Trails fire began, after he was identified by witnesses who saw him kneeling in the brush near the fire’s origin. “He was bent over in the brush, acting nervous,” Paul Child, who was driving in the area with his grandson, told the Associated Press. “You get the feeling this guy’s up to something.” Farinacci had waterproof matches, cigarettes and a butane lighter in his posession, authorities say. Police arrested him on Monday after an investigators ruled out other possible causes of the fire, and learned that he had been questioned in connection with other fires. In July 2025, there were several “bus-sized” fires in an area near the Spokane River and Farinacci’s apartment. Police searching for a wildfire suspect at a state park the following month came upon Farinacci sitting on a bench “seemingly out of breath from possibly running”. Law enforcement took photos of him and according to court documents he was wearing a green T-shirt like the one he was seen in on Saturday. While he was questioned in the two investigations, he was not charged. Since Farinacci’s arrest in connection with the Old Trails fire, a clearer picture of his criminal history has emerged. He previously served roughly a decade in prison for manslaughter and aggravated assault in the 2010 killing of his father. At age 21, he shot and killed his father after an argument in a family home in Arizona. He was released from probation in early 2024, and a probation officer said he had a stable residence with his girlfriend and her family, but had not completed a mental health evaluation or domestic violence treatment. Farinacci is currently being held on $1m bail. Plus: Chaos on the streets of Ceuta Get the Guardian Weekly delivered to your home address Graham Snowdon Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google When Vladimir Putin sent his tanks over the Ukrainian border to seize Kyiv in February 2022, it’s unlikely he evisaged the mess he finds himself in today. Four-and-a-half years later, Russia remains bogged down in what is no longer simply a ground war but one increasingly being fought in the air by drones. After years of nightly attacks from Russian ballistic missiles and Iranian-designed Shahed drones, Ukraine has responded by scaling up to become the world’s leading manufacturer of unmanned systems. Its retaliatory campaign targeting Russian energy and retail infrastructure is bringing the war to the doorsteps of Russians in Moscow, Crimea and beyond, making life distinctly uncomfortable for Putin and his regime’s messaging over a “special military operation” that was expected to last days rather than years. For our big story this week, Luke Harding gained exclusive access to Ukraine’s elite drone strike force, going behind the scenes with senior commanders. Then Robert Tait reports on how Ukraine’s growing defensive knowhow against Iranian drones has unexpectedly brought Volodymyr Zelenskyy back into favour with Donald Trump’s White House. But not all is rosy for the Ukrainian president, who is under growing pressure at home over his decision to sideline a popular military commander, as Michael Segalov explains. https://www.theguardian.com/news/audio/2.text: 00:00:00 00:00:00 Today in Focus Ukraine Russia exploits Ukraine’s air defence shortage in deadly attack on Kyiv - The Latest At least 17 people were killed and more than 40 injured in another round of deadly Russian strikes on the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv. Volodymyr Zelenskyy has pleaded for more air defence weapons, saying ballistic missile interceptors ‘could have saved the lives of those killed today’. For months, Ukraine has been warning about shortages after Donald Trump backtracked on his promise to let Ukraine manufacture missiles locally. In response to the attack, the EU’s Ursula von der Leyen said ‘Russia must pay’ – but will it? https://www.politico.eu/article/washingt.text: PARIS — The United States is dragging its feet on approving President Emmanuel Macron’s pick for French ambassador to Washington amid a spat over human rights at the United Nations, according to three people familiar with the dispute. Macron may have charmed U.S. President Donald Trump with pleasantries and fine dining at Versailles Palace during his June visit to France , but the delay in approving the new envoy reveals that diplomatic tensions between the two countries are still simmering. Aurélien Lechevallier, a longtime Macron ally, was expected to take office next month but his posting is yet to be approved by the U.S. Department of State — a process that is usually a formality between allied countries. Advertisement Advertisement According to two people familiar with the matter, the Trump administration took offense at a social media post from France’s mission to the U.N. in Geneva that criticized Washington’s decision to side with Russia and North Korea against the renewal of U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk’s mandate. “The U.S. used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore,” wrote the French mission on X last month. “And the world no longer listens to it.” The post prompted the U.S. delegation to walk out of a U.N. Security Council meeting in protest. “The United States is very disappointed in the irresponsible and disrespectful rhetoric from the French,” said an official from the Department of State in response to a written question about Lechevallier’s clearance process. “We are responding appropriately to their comments.” Türk, an Austrian national who has been high commissioner since 2022, has drawn U.S. ire for his criticism of the country’s immigration policy and Israel’s war in Gaza. Two of the individuals also expressed hope that the dispute, which was first reported by Reuters, would blow over and Washington would not block Lechevallier’s appointment. Love-hate relationship The spat illustrates the volatile relationship between the U.S. and its oldest ally France. While Macron and Trump have shared moments of camaraderie in front of the cameras, they have polar opposite world views and regularly spar over NATO, Ukraine and trade relations. Advertisement Advertisement Trump’s participation in the June G7 summit in Evian was praised as a high point in the relationship, with the U.S. president showing signs of support for Ukraine and prolonging his visit to France to join Macron and his wife for dinner at the gilded Versailles Palace. “We have our ups and downs in our relationship with the U.S.,” said a former French official, who has kept informed of the transatlantic relationship. Macron is capable of challenging America’s bullying at the Economic Forum of Davos , but “can also hug President Trump and invite him to sign his Iran deal in Versailles.” The hold-up in Lechevallier’s approval process will end up being “an anecdote,” said the former official, who, like others quoted here, was granted anonymity to discuss a sensitive topic. “But it confirms we are not afraid of a confrontation” with Washington, they added. For a senior figure from Macron’s Renaissance party, however, the U.S. targeting a senior French diplomat is “staggering.” Lechevallier is currently chief of staff to Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot and was Macron’s classmate at the elite ENA graduate school. “We’ve been extremely cooperative, even considerate, on Iran … We’ve been polite and diplomatic. And we’re faced with something that is a bit humiliating,” said the official. Diplomatic tensions The French foreign ministry declined to comment on Lechevallier’s stalled approval procedure and has not protested publicly. But Paris has not rowed back its criticism of the U.S. human rights record either. Advertisement Advertisement “Our position was known. We supported the renewal of the high commissioner’s mandate,” said a French diplomat. “Differences of opinion over a [U.N.] vote do not call into question the strength of our relationship or our ability to work together.” Last month, the U.S. voted against the renewal of Türk’s term, accusing him of leading the U.N. human rights system “to its deathbed.” Despite the personal relationship between Trump and Macron, the dispute comes at a time of simmering diplomatic tensions with the U.S. Barrot has sharply criticized Washington over its military intervention in Venezuela, as well as its threats against Greenland. He also vowed France would never give in to U.S. “blackmail” over trade tariffs. Relations with U.S. Ambassador to France Charles Kushner have also soured over his perceived lecturing on the fight against antisemitism in France and his alleged interference in French political life. Kushner, the father of Trump’s son-in-law Jared, was twice summoned to the foreign ministry. “Kushner had problems [with the French foreign ministry] … He was humiliated. Maybe this is also payback,” said the former French diplomat. Jerry Wu contributed reporting.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cyvl.text: Figure caption, Watch: 'Scariest night' as Ukraine fails to intercept Russian attack By Dan Johnson Ukraine correspondent in Kyiv Published 1 hour ago At the Kvitneva railway station near Kyiv, workers lift white body bags from the pockmarked platform and carry them to waiting ambulances. Shoes, glasses and some pieces of clothing mark the spot where eight people were killed during Russia's latest massive aerial attack on Ukraine. Overnight, Moscow fired 115 drones and 24 ballistic missiles. Most of the drones were shot down, but Kyiv's depleted air defences did not intercept any of the missiles. Twenty-one people were killed and dozens more were injured. The latest Russian barrage destroyed storage and logistics facilities - from online retailer warehouses to a postal sorting centre. In Kvitneva, it is not clear if the target was the railway itself or the warehouse beside it, which was also hit and was still smouldering hours later. Down the road, another warehouse was still ablaze more than 12 hours after the attack. The attack started just after midnight, with very little warning. It was one of the most intense nights of bombardment Kyiv has endured in recent months. Nearby, Anastasiia Dudley's house was almost totally destroyed but she and her mother survived â shaken but unharmed. Anastasiia has lived through years of war - but Wednesday was her "scariest night" since the start of Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine in February 2022, she says. She looks up at the precariously leaning walls of her house, which she says was hit by a drone a few hours before missiles struck the warehouse and the station nearby. "You see two floors - the first and the second, but it was a three-floor house with a roof," she says. The building's top floor has been sliced off. "So no roof, no third floor, and extensive damage on the second floor. It's pretty unstable". Ukrainians have lived through four-and-a-half years of war, but now air defences are increasingly vulnerable, resulting in dozens of deaths at a time. For years, Ukraine has relied on US supplies of Patriot interceptor missiles to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles. But the US has used many of its stockpiles during its war with Iran and is reluctant to give up more. After initially offering Ukraine the license to make Patriots in early July, last week President Donald Trump denied the US had agreed to "give away that kind of technology". Image caption, Shoes, glasses and some pieces of clothing mark the spot where eight people were killed overnight Wednesday Yet without them, Ukraine's skies are wide open. "Ballistic missile interceptors could have saved the lives of those killed today," President Volodymyr Zelensky said. Last week, following another deadly attack in which only one out of 27 missiles was shot down, he warned that a shortage of interceptors "encourages Russia to launch such attacks that take human lives". On Wednesday again Zelensky made a direct link between the delays in supply and the "horrific casualties and destruction" witnessed regularly across Ukraine. "Quite literally every single day, the lives of people here in Ukraine depend on the decisiveness of our partners in Europe and America," he said later, adding he had spoken to Nato chief Mark Rutte about getting interceptor missiles. Ukraine has an undisclosed number of Patriot systems, but it is the Patriot interceptor missiles which are in short supply. It takes at least two to bring down each incoming ballistic missile and the system has a range of around 160km (99m), so effectively placing units can be difficult. Russia, meanwhile, uses on average between 20 and 30 ballistic missiles each time it carries out large-scale strikes on Ukraine. Ukrainian military expert and former intelligence service officer Ivan Stupak says the lack of interceptors left Kyiv in a situation comparable to having a supercar in the garage but no petrol. "Imagine you own a Lamborghini but have no fuel," he tells the BBC. "You have one of the best cars in the world, but you can't drive anywhere... The situation with Patriot is similar. The systems are there, but there are no interceptor missiles." A lack of Patriot missiles leaves the whole country exposed â including the valuable Patriot systems. "Now the question is how to protect the systems themselves from being destroyed," Stupak says. "Because they could very well become priority targets for the Russian Federation. "Until we receive more interceptor missiles, these systems need to be relocated or concealed somehow so the Russians cannot detect and destroy them. Right now they're extremely vulnerable." At the railway station as the medics leave the scene, another team moves in quickly to repair the power lines above the track so services can resume. This is the rapid recovery and clear-up Ukrainians have become all too familiar with. But they know their skies can still light up with deadly force at a moment's notice. Countering that threat and keeping people here safe can depend on decisions about production and distribution of interceptors made many miles from Ukraine's borders. Beállítom Megölte feleségét és hétéves nevelt lányát egy 26 éves férfi egy Urálhoz közeli kisvárosban. Csitában egy 10 és egy 12 éves lányt erőszakolt meg egy 42 éves támadó. Bemászott az ablakon és megölte barátnőjét annak hároméves fia szeme láttára egy férfi Cseljabinszkban. Asztrahánban leszúrta , majd feldarabolta volt élettársát a 41 éves Ivan Polunyin, majd korábban szinte sosem látott 13 éves lányának azt mondta, hogy az édesanyja elutazott Amerikába. Vlagyikavkazban megölte feleségét és 23 éves lányát egy 58 éves férfi. Megerőszakolt és megölt egy 13 éves lányt egy 34 éves támadó Tver megyében. Egy másik pedig megerőszakolta és megölte mozgássérült szomszédját Szentpéterváron. Az Oroszország különböző pontjain elkövetett súlyos bűncselekmények hosszan folytatható sorában egy közös elem van: nem történtek volna meg, ha Oroszország nem indít háborút Ukrajna ellen, mert az elkövetők mind hosszú évekre börtönben ültek volna korábbi bűncselekményekért – gyakran ugyanúgy gyilkosságért, nemi erőszakért. Csakhogy a háborúval az orosz állam lehetőséget adott nekik arra, hogy amnesztiával szabadulva a frontra menjenek, onnan pedig vissza az orosz társadalomba. Na, megyek az SZVO-ra! A feleségét és annak korábbi kapcsolatból született hétéves lányát megölő Artyom Bucsin például épp 20 éves börtönbüntetését töltötte: az utcán útbaigazítást kért tőle egy 23 éves lány, akit egy erdős részre csalt, megerőszakolt, majd megölt. Mindezért végül csupán hét hónapot ült, mivel 2023 augusztusában egy börtönbeli toborzáskor szerződésesnek állt és elment a frontra. Az Ukrajna elleni háború – Oroszországban hivatalosan csak rendkívüli katonai művelet, orosz rövidítéssel SZVO, amit ebben a cikkben használni fogunk – tömegeknek jelent menekülési útvonalat a legsúlyosabb börtönévek elől, hogy aztán hazatérve, már amennyiben túlélik, rászabaduljanak a társadalomra. Ez annyira a köztudatban van, hogy volt eset, amikor egy, részegen egy nyugdíjas asszonyt megkéselő férfi már a támadás utáni pillanatokban azt ismételgette , hogy „Na, megyek az SZVO-ra”. Akadálya nincs is: ha nagyjából egészséges, nem alacsonyabb 150 centiméternél és nem pedofil bűncselekményért ítélték el, akkor minden további nélkül mehet a börtön helyett a frontra. Az is kizáró ok, ha terrorizmusért vagy hazaárulásért ítéltek el valakit, ezeket ugyanis gyakran ráhúzzák nyíltan ellenzékiekre is , elfedve a valós politikai okot. A cikk kezdetén felsorolt bűncselekmények mindegyikét felesleges részletezni, de a feleségét és annak lányát meggyilkoló Bucsinét érdemes, mert története még az egyébként végletekig kontrollált nyilvánosságban is teret kapott , már az előtt, hogy a második gyilkosságot elkövette volna. A 29 éves férfi ugyanis egy sérülés miatt alig három hónapnyi frontszolgálat után, már 2023 novemberében visszatért a városba, ahol megölte a fiatal ápolónőt. Az áldozat édesanyja már akkoriban arról beszélt , hogyan jár a környékre a férfi és hergeli a gyászoló családot. A bíróság által kiszabott hárommillió rubeles (kb. 12 millió forint) összeget sem kapták meg a gyilkostól – hiszen elnöki kegyelemben részesült. Mellesleg a frontszolgálatért helyi mértékkel mérve komoly pénzt is kapott, ez a háromhavi fizetést, a sérülésért és az akkoriban még a szerződéskor egyben kapott juttatást összesítve 800 ezer rubel is lehetett. Hiába volt a nyilvánvaló igazságtalanság az áldozat családjával szemben, a férfi érintetlen maradt. Alig két évvel később pedig megölte a feleségét és annak kislányát. Idén júniusban életfogytiglant kapott . Toborzó plakát a moszkvai Lefortovo börtön előtt – Fotó: Alexander Nemenov / AFP A börtönben toborzott, majd frontról visszatértek a háború első négy évében legalább 551 embert öltek meg hazatérésük után. Rokont, feleséget, gyereket, ivócimborát. Elméletben megvan a lehetőségük arra, hogy az újabb gyilkosságot is kiváltsák a frontszolgálattal. Visszatérni nehezebb lett Igaz, a mostaniak már kisebb eséllyel térnek haza, ugyanis egy 2023. októberi szabálymódosítás óta már fél év helyett egy évre kell szerződést aláírni. Ez pedig automatikusan meg is újul a háború végéig, ha nem sérül vagy hal meg a börtönből frontra került katona. Ez egyébként a gyakorlatban lényegében mindenkire vonatkozik, aki a frontra került, legyen 2022 őszén az eddigi egyetlen alkalommal alkalmazott mozgósítás alá eső civil, önkéntes szerződéses, vagy börtönből verbuvált katona. A jelenség tehát nem az elítéltekkel kapcsolatos valamiféle morális megfontoláson alapul, valójában csak azt jelzi, hogy az orosz katonai céloktól távol álló orosz hadsereg egyre nehezebben gyűjt katonákat a frontra a mozgósítás nélkül. Az újabb mozgósítást a Kreml mindenképp igyekezett elkerülni, de ukrán hírszerzési információk szerint Vlagyimir Putyin ősszel mégis meglépheti ezt . Az orosz hadsereg súlyos sérültekben és halottakban együttesen mért vesztesége becslések szerint másfél milliónál tart. Ez már a teljes lakosság egy százaléka, ráadásul a demográfiailag egyre szűkösebb részt adó fiatalabbak teszik ki a többséget, és a veszteség gyorsabban nő, mint ahogyan újabb embereket vonnak be a harcokba. De így sem kevesen vannak azok, akik már megjárták a börtön után a frontot és hazatértek. Részleges adatok szerint a visszatérők fele újra bűncselekményt követ el. Ráadásul azok, akik az említett 2023. októberi változtatás előtt szerződtek, egy bűncselekmény esetén nem is számítanak visszaesőnek. Ezt mutatta Pjotr Szutajkin esete is. Hiába ítélték már el korábban a barátnője meggyilkolásáért, amikor a börtönben „aláírt az SZVO-ra”, elnöki kegyelmet kapott. Így, amikor visszatért és a következő barátnőjét is megölte, a bíróság büntetlen előéletűként kezelte, sőt a frontszolgálatot enyhítő körülményként vette számításba. Ezen az abszurd helyzeten az említett 2023-as módosítás változtatott, most már csak feltételes szabadlábra helyezik a frontra vonuló elítélteket, nem kapnak elnöki kegyelmet. Gyilkosokból felemelt hősök „Egyetértek azokkal a kriminológusokkal, akik attól tartanak, hogy ugrásszerűen megnő az erőszakos bűncselekmények száma a háború után, amikor a frontot megjártak visszatérnek” – mondta a Pervij Otgyel (Első Ügyosztály) jogvédő szervezet alapítója, Ivan Pavlov. Erről azonban a putyini rezsimben kevés szó esik, ahogyan arról is, hogy milyen súlyosan demoralizálja a társadalmat és zülleszti szét az állami intézményekbe vetett hitet, hogy a sértettek és az áldozatok hozzátartozói azt látják, milyen könnyen léphetnek meg az elkövetők a felelősségre vonás elől. Sőt, válhatnak hősökké. Az orosz elnök ugyanis többször világossá tette, hogy az „SZVO katonái” hősök. „Sokszor beszéltem már arról, hogy az országnak, a hazának, a népünknek mellékes, hogyan került valaki a frontra. A lényeg, hogy ott van és önként ment oda, hogy küzdjön a hazáért” – mondta Putyin tavaly márciusban. Ugyanekkor mondta azt is, hogy hősi kitüntetést adott egy elítéltnek, ezzel lesöpörve az ezt korábban kizáró szabályozást. Az SZVO tehát Putyin nyomán minden bűnt elmos, így amikor az elnök hősökként, „Oroszország aranytartalékaként” beszél a katonákról, akkor már a gyilkosságokért évtizedes börtönbüntetésük elől menekülő szerződésesekre is érti. Csak részleges adatok vannak arról, hogy mennyien járhatták meg a frontot egyenesen a börtönből indulva. Az első évben a toborzást Jevgenyij Prigozsin Wagner-magánhadserege végezte. Ő 2023 tavaszáig saját bevallása szerint 48 ezer embert toborzott, ebből 32 ezer ember jutott haza. Ám „a Kreml séfjeként” ismertté vált, fiatalon szintén börtönviselt Prigozsin 2023 nyarán hamvába holt lázadást indított, a Wagnert felszámolták, Prigozsin pedig hiába kötött egyezséget Putyinnal, két hónappal később lezuhant a repülőgépe. Közel 180 ezerrel kevesebb börtönlakó A rövid lázadás egyik oka az volt, hogy nem sokkal korábban a védelmi minisztérium kivette Prigozsin kezéből a toborzást. A „Leültetett Oroszország” igazságszolgáltatással, börtönviszonyokkal foglalkozó jogvédő szervezet vezetője, Olga Romanova már 2024 februárjában a wagneresekkel együtt összesen 150 ezer emberről számolt be , akik a börtönből a frontra mentek. Közülük 50 ezer akkoriban már hazamehetett. Számuk azóta bizonyosan nőtt, ha nem is ilyen mértékben, egyrészt a fent említett szigorítások miatt, másrészt, mert közülük sokan újra a frontra mehettek. Jevgenyij Prigozsin foglyokat toboroz 2022. szeptember 14-én a mariföldi régióban található 6. számú büntetés-végrehajtási intézetben – Forrás: X.com Hivatalosan összesített adatok még most sincsenek arról, mennyi börtönből toborzott, frontot megjárt ember van Oroszországban, de beszédes, hogy jelenleg 40 százalékkal kevesebb ember van a börtönökben, mint 2021-ben. Erről májusban az orosz Szövetségi Büntetés-végrehajtási Szolgálat vezetője számolt be . Arkagyij Gosztyev szerint az öt évvel ezelőtti 462 ezerhez képest, jelenleg 285 ezer ember van a bv. intézetekben, ráadásul ebből 85 ezer csak előzetesben. Az elmúlt évek alatt utóbbiak közül is nagy számban kerülnek frontra katonák. Nem mellesleg az egész súlyosbítja a rendőrségi intézmények korrupcióját: a rendőrök ugyanis 10 és 100 ezer rubel közötti prémiumot kapnak mindenki után, aki az eljárás alatt inkább szerződéses katonának áll. Azaz érdekeltek lehetnek abban, hogy minél több embert vonjanak eljárás alá. A háború előtt is élt a gyanú, hogy ez a gyakorlat létezik, csak korábban a korrupciós jutalmat rejtve, az eljárás alá vont személytől remélhették az ügy ejtése érdekében, most pedig legálisan, az államtól kaphatják meg ugyanezt. Ezzel tovább erodálják az irányukban korábban sem túl magas társadalmi bizalmat. Elítéltből elit lett A Kreml viszont ennek ellenére egyre inkább épít a frontra küldött katonákra, köztük a börtönből toborzottakra is, egyúttal figyelmeztetve azokat is, akik a putyini évtizedek eddigi nyertesei voltak. „Milyen elit? Ellopták a pénzeket, most meg eltartott kisujjal azt mondják, ők az elit?! Milyen elit? Itt az elit az, amelyik a hazát védi! Ezek azok az emberek, ők a jövő, ők azok, akiknek érdemes a kezébe adni az országot” – mondta Putyin. Az orosz elnök úgy állította be magát a korruptnak nevezett jelenlegi elittel szemben, mintha az elmúlt 26 évben nem ő irányította volna az országot. Az elnök állami programot is elindított „Hősök ideje” néven, amely képzéseket ígér, hogy akár állami vezetői pozíciókra készítse fel az SZVO résztvevőit, bárhonnan érkezzenek is a frontra. Putyin láthatóan előre menekül, és meglehetős sikerrel teszi a háború cinkosává az állami intézményeket, a rendőrséget, vagy akár a diákok frontszolgálatra ösztönzése érdekében az oktatási intézményeket és általában véve az egész társadalmat is. Ezért is beszélt a múlt héten arról, hogy a háborút közvetve, tiszta szívből segítő asszonyokkal beszélgetve mit hallott tőlük. „Nemrég hallottam egy nagyon érdekes mondatot: ha vége lesz az SZVO-nak, mivel fogunk foglalkozni? Szóval, annyira beleélték magukat, annyira teljes lélekkel vesznek benne részt, érzik, hogy valami hatalmas és Oroszországnak fontos dolog részesei, hogy felmerül bennük az aggodalommal teli érzés: [utána] lesz ránk annyira szükség, mint most?” Elgondolkodtató, mennyire gondolt magára, mint a hivatkozott asszonyokra Putyin, miután a háború ötödik évében is messze áll katonai céljaitól. Ukrajna nem kapitulált, nem vesztette el az összes tengeri kijáratát, de legalább a Donbasz egészét sem sikerült megszerezniük az oroszoknak, nem omlott össze az ukrán politikai vezetés, mégsem sikerült Putyinnak a maga oldalára állítania az amerikai elnököt, noha Donald Trump tavaly még láthatóan kész volt Ukrajna rovására összehozni egy megállapodást. Közben a NATO Finnországgal és Svédországgal bővült, a posztszovjet térségben az orosz befolyás láthatóan csökkent , ráadásul Ukrajna egyre több ellencsapásra képes drónjaival az orosz hátországban, és sikerült a megszálló orosz erők utánpótlási útvonalait is elvágni az Oroszország által 2014-ben elfoglalt Krím felé. Ezek ismeretében nem meglepő, hogy a propaganda révén háborús pszichózissal átitatott, az alternatív lehetőségektől gondolat szintjén is megfosztott orosz társadalomnak a győzelem reményében nemcsak szüksége van az elítéltekre, de ők azok, akikből az állam „új elitet” gyúrhat. Részletesen leírja, hogy a közmédiából 2015-ben az M1 hírcsatornává válása után távozott ahhoz a Hír TV-hez, amely ugyanazon év februárjától, az elhíresült G-nap után megszűnt fideszesnek lenni. „Hírműsorok felelős szerkesztőjeként törekedtem – kollégáimmal együtt – a kiegyensúlyozottság megteremtésére. 2018-ban csakugyan az Echo Televízióba mentem át.” Miután a Hír TV akkori vezetése elkötelezte magát a Jobbik mellett, erről pedig az volt a véleménye, hogy sérti a kiegyensúlyozottság elvét, nem akart benne részt venni. Az Echo TV-ben felelős szerkesztőként szintén hírműsorokat készített „az újságírói normák szerint dolgozó kiváló kollégákkal együtt”. „Noha én nem mozdultam, ugyanannál az asztalnál, ugyanabban a székben ülve lettem újra Hír TV-s. Miután a régi-új vezetőkkel nem volt meg a kémia, önként távoztam onnan.” Ezután következett a Mészáros-csoport, amelyről a köztévéhez való kinevezésekor megjelent közleményben nem tettek említést, csak ezt írták: „az elmúlt években a vállalati kommunikáció és a társadalmi felelősségvállalás területén szerzett tapasztalatokat az üzleti és a civil szférában”. A 24.hu írta meg , hogy Hajdú vállalati munkahelye a Mészáros-csoport volt. „Igen, a Mészáros Csoportnál helyezkedtem el. Újságíróként, azaz hírfelhasználóként kihívást jelentett a másik oldal, a hír kibocsátói oldal szempontjainak megismerése, azaz a vállalati kommunikáció elsajátítása” – írja erről posztjában Hajdú. Ottani feladatairól ezt írja: „Munkám kezdete egybeesett a Covid-időszakkal, amelyben az egyébként is nagy érdeklődést kivívó ügyek mellett nagy figyelmet kellett fordítani a belső kommunikációra, arra, hogy a korlátozások közepette hogyan lehet működtetni egy több mint harmincezer munkavállalót foglalkoztató cégcsoport munkáját. Emellett a mi feladatunk volt a vállalatcsoport társadalmi felelősségvállalási programjának operatív működtetése. Büszkeséggel tölt el, hogy civil szervezetekkel együttműködve munkámmal – sokakkal együtt – hozzájárulhattam több ezer rászoruló mindennapjainak megkönnyítéséhez.” Külön megemlíti, hogy Magyar Péterrel ebben az időben „kollégák voltak”, Magyar ugyanis 2022 és 2024 között a cégcsoporthoz tartozó MBH Bank felügyelőbizottsági tagja volt. „Reagálva az elmúlt napokban megjelent vádakra közlöm mindenkivel, akit érdekel, hogy itt sem és más munkahelyeimen sem szolgáltam soha, de soha egyes személyiségeket, hanem csakis ügyeket. Aljas rágalom, hogy részt vettem kollégák ellehetetlenítésében, ellenkezőleg, pártállástól függetlenül partneri viszonyt ápoltam velük” – írta Hajdú. A Mészáros-csoporttól való eltávolítása után egy civil szervezetnél, a Magyar Kertörökség Alapítványnál sajtófőnökként dolgozott. Hajdú szerint bár most a legtöbben a hírigazgatóságot vezető „Bodacz Balázs felelősségét firtatják, de nem árt tudni, hogy szakmai előéletemmel a teljes menedzsment tisztában volt, a munkaszerződést ennek tudatában a vezérigazgató írta alá”. A posztban leírja, hogyan telt egyetlen napja Híradó-főszerkesztőként, aminek a végén közölték vele, hogy visszavonják a kinevezését. Reggel aláírta a munkaszerződését a Kunigunda útján a tévészékházban, ellátogatott a newsroomba, bejárta a stúdiót, beköltözött az irodájába, részt vett egy arculati megbeszélésen, ebédelt egy régi kollégával, adminisztratív ügyeket, telefonokat intézett, délután 5-kor pedig távozott a székházból. 19:42-kor tette közzé az MTI a kinevezéséről szóló hírt, amelyet átvettek a hírportálok. Ezután a miniszterelnök kommentet fűzött a Telexen megjelent hír alá, miszerint őt nevezték ki főszerkesztőnek, ami alá Magyar azt írta: „nem hinném”.„21:24-kor hívnak, hogy közöljék: olyan teher lettem, amelyet a közmédia nem tud felvállalni.” Augusztus 4-én délután alá is írta a munkaszerződés megszüntetését. „Azok után, hogy a köztévé vezetése által felajánlott munkát korábbi munkahelyemet feladva elfogadtam, a próbaidőszak jogi lehetőségét kihasználva indoklás nélkül utcára tettek. Ugye nem kell magyaráznom, hogy nem azért, mert valamit azon az egy napon rosszul csináltam. A hitelességen alapuló három évtizedes munkásságomat sutba dobva úgy ráztak le, mint kutya a vizet. Finoman fogalmazva is kisszerű” – írja Facebook-bejegyzésében Hajdú. A poszt végén még kérdéseket tesz fel. „Eltűrhető bárkinek is a tényeket nélkülöző meghurcolása, különböző stigmák alapján? Ha én a Hír TV-miatt propagandista voltam, akkor a velem egy időben szintén ott dolgozók (Veiszer Alinda, Kálmán Olga, Láng Balázs, Magyar Márton és sokan mások) is mind propagandisták, akiknek nincs helyük többé a közéletben? nem hinném…Ha valaki az elmúlt 16 évben fideszes cégnél vagy a kormánynak dolgozott akár alkalmazottként, akár vezető beosztásokban (pl. diplomataként, vezérigazgatóként, FB-tagként, államtitkárként stb.), akkor el kell lehetetleníteni, mert a közösségi hálón egy aktív kör vérre szomjazik? nem hinném…Lehet-e úgy független a közmédia, hogy Facebook-bejegyzésekre alapozott vélemények alapján történnek döntések? nem hinném…” Hajdu szerint mindenki pótolható, számos jó szakember van, házon belül és kívül is, akikkel kivitelezhető egy modern közszolgálati hírszolgáltatás. „Mindannyiunknak ez az érdeke. És talán az utolsó lehetőség. A szakmánkat is érintő technológiai ugrás okozta kihívás óriási. Őszintén szurkolok!” A teljes bejegyzés itt olvasható: Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! Friss az Afteren

(AP file photo) BUDAPEST—Prosecutors and investigators with Hungary's tax authority on Tuesday raided offices housing data servers used by former prime minister Viktor Orbán 's Fidesz party as part of a probe into suspected embezzlement and other crimes, a prosecutor's office spokesperson told The Associated Press. Fidesz accused the governing Tisza party, led by pro-European Prime Minister Péter Magyar, of seeking to use legal means to destroy it. Marianna Bodó, a spokesperson for the Bács-Kiskun County chief prosecutor’s office, said in an email that the raid was part of an investigation into the suspected misuse of grant money through Hungary's National Cultural Fund while Orbán's government was in office. The county lies south of the capital, Budapest. Six current and former officials have been charged in connection with the misuse of some 17 billion forints ($53.5 million) through the fund. They have denied wrongdoing. The officials have been accused of distributing the money in an opaque manner to artists and performers linked to Fidesz. Some of them actively campaigned for the party leading up April's national election. A regional criminal directorate of the National Tax and Customs Administration assisted in Tuesday's raid, Bodó wrote, adding that no further information could be provided “in the interests of the investigation.” Fidesz said in a statement on Facebook that investigators had launched the raid “without prior notice” and “with the intention of seizing the party’s entire communications system and databases.” “There has been no precedent for this in Hungary since the end of Communism in 1990!” Fidesz asserted. Orbán and Fidesz governed Hungary for 16 years until their blowout election loss in April. While in office, they were routinely accused of overseeing unchecked corruption, seizing control of Hungary's institutions and undermining democracy and the rule of law. After taking office in May, Magyar has taken action to dismantle what he calls Orbán’s “mafia” by removing numerous political appointees — including the president — and heads of institutions viewed as having facilitated Orbán’s autocratic government. Since their election defeat, Fidesz has accused Magyar and Tisza of “tyranny” in their steps to dismantle Orbán's political and economic system. Tisza argues it is using its overwhelming electoral mandate to fulfill campaign promises. Magyar wrote on Facebook on Tuesday that he was awaiting further information on the raid from prosecutors.
